● Android Interview Prep

1D — Kotlin OOP

Classes, constructors, init, inheritance, interfaces, abstract classes, visibility modifiers, and open/final/abstract — how Kotlin's OOP differs from Java and why it matters for Android architecture.

ID: 1D ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

What it is

Kotlin's OOP system is a safer, more concise evolution of Java's. Key differences: classes are final by default (must opt-in to inheritance with open), constructors are inline in the class header, interfaces can have default implementations and properties, and visibility modifiers have Android-relevant scoping differences.

Why it matters for Android

  • Every Activity, Fragment, ViewModel, Repository, UseCase is a class — OOP fundamentals underpin every layer.
  • Clean Architecture is built on interfaces (abstractions) and classes (implementations) — understanding visibility and inheritance is mandatory.
  • Hilt DI relies on constructor injection — understanding primary constructors and @Inject is critical.
  • Compose uses open/abstract sparingly — final-by-default aligns with the immutability preference in reactive code.
Key Kotlin vs Java Difference
In Java, classes are open (extensible) by default. In Kotlin, classes are final by default. You must explicitly mark a class open to allow subclassing. This is a deliberate design choice — it enforces the Effective Java principle "design and document for inheritance, or else prohibit it."
⚙
2. How It Works

Classes and Primary Constructor

// Primary constructor in class header — no separate constructor block needed
class UserRepository @Inject constructor(   // @Inject on primary constructor
    private val api: UserApi,
    private val dao: UserDao
) {
    // class body
}

init block

class TokenManager(private val prefs: SharedPreferences) {
    private val encryptionKey: String

    init {
        // Runs after primary constructor, before secondary constructors
        encryptionKey = prefs.getString("enc_key", "") ?: generateKey()
        require(encryptionKey.isNotBlank()) { "Encryption key must not be blank" }
    }
}
// Multiple init blocks run top-to-bottom in declaration order

Secondary Constructors

class ApiException(val code: Int, message: String) : Exception(message) {
    // Secondary constructor — must delegate to primary via this()
    constructor(code: Int) : this(code, "HTTP error $code")
}
// Prefer default arguments over secondary constructors in most cases

Inheritance

// Base class MUST be 'open' to be subclassed
open class BaseViewModel : ViewModel() {
    open fun onError(e: Throwable) {  // also 'open' for override
        Timber.e(e)
    }
}

class PaymentViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val useCase: ProcessPaymentUseCase
) : BaseViewModel() {
    override fun onError(e: Throwable) {
        super.onError(e)              // call super explicitly
        _uiState.value = UiState.Error(e.message)
    }
}

Interfaces

// Kotlin interfaces can have: abstract methods, default implementations, properties
interface PaymentRepository {
    // Abstract — must be implemented
    suspend fun initiatePayment(request: PaymentRequest): Result<PaymentResponse>

    // Default implementation — can be overridden but doesn't have to be
    suspend fun cancelPayment(id: String): Result<Unit> =
        Result.failure(UnsupportedOperationException("Cancel not supported"))

    // Property in interface (no backing field)
    val maxRetries: Int get() = 3
}

Abstract Classes

// abstract class: cannot be instantiated, can have state (fields), constructors
abstract class BaseUseCase<P, R> {
    protected abstract suspend fun execute(params: P): R

    suspend operator fun invoke(params: P): Result<R> = try {
        Result.success(execute(params))
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        Result.failure(e)
    }
}

class GetUserProfileUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val repo: UserRepository
) : BaseUseCase<String, UserProfile>() {
    override suspend fun execute(params: String) = repo.getUser(params)
}

Visibility Modifiers

ModifierClass memberTop-levelAndroid use
publicVisible everywhere (default)Visible everywhere (default)Public API — interface methods, ViewModel state
internalVisible in same moduleVisible in same moduleModule-internal implementations — hide from other modules
protectedVisible in class + subclassesNot allowed on top-levelBase class helpers used by subclasses only
privateVisible in the class onlyVisible in the file onlyImplementation details, backing StateFlow fields

open / final / abstract

// final (default) — cannot subclass
class LoginUseCase { }        // final by default

// open — opt-in to inheritance
open class BaseActivity : AppCompatActivity()

// abstract — cannot instantiate, must subclass
abstract class BaseViewModel : ViewModel()

// Members follow the same rule
open class Foo {
    open fun bar()  = "open"    // can be overridden
    final fun baz() = "final"   // cannot be overridden in subclass
}

Key Terms

TermKotlin defaultJava defaultNote
ClassfinalopenAdd open to allow subclassing
Methodfinalopen (virtual)Add open to allow override
Visibilitypublicpackage-privateKotlin has no package-private; use internal
Interface methodabstract (or default)abstract (pre-Java 8)Kotlin interfaces can have default impls
Abstract classcan have constructors + statesameInterface cannot have constructor or backing fields
🎯
3. Why and When to Use It

Interface vs Abstract Class — Decision Guide

UseWhenAndroid Example
InterfaceDefine a contract with no state; multiple implementations; testability (mock/fake); DI abstraction layerUserRepository, AuthService, AnalyticsTracker
Abstract classShare state + behaviour across subclasses; template method pattern; partial implementationBaseViewModel, BaseUseCase<P,R>, BaseFragment
Open classAllow subclassing but provide a complete default implementationCustom view base class, library classes that need extension
Final class (default)Implementation classes that should not be subclassed (most use cases, use cases, ViewModels)LoginUseCase, ProductRepositoryImpl

Visibility in Multi-Module Architecture

Production Rule
In a multi-module app, internal is your friend. Mark implementation classes internal so the :feature-payment module cannot directly instantiate PaymentRepositoryImpl from :data. Only the interface (PaymentRepository) is public. Hilt binds them — the consumer never sees the implementation class.

When NOT to Use Inheritance

Do NOT
  • Use inheritance for code reuse alone — prefer composition or extension functions
  • Mark every class open "just in case" — final-by-default is a safety feature
  • Use abstract classes for pure contracts — that's what interfaces are for
  • Deep inheritance hierarchies — 2 levels max; beyond that, extract shared logic differently
🏭
4. Production Example
Scenario
Automotive app — a Clean Architecture payment module demonstrating interface, abstract class, open class, visibility modifiers, constructors, and init blocks together.

Interface — contract for DI

// domain/repository/PaymentRepository.kt  (public — crosses module boundary)
interface PaymentRepository {
    suspend fun initiatePayment(req: PaymentRequest): Result<PaymentResponse>
    suspend fun getPaymentStatus(id: String): Result<PaymentStatus>
}

Abstract Base UseCase — template method pattern

// domain/usecase/BaseUseCase.kt  (internal to :domain module)
internal abstract class BaseUseCase<in P, out R> {
    protected abstract suspend fun execute(params: P): R

    // Template method: wraps execute() with error handling
    suspend operator fun invoke(params: P): Result<R> = try {
        Result.success(execute(params))
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        throw e   // never swallow cancellation
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        Result.failure(e)
    }
}

Concrete UseCase — final (default)

// domain/usecase/ProcessPaymentUseCase.kt
class ProcessPaymentUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val repo: PaymentRepository,       // depends on interface, not impl
    private val validator: PaymentValidator
) : BaseUseCase<PaymentRequest, PaymentResponse>() {

    override suspend fun execute(params: PaymentRequest): PaymentResponse {
        validator.validate(params)          // throws on invalid — caught by base
        return repo.initiatePayment(params).getOrThrow()
    }
}

Repository Implementation — internal, hides from other modules

// data/repository/PaymentRepositoryImpl.kt
internal class PaymentRepositoryImpl @Inject constructor(
    private val api: PaymentApi,
    private val dao: PaymentDao
) : PaymentRepository {

    private val cache = HashMap<String, PaymentStatus>()  // private state

    override suspend fun initiatePayment(req: PaymentRequest) =
        safeApiCall { api.pay(req.toDto()).toDomain() }

    override suspend fun getPaymentStatus(id: String) =
        safeApiCall { cache.getOrPut(id) { api.getStatus(id).toDomain() } }
}

ViewModel — open base class pattern

// presentation/base/BaseViewModel.kt
open class BaseViewModel : ViewModel() {
    protected val _error = MutableSharedFlow<String>()
    val error = _error.asSharedFlow()

    protected open fun handleError(e: Throwable) {
        viewModelScope.launch { _error.emit(e.message ?: "Unknown error") }
    }
}

// presentation/payment/PaymentViewModel.kt
@HiltViewModel
class PaymentViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val processPayment: ProcessPaymentUseCase
) : BaseViewModel() {

    private val _state = MutableStateFlow<PaymentUiState>(PaymentUiState.Idle)
    val state = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun pay(req: PaymentRequest) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _state.value = PaymentUiState.Loading
            processPayment(req)
                .onSuccess { _state.value = PaymentUiState.Success(it) }
                .onFailure { handleError(it) }  // calls base class method
        }
    }
}

Key Architecture Points

  • PaymentRepository is a public interface — crosses module boundaries; consumers depend on abstraction.
  • PaymentRepositoryImpl is internal — hidden from feature modules; only Hilt wires it.
  • BaseUseCase is internal abstract — template method pattern; error handling once, reused across all use cases.
  • BaseViewModel is open with protected open fun handleError — subclasses can override but get sensible defaults.
  • No !!, no mutable public state, constructor injection throughout.
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs
ApproachProsConsWhen to pick
Interface + implementationTestable, mockable, DI-friendly, loose couplingMore files; interface must be maintained in syncRepository, Service, UseCase contracts — always for cross-layer boundaries
Abstract classShare state + behaviour; template method; constructor paramsSingle inheritance limit; tighter coupling than interfaceBaseViewModel, BaseUseCase — shared implementation, not pure contract
Open classFull default implementation + extensibilitySubclasses may break parent invariants (fragile base class)Library/base classes where extension is explicitly intended
Composition over inheritanceFlexible, no inheritance hierarchy, testableMore delegation boilerplatePreferred over deep inheritance; Kotlin's by delegation helps
Extension functionsAdd behaviour without subclassing, statically safeNo access to private members, no polymorphismUtility methods on existing types

Interface vs Abstract Class — Quick Decider

NeedUse
Multiple implementations + mockabilityInterface
Shared state (fields) across subclassesAbstract class
Constructor parameters in baseAbstract class
Multiple "contracts" on one classMultiple interfaces
Default method logic + contractEither (interface has defaults since Kotlin/Java 8)
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Forgetting open on a class that needs to be subclassed

// ❌ BAD — Hilt proxy / Mockito subclassing will fail at runtime
class BaseViewModel : ViewModel()  // final — cannot mock or proxy
// ✅ GOOD
open class BaseViewModel : ViewModel()

Leaking implementation through public visibility

// ❌ BAD — implementation class is public; other modules can depend on it directly
class UserRepositoryImpl : UserRepository { ... }  // public by default
// ✅ GOOD — internal hides it from other modules; only Hilt module sees it
internal class UserRepositoryImpl : UserRepository { ... }

init block ordering trap

class Foo(val x: Int) {
    val doubled = x * 2   // ✅ property initializers run top-to-bottom

    init {
        // ❌ BAD: if 'tripled' is declared AFTER this init block,
        // accessing it here throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException
        println(tripled)
    }

    val tripled = x * 3   // declared AFTER init — not yet initialized when init runs
}

Property initializers and init blocks run in declaration order. Never access a property in an init block that is declared after it.

Abstract class vs interface — wrong choice

// ❌ BAD — abstract class used as a pure contract (no state, no constructors)
abstract class UserRepository {
    abstract suspend fun getUser(id: String): User
}
// ✅ GOOD — interface is the right tool for a pure contract
interface UserRepository {
    suspend fun getUser(id: String): User
}
// Benefit: implementation can implement multiple interfaces; can be mocked

Production Best Practices

  1. Classes are final by default — only add open when inheritance is deliberately designed and documented.
  2. Keep implementation classes internal in multi-module apps — expose only interfaces across module boundaries.
  3. Prefer interfaces for cross-layer contracts (Repository, Service); abstract classes for shared state (BaseViewModel).
  4. Use protected for base class helpers intended only for subclasses — don't make them public.
  5. Prefer constructor injection — Hilt's @Inject constructor documents all dependencies explicitly.
  6. Declare properties before the init block that needs them — or initialize them in the init block itself.
  7. Prefer composition over inheritance beyond 1–2 levels deep.
🎤
7. Interview Answer Framework

30-Second Answer

"Kotlin's OOP differs from Java in one critical way: classes are final by default. You must explicitly mark a class open to allow subclassing. This enforces 'design for inheritance or prohibit it.' For contracts, I use interfaces — they support multiple implementations, default methods, and are mockable. For shared state and behaviour, I use abstract classes. Visibility-wise, I use internal heavily in multi-module apps to hide implementation classes from other modules, exposing only the interface."

2-Minute Structured Answer

"Three areas stand out in Kotlin OOP compared to Java.

First, final-by-default. In Java, any class can be subclassed unless you mark it final. In Kotlin it's the opposite — you have to opt-in with open. This is an intentional design decision that aligns with Clean Architecture: use cases, repository implementations, and most concrete classes should not be extended — they should be replaced or wrapped.

Second, interface vs abstract class. I use interfaces for cross-layer contracts — UserRepository, AnalyticsTracker — because they're mockable, support multiple implementations, and implementations can implement multiple interfaces. I use abstract classes when I need shared state: a BaseViewModel with a protected _error: SharedFlow, or a BaseUseCase<P,R> that wraps execute() with error handling once for all use cases.

Third, visibility in multi-module apps. internal is the key modifier. Repository implementations are internal — the feature module only sees the interface. Only Hilt's module sees the implementation. This enforces the Dependency Inversion Principle at the module level."

Must-Mention Points

1
Classes are final by default in Kotlin — must explicitly mark open to allow inheritance
2
Interface for pure contracts (no state); abstract class for shared state + behaviour (has constructor, fields)
3
internal visibility = visible within the same Gradle module — key for multi-module encapsulation
4
Kotlin has no package-private — use internal where Java would use package-private
5
Primary constructor in class header; init blocks run in declaration order after primary constructor
6
Interface properties have no backing field — only an abstract getter (or custom getter with a default)
7
Prefer composition over inheritance beyond 2 levels — Kotlin by delegation makes composition clean

Do NOT Go Deeper Unless Asked

  • JVM bytecode for Kotlin interfaces with default methods (DefaultImpls class)
  • Kotlin's delegation (by) internals — covered in 1G
  • Data classes, sealed classes, objects — covered in 1E

Likely Follow-up Questions

QuestionShort Answer
Why are Kotlin classes final by default?Enforces "design and document for inheritance, or prohibit it" (Effective Java Item 19). Prevents accidental subclassing that breaks invariants. Aligns with Kotlin's philosophy of explicit opt-in for unsafe operations.
Can an interface have a constructor in Kotlin?No. Interfaces cannot have constructors or backing fields. If you need constructor parameters, use an abstract class. Interface properties are abstract getters (or have custom getters) — no stored state.
What's the difference between internal and private?private on a class member = visible only within that class. private on a top-level declaration = visible only within that file. internal = visible within the same Gradle module — used to hide implementation classes from other modules.
Can a Kotlin class implement multiple interfaces?Yes — unlike abstract classes, a class can implement multiple interfaces. If two interfaces have the same default method, the implementing class must override it and explicitly call which super it wants.
What happens if two interfaces both provide a default for the same method?Compile error — the implementing class must override the method and call super<InterfaceName>.method() to disambiguate.

Senior-Level Insight (Stand Out)

Say This
"In a multi-module Clean Architecture, I combine Kotlin's visibility system with Hilt's DI to enforce the Dependency Inversion Principle at the build-system level. The :data module exposes only public interface UserRepository. The implementation UserRepositoryImpl is internal — literally impossible for the :feature module to reference it directly. Hilt's module in :data binds them. This means you get compile-time enforcement of 'depend on abstractions, not concretions' — not just a convention. That's a stronger guarantee than any code review."
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

CLASS DEFAULTS

class Foo      // final, public
open class Foo // extensible
abstract class Foo // no instantiate
// Members also final by default
open fun bar() // can override
final fun baz() // cannot override

CONSTRUCTORS

class Foo(val x: Int) // primary
// init runs after primary
init { require(x > 0) }
// secondary must delegate
constructor(s: String) : this(s.toInt())
// prefer default args over secondary

INTERFACE vs ABSTRACT

Interface:
  - no constructor, no backing fields
  - multiple implementations
  - mockable / fake-able
  - default methods OK

Abstract class:
  - has constructor + state
  - single inheritance
  - template method pattern

VISIBILITY

public    → everywhere (default)
internal  → same Gradle module
protected → class + subclasses
private   → class only (or file)
// No package-private in Kotlin
// Use internal for module encap

ANDROID PATTERNS

interface UserRepository   // contract
internal class UserRepositoryImpl // hidden
open class BaseViewModel          // extensible
abstract class BaseUseCase  // template
@HiltViewModel class PayVM       // final+DI

KEY GOTCHAS

final-by-default → add open to allow mock
internal → same module, not same package
init order = declaration order
interface property = no backing field
2 interfaces same default → must override
composition > deep inheritance
❓
9. Interview Questions (Self-Check)
How to use
Answer first, then reveal.

Basic

B1 — What is the default visibility of a Kotlin class and its members? How does it differ from Java?
Easy▼
In Kotlin, the default visibility is public (unlike Java where it's package-private). However, classes in Kotlin are final by default (unlike Java where they're open/extensible). To allow subclassing in Kotlin you must mark the class open. Java requires final to prohibit subclassing — the opposite approach.
B2 — What is the init block? When does it run?
Easy▼
The init block is a body of code that runs as part of the primary constructor, immediately after property initializers. Multiple init blocks are allowed — they run in top-to-bottom declaration order, interleaved with property initializers. Use it for validation (require()), complex initialization that can't be expressed in a single expression, or initialization that depends on constructor parameters.
B3 — What is the difference between interface and abstract class in Kotlin?
Easy▼
Interface: no constructors, no backing fields (only abstract getters), can have default method implementations, a class can implement multiple interfaces.

Abstract class: can have constructors, backing fields (actual state), both abstract and concrete methods. A class can only extend one abstract class.

Use interface for pure contracts (testability, DI); use abstract class when shared state or constructor parameters are needed.

Intermediate

I1 — What does internal mean? How is it different from private? Give an Android multi-module example.
Medium▼
internal means visible within the same Gradle module. private on a class member means visible only within that class; on a top-level declaration it means visible only within that file.

Multi-module example: In :data module, UserRepositoryImpl is marked internal. The :feature-profile module cannot reference it directly even though it depends on :data. It can only use the public interface UserRepository. Hilt's module in :data (which is in the same module as the impl) binds the interface to the implementation.
I2 — (Coding) What is wrong with this code and how do you fix it?
MediumCoding▼
class Config(val env: String) {
    init {
        println(label)   // ❌ — 'label' declared AFTER this init block
    }
    val label = "$env config"
}
Problem: Property initializers and init blocks run in declaration order. label is declared after the init block, so when init runs, label has not been initialized yet → UninitializedPropertyAccessException at runtime.

Fix: Move label before the init block, or access it in a later init block: 
class Config(val env: String) {
    val label = "$env config"  // declared first
    init { println(label) }    // ✅ now initialized
}
I3 — Can a Kotlin class implement two interfaces that both define a default implementation for the same method? What happens?
Medium▼
Yes, a class can implement two such interfaces, but if both provide a default implementation for the same method, the implementing class must override that method — otherwise it's a compile error. Inside the override, you can delegate to either interface's default with super<InterfaceName>.method(): 
interface A { fun greet() = println("Hello from A") }
interface B { fun greet() = println("Hello from B") }
class C : A, B {
    override fun greet() { super<A>.greet() }  // must disambiguate
}
I4 — When would you use a secondary constructor vs default arguments in Kotlin?
Medium▼
Almost always prefer default arguments — they're more concise, idiomatic, and work with named arguments. Secondary constructors should be used when: (1) the class needs completely different initialization paths that can't be captured by defaults (e.g., constructing from a JSON string vs individual fields); (2) interoperability with Java requires overloaded constructors (@JvmOverloads is the cleaner alternative); (3) you're subclassing a Java class with multiple constructors and need to delegate to different parent constructors.

Senior / Scenario

S1 — (Scenario) A teammate made UserRepositoryImpl public. What are the risks? How do you enforce the right pattern?
HardScenario▼
Risks: (1) Feature modules can depend directly on the implementation — violating DIP. If the implementation changes (e.g., adding a constructor parameter), every direct user breaks. (2) Tests may use the concrete class instead of the interface, making them harder to fake. (3) The implementation's internal details (caching, retries) are now part of the "public API" — any refactor becomes a breaking change.

Fix: Mark UserRepositoryImpl as internal. The Hilt module that binds it is in the same module so it still works. Add a lint rule or ArchUnit test to prevent cross-module direct usage of impl classes. In code review, flag any import of an Impl class in a feature module.
S2 — Design a BaseUseCase abstract class that wraps all use cases in a Result with correct CancellationException handling.
HardCoding▼
abstract class BaseUseCase<in P, out R> {
    // Subclasses implement this — business logic only
    protected abstract suspend fun execute(params: P): R

    // Callers use invoke() — gets error handling for free
    suspend operator fun invoke(params: P): Result<R> = try {
        Result.success(execute(params))
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        throw e  // CRITICAL: never swallow coroutine cancellation
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        Result.failure(e)
    }
}

// Usage:
class GetUserUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val repo: UserRepository
) : BaseUseCase<String, User>() {
    override suspend fun execute(params: String) = repo.getUser(params)
}
Key point: CancellationException must be rethrown — swallowing it breaks coroutine cancellation throughout the scope.
S3 — When would you choose composition over inheritance for a ViewModel scenario? Give a concrete example.
HardScenario▼
Scenario: You have BaseViewModel with error handling, and now you need two orthogonal concerns: pagination logic and analytics tracking. You could add both to the base class or create a deep hierarchy — but that couples all ViewModels to pagination and analytics whether they need it or not.

Composition approach: 
// Each concern is a separate class injected via constructor
class PaginationController(private val pageSize: Int = 20) {
    fun nextPage() = ...
}

class AnalyticsDelegate @Inject constructor(private val tracker: Tracker) {
    fun trackScreen(name: String) = tracker.track(name)
}

@HiltViewModel
class ProductListViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val pagination: PaginationController,  // composed
    private val analytics: AnalyticsDelegate        // composed
) : ViewModel() { ... }
This is testable (mock each dependency independently), avoids a bloated base class, and each concern is independently reusable. Kotlin's by delegation can make this even cleaner by auto-delegating interface calls.

● Android Interview Prep

1E — Kotlin Special Classes

data classes, enum classes, sealed classes & interfaces, object declarations, companion objects, anonymous objects — the Kotlin class variants that power Android architecture daily.

ID: 1E ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

What they are

Kotlin's special class variants solve recurring patterns that require verbose boilerplate in Java: value objects (data classes), fixed sets of constants (enum), exhaustive type hierarchies (sealed), singletons (object), static-like members (companion object), and one-off anonymous implementations (anonymous object).

Why they matter for Android

  • data class — domain models, DTOs, UI states, events
  • sealed class/interface — UiState, Result, navigation events, one-time UI effects
  • enum class — fixed sets: order status, payment type, network state
  • object — singleton services, Retrofit instance, constants file
  • companion object — factory methods, constants, newInstance() for Fragments
  • anonymous object — one-off interface implementations, test fakes inline
Senior Mental Model
sealed class is the most interview-critical here. It models closed type hierarchies — the compiler knows every possible subtype, enabling exhaustive when expressions. This is the foundation of safe, compile-time-checked UiState machines in MVVM.
⚙
2. How It Works

data class

data class UserProfile(
    val userId: String,
    val name: String,
    val email: String?
)

The compiler auto-generates: equals() / hashCode() (structural equality), toString(), copy(), and componentN() functions (for destructuring). All based on properties declared in the primary constructor.

val u1 = UserProfile("1", "Alice", "a@b.com")
val u2 = u1.copy(name = "Bob")          // new object, only name changed
val (id, name, email) = u1               // destructuring via componentN()
u1 == u2                                  // false — structural equality
Key Rules
  • Properties in body (not primary constructor) are NOT included in equals/hashCode/copy
  • Data classes cannot be abstract, open, sealed, or inner
  • At least one primary constructor parameter required
  • All primary constructor params should be val — mutability with var in data classes breaks structural equality invariants

enum class

enum class PaymentStatus(val displayName: String) {
    PENDING("Pending"),
    PROCESSING("Processing"),
    SUCCESS("Paid"),
    FAILED("Failed"),
    REFUNDED("Refunded");

    fun isFinal(): Boolean = this == SUCCESS || this == FAILED || this == REFUNDED
}

val status = PaymentStatus.SUCCESS
println(status.displayName)   // "Paid"
println(status.name)          // "SUCCESS" — built-in
println(status.ordinal)       // 2 — zero-based index
PaymentStatus.valueOf("PENDING")  // by name string
PaymentStatus.entries           // all values (Kotlin 1.9+), replaces values()

sealed class

sealed class UiState<out T> {
    data object Loading : UiState<Nothing>()
    data class  Success<T>(val data: T) : UiState<T>()
    data class  Error(val message: String) : UiState<Nothing>()
}

// Exhaustive when — compiler error if a subtype is missing
when (val state = uiState) {
    is UiState.Loading  -> showLoading()
    is UiState.Success  -> showData(state.data)
    is UiState.Error    -> showError(state.message)
    // No else needed — compiler guarantees exhaustiveness
}
sealed class vs sealed interface
sealed class: subclasses can only be in the same package (Kotlin 1.5+: same compilation unit). Can hold state via constructor. sealed interface: subclasses/implementors can be data classes, objects, or regular classes — more flexible. Preferred for pure type hierarchies with no shared state. Use sealed interface when subtypes need to implement multiple interfaces.

object declaration (Singleton)

// Thread-safe singleton — initialized on first access
object NetworkConfig {
    const val BASE_URL = "https://api.bank.com/"
    const val TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 30L

    fun buildOkHttpClient(): OkHttpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
        .connectTimeout(TIMEOUT_SECONDS, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
        .build()
}
// Usage: NetworkConfig.BASE_URL
// Compiled to: public final class NetworkConfig with static INSTANCE field

companion object

class PaymentFragment : Fragment() {
    companion object {
        private const val ARG_PAYMENT_ID = "payment_id"

        // Factory method — idiomatic Fragment instantiation
        fun newInstance(paymentId: String): PaymentFragment =
            PaymentFragment().apply {
                arguments = Bundle().apply { putString(ARG_PAYMENT_ID, paymentId) }
            }
    }

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, ...) {
        val paymentId = arguments?.getString(ARG_PAYMENT_ID)
    }
}
// Usage: PaymentFragment.newInstance("pay_123")
// companion object members are NOT truly static — accessed via INSTANCE
// Add @JvmStatic for Java interop

anonymous object

// One-off implementation — no need for a named class
val loginListener = object : AuthListener {
    override fun onSuccess(token: String) { navigateToHome() }
    override fun onFailure(e: Exception) { showError(e.message) }
}

// Anonymous object with no supertype — local temporary state
val counter = object {
    var count = 0
    fun increment() = ++count
}

data object (Kotlin 1.9+)

// Singleton with proper equals/hashCode/toString — perfect for sealed subtypes
sealed class NetworkState {
    data object Connected    : NetworkState()
    data object Disconnected : NetworkState()
    data class  Error(val code: Int) : NetworkState()
}
// data object: toString() = "Connected", equals() works correctly
// plain object: toString() = "NetworkState$Connected@1234abc" — ugly
TypeInstancesAuto-generatedPrimary use
data classManyequals, hashCode, toString, copy, componentNDomain models, DTOs, UI states
enum classFixed setname, ordinal, valueOf, entriesClosed constants with behaviour
sealed classClosed hierarchyExhaustive whenUiState, Result, navigation events
sealed interfaceClosed hierarchyExhaustive whenMulti-interface subtypes, pure type unions
object1 (singleton)Thread-safe initSingletons, constants holders
companion object1 per class—Factory methods, constants, @JvmStatic
anonymous object1 inline—One-off interface implementation
data object1 (singleton)equals, hashCode, toStringSingleton sealed subtypes (Loading, Idle)
🎯
3. Why and When to Use It

Decision Guide

NeedUseAndroid Example
Value object — structural equality, copy, destructuringdata classUserProfile, ProductDto, CartItem
Fixed named constants with optional behaviour/propertiesenum classPaymentStatus, OrderState, Theme
Closed type hierarchy — exhaustive whensealed class or sealed interfaceUiState, ViewEvent, ApiResult
App-wide singleton with no DIobjectNetworkConfig, AppConstants
Factory method / constants tied to a classcompanion objectFragment.newInstance(), TAG constant
One-off multi-method interface implementationanonymous objectAuth callback, test fake inline
Singleton sealed subtype (no data)data objectUiState.Loading, UiState.Idle

sealed class vs enum class — when to pick which

Criterionenum classsealed class
Number of instancesFixed at compile timeFixed subtypes, unlimited instances per subtype
Each variant carries dataSame fields for allEach subtype has its own fields
Hierarchy depthFlat onlyCan nest further
Exhaustive whenYesYes
ExamplePaymentStatus.SUCCESSUiState.Success(data)

When NOT to Use

Do NOT
  • Use data class for mutable state — all properties should be val
  • Put business logic in a data class body — keep it a dumb value object
  • Use object for things that need DI or testing — use Hilt @Singleton instead
  • Use enum when subtypes need different data shapes — use sealed class
  • Use companion object as a dumping ground for utility functions — extract to top-level or proper class
  • Use a plain object for sealed singleton subtypes (use data object instead — better toString() / equality)
🏭
4. Production Example
Scenario
E-commerce app — order management. Each special class type appears in its natural production context across Clean Architecture layers.

data class — Domain Model

// domain/model/Order.kt
data class Order(
    val id: String,
    val items: List<OrderItem>,
    val status: OrderStatus,
    val totalAmount: Double,
    val createdAt: Long
) {
    // Body properties excluded from equals/hashCode/copy
    val formattedTotal: String
        get() = "₹${String.format("%.2f", totalAmount)}"
}

// Deep copy with modification — immutable update pattern
val updatedOrder = order.copy(status = OrderStatus.DELIVERED)

enum class — Order Status

// domain/model/OrderStatus.kt
enum class OrderStatus(
    val displayName: String,
    val colorRes: Int
) {
    PLACED("Order Placed", R.color.status_blue),
    CONFIRMED("Confirmed", R.color.status_indigo),
    SHIPPED("Shipped", R.color.status_orange),
    DELIVERED("Delivered", R.color.status_green),
    CANCELLED("Cancelled", R.color.status_red);

    val isFinal: Boolean
        get() = this == DELIVERED || this == CANCELLED
}

sealed interface — UiState

// presentation/orders/OrderListUiState.kt
sealed interface OrderListUiState {
    data object Loading  : OrderListUiState
    data object Empty    : OrderListUiState
    data class  Success(val orders: List<Order>) : OrderListUiState
    data class  Error(val message: String, val retryable: Boolean = true) : OrderListUiState
}

// One-time events (side effects) — also sealed
sealed interface OrderEvent {
    data class NavigateToDetail(val orderId: String) : OrderEvent
    data class ShowSnackbar(val message: String) : OrderEvent
    data object ShowCancelConfirmation : OrderEvent
}

ViewModel — sealed state + events

// presentation/orders/OrderListViewModel.kt
@HiltViewModel
class OrderListViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val getOrders: GetOrdersUseCase
) : ViewModel() {

    private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow<OrderListUiState>(OrderListUiState.Loading)
    val uiState = _uiState.asStateFlow()

    private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<OrderEvent>()
    val events = _events.asSharedFlow()

    fun loadOrders() {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            getOrders()
                .onSuccess { orders ->
                    _uiState.value = if (orders.isEmpty())
                        OrderListUiState.Empty
                    else
                        OrderListUiState.Success(orders)
                }
                .onFailure {
                    _uiState.value = OrderListUiState.Error(it.message ?: "Unknown")
                }
        }
    }

    fun onOrderClicked(orderId: String) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _events.emit(OrderEvent.NavigateToDetail(orderId))
        }
    }
}

Compose UI — exhaustive when on sealed

@Composable
fun OrderListScreen(viewModel: OrderListViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val uiState by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

    when (uiState) {                                     // exhaustive — no else needed
        OrderListUiState.Loading -> LoadingIndicator()
        OrderListUiState.Empty   -> EmptyState()
        is OrderListUiState.Success -> OrderList((uiState as OrderListUiState.Success).orders)
        is OrderListUiState.Error   -> ErrorView((uiState as OrderListUiState.Error).message)
    }
}

companion object — Fragment factory + TAG

class OrderDetailFragment : Fragment() {
    companion object {
        const val TAG = "OrderDetailFragment"              // compile-time constant
        private const val ARG_ORDER_ID = "order_id"

        fun newInstance(orderId: String) =
            OrderDetailFragment().apply {
                arguments = Bundle().apply { putString(ARG_ORDER_ID, orderId) }
            }
    }
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs
ApproachProsConsWhen to pick
data classAuto equals/hashCode/copy, immutable by conventionCan't be open/abstract; body props excluded from equalsAlways for value objects and domain models
Regular classFlexibleManual equals/hashCode, no copy()When mutable state or inheritance needed
sealed classExhaustive when, type safety, can hold state per subtypeAll subtypes in same packageUiState, Result, navigation events
sealed interfaceSubtypes can implement multiple interfaces, more flexibleNo shared constructor/fieldsPure type hierarchy, multi-interface subtypes
enum classSimple, ordinal, valueOf, exhaustive whenAll instances have same fields; no per-instance data shapesFixed constant set with optional shared behaviour
Kotlin Result<T>Built-in, interops with coroutinesOnly Success/Failure — no Loading, no custom error typesSimple success/failure; use sealed UiState for UI layer
object singletonThread-safe, simpleHard to test (no DI), global stateConstants, config — not for service classes
Hilt @SingletonTestable, injectable, lifecycle-awareMore setupServices, repositories — always over raw object

Interviewer Comparisons

Expect These
  • sealed class vs enum — enum: fixed instances, same data shape; sealed: fixed subtypes, different data per subtype
  • sealed class vs sealed interface — interface: more flexible (multi-interface), no shared state; class: shared constructor/fields
  • data class vs regular class — data: auto value semantics; regular: manual, needed for inheritance
  • object vs companion object — object is standalone singleton; companion is tied to an enclosing class
  • object vs Hilt @Singleton — object is hard to test; Hilt singleton is injectable and mockable
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

data class with var — breaks equals/hashCode contract

// ❌ BAD — mutable data class breaks structural equality guarantees
data class CartItem(var quantity: Int, val productId: String)
val item = CartItem(1, "p1")
val set = hashSetOf(item)
item.quantity = 2    // mutates! hashCode changes → item "lost" in the set
println(item in set)  // false! bucket changed
// ✅ GOOD — all val; use copy() for updates
data class CartItem(val quantity: Int, val productId: String)
val updated = item.copy(quantity = 2)   // new object

Body property included in equals — invisible bug

// ❌ BAD — 'displayName' is in the body; NOT compared in equals()
data class Product(val id: String) {
    var displayName: String = ""   // body property — ignored by equals/hashCode
}
val a = Product("1").apply { displayName = "Phone" }
val b = Product("1").apply { displayName = "Laptop" }
println(a == b)  // true! displayName not in equals
// ✅ GOOD — all meaningful fields in primary constructor
data class Product(val id: String, val displayName: String)

sealed class when without else — missing new subtype

// ❌ BAD — using else loses the compile-time exhaustiveness guarantee
when (state) {
    is UiState.Loading -> showLoading()
    is UiState.Success -> showData()
    else -> showError()  // silently swallows new subtypes added later
}
// ✅ GOOD — no else; adding a new sealed subtype causes compile error here
when (state) {
    is UiState.Loading -> showLoading()
    is UiState.Success -> showData()
    is UiState.Error   -> showError()
}

object singleton vs Hilt — testability trap

// ❌ BAD — singleton object impossible to replace in tests
object AnalyticsManager {
    fun track(event: String) { /* sends to Firebase */ }
}
// In tests: can't inject a no-op; real events fire
// ✅ GOOD — interface + Hilt @Singleton
interface Analytics { fun track(event: String) }
class FirebaseAnalytics @Inject constructor() : Analytics { ... }
// Test: inject FakeAnalytics that does nothing

enum ordinal as persisted value — fragile

// ❌ BAD — storing ordinal in DB; reordering enum breaks all stored data
dao.insert(order.copy(statusCode = status.ordinal))

// ✅ GOOD — store name or a stable Int field
enum class OrderStatus(val code: Int) {
    PLACED(1), SHIPPED(2), DELIVERED(3), CANCELLED(4)
}
dao.insert(order.copy(statusCode = status.code))  // stable

Production Best Practices

  1. All data class primary constructor properties should be val — use copy() for updates.
  2. Use sealed interface over sealed class when subtypes need no shared state — more flexible.
  3. Never use else in a when on a sealed type — defeats the exhaustiveness guarantee.
  4. Use data object (Kotlin 1.9+) for no-data sealed subtypes — correct toString() and equality.
  5. Use enum class for fixed constants; use a stable explicit code: Int field if persisting to DB.
  6. Keep companion object lean — factory methods and constants only, not utility functions.
  7. Prefer Hilt @Singleton over raw object for anything that needs to be replaced in tests.
🎤
7. Interview Answer Framework

30-Second Answer

"Kotlin's special classes each solve a specific pattern. Data classes give you value semantics — equals, hashCode, copy, destructuring — auto-generated from primary constructor properties. Sealed classes and interfaces model closed type hierarchies, enabling exhaustive when expressions — the compiler guarantees you handle every subtype. I use sealed interface for UiState and UI events throughout my ViewModels. Enum classes handle fixed constant sets. Object declarations are thread-safe singletons. Companion objects provide factory methods and constants scoped to a class."

2-Minute Structured Answer

"I'll focus on the ones that come up most in Android work.

Data classes: I use these for domain models, DTOs, and UI states. The key thing is they provide structural equality — two instances with the same property values are equal. All primary constructor properties should be val. Properties in the body are NOT included in equals or copy, which is a common source of subtle bugs. I use copy() for immutable updates — never mutate.

Sealed classes/interfaces: this is the most powerful one. A sealed type has a closed set of subtypes known at compile time. This makes when exhaustive — no else branch needed, and if I add a new subtype later, every when expression that doesn't handle it becomes a compile error. I model every ViewModel's state as a sealed interface with data object Loading, data object Empty, data class Success(val data), and data class Error(val message). I also use a separate sealed interface for one-time events like navigation and snackbars.

Sealed vs enum: enum is for a fixed set of named constants where all instances share the same fields. Sealed is for when each subtype needs different data — Success needs a result, Error needs a message, Loading needs nothing.

Object vs companion: object is a standalone singleton. Companion object lives inside a class and gives you factory methods and constants scoped to that class — the idiomatic way to do Fragment.newInstance()."

Must-Mention Points

1
data class: equals/hashCode/copy/componentN auto-generated from primary constructor properties only
2
All data class primary constructor params should be val — mutable data class breaks equals/hashCode in collections
3
sealed = closed type hierarchy; compiler-enforced exhaustive when — never add else on a sealed type
4
sealed class vs enum: enum = same data shape for all instances; sealed = different data per subtype
5
sealed interface preferred over sealed class when no shared state needed — subtypes can implement multiple interfaces
6
data object (Kotlin 1.9+) for no-data sealed subtypes — gives correct toString() and equality vs plain object
7
object = thread-safe singleton; prefer Hilt @Singleton for anything testable

Do NOT Go Deeper Unless Asked

  • Bytecode representation of data classes (componentN, Intrinsics checks)
  • Kotlin value class (inline classes) — different concept
  • Enum reflection / enumValueOf internals

Likely Follow-up Questions

QuestionShort Answer
Can a data class extend another class?It can extend a non-data class or implement interfaces. It cannot extend another data class (data classes cannot be open).
What does copy() do?Creates a new instance with the same values as the original, overriding only the specified properties. It does a shallow copy — nested objects are not deep-copied.
What's the difference between object and companion object?object = standalone singleton class. companion object = singleton tied to the enclosing class — members accessed via the class name. Only one companion object per class. Neither generates truly static JVM members — add @JvmStatic for Java interop.
Why use sealed interface over sealed class?A sealed interface's subtypes can implement multiple other interfaces, and can be data classes or regular classes independently. A sealed class requires subtypes to extend it — they can't extend another class. Prefer sealed interface unless you need shared constructor parameters or state in the base.
How do you make when exhaustive in Compose when it's used as a statement, not expression?Use the when extension trick: val exhaustive = when(state) { ... } as an expression, or use a custom exhaustive extension property. Compose smart recomposition also benefits from sealed state changes being distinct object types.

Senior-Level Insight (Stand Out)

Say This
"I model UI state as a sealed interface with data object for no-data states and data class for states with data. I keep state and one-time events separate — state goes in StateFlow, events go in SharedFlow (replay=0). The sealed interface guarantees the UI handles every state, and adding a new state (e.g., Refreshing) causes compile errors at every when expression — you can't miss it. That's architecture enforced by the type system, not by documentation or convention."
⚡

DATA CLASS

Auto: equals/hashCode/toString
      copy() / componentN()

All params → val (avoid var!)
Body props excluded from equals
Can't be open/abstract/sealed

entries (1.9+) replaces values()

NEVER use else on sealed when
Prefer sealed interface in new code

OBJECT / COMPANION

object Foo { }  // singleton
companion object { }  // tied to class
// Both: not truly static JVM
// Add @JvmStatic for Java interop
// object = hard to test → use Hilt
// companion = factory + constants

ANONYMOUS OBJECT

val x = object : SomeInterface {
  override fun method() { }
}
// One-off, local scope
// Captures outer this → leak risk
// For SAM → use lambda instead

KEY GOTCHAS

data class var → breaks hashSet
body props excluded from copy/equals
enum ordinal → fragile for DB/API
object singleton → untestable
else on sealed when → misses new types
data object toString = "Loading"
plain object toString = "Foo@abc123"
❓
9. Interview Questions (Self-Check)
How to use
Answer first, then reveal.

Basic

B1 — What does a data class auto-generate? What is NOT included in equals/hashCode?
Easy▼
Auto-generated: equals(), hashCode(), toString(), copy(), and componentN() functions for destructuring — all based on properties declared in the primary constructor only.

NOT included: properties declared in the class body (outside the primary constructor). This is a common source of bugs — if you add a var property in the body, two instances with different body-property values will still be considered equal if their constructor properties match.
B2 — What is a sealed class? How does it enable exhaustive when?
Easy▼
A sealed class defines a closed type hierarchy — all direct subclasses must be in the same compilation unit (package in Kotlin 1.5+). Because the compiler knows every possible subtype at compile time, a when expression on a sealed type can be exhaustive without an else branch. If you add a new subtype later, every when expression that doesn't handle it becomes a compile error — preventing silent bugs.
B3 — What is the difference between object and companion object?
Easy▼
object is a standalone singleton class declaration — it exists independently. companion object lives inside another class and its members are accessed via the enclosing class name (like Java static members, but not truly static in JVM bytecode). Only one companion object per class is allowed. Add @JvmStatic to companion members for actual Java static interop. Common use: companion object { fun newInstance() } for Fragment factories.

Intermediate

I1 — When would you use a sealed class vs an enum class?
Medium▼
Enum: fixed set of named constants where all instances share the same data shape. Good for: PaymentStatus, Theme, NetworkType. Each enum value is a singleton.

Sealed class: fixed set of subtypes where each subtype can carry different data. Good for: UiState (Loading has no data, Success has a list, Error has a message), Result, navigation events. Each subtype can have its own constructor and multiple instances.

Rule: if the variants have the same fields → enum. If each variant needs different data → sealed.
I2 — (Coding) What is wrong? data class User(val id: String) { var name = "" }; val a = User("1").apply { name = "Alice" }; val b = User("1").apply { name = "Bob" }; println(a == b)
MediumCoding▼
Prints true — which is likely NOT what the developer intended.

name is declared in the class body, not the primary constructor. Data class equals() and hashCode() are generated only from primary constructor properties (id here). So two User objects with the same id but different name values are considered equal.

Fix: move name to the primary constructor: data class User(val id: String, val name: String)
I3 — What is data object? Why is it better than plain object for sealed subtypes?
Medium▼
data object (Kotlin 1.9+) is a singleton with auto-generated equals(), hashCode(), and toString() — like a data class with no properties.

Why better for sealed subtypes: a plain object's toString() returns the JVM identity string like "UiState$Loading@1a2b3c" — useless for logging and debugging. A data object's toString() returns "Loading" — much cleaner. Also, equals() works correctly (two references to the same singleton are equal), though for objects this is true anyway since there's only one instance.
I4 — Why should you never use else in a when expression on a sealed type?
Medium▼
Using else defeats the compile-time exhaustiveness guarantee. If you add a new subtype to the sealed hierarchy later, the when with else will silently handle it with the else branch — the compiler won't warn you. You could be rendering the wrong UI for a new state for weeks without realizing.

Without else, adding a new sealed subtype causes a compile error at every when expression that doesn't handle it. This is intentional — it forces you to explicitly handle every state, making the system fail fast at compile time rather than silently at runtime.

Senior / Scenario

S1 — Design a complete UiState and ViewEvent sealed hierarchy for a payment screen. Justify your choices.
HardCoding▼
// State — flows in StateFlow, represents current screen state
sealed interface PaymentUiState {
    data object Idle       : PaymentUiState
    data object Loading    : PaymentUiState
    data class  Success(val transactionId: String) : PaymentUiState
    data class  Error(val message: String, val retryable: Boolean) : PaymentUiState
}

// Events — one-time side effects in SharedFlow(replay=0)
sealed interface PaymentEvent {
    data class  NavigateToReceipt(val txId: String) : PaymentEvent
    data class  ShowSnackbar(val msg: String) : PaymentEvent
    data object NavigateBack : PaymentEvent
}
Justifications: sealed interface (not class) — no shared state; subtypes can implement other interfaces. data object for Idle/Loading — no data, but clean toString(). data class for Success/Error — each has different fields. Events separate from state — state is persistent (StateFlow), events fire once (SharedFlow replay=0) to prevent re-delivery on recomposition.
S2 — (Scenario) A junior dev stored PaymentStatus.ordinal in the Room database. Three months later, the team added a new status between PROCESSING and SUCCESS. What broke and how do you fix it?
HardScenario▼
What broke: ordinal is the zero-based position in the enum declaration. Adding a new status shifted all ordinals after it by 1. Every row in the DB that had ordinal 2 (SUCCESS) is now interpreted as the new status. Orders that were previously marked SUCCESS are now read back as the wrong status — silent data corruption.

Fix: Add a stable code: Int field to the enum that never changes regardless of declaration order: 
enum class PaymentStatus(val code: Int) {
    PENDING(1), PROCESSING(2), UNDER_REVIEW(5), SUCCESS(3), FAILED(4)
}
Write a Room migration to convert stored ordinal values to the new stable codes. Going forward, always persist status.code, not status.ordinal. Add a Room TypeConverter that converts by code.
S3 — (Scenario) copy() on a data class gives you a "deep copy" — true or false? What are the implications in an Android app?
HardScenario▼
False. copy() performs a shallow copy — only the top-level object is a new instance. Any nested objects (lists, other data classes) are shared references.

Implications: 
data class Cart(val items: MutableList<Item>)
val cart1 = Cart(mutableListOf(Item("A")))
val cart2 = cart1.copy()
cart2.items.add(Item("B"))   // MUTATES cart1.items too!
Fix: use immutable collections (List not MutableList) in data classes. If you need a deep copy, manually create new instances. In StateFlow with Compose, sharing mutable lists between states causes incorrect recomposition — Compose compares by reference for stability. Always use immutable List<T> in your UI state data classes.

● Android Interview Prep

1F — Generics & Variance

Generics, in/out variance annotations, covariance, contravariance — the type-system mechanics behind Flow, StateFlow, Result, and Clean Architecture generics.

ID: 1F ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

What it is

Generics let you write type-safe code that works with multiple types without duplication. Variance (in/out) controls how generic types relate when their type parameters are in a subtype relationship — determining whether List<Dog> can be used as a List<Animal>.

Why it matters for Android

  • Flow<T>, StateFlow<T>, Result<T>, LiveData<T> are all generic — understanding variance explains why StateFlow<UiState> is safe to assign to Flow<UiState>.
  • BaseUseCase<in P, out R> — the variance annotations are meaningful and necessary.
  • Repository generics: Resource<T>, ApiResult<T> — you need to design these correctly.
  • Compose: @Composable functions with generic state types.
Senior Mental Model
out T (covariant) = T only comes OUT (returned). Safe to read, not write. A Producer<Dog> IS-A Producer<Animal>.
in T (contravariant) = T only goes IN (consumed). Safe to write, not read. A Consumer<Animal> IS-A Consumer<Dog>.
Invariant (no annotation) = T both in and out. No subtype relationship. MutableList<Dog> is NOT a MutableList<Animal>.
⚙
2. How It Works

Basic Generics

// Generic function
fun <T> wrapInResult(value: T): Result<T> = Result.success(value)

// Generic class
class Box<T>(val value: T)

// Multiple type params
class Pair<A, B>(val first: A, val second: B)

// Upper bound constraint
fun <T : Comparable<T>> max(a: T, b: T): T = if (a > b) a else b

// Multiple bounds — use where
fun <T> process(item: T) where T : Serializable, T : Comparable<T> { }

The Variance Problem — Why Invariance Exists

// Dogs are Animals — OK
val dog: Animal = Dog()  // fine

// But MutableList<Dog> is NOT a MutableList<Animal> — why?
val dogs: MutableList<Dog> = mutableListOf(Dog())
// val animals: MutableList<Animal> = dogs  // ❌ compile error

// If it were allowed:
// animals.add(Cat())  // would corrupt the dogs list!
// dogs[0] is now a Cat — type safety broken

This is why generic types are invariant by default — to prevent type-unsafe writes.

out T — Covariance (Producer)

// out T: T only appears in OUT position (return type / val)
interface Producer<out T> {
    fun produce(): T   // ✅ T in out position
    // fun consume(item: T)  // ❌ compile error: T in in-position
}

val dogProducer: Producer<Dog> = DogFactory()
val animalProducer: Producer<Animal> = dogProducer  // ✅ safe — can only read

// Real example: Flow is covariant
val dogFlow: Flow<Dog> = flowOf(Dog())
val animalFlow: Flow<Animal> = dogFlow  // ✅ Flow<out T>

in T — Contravariance (Consumer)

// in T: T only appears in IN position (parameter)
interface Consumer<in T> {
    fun consume(item: T)   // ✅ T in in-position
    // fun produce(): T     // ❌ T in out-position — not allowed
}

val animalConsumer: Consumer<Animal> = AnimalPrinter()
val dogConsumer: Consumer<Dog> = animalConsumer  // ✅ Animal consumer can handle Dog

// Real example: Comparator is contravariant
val animalComparator: Comparator<Animal> = compareBy { it.name }
val dogComparator: Comparator<Dog> = animalComparator  // ✅ works

Declaration-site vs Use-site Variance

// Declaration-site: variance on the class/interface itself
interface Flow<out T>   // covariant — defined by the library

// Use-site: variance at the call site (type projection)
fun copy(from: Array<out Animal>, to: Array<Animal>) {
    // 'from' is projected — can only read from it
    for (item in from) to[0] = item
}
// Array is invariant, but use-site 'out' projects it to read-only

Star Projection *

// * = "I don't know the type parameter"
fun printList(list: List<*>) {
    list.forEach { println(it) }  // elements are Any? — read-only
}
// Equivalent to List<out Any?> for reading
// Cannot add elements — type unknown

Key Terms Summary

TermAnnotationDirectionSubtype relationReal example
Invariant(none)In + OutNone — exact type onlyMutableList<T>
Covariantout TOut onlyC<Dog> is C<Animal>Flow<T>, List<T>
Contravariantin TIn onlyC<Animal> is C<Dog>Comparator<T>
Star projection*Read-only unknownLike out Any?List<*>

Nothing and Any? in variance

// Nothing is a subtype of everything — bottom type
data object Loading : UiState<Nothing>()
// With UiState<out T>, Loading (UiState<Nothing>) is assignable to UiState<Any>

// Any? is supertype of everything — top type
fun <T : Any> nonNull(value: T): T = value  // T is non-nullable
🎯
3. Why and When to Use It

Real Android Use Cases

SituationVariance usedWhy
Flow<out T>CovariantFlow only emits (produces) T — safe to assign Flow<Dog> to Flow<Animal>
StateFlow<out T>CovariantSame — value is read-only from the outside
BaseUseCase<in P, out R>Contravariant P, Covariant RP is consumed (input), R is produced (output)
sealed class UiState<out T>CovariantAllows UiState.Loading : UiState<Nothing> to be used as UiState<SomeData>
Resource<T> wrapperCovariantResource only wraps and exposes data — never mutates it
Generic RepositoryInvariant (usually)Both reads and writes needed

When NOT to annotate variance

Do NOT
  • Add out if T appears in a function parameter — compile error
  • Add in if T appears as a return type — compile error
  • Use * when you know the type — use the concrete type or bound instead
  • Over-engineer variance for simple use cases — most app-level classes don't need it
🏭
4. Production Example
Scenario
Banking app — generic result wrapper, covariant UiState, contravariant use case base — all in Clean Architecture.

Covariant UiState — Loading works for any T

// domain/state/UiState.kt
sealed class UiState<out T> {           // out T: only produced, never consumed
    data object Loading : UiState<Nothing>()   // Nothing = valid subtype of any T
    data class  Success<T>(val data: T) : UiState<T>()
    data class  Error(val msg: String) : UiState<Nothing>()
}

// Because UiState is covariant:
val state: UiState<List<Transaction>> = UiState.Loading  // ✅
val state2: UiState<UserProfile> = UiState.Loading       // ✅ same Loading instance

Covariant Flow — StateFlow assignable to Flow

// presentation/TransactionViewModel.kt
@HiltViewModel
class TransactionViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val getTransactions: GetTransactionsUseCase
) : ViewModel() {

    private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow<UiState<List<Transaction>>>(UiState.Loading)

    // Exposed as Flow — safe because StateFlow is covariant (out T)
    val uiState: StateFlow<UiState<List<Transaction>>> = _uiState.asStateFlow()
    // Could also expose as Flow<UiState<...>> — valid because Flow<out T>
}

Generic BaseUseCase with in/out

// domain/usecase/BaseUseCase.kt
abstract class BaseUseCase<in P, out R> {
    // P is consumed (input param) → in P
    // R is produced (return value) → out R
    protected abstract suspend fun execute(params: P): R

    suspend operator fun invoke(params: P): Result<R> = try {
        Result.success(execute(params))
    } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
      catch (e: Exception) { Result.failure(e) }
}

// Usage: P=String (userId), R=UserProfile
class GetUserProfileUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val repo: UserRepository
) : BaseUseCase<String, UserProfile>() {
    override suspend fun execute(params: String) = repo.getUser(params)
}

Generic ApiResult wrapper

// data/remote/ApiResult.kt
sealed class ApiResult<out T> {
    data class  Success<T>(val data: T) : ApiResult<T>()
    data class  HttpError(val code: Int, val message: String) : ApiResult<Nothing>()
    data class  NetworkError(val cause: Throwable) : ApiResult<Nothing>()
    data object Loading : ApiResult<Nothing>()
}

// Map the data while preserving error cases
fun <T, R> ApiResult<T>.map(transform: (T) -> R): ApiResult<R> = when (this) {
    is ApiResult.Success      -> ApiResult.Success(transform(data))
    is ApiResult.HttpError    -> this
    is ApiResult.NetworkError -> this
    ApiResult.Loading          -> ApiResult.Loading
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs
ApproachProsConsWhen to pick
Invariant generic (default)Simple, safe, no annotationNo subtype flexibilityMutable containers, classes with both reads + writes
out T (covariant)Subtype flexibility for producersCannot accept T as inputRead-only wrappers: Flow, UiState, Result, ApiResult
in T (contravariant)Supertype flexibility for consumersCannot return TConsumers: Comparator, event sinks, callbacks
Use-site variance (Array<out T>)Project invariant types read-only at call siteVerbose; type projection loses write capabilityWhen working with Java invariant types like Array
Star projection *Works when type unknownLoses type info; can only read as Any?Logging, reflection, type-erasure scenarios

Interviewer Comparisons

Expect These
  • Java wildcards vs Kotlin variance — Java uses ? extends T (covariant) and ? super T (contravariant) at use-site. Kotlin uses out/in at declaration-site (cleaner) or use-site projection.
  • List vs MutableList variance — List<out T> is covariant (read-only). MutableList<T> is invariant (read+write).
  • Flow vs StateFlow vs SharedFlow — all are out T covariant; StateFlow is a subtype of Flow, which is why it can be assigned to a Flow reference.
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

out T with mutable state — type safety violation attempt

// ❌ Won't compile — correctly rejected by the compiler
class BadBox<out T>(var value: T) // ❌ var exposes T in in-position (setter)

// ✅ GOOD — val only for covariant types
class Box<out T>(val value: T)   // ✅ read-only property

Forgetting Nothing for no-data sealed subtypes

// ❌ BAD — UiState.Loading has type param UiState<Unit> — awkward
sealed class UiState<out T> {
    object Loading : UiState<Unit>()   // Unit — leaks into type signature
}
val s: UiState<List<User>> = UiState.Loading  // ❌ won't compile
// ✅ GOOD — Nothing is subtype of every type; works with covariant out T
data object Loading : UiState<Nothing>()
val s: UiState<List<User>> = UiState.Loading  // ✅

Type erasure at runtime

// ❌ BAD — generic type erased at runtime
fun <T> isListOf(list: List<*>): Boolean = list is List<T>  // ❌ unchecked cast warning

// ✅ GOOD — use reified with inline (covered in 1I)
inline fun <reified T> isListOf(list: List<*>): Boolean =
    list.all { it is T }

Production Best Practices

  1. Use out T for read-only wrappers: UiState<out T>, ApiResult<out T>, Resource<out T>.
  2. Use Nothing as type arg for no-data sealed subtypes — allows assignment to any covariant generic.
  3. Expose StateFlow as StateFlow (not Flow) in ViewModels — provides .value access; covariance means it's still assignable to Flow when needed.
  4. Don't over-annotate — most application-level classes are invariant and that's fine.
  5. Use where T : SomeInterface for multiple type bounds instead of complex inheritance.
🎤
7. Interview Answer Framework

30-Second Answer

"Generics let you write type-safe code that works across multiple types. Variance controls how generic types relate under subtyping. out T means covariant — T is only produced, never consumed, so Producer<Dog> is safely assignable to Producer<Animal>. in T means contravariant — T is only consumed, so Consumer<Animal> works as a Consumer<Dog>. This is why Flow<out T> allows StateFlow<T> to be used as a Flow<T>, and why I annotate UiState<out T> so UiState.Loading : UiState<Nothing> works for any state type."

2-Minute Structured Answer

"The core question variance answers is: if Dog is a subtype of Animal, is Box<Dog> a subtype of Box<Animal>? By default, no — because if it were, you could write a Cat into a Dog box.

out T (covariant) makes it safe by restricting T to output positions only — return types and val properties. You can only read T, never write it. So Producer<Dog> is safe as Producer<Animal> — you can only get animals out, and dogs are animals.

in T (contravariant) restricts T to input positions only. A Consumer<Animal> can handle dogs since dogs are animals — so Consumer<Animal> works as Consumer<Dog>.

In my Android code: I annotate all read-only result wrappers — UiState<out T>, ApiResult<out T> — as covariant. This lets me use Nothing as the type arg for no-data states like Loading, which then satisfies any UiState<SomeDataType> requirement. This is exactly how Kotlin's built-in Flow<out T> works — StateFlow is a subtype of Flow because of covariance."

Must-Mention Points

1
Generic types are invariant by default — MutableList<Dog> is NOT a MutableList<Animal>
2
out T = covariant = T only in output positions = producer; subtype relationship follows type param
3
in T = contravariant = T only in input positions = consumer; subtype relationship reverses
4
Flow<out T> — that's why StateFlow<T> is assignable to Flow<T>
5
Nothing is the bottom type — subtype of everything; enables UiState.Loading : UiState<Nothing> to satisfy any UiState<T> with covariance
6
Declaration-site variance (on the class) is cleaner than use-site projection (on each call site)

Do NOT Go Deeper Unless Asked

  • JVM type erasure and how generics are implemented at bytecode level
  • reified type parameters with inline functions — covered in 1I
  • Kotlin's @UnsafeVariance annotation

Likely Follow-up Questions

QuestionShort Answer
Why is MutableList invariant but List covariant?List is read-only — T only in output positions → safe to be covariant. MutableList has add(T) — T in input position → must be invariant to prevent type-unsafe writes.
What is Nothing in Kotlin?The bottom type — a subtype of every type. No instance can ever be created. Used as type arg for sealed subtypes that carry no data, and as return type of functions that never return (throw or infinite loop).
What is star projection?List<*> means "a list of some unknown type." Equivalent to List<out Any?> for reading. You can read elements as Any? but cannot add anything (type unknown).
How does Java handle variance vs Kotlin?Java uses use-site wildcards: List<? extends Animal> (covariant) and List<? super Dog> (contravariant) — specified at every call site. Kotlin uses declaration-site variance with out/in on the class itself — less repetitive and clearer.

Senior-Level Insight (Stand Out)

Say This
"The practical payoff of understanding variance in Android is the UiState<out T> + Nothing pattern. By making UiState covariant, a single data object Loading : UiState<Nothing> satisfies every screen's state type — UiState<List<Transaction>>, UiState<UserProfile>, whatever. Without out T, you'd need a Loading instance per generic type, or use UiState<*> and lose type safety. This is the same pattern Kotlin's stdlib uses for Result<out T>."
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

VARIANCE AT A GLANCE

Invariant (default):
  MutableList<Dog> ≠ MutableList<Animal>

out T (covariant = producer):
  List<Dog> IS-A List<Animal>
  Flow<Dog> IS-A Flow<Animal>
  T only in OUT positions (return/val)

in T (contravariant = consumer):
  Comparator<Animal> IS-A Comparator<Dog>
  T only in IN positions (params)

ANDROID EXAMPLES

Flow<out T>       → covariant
StateFlow<out T>  → covariant (subtype of Flow)
List<out T>       → covariant (read-only)
MutableList<T>    → invariant
Comparator<in T>  → contravariant
UiState<out T>    → covariant (design pattern)
BaseUseCase<in P, out R>

NOTHING + COVARIANCE

Nothing = bottom type = subtype of all
// With sealed class UiState<out T>:
data object Loading : UiState<Nothing>()
// Assignable to UiState<List<User>> ✅
// Because Nothing IS-A List<User>
// and UiState is covariant

TYPE BOUNDS

fun <T : Comparable<T>> max(a: T, b: T): T
// multiple bounds:
fun <T> f(x: T) where T : A, T : B

// Star projection:
fun print(list: List<*>)
// = List<out Any?> — read-only unknown

GOTCHAS

out T: var property ❌ (in-position)
out T: val property ✅
in T: return type ❌ (out-position)
in T: fun param ✅
Type erasure: List<Dog> == List<Cat> at runtime
Use reified inline for runtime type checks

JAVA COMPARISON

Java use-site:
  List<? extends Animal> = out Animal
  List<? super Dog>       = in Dog

Kotlin declaration-site (cleaner):
  class Box<out T>  // annotated once
  // no per-call-site repetition
❓
9. Interview Questions (Self-Check)
How to use
Answer first, then reveal.

Basic

B1 — What does it mean for a generic type to be invariant? Give an Android example.
Easy▼
Invariant means no subtype relationship exists between generic types even if their type arguments have a subtype relationship. MutableList<Dog> is NOT a subtype of MutableList<Animal>, even though Dog extends Animal. This prevents type-unsafe mutations: if it were allowed, you could add a Cat to a list that was expected to contain only Dogs. Android example: MutableStateFlow<UiState> — invariant because it supports both reads and writes.
B2 — What does out T mean? Give a real Kotlin/Android example.
Easy▼
out T declares covariance — T appears only in output positions (return types, val properties). This means if Dog is a subtype of Animal, then Producer<Dog> is a subtype of Producer<Animal>.

Real example: Flow<out T> in Kotlin coroutines. Because Flow is covariant, StateFlow<Dog> (which extends Flow<Dog>) can be assigned to a Flow<Animal> variable. Also: List<out T> is covariant because it's read-only — no add() method takes T as a parameter.
B3 — What is Nothing and why is it used with covariant sealed classes?
Easy▼
Nothing is Kotlin's bottom type — a subtype of every type. No instance of Nothing can be created. Because of covariance: if Nothing is a subtype of T, and UiState is covariant (out T), then UiState<Nothing> is a subtype of UiState<T> for ANY T. This means data object Loading : UiState<Nothing> is assignable to UiState<List<Transaction>>, UiState<UserProfile>, etc. — one Loading object works for all generic types.

Intermediate

I1 — Why is List covariant but MutableList invariant in Kotlin?
Medium▼
List<out T> is read-only — it has no add(T) or set(T) methods. T only appears in output positions (get, iterator, etc.). Because it can never be used to write a T, it's safe to treat a List<Dog> as a List<Animal> — you can only read animals from it, and dogs are animals.

MutableList<T> has add(T) where T is in an input position. If it were covariant, you could assign a MutableList<Dog> to MutableList<Animal> and call add(Cat()) — corrupting the dog list. Invariance prevents this.
I2 — (Coding) Why won't this compile? How do you fix it?
MediumCoding▼
class Box<out T>(var value: T)  // ❌
Problem: var value: T generates a setter that takes T as a parameter — an input position. out T restricts T to output positions only. The setter violates this, so the compiler rejects it.

Fix: Use val instead of var: 
class Box<out T>(val value: T)  // ✅ val = getter only = out position
I3 — What is declaration-site variance vs use-site variance? Which does Kotlin prefer?
Medium▼
Declaration-site variance: annotate the class/interface once — class Flow<out T>. Every usage site automatically gets the covariance. Kotlin-idiomatic.

Use-site variance (type projection): annotate at each call site — fun copy(src: Array<out T>). Used when the class itself can't be annotated (e.g., invariant Java classes like Array).

Kotlin prefers declaration-site — less repetition, clearer intent. Java only has use-site wildcards (? extends T, ? super T). Kotlin supports both but declaration-site is idiomatic for your own code.
I4 — What is contravariance? Give a real Android/Kotlin use case.
Medium▼
Contravariance (in T): T appears only in input positions. The subtype relationship is reversed — Consumer<Animal> is a subtype of Consumer<Dog> because a consumer that can handle animals can certainly handle dogs.

Real Kotlin example: Comparator<in T>. A Comparator<Animal> that compares by name can be used to sort a list of dogs — dogs are animals, so the comparator works. You can pass an animalComparator wherever a dogComparator is needed.

Android example: BaseUseCase<in P, out R> — the params type P is consumed (input), so contravariant; the result R is produced (output), so covariant.

Senior / Scenario

S1 — Design a generic Resource<T> sealed class for the data layer. Justify the variance annotation.
HardCoding▼
sealed class Resource<out T> {           // out T: only produced, never consumed
    data class  Success<T>(val data: T) : Resource<T>()
    data class  Error(val exception: Throwable) : Resource<Nothing>()
    data object Loading : Resource<Nothing>()
}

// Extension to transform the data
fun <T, R> Resource<T>.map(f: (T) -> R): Resource<R> = when (this) {
    is Resource.Success -> Resource.Success(f(data))
    is Resource.Error   -> this
    Resource.Loading    -> Resource.Loading
}
Justification: out T because Resource only wraps and exposes data — it never accepts T as input anywhere. This allows: (1) Resource.Loading and Resource.Error with Nothing to satisfy any Resource<T>; (2) a Resource<Dog> to be assigned to Resource<Animal> when the consuming code only reads.
S2 — (Scenario) A teammate asks: "Why can I assign a StateFlow<UiState> to a Flow<UiState> variable but not a MutableStateFlow to a MutableSharedFlow?" Explain.
HardScenario▼
StateFlow → Flow is valid because both are declared as interface Flow<out T> and interface StateFlow<out T> : Flow<T>. StateFlow IS-A Flow — it extends it. The covariance (out T) isn't even needed here; it's a direct subtype relationship via interface inheritance.

MutableStateFlow → MutableSharedFlow is invalid because MutableStateFlow and MutableSharedFlow are separate interfaces in different parts of the hierarchy. MutableStateFlow<T> extends both StateFlow<T> and MutableSharedFlow<T>, so a MutableStateFlow IS-A MutableSharedFlow — actually this assignment IS valid. If it fails in practice it may be a generics invariance issue with a specific type argument.

The key insight: variance enables subtype relationships based on type params. Direct interface inheritance enables them based on the class hierarchy. Both matter.
S3 — When would you use star projection * vs a bounded type parameter vs a concrete type?
Hard▼
Concrete type (List<String>): use when you know and care about the exact type at compile time. Most common case.

Bounded type parameter (<T : Serializable>): use when you don't know the exact type but need it to satisfy a constraint. The type is known within the function scope. Use this for generic utility functions.

Star projection (List<*>): use when you truly don't care about the type and only need to work with the container, not the elements — e.g., logging a list's size, checking if it's empty, or passing to a reflection API. Elements read as Any?. Cannot write. Use sparingly — it loses type information.
