● Android Interview Prep

1J — Equality, Interop & Errors

== vs ===, Kotlin–JVM interoperability, Kotlin compilation basics, exceptions, and the Result type — the final Kotlin unit before moving into Android fundamentals.

ID: 1J ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

What it covers

  • == vs ===: structural equality vs referential equality — critical for data classes, caches, state comparison
  • Kotlin–JVM interop: how Kotlin and Java code call each other, platform types, @JvmStatic, @JvmOverloads, @JvmField
  • Kotlin compilation: source → IR → JVM bytecode (or JS/Native); how the compiler outputs .class files; what kotlinc does differently from javac
  • Exceptions: Kotlin's unchecked exception model, try/catch/finally, runCatching, exception hierarchy
  • Result type: Result<T>, runCatching, fold, onSuccess/onFailure, when to use vs sealed class
Senior Mental Model
In Android, == vs === is critical for StateFlow: MutableStateFlow uses structural equality (==) to decide whether to emit a new value. If your state object doesn't override equals() correctly, state updates get silently dropped. This is the most common source of "my UI isn't updating" bugs.
⚙
2. How It Works

== vs ===

// == : structural equality — calls equals()
// === : referential equality — same object in memory

data class User(val id: String, val name: String)

val a = User("1", "Alice")
val b = User("1", "Alice")
val c = a

println(a == b)   // true  — same content (data class equals)
println(a === b)  // false — different objects in memory
println(a === c)  // true  — same reference

// For nullable types: a == null calls a?.equals(null) ?: (a === null)
val x: String? = null
println(x == null)   // true — safe null check
println(x === null)  // true — referential null check
StateFlow & Equality
MutableStateFlow.value = newValue compares newValue == currentValue. If equal, no emission. This is why data class with all val properties is critical for UI state — equals() auto-generated from constructor properties. Regular classes with no equals() override use reference equality — the state object is "new" even if content is identical, always emitting.

Kotlin–JVM Interoperability

// Platform types — Java's String (without annotation) becomes String! in Kotlin
// String! means "may or may not be null" — Kotlin trusts you
val result: String = javaObject.getName()  // could be null if Java doesn't annotate!

// Fix: annotate Java side with @Nullable / @NotNull
// Or handle defensively:
val safe = javaObject.getName() ?: "default"
// @JvmStatic — generate a true Java static method from companion object
class Analytics {
    companion object {
        @JvmStatic
        fun track(event: String) { }  // callable as Analytics.track() from Java
    }
}

// @JvmOverloads — generate overloaded Java methods for default args
@JvmOverloads
fun createRequest(url: String, timeout: Int = 30, retries: Int = 3) { }
// Java sees: createRequest(url), createRequest(url, timeout), createRequest(url, timeout, retries)

// @JvmField — expose Kotlin property as Java field (no getter/setter)
class Config {
    @JvmField val MAX_RETRY = 3   // Java: config.MAX_RETRY (no getMAX_RETRY())
}

// @Throws — declare checked exceptions for Java callers
@Throws(IOException::class)
fun readFile(path: String): String { ... }

Kotlin Compilation Basics

// Kotlin source (.kt) → Kotlin IR → JVM bytecode (.class)
// Android build: .kt → .class → D8/R8 → .dex → .apk/.aab

// Key compiler outputs for interop:
// - data class generates: equals, hashCode, toString, copy, componentN
// - companion object generates: inner static class + INSTANCE field
// - extension functions compile to: static methods (receiver as first param)
// - default params compile to: $default synthetic method + bitmask
// - inline functions: body copied at each call site

// KAPT (Kotlin Annotation Processing Tool) — runs before compilation
// KSP (Kotlin Symbol Processing) — faster, processes Kotlin symbols directly
// Hilt uses KSP; Room uses KSP (or KAPT)

Exceptions in Kotlin

// ALL Kotlin exceptions are unchecked (unlike Java checked exceptions)
// No 'throws' declaration required (unlike Java)

try {
    val result = riskyOperation()
} catch (e: SpecificException) {
    handleSpecific(e)
} catch (e: Exception) {
    handleGeneral(e)
} finally {
    cleanup()   // always runs
}

// try is an expression — returns the last value
val parsed = try { input.toInt() } catch (e: NumberFormatException) { 0 }

// throw is also an expression (type: Nothing)
val port = config.port ?: throw IllegalStateException("Port not configured")

Result<T>

// Result<T> = either Success(value: T) or Failure(exception: Throwable)
val result: Result<User> = runCatching { api.getUser(id) }

// Access:
result.getOrNull()                       // T? — null on failure
result.getOrDefault(User.empty())        // T — default on failure
result.getOrElse { e -> User.fromError(e) }
result.getOrThrow()                       // T — rethrows exception
result.isSuccess; result.isFailure

// Chain transformations:
result
    .map { user -> user.toDomain() }       // transform on success
    .mapCatching { user -> enrich(user) }  // transform, catches exceptions
    .onSuccess { user -> cacheUser(user) } // side effect on success
    .onFailure { e -> logError(e) }         // side effect on failure
    .fold(
        onSuccess = { user -> UiState.Success(user) },
        onFailure = { e    -> UiState.Error(e.message) }
    )

// runCatching — wraps a block in Result
val r: Result<Int> = runCatching { "42".toInt() }   // Success(42)
val r2: Result<Int> = runCatching { "abc".toInt() }  // Failure(NumberFormatException)

Key Terms

TermMeaning
==Structural equality — calls equals()
===Referential equality — same object in memory
Platform type T!Java type with unknown nullability — Kotlin trusts the developer
@JvmStaticGenerate true Java static method from companion object member
@JvmOverloadsGenerate Java-visible overloads for Kotlin default arguments
runCatchingExecute a block and wrap result/exception in Result<T>
KSPKotlin Symbol Processing — faster annotation processing, replaces KAPT
🎯
3. Why and When to Use It

== vs === — When it matters in Android

SituationUseWhy
Compare UI state objects== (structural)StateFlow uses == to detect changes
Check if two references point to the same singleton===Singletons (object, Hilt @Singleton) should be referentially equal
Null check in smart cast== null or === nullBoth work; == null is idiomatic Kotlin
Check enum values==Enums are singletons; structural and referential equality are the same

Result<T> vs Sealed Class — Decision

Use Result<T>Use Sealed Class
Repository / data layer wrapping exceptionsPresentation layer UiState (Loading, Success, Error)
Simple success/failure from a use caseMultiple distinct error types with different data
Wrapping existing exception-throwing codeOne-time UI events (navigation, snackbar)
When stdlib operators (map, fold, onSuccess) are sufficientWhen you need exhaustive when + compile-time safety for all states

When NOT to use Result<T>

Do NOT
  • Use Result as a return type in public API — use sealed class for explicit, exhaustive error handling
  • Wrap CancellationException in Result — always rethrow it
  • Use runCatching to swallow exceptions silently without logging
  • Use === for value comparison of data classes — use ==
🏭
4. Production Example
Scenario
Banking app — repository wraps API calls in Result, ViewModel converts to sealed UiState, Java interop layer uses @JvmStatic and @JvmOverloads.

Repository — Result wrapping

// data/repository/AccountRepositoryImpl.kt
internal class AccountRepositoryImpl @Inject constructor(
    private val api: AccountApi
) : AccountRepository {

    override suspend fun getBalance(accountId: String): Result<Balance> =
        runCatching {
            api.getBalance(accountId).toDomain()
        }.onFailure { e ->
            if (e is CancellationException) throw e  // never swallow cancellation
            Timber.e(e, "getBalance failed for $accountId")
        }
}

UseCase — Result propagation

// domain/usecase/GetAccountSummaryUseCase.kt
class GetAccountSummaryUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val accountRepo: AccountRepository,
    private val txRepo: TransactionRepository
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(accountId: String): Result<AccountSummary> =
        runCatching {
            val balance = accountRepo.getBalance(accountId).getOrThrow()
            val recentTx = txRepo.getRecent(accountId, limit = 5).getOrThrow()
            AccountSummary(balance, recentTx)
        }

ViewModel — Result → sealed UiState

// presentation/account/AccountViewModel.kt
@HiltViewModel
class AccountViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val getAccountSummary: GetAccountSummaryUseCase
) : ViewModel() {

    private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow<AccountUiState>(AccountUiState.Loading)
    val uiState = _uiState.asStateFlow()

    fun load(accountId: String) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _uiState.value = AccountUiState.Loading

            val newState = getAccountSummary(accountId)
                .fold(
                    onSuccess = { AccountUiState.Success(it) },
                    onFailure = { AccountUiState.Error(it.message ?: "Unknown error") }
                )

            // StateFlow uses == to detect change — data class AccountUiState needed
            _uiState.value = newState
        }
    }
}

sealed interface AccountUiState {
    data object Loading                                    : AccountUiState
    data class  Success(val summary: AccountSummary)        : AccountUiState
    data class  Error(val message: String)                  : AccountUiState
}

Java Interop — Analytics SDK wrapper

// data/analytics/AnalyticsManager.kt (consumed from Java legacy code)
class AnalyticsManager private constructor() {

    companion object {
        @JvmStatic
        val instance: AnalyticsManager by lazy { AnalyticsManager() }

        @JvmStatic
        @JvmOverloads
        fun track(
            event: String,
            properties: Map<String, Any> = emptyMap(),
            userId: String? = null
        ) { /* ... */ }
    }
}
// Java: AnalyticsManager.track("login") — works due to @JvmStatic + @JvmOverloads

Equality in StateFlow — == matters

// ❌ If UiState is a regular class (no data), StateFlow may not emit
class UiState(val count: Int)  // no equals() override
_state.value = UiState(5)     // always emits — new object ≠ old (reference)
_state.value = UiState(5)     // emits again even with same content! (5 == 5 but different obj)

// ✅ data class: equals() uses structural comparison
data class UiState(val count: Int)
_state.value = UiState(5)     // emits
_state.value = UiState(5)     // NOT emitted — same content, == returns true
_state.value = UiState(6)     // emits — content changed
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs
ApproachProsConsWhen to pick
Result<T>Stdlib, no extra type, good operators (map, fold, onSuccess)Only Success/Failure — no Loading, no typed error subtypesData/domain layer simple success/failure
Sealed class (UiState)Exhaustive when, typed subtypes, Loading state, custom data per errorMore boilerplate; not interoperable with coroutine exceptions directlyUI layer state — always
Try/catchDirect, familiar, fine-grained controlImperative; easy to forget to handle; no functional chainingLow-level code; specific exception type handling
runCatchingWraps any block safely; functional operatorsSwallows CancellationException if you're not carefulWrapping existing exception-throwing APIs
Arrow's Either/ValidatedTyped errors, functional programming styleExternal dependency; learning curveAdvanced FP style; not typical Android production

Equality: == vs ===

Type== behaviour=== behaviour
data classStructural (auto-generated)Referential
Regular class (no override)Referential (inherited from Any)Referential
StringStructural (value comparison)Referential (may differ for string pool)
Primitive types (Int, etc.)Value comparisonValue comparison (boxed: referential on JVM)
enumReferential (singletons) = structuralSame as ==
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

runCatching swallows CancellationException

// ❌ BAD — CancellationException caught and wrapped, coroutine not cancelled
val result = runCatching { api.call() }
// If coroutine is cancelled during api.call(), CancellationException is swallowed!
// ✅ GOOD — always rethrow CancellationException
val result = runCatching { api.call() }
    .onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }

// Or use a safeRunCatching wrapper:
suspend inline fun <T> safeRunCatching(block: suspend () -> T): Result<T> = try {
    Result.success(block())
} catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
  catch (e: Exception) { Result.failure(e) }

StateFlow with regular class — no emission

// ❌ BAD — regular class; StateFlow.value = x checks x == current
// Regular class inherits equals() from Any → reference comparison
class ProfileState(val name: String)
_state.value = ProfileState("Alice")
_state.value = ProfileState("Alice")  // emits again! different object references
// ✅ GOOD — data class; structural equality prevents duplicate emissions
data class ProfileState(val name: String)
_state.value = ProfileState("Alice")
_state.value = ProfileState("Alice")  // NOT emitted — == returns true

Platform types — silent NPE from Java

// ❌ BAD — Java returns String! (platform type); assigned as non-null
val name: String = javaApi.getName()  // crashes if getName() returns null
// ✅ GOOD — treat Java returns defensively
val name: String = javaApi.getName() ?: "Unknown"
// Or: annotate the Java side with @NotNull / @Nullable

Production Best Practices

  1. Use data class for all StateFlow state types — structural equality ensures correct emission/de-dup.
  2. Always rethrow CancellationException — wrap all runCatching with a re-throw check.
  3. Use Result<T> in data/domain layer, sealed UiState in presentation layer — they serve different purposes.
  4. Add @Throws to Kotlin functions called from Java that may throw checked exceptions.
  5. Add @JvmStatic to companion object methods used from Java — avoids MyClass.Companion.method() verbosity.
  6. Prefer KSP over KAPT for annotation processors in new code — significantly faster build times.
  7. Use try as an expression for simple parse operations: val n = try { s.toInt() } catch { 0 }.
🎤
7. Interview Answer Framework

30-Second Answer

"== is structural equality — calls equals(). === is referential equality — same object in memory. This matters critically for StateFlow: it uses == to decide whether to emit. A regular class with no equals() will always emit; a data class correctly de-duplicates identical states. For error handling, Result<T> with runCatching is good for data/domain layer wrapping; sealed UiState is right for the presentation layer. Java interop uses @JvmStatic, @JvmOverloads, and @JvmField to make Kotlin code natural to call from Java. All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked — no forced try/catch."

2-Minute Structured Answer

"Three topics. Equality: == calls equals() — structural. === is the same-object check. The most practically important implication in Android is StateFlow: it internally uses == to compare the new and current value. If they're equal, no emission happens. With a data class, this correctly suppresses duplicate state pushes. With a regular class that hasn't overridden equals(), you get reference comparison — every new object emits, even if content is identical. That can cause unnecessary recomposition or repeated side effects.

Errors and Result: Kotlin has no checked exceptions — unlike Java, you're never forced to declare or catch. For wrapping exception-throwing code I use runCatching { } which produces a Result<T>. I chain map, onSuccess, onFailure, and fold on it. The one trap: runCatching catches ALL exceptions including CancellationException, which breaks coroutine cancellation. I always add a rethrow for CancellationException inside onFailure, or use a custom safeRunCatching.

Java interop: Kotlin companion object members aren't static on the JVM — they need @JvmStatic for Java to call without .Companion. Default arguments don't generate Java overloads — use @JvmOverloads. Platform types from Java (T!) have unknown nullability — treat them defensively with ?:."

Must-Mention Points

1
== = structural (calls equals()); === = referential (same object)
2
StateFlow uses == for emission — data class required for correct de-duplication of state
3
All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked — no forced declarations or catches unlike Java
4
runCatching catches CancellationException — always rethrow it to preserve coroutine cancellation
5
Result<T> = data/domain layer; sealed UiState = presentation layer — different responsibilities
6
Platform types (T!) from Java have unknown nullability — treat defensively with ?:
7
@JvmStatic, @JvmOverloads, @JvmField — Kotlin annotations for clean Java interop

  • JVM string interning and how it affects === for String literals
  • Kotlin IR compiler pipeline details
  • Kotlin/Native and Kotlin/JS compilation targets

Likely Follow-up Questions

QuestionShort Answer
Does Kotlin have checked exceptions?No. All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked. You're never forced to declare or catch them. Use @Throws to expose checked exception contracts to Java callers.
What is a platform type?A type from Java that has no nullability annotation — Kotlin expresses it as T!. Kotlin trusts you — you can treat it as non-null, but if Java returns null you get a NPE. Annotate the Java side with @Nullable/@NotNull to fix.
Difference between KAPT and KSP?KAPT (Kotlin Annotation Processing Tool) converts Kotlin to Java stubs first, then runs Java annotation processors — slow. KSP (Kotlin Symbol Processing) reads Kotlin symbols directly — typically 2x faster. KSP is the modern standard; Hilt and Room support it.
What does Result.fold do?Transforms a Result<T> into a single value by providing two lambdas: onSuccess receives the value, onFailure receives the exception. Always returns a value — no exceptions thrown.

Senior-Level Insight (Stand Out)

Say This
"The == vs === distinction has a concrete production implication that I always explain in code reviews: StateFlow.value setter calls value.equals(newValue). If the state is a regular class, the default equals() is reference-based — so _state.value = SomeState() always emits, even if the content is identical. This causes unnecessary recomposition and potential infinite loops if the state emission triggers the same state assignment again. Making state a data class with immutable val fields is the correct fix — structural equality only emits when something actually changed."

9. Interview Questions (Self-Check)
How to use
Answer first, then reveal.

Basic

B1 — What is the difference between == and === in Kotlin?
Easy▼
== is structural equality — it calls equals(). === is referential equality — it checks whether two variables point to the exact same object in memory. For a data class, == compares field values (auto-generated equals()). For a regular class with no equals() override, == behaves the same as === (reference comparison, inherited from Any).
B2 — Does Kotlin have checked exceptions? How do you expose checked exceptions to Java callers?
Easy▼
No — all Kotlin exceptions are unchecked. You are never forced to declare which exceptions a function throws, nor are callers forced to catch them. This is a deliberate design decision that avoids Java's checked exception verbosity.

To expose a checked exception contract to Java callers, annotate the Kotlin function with @Throws(IOException::class). This tells the Java compiler to treat it as a checked exception, enabling Java's try/catch requirement.
B3 — What is runCatching and what does it return?
Easy▼
runCatching { block } executes a block and wraps the result in a Result<T>. If the block succeeds, it returns Result.success(value). If it throws any exception, it returns Result.failure(exception). You can then chain map, onSuccess, onFailure, fold, and getOrNull on the result.

Intermediate

I1 — Why is StateFlow UI state broken if you use a regular class instead of a data class?
Medium▼
MutableStateFlow.value = newValue checks if newValue == currentValue before emitting. If they're equal, no emission occurs — this is the de-duplication mechanism.

A regular class inherits equals() from Any, which compares by reference. So every new instance is "different" even if the content is identical — the state always emits. This can cause unnecessary recompositions.

Conversely, if the same instance is mutated in-place (mutable properties), the reference stays the same — == returns true — and no emission occurs even though the content changed. Either way breaks the reactive contract. Fix: use data class with all val properties.
I2 — What is a platform type in Kotlin? How do you handle it safely?
Medium▼
A platform type (expressed as T! in error messages) is a type from Java code that has no nullability annotation. Kotlin cannot determine if it's nullable or non-null, so it defers to the developer. You can assign it to either T or T? — but if you assign to T and Java returns null, you get a NPE.

Safe handling: (1) Annotate the Java side with @Nullable/@NotNull — Kotlin then knows the contract. (2) Defensively treat all Java returns as nullable: javaApi.getName() ?: "default". (3) In modern code, use Kotlin APIs that are already annotated.
I3 — (Coding) What's the critical bug in this code? Fix it.
MediumCoding▼
// ❌ BUG
suspend fun fetchUser(id: String): Result<User> =
    runCatching { api.getUser(id) }
Bug: runCatching catches ALL exceptions, including CancellationException. When the coroutine is cancelled (e.g., user navigates away), the cancellation exception is caught and wrapped in a Result.failure. The coroutine thinks it completed normally — it doesn't propagate the cancellation. The scope doesn't cancel properly, causing leaked coroutines.

// ✅ Fixed
suspend fun fetchUser(id: String): Result<User> =
    runCatching { api.getUser(id) }
        .onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }
I4 — What is the difference between KAPT and KSP? Which should you use in new projects?
Medium▼
KAPT (Kotlin Annotation Processing Tool): converts Kotlin source to Java stubs, then runs Java annotation processors. Works with all Java annotation processors but adds a full compilation step — significantly slower, especially on incremental builds.

KSP (Kotlin Symbol Processing): processes Kotlin symbols directly without Java stub generation — typically 2x faster than KAPT. Has a Kotlin-first API. Supported by major Android libraries: Hilt (1.0.0+), Room (2.4.0+), Moshi, Glide.

Use KSP in new projects wherever the library supports it. Only fall back to KAPT for processors that haven't migrated to KSP yet.

Senior / Scenario

S1 — (Scenario) A developer reports "my UI sometimes doesn't update when the state changes." You look at the ViewModel and see _state.value = ProfileState(name = newName) where ProfileState is a regular class. Diagnose and fix.
HardScenario▼
Diagnosis: MutableStateFlow.value = x uses == (structural equality) to decide whether to emit. ProfileState is a regular class — it inherits equals() from Any, which compares by reference. So every ProfileState(name = newName) creates a new object, and ===-based comparison makes it always emit (new reference ≠ old reference) — that would actually cause over-emission.

But the "UI doesn't update" scenario happens if the developer is mutating the existing object: profileState.name = newName (if name is a var). The reference hasn't changed, so == (reference for non-data class) returns true — no emission.

Fix: 1. Make ProfileState a data class with val properties — now == compares field values. 2. Never mutate state in-place; always create a new object: _state.value = _state.value.copy(name = newName) 
data class ProfileState(val name: String)
_state.value = _state.value.copy(name = newName)  // emits if name changed
S2 — When would you choose Result<T> over a sealed class for error handling? Give a specific architecture example.
HardScenario▼
Use Result<T> at the repository and use-case layer — it's the boundary between exception-throwing code (network, database) and your clean domain logic. The repository wraps a Retrofit call with runCatching; the use case propagates or maps the result. No custom state is needed here — it's just success/failure.

Use sealed class at the presentation layer — because UI has states beyond just success/failure: Loading, Empty, Refreshing, etc. Each state may carry different data, and the when expression must be exhaustive.

The pattern in production: 
// Data layer → Result
suspend fun getUser(): Result<User> = runCatching { api.getUser() }

// Presentation layer → sealed UiState
getUser().fold(
    onSuccess = { UiState.Success(it) },
    onFailure = { UiState.Error(it.message) }
)
They complement each other — Result handles the exception boundary; sealed UiState handles the display contract.
S3 — You have a Kotlin library consumed by a Java project. List all the annotations you'd apply and why.
HardScenario▼
@JvmStatic — on companion object members: generates a true Java static method so Java can call MyClass.method() instead of MyClass.Companion.method().

@JvmOverloads — on functions with default parameters: generates Java-visible overloaded methods so Java callers can omit optional parameters.

@JvmField — on val/var properties you want exposed as Java fields: removes the getter/setter and exposes the field directly. Useful for constants.

@Throws(ExceptionType::class) — on suspend functions or functions that throw: tells Java's compiler to treat them as checked exceptions.

@JvmName — when Kotlin generates a method name that clashes with another JVM method name (e.g., extension functions on the same receiver type).

@Nullable / @NotNull — on all public function parameters and return types: prevents Java from treating them as platform types, giving Java callers proper nullability warnings.

Also: avoid using Kotlin-specific features in the public API surface (default arguments without @JvmOverloads, companion objects without @JvmStatic, extension functions in interfaces).

2A — Android Components Overview

Tier 2 Activity · Fragment · Service · BroadcastReceiver · ContentProvider · Application · Context

1 · Overview

Android apps are not traditional programs with a single main() entry point. Instead, the OS selects and instantiates discrete components on demand. This allows the system to optimise memory, lifecycle, and inter-app collaboration without the app running as a monolithic process.

Activity

A single, focused screen with a UI. The entry point for user interaction. Managed by the Activity back stack.

Fragment

A reusable UI/logic portion hosted inside an Activity. Has its own lifecycle, view lifecycle, and back stack entry.

Service

Long-running background operation, no UI. Three types: Started, Bound, Foreground.

BroadcastReceiver

Listens for system-wide or app-scoped intents (events). Very short-lived — no UI, minimal work.

ContentProvider

Structured data sharing across apps/processes via a URI-based CRUD API backed by SQLite / file / network.

Application

Singleton that exists for the process lifetime. Global init (DI graph, logging). Extended via Application subclass.

Context

Context is the bridge to the Android system: access resources, start components, get system services. Every component is a Context (or wraps one). Two main flavours:

  • Application Context — process lifetime, safe for singletons, DI graphs, database instances.
  • Activity/Fragment Context — tied to UI lifecycle; use only for UI operations (inflate views, show dialogs).

2 · How It Works

AndroidManifest.xml — The Registry

Every component must be declared (or exported) in AndroidManifest.xml. The PackageManagerService reads this at install time to build a component registry.

<!-- Activity: visible screen -->
<activity android:name=".MainActivity"
           android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
    </intent-filter>
</activity>

<!-- Service: background work -->
<service android:name=".sync.SyncService"
          android:exported="false" />

<!-- BroadcastReceiver: event listener -->
<receiver android:name=".receiver.BootReceiver"
            android:exported="false">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED" />
    </intent-filter>
</receiver>

<!-- ContentProvider: structured data sharing -->
<provider android:name=".provider.ContactsProvider"
            android:authorities="com.example.app.contacts"
            android:exported="false" />

Component Lifecycle (high-level)

Activity: onCreate → onStart → onResume ←→ onPause → onStop → onDestroy Fragment: onAttach → onCreate → onCreateView → onViewCreated → onStart → onResume ↕ symmetric teardown: onPause → onStop → onDestroyView → onDestroy → onDetach Service: onCreate → onStartCommand / onBind → ... → onDestroy BroadcastReceiver: onReceive() — one method, exits immediately ContentProvider: onCreate() → query / insert / update / delete / getType

Activity Back Stack

Task (back stack) ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ [Top] ProfileActivity │ ← currently visible │ OrderActivity │ │ HomeActivity │ ← bottom of stack └─────────────────────────────┘ BACK press pops top activity

Context Hierarchy

Context (abstract) ├── ContextWrapper │ ├── Application ← process lifetime │ ├── Activity ← UI lifetime │ └── Service ← service lifetime └── ContextImpl (system implementation)

Key Terms

TermMeaning
ContextInterface to global app info; access resources, start components, get services
IntentMessaging object to start components or broadcast events
AndroidManifest.xmlApp declaration: components, permissions, features
ApplicationProcess-level singleton; created first, destroyed last
TaskA stack of Activities representing a user flow
Component lifecycleCallbacks the OS calls to manage component state transitions

3 · Why and When to Use Each

ComponentUse when…Do NOT use when…
Activity You need a distinct full-screen user interaction point; app entry points; launcher screens You have a single-activity app (prefer Fragments/Compose for sub-screens)
Fragment Reusable UI segments; tablet dual-pane; modal bottom sheets; navigation destinations Logic-only modules with no UI (use ViewModel / UseCase instead)
Service (started) Long-running work decoupled from UI (legacy); background music (foreground service) One-off background tasks — use WorkManager / Coroutine instead
Service (bound) IPC to another app or process; MediaBrowser; Bluetooth In-process communication — use ViewModel/Repository instead
BroadcastReceiver React to system events (network change, boot, battery); app-global events between components Ongoing processing — receivers must finish in <10 s; no long work here
ContentProvider Expose structured data to other apps (Contacts, Media); share data with widgets Internal-only data access — use Room/DataStore directly
Application Process-level singletons: DI init (Hilt), analytics setup, crash reporting init Storing UI state or large objects — will cause memory leaks
Application Context Singletons, Room database, Retrofit, DataStore, WorkManager Inflating views, showing dialogs — causes WindowManager leaks

4 · Production Example (Banking App)

Multi-module banking app: :app → single Activity, Navigation Compose, Hilt, Room, WorkManager. Each component plays its proper role.

Application — DI + Crash Init

@HiltAndroidApp
class BankingApp : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        // Hilt builds the DI graph here — process-scoped singletons created
        // Crashlytics, Timber, StrictMode init in debug builds
        if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) StrictMode.enableDefaults()
    }
}

Single Activity — Navigation Host

@AndroidEntryPoint
class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContent {
            BankingTheme {
                // NavHost owns back stack; all screens are Composables
                AppNavHost()
            }
        }
    }
}

BroadcastReceiver — Network Change

// Registered dynamically (API 26+: static receivers restricted for most actions)
class NetworkReceiver : BroadcastReceiver() {
    override fun onReceive(context: Context, intent: Intent) {
        // Must exit quickly — no coroutines, no blocking IO here
        // Use goAsync() + coroutine only if you MUST; prefer WorkManager
        val isConnected = NetworkUtils.isOnline(context)
        SyncManager.onNetworkChanged(isConnected)   // triggers WorkManager enqueue
    }
}

// In Activity.onStart / ViewModel init:
private val networkReceiver = NetworkReceiver()
registerReceiver(networkReceiver, IntentFilter(ConnectivityManager.CONNECTIVITY_ACTION))

Foreground Service — Transaction Sync

class SyncForegroundService : LifecycleService() {

    @Inject lateinit var syncUseCase: SyncTransactionsUseCase

    override fun onStartCommand(intent: Intent?, flags: Int, startId: Int): Int {
        startForeground(NOTIF_ID, buildNotification())   // must call within 5 s
        lifecycleScope.launch {
            syncUseCase.invoke()
            stopSelf()                                    // stop when done
        }
        return START_NOT_STICKY
    }
}

Context — Safe Usage

// ✅ ApplicationContext for long-lived singletons
@Singleton
class AppDatabase @Inject constructor(
    @ApplicationContext context: Context   // Hilt qualifier — no leaks
) {
    val db = Room.databaseBuilder(context, BankDatabase::class.java, "bank.db").build()
}

// ❌ Never store Activity context in a singleton — causes memory leak
object BadSingleton {
    var ctx: Context? = null  // LEAK if ctx is an Activity
}

5 · Alternatives and Trade-offs

ApproachProsConsWhen to pick
Multiple Activities Clean separation, independent back stacks, deep-link targets Cross-activity communication is hard; more boilerplate; harder to share ViewModels Legacy codebases; distinct user flows that rarely share state
Single Activity + Fragments Shared ViewModel, Navigation Component, easy transitions Fragment lifecycle complexity, FragmentManager bugs in older APIs Standard modern Android pre-Compose
Single Activity + Compose No Fragment lifecycle; composable back stack; simplest model Requires migration effort; less mature tooling for very large apps New projects / greenfield
Service for background Always-running, flexible IPC Background execution restrictions (API 26+); battery drain; complex lifecycle Foreground service (audio, location); IPC to other processes
WorkManager instead of Service Constraint-aware, persisted, battery-efficient, simpler API Not guaranteed immediate execution; not for real-time tasks Deferrable background work (sync, upload, cleanup)
DataStore instead of ContentProvider Type-safe, coroutine-native, simpler API No cross-app sharing App-internal preferences/proto data

6 · Pitfalls and Best Practices

Context Leaks

❌ Bad

// Stores Activity context in a long-lived object
class ImageLoader(val ctx: Context)

// Passed from Fragment — leaks Fragment/Activity
ImageLoader(requireContext())

✅ Good

// Use applicationContext for singletons
class ImageLoader(val ctx: Context)

ImageLoader(requireContext().applicationContext)

BroadcastReceiver — Long Work

❌ Bad

override fun onReceive(ctx: Context, intent: Intent) {
    // Blocking network call — ANR risk
    apiClient.syncNow()
}

✅ Good

override fun onReceive(ctx: Context, intent: Intent) {
    // Enqueue WorkManager — fast, non-blocking
    WorkManager.getInstance(ctx).enqueue(syncRequest)
}

Other Critical Pitfalls

  • Static Activity reference: companion object { var activity: Activity? } — will leak. Never do this.
  • Starting Activity from Application context: requires FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK — avoid unless necessary (notifications, deep links from services).
  • Fragment over-creation: Not using findFragmentByTag before add leads to duplicate fragments after rotation.
  • Service not stopped: Started services that never call stopSelf() or stopService() drain battery.
  • Exported components without permission: android:exported="true" without android:permission exposes your components to any app (security hole).
  • Application class bloat: Heavy sync init in Application.onCreate() slows cold start. Use App Startup library or lazy init.
  • ContentProvider in multi-process: Accessing your own ContentProvider from multiple processes leads to unexpected instantiation. Prefer single-process with explicit initialization order.
API 26+ Background Restrictions: Apps in background cannot start Services. Use startForegroundService() + call startForeground() within 5 seconds, or use WorkManager for deferrable tasks.

7 · Interview Answer Framework

30-Second Answer

"Android apps are component-based rather than having a single entry point. The four main components — Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver, and ContentProvider — each have a distinct lifecycle and purpose. On top of that, Fragment gives you reusable UI inside an Activity, Application provides process-level initialisation, and Context is the bridge to the Android system. In modern apps I typically use a single Activity with Compose or Fragments for navigation, Services only when truly needed for IPC or foreground work, and WorkManager instead of started Services for background tasks."

2-Minute Structured Answer

What they are: Android's app model is component-based. PackageManagerService reads AndroidManifest.xml at install time, and ActivityManagerService instantiates components on demand. The four main component types are Activity (UI screen), Service (background work), BroadcastReceiver (system/app events), and ContentProvider (structured data sharing).

Key distinctions: Activities are UI-centric and managed in a task back stack. Fragments are hosted by Activities, with their own view lifecycle. Services run without UI; post-API-26, background services are heavily restricted, so foreground services + WorkManager are the production choices. BroadcastReceivers must finish fast — any heavy work goes to WorkManager. ContentProviders are for cross-app data sharing; for internal data I use Room + DataStore directly.

Context: Application context is safe for singletons; Activity context is needed only for UI operations — using it in long-lived objects causes memory leaks. With Hilt, I use @ApplicationContext qualifier to inject the right context automatically.

Modern pattern: Single Activity + Navigation Compose/Fragments; Hilt for DI bootstrapped in Application; WorkManager for background; foreground service only for ongoing user-aware operations like audio playback or live location.

Must-Mention Points

  1. Four app components declared in AndroidManifest; AMS instantiates them on demand.
  2. Activity = UI + back stack; Fragment = reusable UI inside Activity with own view lifecycle.
  3. Service types: Started (no UI, fire-and-forget), Bound (IPC), Foreground (ongoing, visible notification).
  4. BroadcastReceiver is ephemeral — onReceive() must finish fast; post-API-26 most static receivers are restricted.
  5. ContentProvider is for cross-app data sharing; internal apps should use Room / DataStore directly.
  6. Application context vs Activity context: lifespan and leak implications.
  7. Modern recommendation: Single Activity + Compose + WorkManager + Foreground Service only when necessary.
  8. Background execution restrictions since API 26 changed the Service usage pattern fundamentally.

Do Not Go Deeper Unless Asked

  • AIDL / Binder internals for IPC (wait for 3C)
  • ContentProvider cursor implementations
  • IntentService (deprecated) — just note it's replaced by WorkManager
  • Specific Fragment backstack transactions

Likely Follow-up Questions

QuestionShort Answer
What's the difference between Application context and Activity context?Lifespan: Application lives for the process; Activity lives until destroyed. Use Activity context only for UI operations to avoid leaks.
When would you use a bound Service vs WorkManager?Bound Service for IPC / ongoing connection with another process (e.g., MediaBrowser, Bluetooth). WorkManager for deferrable, constraint-aware, persisted background tasks.
Why are static BroadcastReceivers restricted in API 26+?Background execution restrictions. Apps were abusing implicit broadcasts to wake up in background and drain battery. Google restricted most implicit broadcasts to dynamic registration only.
Why single-activity architecture?Simplifies back stack, enables shared ViewModels, works natively with Navigation Component / Compose NavHost, reduces Activity transition complexity.

Senior-Level Insight

"The shift to single-activity architecture isn't just a style preference — it aligns with the process model. Sharing a ViewModel across screens requires a common scope (the Activity's ViewModelStore). Multiple Activities create multiple ViewModelStores, making shared state hard. Compose NavHost takes this further: there's no Fragment back stack at all — the Composable function call stack IS the UI tree, which means no lifecycle edge cases from Fragment transactions. This directly improves testability because screens are just Composable functions with no component lifecycle boilerplate."

Context Golden Rules

  • Singleton / long-lived object → applicationContext (never Activity context)
  • Inflate view / show dialog → Activity/Fragment context
  • Hilt DI → use @ApplicationContext qualifier for non-UI injection
  • Never store Activity in static / companion object field

Background Restrictions (API 26+)

  • Cannot call startService() from background → use startForegroundService() + startForeground() within 5 s
  • Most implicit broadcasts cannot have static receivers → register dynamically
  • Deferrable work → WorkManager

Component Security

  • Set android:exported="false" unless cross-app access is needed
  • Add android:permission for exported components that should be restricted
  • Required: android:exported must be explicit on API 31+ for components with intent-filters

9 · Interview Questions (Self-Check)

Try to answer before expanding each card.

Basic What are the four main Android app components?
Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver, ContentProvider. All must be declared in AndroidManifest.xml. Each has a distinct lifecycle and purpose managed by the Android system (ActivityManagerService).
Basic What is the difference between Application context and Activity context?
Application context lives for the process lifetime; Activity context lives until the Activity is destroyed. Use Application context for long-lived singletons (databases, Retrofit, DI). Use Activity context only for UI operations (inflate views, show dialogs, start activities). Storing Activity context in a singleton causes memory leaks because the Activity cannot be GC'd.
Basic What restrictions apply to BroadcastReceivers?
onReceive() must complete quickly (ideally <10 s). No long-running or async work. Post-API 26, most implicit broadcasts cannot use statically declared receivers in the manifest — use dynamic registration. If work is needed, enqueue a WorkManager task inside onReceive().
Intermediate Explain the difference between a started Service, bound Service, and foreground Service.
Started: Launched via startService(); runs until stopSelf() is called; no IPC interface. Mostly obsolete for pure background work.
Bound: Launched via bindService(); client-server relationship; provides IBinder for IPC; stops when all clients unbind.
Foreground: Started via startForegroundService(); must show a persistent notification; survives background restrictions; used for ongoing user-aware operations (music, navigation, workout tracking).
Intermediate Why is single-activity architecture preferred in modern Android?
Single Activity means one ViewModelStore, enabling easy state sharing across screens. Navigation Component / Compose NavHost manage the back stack without inter-Activity complexity. Transitions are smoother (within one window). Fragment / Composable lifecycles are simpler than Activity-to-Activity transitions. Deep links are easier to handle in one NavGraph. No need to pass data via Intent extras across Activity boundaries.
Intermediate When should you use ContentProvider for internal data access?
You generally should NOT use ContentProvider for internal-only access. ContentProvider adds overhead (URI resolver, cursor conversion) and was designed for cross-app data sharing. For internal storage use Room (SQL), DataStore (preferences/proto), or files directly. ContentProvider is appropriate when: sharing data with other apps, exposing data to Search/Android Auto/widgets, or implementing SyncAdapter integration.
Intermediate What is the correct way to start a Service on API 26+ from the background?
You cannot call startService() from a background app — it throws IllegalStateException. Use startForegroundService() instead, then call startForeground(notifId, notification) within 5 seconds or the system throws ForegroundServiceDidNotStartInTimeException. For deferrable work, use WorkManager instead of a service entirely.
Senior/Scenario You have a foreground service that syncs banking transactions. It must stop if the user logs out, even if it's mid-sync. How do you architect this?
Use LifecycleService so the service has a lifecycleScope. Expose a cancellation signal — e.g., a SharedFlow in a singleton SyncCoordinator. The sync coroutine collects this flow: if a logout event arrives, cancel the job and call stopSelf(). The ViewModel (or logout UseCase) emits to the SharedFlow. This decouples the logout trigger from the service without needing to call stopService() directly, and the coroutine cooperatively cancels. Also enqueue a WorkManager task post-logout to do any cleanup that must survive process death.
Senior/Scenario [Coding] Register and unregister a BroadcastReceiver safely in a Fragment. Write the code. 
class DashboardFragment : Fragment() {
    private val networkReceiver = object : BroadcastReceiver() {
        override fun onReceive(ctx: Context, intent: Intent) {
            viewModel.onNetworkChanged(NetworkUtils.isOnline(ctx))
        }
    }

    override fun onStart() {
        super.onStart()
        // Register when Fragment is visible
        requireContext().registerReceiver(
            networkReceiver,
            IntentFilter(ConnectivityManager.CONNECTIVITY_ACTION)
        )
    }

    override fun onStop() {
        super.onStop()
        // Unregister symmetric to onStart — prevents leaks
        requireContext().unregisterReceiver(networkReceiver)
    }
}
Key: register/unregister in symmetric lifecycle callbacks (onStart/onStop). Never in onCreate/onDestroy for a dynamic receiver — Fragment view may exist longer than needed.
Senior/Scenario [Debug] Your app throws "Context is not an Activity" when inflating a view inside a ViewModel. What happened and how do you fix it?
The ViewModel was injected with Application context (correct for non-UI work), but the code tried to use it to inflate a View — which requires an Activity context (a ContextThemeWrapper with a window). Fix: Never inflate views in ViewModel. Move inflation to Fragment/Activity. If creating a custom View programmatically for testing, pass Activity context explicitly. Alternatively, if absolutely necessary, wrap applicationContext in a ContextThemeWrapper with the app theme, but this is a code-smell — views belong in the UI layer.

Answer Key Summary

Expand each card above to see full model answers. Key themes to self-assess:

  • Can you name all 4 components + Application + Context without hesitation?
  • Can you explain the API 26 background restrictions and their implications?
  • Can you justify single-activity architecture in one sentence?
  • Can you write register/unregister receiver code correctly in a Fragment?
  • Do you know when NOT to use ContentProvider, Service, and static receivers?

2B — Activity Lifecycle & State

Tier 2 onCreate · onStart · onResume · onPause · onStop · onDestroy · config changes · process death · onSaveInstanceState

1 · Overview

An Activity's lifecycle is the sequence of callbacks the Android OS calls as it creates, shows, hides, and destroys the Activity. Understanding it is mandatory for correctness: doing the wrong work in the wrong callback causes ANRs, memory leaks, UI glitches, and data loss.

The lifecycle exists because Android is a resource-constrained, multi-app environment. The OS can pause, stop, or kill your Activity at any time to reclaim memory. Your job is to react correctly to each transition so the app remains consistent regardless of interruptions.

Key problems the lifecycle solves:
  • Releasing resources (camera, GPS, network) when not visible
  • Saving and restoring UI state across configuration changes and process death
  • Knowing when to start / stop work (animation, polling, observers)

2 · How It Works

Callback Flow

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Activity Created │ └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘ ▼ onCreate() ← setContentView, init ViewModel, observe ▼ onStart() ← Activity becomes visible (not interactive) ▼ onResume() ← Activity in foreground, user can interact │ ┌────────────────────┴────────────────────┐ │ Another Activity / dialog in front │ ▼ │ onPause() ← still partially visible │ │ │ ▼ (fully hidden) │ onStop() ← not visible │ │ │ ├──── onRestart() ──────────────────────► onStart() │ ▼ onDestroy() ← finishing OR config change Config change (rotation): onPause → onStop → onDestroy → onCreate → onStart → onResume Process death: OS silently kills; no callbacks after onStop

Callback Responsibilities

CallbackWhat to do hereWhat NOT to do
onCreate()setContentView / setContent, init ViewModel, observe LiveData/Flow, restore state from savedInstanceStateLong blocking work, animations
onStart()Register lightweight observers, start animations that should show when visibleAcquire exclusive resources (camera)
onResume()Acquire exclusive resources (camera, sensor), resume paused mediaHeavy init (already done in onCreate)
onPause()Release exclusive resources, pause media, commit critical unsaved dataHeavy operations — this must be fast; blocks the new Activity from showing
onStop()Release observers, stop network polling, unregister receiversSaving data that must not be lost — use onPause or ViewModel
onDestroy()Release anything not yet released; called on finish() OR config changeSaving state — too late; use onSaveInstanceState
onRestart()Refresh data that may have changed while stopped (rare)Heavy re-init — use ViewModel

Configuration Change Flow

A rotation, locale change, or dark-mode toggle triggers a full Activity teardown and recreation by default. The OS calls onSaveInstanceState before onStop, then recreates the Activity passing the saved Bundle to onCreate.

Rotation detected → onPause() → onStop() → onSaveInstanceState(bundle) ← save cheap UI state (scroll pos, selected tab) → onDestroy() ← ViewModel NOT destroyed (ViewModelStore survives) → onCreate(savedInstanceState) ← restore from bundle → onStart() → onResume()

Process Death

When the OS kills your process (low memory), it calls nothing after onStop(). On relaunch, the OS restores the back stack and passes the saved instance state Bundle to onCreate() — but only if onSaveInstanceState() was called before death.

Process death ≠ normal finish: onDestroy() is NOT called on process death. Never rely on onDestroy to save critical data.

State Saving Mechanisms

MechanismSurvives rotation?Survives process death?Best for
ViewModel✅❌In-memory UI state, loaded data
onSaveInstanceState Bundle✅✅Small, cheap UI state (selected tab, scroll offset)
SavedStateHandle (in ViewModel)✅✅ViewModel state that must survive death
Room / DataStore✅✅Persistent user data

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Configuration changeDevice rotation, locale/language change, dark mode toggle, font size — causes Activity recreation by default
Process deathOS kills app process silently when memory is needed; app is in background
Saved instance stateSmall Bundle persisted by system across recreation; passed to onCreate
ViewModelStoreContainer that holds ViewModels; survives configuration changes but not process death
SavedStateHandleKey-value map inside ViewModel backed by saved instance state; survives process death

3 · Why and When to Use It

You cannot opt out of the Activity lifecycle — it is the contract between your app and the OS. What you control is where you put your logic:

ScenarioRight callback / mechanism
Initialize ViewModel, observe data streamsonCreate()
Start camera or audio recordingonResume()
Stop camera or audio recordingonPause()
Unregister BroadcastReceiveronStop()
Persist critical unsaved form dataonPause() (guaranteed) or autosave in ViewModel
Save selected tab / scroll positiononSaveInstanceState()
Survive rotation with loaded dataViewModel
Survive process death with small stateSavedStateHandle in ViewModel
When NOT to: Never start long-running coroutines or network calls directly inside lifecycle callbacks — use ViewModel + lifecycleScope with repeatOnLifecycle so they auto-cancel when appropriate.

4 · Production Example (E-Commerce: Product Detail Screen)

An e-commerce product detail Activity that loads product data, tracks analytics, and saves the selected variant across rotation and process death.

ViewModel with SavedStateHandle

@HiltViewModel
class ProductDetailViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val getProductUseCase: GetProductUseCase,
    private val savedState: SavedStateHandle   // survives process death
) : ViewModel() {

    // Reads productId from navigation argument via SavedStateHandle
    private val productId: String = checkNotNull(savedState["productId"])

    // Selected variant persisted across rotation AND process death
    var selectedVariant: String?
        get() = savedState["selectedVariant"]
        set(value) { savedState["selectedVariant"] = value }

    val uiState: StateFlow<ProductUiState> = flow {
        emit(ProductUiState.Loading)
        emit(getProductUseCase(productId).fold(
            onSuccess = { ProductUiState.Success(it) },
            onFailure = { ProductUiState.Error(it.message) }
        ))
    }.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), ProductUiState.Loading)
}

Activity — Lifecycle-Aware Observation

@AndroidEntryPoint
class ProductDetailActivity : ComponentActivity() {

    private val viewModel: ProductDetailViewModel by viewModels()

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContent {
            ProductDetailScreen(viewModel)
        }
        // Collect Flow safely: pauses when Activity goes to background
        lifecycleScope.launch {
            repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                viewModel.uiState.collect { state ->
                    // update UI based on state
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

// Note: In Compose, you would use collectAsStateWithLifecycle() instead —
// it handles lifecycle awareness automatically.

onSaveInstanceState — Light UI State Only

// Use ONLY for cheap, non-sensitive UI state
override fun onSaveInstanceState(outState: Bundle) {
    super.onSaveInstanceState(outState)
    // scroll position, selected tab — NOT loaded data (that's ViewModel's job)
    outState.putInt("scrollY", binding.scrollView.scrollY)
}

override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    savedInstanceState?.getInt("scrollY")?.let { binding.scrollView.scrollTo(0, it) }
}

Handling Configuration Changes in Manifest (opt-out — use sparingly)

<!-- Only for Activities that manually handle config changes (e.g., video player) -->
<activity
    android:name=".player.VideoPlayerActivity"
    android:configChanges="orientation|screenSize|keyboardHidden"
    />

// Then in Activity:
override fun onConfigurationChanged(newConfig: Configuration) {
    super.onConfigurationChanged(newConfig)
    // Manually adjust layout; no onCreate called — ViewModel already has state
}
Opting out of configuration changes with android:configChanges is acceptable for media players and maps. For most screens, letting the system recreate and using ViewModel is cleaner.

5 · Alternatives and Trade-offs

ApproachProsConsWhen to pick
ViewModel (default) Survives rotation; no Bundle size limits; clean separation Lost on process death unless combined with SavedStateHandle All UI state and loaded data — always use
SavedStateHandle in ViewModel Survives rotation + process death; type-safe with Kotlin delegation Size limits (~1 MB Bundle); serialisation overhead Small critical state: selected IDs, input text, filters
onSaveInstanceState (Activity) Simple for small primitive state Limited size; manual save/restore boilerplate; only for small data Scroll position, selected tab in legacy code; prefer SavedStateHandle
android:configChanges No recreation overhead; useful for video/camera Manual layout adjustment; easy to miss edge cases; not recommended generally Video player, map screen where recreation cost is prohibitive
Room / DataStore Survives everything; user data persists Disk I/O; not for transient UI state Actual user data that must persist beyond session

6 · Pitfalls and Best Practices

Collecting Flow in onCreate Without repeatOnLifecycle

❌ Bad — collects in background, wastes resources

override fun onCreate(...) {
    lifecycleScope.launch {
        // Keeps collecting even when Activity is stopped
        viewModel.uiState.collect { render(it) }
    }
}

✅ Good — pauses when not STARTED

override fun onCreate(...) {
    lifecycleScope.launch {
        repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
            viewModel.uiState.collect { render(it) }
        }
    }
}

Doing Work in onDestroy

onDestroy() is NOT guaranteed to be called (process death). Never save critical data here. Use onPause() for must-save data or a ViewModel + Room for persistence.

Other Critical Pitfalls

  • Heavy work in onCreate/onResume: Causes jank and slow start. Move I/O to ViewModel/coroutine.
  • Leak via anonymous inner class: An inner class in Activity captures Activity reference. If passed to a background thread, leaks the Activity.
  • Not restoring state from Bundle: After process death + relaunch, the user sees a blank screen instead of their previous position.
  • Forgetting isFinishing() check in onStop: Some cleanup (like analytics flush) should only happen if actually finishing, not just hiding.
  • Starting Activity from onResume in a loop: If you start another Activity in onResume and that Activity finishes back to you, you get an infinite loop.
  • Network calls in lifecycle callbacks: Put them in ViewModel with viewModelScope. Callbacks may be called multiple times on rotation.
Best Practice checklist:
  • Use ViewModel for all UI state — it survives rotation automatically
  • Use SavedStateHandle for small state that must survive process death
  • Use repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) to collect Flows
  • In Compose, use collectAsStateWithLifecycle() from lifecycle-runtime-compose
  • Never call blocking operations in lifecycle callbacks
  • Release exclusive resources (camera, GPS) in onPause(), not onStop()

7 · Interview Answer Framework

30-Second Answer

"The Activity lifecycle is a series of callbacks the OS uses to manage screen visibility and memory. The key transitions are onCreate → onStart → onResume for coming to foreground, and onPause → onStop → onDestroy for leaving. The critical insight is: configuration changes like rotation destroy and recreate the Activity, but ViewModel survives. Process death is silent — no callbacks after onStop — so I use SavedStateHandle for small state that must survive that. In modern code with Compose, I use collectAsStateWithLifecycle() to observe flows safely."

2-Minute Structured Answer

The six main callbacks: onCreate (setup), onStart (visible), onResume (interactive), onPause (partially hidden — release exclusive resources), onStop (fully hidden), onDestroy (finishing or config change).

Configuration changes: Rotation triggers full teardown + recreation. onSaveInstanceState is called before onStop, letting you save cheap UI state. ViewModel survives via ViewModelStore — it's retained across config changes by the framework.

Process death: The OS kills the process silently when memory is needed. Callbacks stop after onStop. On relaunch the system reconstructs the back stack and passes saved instance state to onCreate. For critical ViewModel state I use SavedStateHandle, which is backed by the saved instance state Bundle.

In production: I put data loading in ViewModel with viewModelScope. UI observes via StateFlow using repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) — or collectAsStateWithLifecycle() in Compose — to automatically pause collection when the Activity is in background, preventing unnecessary work and wasted resources.

Must-Mention Points

  1. Six main callbacks and what belongs in each (especially onCreate vs onResume).
  2. Configuration change = full Activity recreation; ViewModel survives via ViewModelStore.
  3. Process death is silent — onDestroy is NOT guaranteed.
  4. onSaveInstanceState called before onStop, Bundle size limited — for small UI state only.
  5. SavedStateHandle in ViewModel for state that survives both rotation AND process death.
  6. repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) for safe Flow collection (or collectAsStateWithLifecycle in Compose).
  7. Release exclusive resources (camera, sensors) in onPause — not onStop.
  8. Never do blocking/heavy work in lifecycle callbacks — always delegate to ViewModel/coroutine.

Do Not Go Deeper Unless Asked

  • ViewModelStore implementation details (wait for 4A)
  • repeatOnLifecycle implementation internals (4C)
  • Parcelable vs Bundle serialisation
  • Multi-Activity back stack and launch modes (2C)

Likely Follow-up Questions

QuestionShort Answer
What's the difference between onStop and onDestroy?onStop = Activity is no longer visible but still in memory. onDestroy = Activity is being destroyed (finish() called or config change). onStop is always called; onDestroy may not be called on process death.
Why does ViewModel survive rotation but not process death?ViewModel is held by ViewModelStore, which is retained by the framework's NonConfigurationInstance mechanism during config changes. Process death kills the entire process — all in-memory objects are gone. SavedStateHandle bridges this by persisting data in the Bundle.
What's the difference between finish() and pressing Back?Back navigates up the back stack (can be intercepted via OnBackPressedDispatcher). finish() explicitly destroys the Activity and removes it from the task.
When is onSaveInstanceState called?Before onStop — guaranteed even if onDestroy is not called. Called for rotation, going to home screen, receiving a call — any time the Activity might be destroyed and recreated.

Senior-Level Insight

"The important distinction is that there are three kinds of 'death' for an Activity: (1) config change — only Activity dies, ViewModel survives; (2) user presses Back/finish() — ViewModel also dies, back stack removed, no state to restore; (3) process death — everything dies, system restores back stack and Bundle only. Many bugs come from conflating these three. SavedStateHandle is only for case 3. ViewModel is for case 1. Room/DataStore is for persistent user data across all cases. In a Compose+ViewModel architecture this is clean: ViewModel holds all state, SavedStateHandle holds the survival-critical subset, and Room holds user data — no onSaveInstanceState override needed in most Activity code."

8 · Quick Revision Sheet

Lifecycle at a Glance

CallbackActivity Visible?Interactive?Key Work
onCreateNoNosetContentView, ViewModel init, observe
onStartYes (partial)NoStart lightweight observers
onResumeYesYes ✅Acquire camera/sensors, resume media
onPausePartialNoRelease camera/sensors, pause media, save critical data
onStopNoNoUnregister receivers, stop polling
onDestroyNoNoLast cleanup; NOT guaranteed on process death

State Survival Matrix

MechanismRotationProcess DeathBack pressed
ViewModel✅❌❌
SavedStateHandle✅✅❌
onSaveInstanceState Bundle✅✅❌
Room / DataStore✅✅✅

Golden Rules

  • Use ViewModel for all UI state
  • Use SavedStateHandle for small survival-critical state
  • Collect Flows with repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) or collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
  • Release exclusive resources in onPause()
  • Never rely on onDestroy() for critical saves
  • onSaveInstanceState → small primitives / IDs only (Bundle size ~1 MB limit)

9 · Interview Questions (Self-Check)

Basic List the six Activity lifecycle callbacks in order and describe what each one means.
onCreate → Activity created; onStart → visible but not interactive; onResume → foreground, interactive; onPause → partially hidden (another Activity/dialog in front), release exclusive resources; onStop → fully hidden; onDestroy → being destroyed (finish or config change). onRestart is called between onStop and onStart when coming back to a stopped Activity.
Basic What is the difference between a configuration change and process death?
Configuration change (rotation, locale): Activity is torn down and recreated. ViewModel survives via ViewModelStore. onSaveInstanceState is called.
Process death: OS kills entire process silently. No callbacks after onStop. ViewModel is gone. Only saved instance state Bundle + Room/DataStore data survives. On relaunch, the system reconstructs the back stack and passes the Bundle to onCreate.
Basic When is onSaveInstanceState called?
Before onStop, when the Activity may be destroyed and recreated. This includes rotation, going to home screen, receiving a phone call, going to another app. It is NOT called when the user presses Back (intentional finish) because there's no expectation of restoration.
Intermediate Why does ViewModel survive rotation but not process death?
ViewModel is stored in ViewModelStore, which is attached to the Activity's NonConfigurationInstance. When a configuration change occurs, the framework retains NonConfigurationInstance across teardown/recreation, so ViewModelStore (and thus ViewModel) survives. During process death, the OS terminates the process entirely — all JVM objects are gone, including ViewModelStore. SavedStateHandle bridges this by serialising ViewModel state into the saved instance Bundle, which the OS does persist across process death.
Intermediate What is the correct way to collect a StateFlow from an Activity in 2025?
Two correct approaches:
1. lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) { flow.collect { ... } } }
2. In Compose: val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle() from lifecycle-runtime-compose.
Both automatically pause collection when the Activity goes below STARTED (background), preventing unnecessary work. The anti-pattern is plain lifecycleScope.launch { flow.collect { ... } } with no repeatOnLifecycle, which keeps collecting even in background.
Intermediate When should you release the camera — in onPause or onStop?
onPause. Camera is an exclusive resource. Another Activity (like the system camera app) may need it while your Activity is partially hidden (onPause state). If you release in onStop, the other app may fail to open the camera. Release exclusive hardware resources (camera, microphone, GPS with FINE location via requestSingleUpdate) in onPause.
Intermediate What happens to a ViewModel when the user presses Back?
When the user presses Back and the Activity finishes (not just a config change), the Activity's ViewModelStore is cleared. ViewModel.onCleared() is called. The ViewModel is destroyed. This is intentional — the user left that screen. SavedStateHandle also loses its data since the system discards the saved state for a finished Activity.
Senior/Scenario [Scenario] After a rotation, users report that a form they were filling out is blank. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
Root cause: Form state (text fields, selections) was stored only in the View/Composable local state without being backed by ViewModel or SavedStateHandle. On rotation, the Activity recreates, the View is re-inflated, and state is lost.

Fix in Compose: Use rememberSaveable for local UI state (it's backed by saved instance state). For important form fields, hoist state to ViewModel using MutableStateFlow or SavedStateHandle — savedState.getStateFlow("email", "").

Fix in XML Views: Use EditText's built-in state saving (it saves if the view has an android:id) for simple cases. For complex forms, use ViewModel with SavedStateHandle. Never reconstruct form state from scratch in onCreate without checking savedInstanceState.
Senior/Scenario [Coding] Show how to use SavedStateHandle in a ViewModel to persist a search query across process death. 
@HiltViewModel
class SearchViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val searchUseCase: SearchProductsUseCase,
    private val savedState: SavedStateHandle
) : ViewModel() {

    // StateFlow backed by SavedStateHandle — survives process death
    val query: StateFlow<String> =
        savedState.getStateFlow("query", "")

    val results: StateFlow<List<Product>> = query
        .debounce(300)
        .flatMapLatest { searchUseCase(it) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())

    fun onQueryChanged(newQuery: String) {
        savedState["query"] = newQuery   // persisted immediately
    }
}
savedState.getStateFlow() returns a StateFlow directly backed by the Bundle. Any assignment to savedState["query"] is immediately persisted.
Senior/Scenario [Debug] Your app crashes with "IllegalStateException: Fragment already added" after rotation. What caused it and how do you fix it?
Caused by adding a Fragment in onCreate without checking if it already exists. On rotation, the FragmentManager automatically restores previously added Fragments from the back stack. If your code then calls fragmentManager.beginTransaction().add(MyFragment()) unconditionally, the Fragment is added twice — crash.

Fix: Check before adding:
if (supportFragmentManager.findFragmentByTag("myFragment") == null) { supportFragmentManager.beginTransaction().add(R.id.container, MyFragment(), "myFragment").commit() }

Better: Prefer Navigation Component (manages back stack for you) or Compose (no Fragment add/remove boilerplate).

Answer Key Summary

Self-assessment checklist:

  • Can you recite all 6 callbacks + what work belongs in each?
  • Can you explain why ViewModel survives rotation but not process death?
  • Can you write a StateFlow + SavedStateHandle ViewModel from memory?
  • Do you know the difference between repeatOnLifecycle and a plain launch?
  • Can you debug the "Fragment already added" crash and explain the root cause?
