2C — Launch Modes & Back Stack

Tier 2 standard · singleTop · singleTask · singleInstance · Tasks · Back Stack · Intent Flags

1 · Overview

Android manages Activities in a task — a stack of Activities forming a logical user flow. A task has a back stack: pressing Back pops the top Activity and returns to the previous one. Launch modes control how and whether a new Activity instance is created when it is started.

Why it matters: Without understanding launch modes, apps produce duplicate Activities, broken back navigation, unexpected task switches, and deep-link bugs. Senior engineers are expected to know exactly what happens to the back stack in each mode and when to pick each one.

Core question launch modes answer: "When Activity A starts Activity B, should Android create a new instance of B, bring an existing one to the front, or pop everything above B?"

2 · How It Works

Task and Back Stack

Task (user flow) ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ [TOP] CheckoutActivity (currently shown) │ │ CartActivity │ │ ProductActivity │ │ HomeActivity (bottom) │ └────────────────────────────────────────────┘ BACK press: CheckoutActivity popped → CartActivity shown Each app launch creates a new Task (unless reusing existing)

The Four Launch Modes

standard (default)

A new instance is created every time the Activity is started, pushed onto the top of the current task.

Stack before: [Home][Product] Start ProductActivity again: Stack after: [Home][Product][Product] ← second instance pushed

singleTop

If an instance of this Activity is already at the top of the current task, no new instance is created. onNewIntent() is called on the existing instance. If it is NOT at the top, a new instance is created normally.

Stack before: [Home][Product] (Product is at top) Start ProductActivity: Stack after: [Home][Product] ← same instance, onNewIntent() called Stack before: [Home][Product][Cart] (Product NOT at top) Start ProductActivity: Stack after: [Home][Product][Cart][Product] ← new instance

singleTask

Only one instance of this Activity exists in the system at a time (within a task). If an instance exists anywhere in the task, all Activities above it are popped (destroyed) and onNewIntent() is called on the existing instance. If no instance exists, a new one is created.

Stack before: [Home][Dashboard][Profile] Start Dashboard (singleTask): Stack after: [Home][Dashboard] ← Profile popped, onNewIntent() called on Dashboard

singleInstance

Like singleTask, but the Activity is the only one in its task — it has its own private task. Any Activity started from it goes into a different task.

Task 1: [Home][App screens...] Task 2: [CallActivity] ← singleInstance; exclusive task User presses Back from CallActivity → returns to Task 1

Intent Flags — Programmatic Control

Launch modes can also be set via Intent flags at runtime, overriding the manifest declaration (flags take priority).

FlagEffectEquivalent Mode
FLAG_ACTIVITY_SINGLE_TOPsingleTop behaviour for this launchsingleTop
FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOPIf instance exists in task, pop all above it; onNewIntent called. No manifest equivalent.≈ singleTask (within task)
FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASKStart Activity in a new task (or bring existing task to foreground)Required when starting from non-Activity context
FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASKClears entire task before starting; always used with NEW_TASKUsed for logout → login flow
FLAG_ACTIVITY_NO_HISTORYActivity not kept in back stack; removed when user leavesSplash screen, auth redirect
FLAG_ACTIVITY_REORDER_TO_FRONTBring existing instance to front without destroying others—

onNewIntent()

Called when an existing Activity instance receives a new Intent (singleTop if at top, or singleTask). The old intent is still accessible via getIntent() until you call setIntent(intent).

override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
    super.onNewIntent(intent)
    setIntent(intent)               // Update getIntent() to return new intent
    val orderId = intent.getStringExtra("orderId")
    viewModel.loadOrder(orderId)   // Handle new navigation target
}

3 · Why and When to Use Each

ModeUse when…Real example
standard Default for most screens. Multiple independent instances make sense. Product detail screen (user can open multiple products in back stack)
singleTop Re-triggering the same screen with new data (notification tap, push notification deep link) Notification taps to NewsDetailActivity — don't stack duplicates if already open
singleTask App's root/home screen that should not be duplicated; deep-link destination that must clear back stack above it HomeActivity (main tab), Login screen after logout, deep link to dashboard
singleInstance Standalone utility with its own isolated task; must not share task with any other Activity System alarm screen, incoming call screen, floating assistant

When NOT to Use

  • singleTask for most screens: Popping the back stack above it is destructive. Users lose navigation history unexpectedly.
  • singleInstance for regular screens: Having Activities in separate tasks breaks the expected back navigation and ViewModel sharing.
  • Launch modes at all (modern apps): Single-activity with Navigation Component / Compose NavHost — you manage the back stack in NavGraph, not via launch modes. Launch modes matter only for the single root Activity and for cross-app scenarios.

4 · Production Example (Banking App — Logout + Deep Link)

Scenario 1: Logout — Clear Entire Task

// After successful logout, navigate to LoginActivity and clear everything
fun navigateToLoginAfterLogout() {
    val intent = Intent(this, LoginActivity::class.java).apply {
        // FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK: start in the task stack root
        // FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK: destroy all existing Activities in task
        flags = Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK or Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK
    }
    startActivity(intent)
    // User cannot press Back to return to account screens
}

Scenario 2: Notification Deep Link with singleTop

// In AndroidManifest.xml — singleTop prevents stacking notification taps
<activity
    android:name=".ui.transaction.TransactionDetailActivity"
    android:launchMode="singleTop"
    android:exported="false" />

// Activity handles new intent from FCM notification
override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
    super.onNewIntent(intent)
    setIntent(intent)
    val txId = intent.getStringExtra("transactionId") ?: return
    viewModel.loadTransaction(txId)
    // If Activity already open at top, just refreshes with new transaction
}

Scenario 3: Home Activity as singleTask Root

<activity
    android:name=".ui.HomeActivity"
    android:launchMode="singleTask"
    android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
    </intent-filter>
</activity>

// Deep link from push notification: go home, clear sub-screens
fun goHome() {
    val intent = Intent(this, HomeActivity::class.java).apply {
        // With singleTask declared, FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP pops Activities above
        flags = Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP
    }
    startActivity(intent)
}

Modern Approach: Navigation Component (Single Activity)

// In a single-activity + Navigation Compose app, launch modes are mostly irrelevant.
// Navigation Component handles back stack with popUpTo and launchSingleTop.
navController.navigate(Route.Home) {
    popUpTo(Route.Home) {
        inclusive = true              // remove Home itself from back stack before re-adding
    }
    launchSingleTop = true          // don't stack if already at top
}

// Logout in Navigation Compose — equivalent of FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK
navController.navigate(Route.Login) {
    popUpTo(navController.graph.startDestinationId) { inclusive = true }
}

5 · Alternatives and Trade-offs

ApproachProsConsWhen to pick
Manifest launch modes Declarative, always applied Cannot be overridden per-launch; limited flexibility; can't combine with flags cleanly Simple, stable navigation patterns; single-Activity root screens
Intent flags Per-launch flexibility; can be combined; usable from non-Activity contexts Verbose; easy to misuse; scatters navigation logic Logout flows, notification deep links, programmatic navigation decisions
Navigation Component (NavController) Centralized NavGraph; type-safe; handles deep links; launchSingleTop / popUpTo built-in; works with Compose Requires migration; learning curve for complex nested graphs All new projects; preferred over manifest launch modes for single-activity apps
Single Activity + Compose NavHost Simplest model; no Activity back stack concerns; composable back stack Full migration required; some limitations for very complex multi-module graphs Greenfield projects; modern standard

6 · Pitfalls and Best Practices

Forgetting setIntent() in onNewIntent()

❌ Bad — stale intent after restart

override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
    super.onNewIntent(intent)
    // Does NOT call setIntent(intent)
    // If Activity is recreated, getIntent() returns OLD intent
    val id = getIntent().getStringExtra("id")
}

✅ Good

override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
    super.onNewIntent(intent)
    setIntent(intent)    // Update so getIntent() returns new one
    val id = intent.getStringExtra("id")
}

singleTask Unexpectedly Destroys Back Stack

Gotcha: Declaring your HomeActivity as singleTask means that whenever it is launched (e.g. from a notification), ALL Activities above it in the task are destroyed. Users lose navigation state. Only use singleTask when popping the back stack is intentional.

Other Critical Pitfalls

  • Using singleInstance for regular screens: Activities in separate tasks cannot share ViewModels and have broken Back navigation. Only use for truly isolated system-level screens.
  • Not handling FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK correctly: When starting an Activity from a Service, Application, or BroadcastReceiver (non-Activity context), FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK is required. Omitting it causes RuntimeException.
  • Deep links with wrong launch mode: A deep link to a singleTask Activity destroys the back stack the user had. Prefer Navigation Component's deep link handling with addToBackStack.
  • Duplicate Activities from double-tap: Users tapping a button twice quickly can start two Activities. Use singleTop or disable the button after first tap + re-enable in onResume.
  • Ignoring task affinity: android:taskAffinity combined with singleTask can route Activities to unexpected tasks. Default affinity is the package name.
Modern best practice: In single-activity apps with Navigation Component, you rarely need launch modes. Use launchSingleTop = true and popUpTo in NavOptions for the equivalent behaviour. Reserve manifest launch modes for the MainActivity and cross-app deep-link scenarios.

7 · Interview Answer Framework

30-Second Answer

"Launch modes control how Android creates Activity instances and manages the back stack. There are four: standard creates a new instance every time; singleTop reuses if already at the top of the stack; singleTask ensures one instance per task and pops everything above it on re-launch; singleInstance is like singleTask but the Activity has its own isolated task. In modern single-activity apps with Navigation Component, I rarely use launch modes — launchSingleTop and popUpTo in NavOptions give the same control in a cleaner way."

2-Minute Structured Answer

The four modes: standard (new instance always), singleTop (reuse if at stack top → onNewIntent called), singleTask (one instance, pop above on re-launch → onNewIntent called), singleInstance (own private task).

Intent flags override manifest: FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP pops everything above an existing instance. FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK + FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK is the classic logout pattern — clears the task and starts fresh with LoginActivity so the user cannot press Back into the account screens.

onNewIntent: Called on singleTop (at top) and singleTask re-launches. Must call setIntent(intent) to update what getIntent() returns — otherwise after rotation the stale original intent is restored.

Modern practice: Single-activity apps use Navigation Component. NavController.navigate with launchSingleTop = true and popUpTo replace singleTop and singleTask respectively. This keeps all navigation logic in one NavGraph rather than scattered across manifests and flag combinations.

Must-Mention Points

  1. Four modes and what each does to the back stack.
  2. singleTask pops ALL activities above it — the most dangerous / commonly misused mode.
  3. onNewIntent() — when it's called and why setIntent() is necessary.
  4. Intent flags: CLEAR_TOP, CLEAR_TASK + NEW_TASK for logout.
  5. FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK required when starting from non-Activity context.
  6. Navigation Component replaces launch modes for in-app navigation.
  7. taskAffinity and its interaction with singleTask.

Do Not Go Deeper Unless Asked

  • taskAffinity details and multi-task scenarios
  • allowTaskReparenting attribute
  • Recents (Overview) screen task management
  • Navigation Component internals (covered in 18A)

Likely Follow-up Questions

QuestionShort Answer
What's the difference between singleTask and singleInstance?Both allow one instance. singleTask lives in a task that can contain other Activities too. singleInstance lives in its own exclusive task — no other Activity can be in that task.
When is onNewIntent() called?When an Activity with singleTop launch mode (and it's at the top of the stack) or singleTask (existing instance anywhere in task) receives a new Intent. The existing instance is reused instead of creating a new one.
How do you implement logout so the user can't press Back to the dashboard?startActivity with FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK + FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK to clear the entire task. Or in Navigation Compose: navController.navigate(login) { popUpTo(graph.startDestination) { inclusive = true } }
How does Navigation Component relate to launch modes?Navigation Component's NavController handles its own back stack (Fragment back stack or Compose composable back stack). launchSingleTop and popUpTo/inclusive give equivalent control to singleTop/singleTask without needing manifest launch modes.

Senior-Level Insight

"The real problem with launch modes is that they're a global, declarative contract set in the manifest, but navigation decisions are often context-dependent. A screen may sometimes need to clear the back stack (on logout deep link) and sometimes not (regular navigation). Intent flags give per-launch control, but scatter navigation logic. Navigation Component solves this by centralising all back-stack decisions in one NavGraph with per-navigate NavOptions — and in Compose, there's no Activity back stack at all, only a Composable call back stack managed by NavHost. For any new project I treat manifest launch modes as a last resort, used only for the root MainActivity (often singleTask for deep-link correctness) and cross-app Activities."

9 · Interview Questions (Self-Check)

Basic What are the four Activity launch modes?
standard, singleTop, singleTask, singleInstance.
• standard: new instance every launch
• singleTop: reuse if at stack top (onNewIntent called), else new instance
• singleTask: one instance per task; pops all above it on re-launch (onNewIntent called)
• singleInstance: one instance, own exclusive task
Basic What is onNewIntent() and when is it called?
onNewIntent() is called when a new Intent arrives for an existing Activity instance (instead of creating a new one). Called for singleTop if the Activity is at the top of the stack, and for singleTask/singleInstance when the instance already exists. Always call setIntent(intent) inside onNewIntent() to keep getIntent() up-to-date after potential future recreations.
Basic What Intent flags would you use to implement a logout flow where the user cannot go Back to the account screens?
FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK combined with FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK:
intent.flags = Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK or Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK
This clears all Activities in the task before starting LoginActivity, so Back press exits the app rather than returning to any account screen.
Intermediate What is the difference between singleTask and FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP?
singleTask is a manifest property — it applies every time the Activity is started and ensures one instance in the system. FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP is a per-launch flag that pops everything above an existing instance in the current task. CLEAR_TOP does not enforce one global instance; it only affects the current task and the current launch. singleTask implies CLEAR_TOP behaviour plus the one-instance guarantee. For in-task navigation, CLEAR_TOP is often preferred as it's less aggressive.
Intermediate When is FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK required?
When starting an Activity from a context that is not an Activity — a Service, BroadcastReceiver, Application class, or any non-Activity Context. Omitting it in these scenarios throws: "Calling startActivity() from outside of an Activity context requires the FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK flag."
Intermediate How does singleTop differ from singleTask when the target Activity is NOT at the top of the stack?
singleTop: if the Activity is NOT at the stack top, a new instance is created and pushed normally — no special back-stack manipulation. singleTask: if an instance exists ANYWHERE in the task (even buried), all Activities above it are popped and onNewIntent() is called on the existing instance. If no instance exists, a new one is created. singleTop is the "gentle" version; singleTask is "destructive."
Intermediate In Navigation Compose, how do you achieve singleTop behaviour when navigating? 
navController.navigate(Route.Home) {
    launchSingleTop = true  // Don't create duplicate if already at top
}
For singleTask-like clearing (e.g. going to Home from deep stack):
navController.navigate(Route.Home) {
    popUpTo(Route.Home) { inclusive = false }  // pop above Home, keep Home
    launchSingleTop = true
}
Senior/Scenario [Scenario] A user taps a push notification for Order #123 while they already have the OrderDetailActivity open showing Order #456. What launch mode/flag strategy ensures Order #123 loads without stacking a duplicate Activity?
Declare OrderDetailActivity as singleTop in the manifest. When the notification PendingIntent fires with the new orderId, Android calls onNewIntent() on the existing instance instead of creating a new one (if it's at the top of the stack). In onNewIntent(), call setIntent(intent) and then viewModel.loadOrder(newOrderId). If OrderDetailActivity is NOT at the top (other screens stacked above), you might also add FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP to pop those and reach the existing instance. In Navigation Compose with a single Activity, handle this in the notification tap by navigating with launchSingleTop = true and popUpTo to ensure clean state.
Senior/Scenario [Debug] After the user taps a notification, they see the correct screen, but pressing Back takes them to the wrong screen (an unrelated Activity from a different flow). What's the problem?
The PendingIntent is launching the Activity with FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK into a task that already has a different activity history. When the user presses Back, they're navigating through that existing task's back stack, not the expected flow. Fix: Use TaskStackBuilder to construct a synthetic back stack that matches the expected navigation hierarchy. Example:
val stackBuilder = TaskStackBuilder.create(context).apply {
    addNextIntentWithParentStack(orderDetailIntent)  // auto-adds HomeActivity → OrderListActivity → OrderDetailActivity
}
val pendingIntent = stackBuilder.getPendingIntent(0, PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE)
This ensures a proper back stack even when the app was killed.
Senior/Scenario [Coding] Write the logout navigation code for both a multi-Activity app and a single-Activity Compose app.
Multi-Activity:
fun logout() {
    authRepository.clearSession()
    val intent = Intent(this, LoginActivity::class.java).apply {
        flags = Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK or Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK
    }
    startActivity(intent)
    // No finish() needed — CLEAR_TASK destroys all Activities
}
Single Activity + Compose NavHost:
// In ViewModel
fun logout() {
    viewModelScope.launch {
        authRepository.clearSession()
        _navigationEvent.emit(NavigationEvent.LoggedOut)
    }
}

// In Composable / NavHost
LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
    viewModel.navigationEvent.collect { event ->
        if (event is NavigationEvent.LoggedOut) {
            navController.navigate(Route.Login) {
                popUpTo(0) { inclusive = true }  // pop entire graph
            }
        }
    }
}

Answer Key Summary

  • Can you describe all 4 launch modes and their back-stack effects without hesitation?
  • Can you explain singleTask vs CLEAR_TOP precisely?
  • Can you write a logout flow with correct flags from memory?
  • Can you write onNewIntent with setIntent correctly?
  • Do you know the TaskStackBuilder pattern for notification back stacks?

2D — Fragments

Tier 2 Fragment lifecycle · View lifecycle · FragmentManager · transactions · back stack · communication · Navigation Component

1 · Overview

A Fragment is a reusable UI component hosted inside an Activity. It has its own lifecycle, view hierarchy, and can be added/removed/replaced dynamically. Fragments enable modular, adaptive UI — the same Fragment can be used on phone (one at a time) and tablet (dual-pane side by side).

Why Fragments exist: Before Fragments (introduced API 11), building adaptive UIs required multiple Activities with duplicated logic. Fragments allow one codebase, one Activity, multiple interchangeable screen segments.

Two separate lifecycles: Fragments have a Fragment lifecycle (the Fragment object) and a View lifecycle (the View tree). This distinction is the source of the most common Fragment bugs. Observers should be tied to viewLifecycleOwner, not the Fragment itself.

2 · How It Works

Fragment Lifecycle (Fragment object)

onAttach() ← Fragment attached to Activity; context available onCreate() ← Fragment created; init non-UI state, args onCreateView() ← Inflate layout, return View onViewCreated() ← View ready; set up UI, observers, listeners onStart() ← Fragment visible onResume() ← Fragment interactive --- USER INTERACTION --- onPause() ← Fragment partially hidden onStop() ← Fragment hidden onDestroyView() ← View destroyed (but Fragment object still exists in back stack) onDestroy() ← Fragment object destroyed onDetach() ← Fragment detached from Activity

Fragment View Lifecycle (viewLifecycleOwner)

Fragment back-stacked: onDestroyView() called — View destroyed Fragment object STAYS ALIVE (in back stack) onCreateView() called again when Fragment returns to foreground Activity rotation: Fragment onDestroyView() → onDestroy() → onCreate() → onCreateView() → onViewCreated() (But Fragment TAG matches — FragmentManager restores it automatically)

Fragment vs Activity Lifecycle Comparison

ActivityFragment equivalentNotes
onCreateonCreateFragment: no view yet
—onCreateViewInflate layout; return view
—onViewCreatedView available; setup UI here
onStartonStartFragment visible
onResumeonResumeFragment interactive
onPauseonPause—
onStoponStop—
onDestroyonDestroyView + onDestroyTWO steps in Fragment
—onDetachNo Activity equivalent

FragmentManager and Transactions

// Get FragmentManager
val fm = supportFragmentManager           // from Activity
val fm = childFragmentManager             // from Fragment (for nested fragments)
val fm = parentFragmentManager            // from Fragment (host's FM)

// Transaction — atomic set of operations
fm.beginTransaction()
    .replace(R.id.container, HomeFragment(), "home")  // replace with tag
    .addToBackStack("home")                              // add to back stack
    .commit()                                             // async commit

// commitNow() — synchronous; cannot be used with addToBackStack
// commitAllowingStateLoss() — use when state may be lost (risky)

add() vs replace()

add()

Adds Fragment on top of existing ones. Both are alive simultaneously. Used for overlapping UIs (bottom sheets, dialogs).

replace()

Removes existing Fragment in container and replaces with new one. Used for full-screen navigation. Previous Fragment's view is destroyed (onDestroyView called).

Fragment Communication Patterns

PatternHowWhen to use
Shared ViewModelBoth Fragments use activityViewModels() to share one ViewModel scoped to ActivitySibling Fragments needing shared state — preferred modern pattern
Fragment Result APIsetFragmentResult() + setFragmentResultListener()One-shot result passing (like startActivityForResult replacement)
Interface callbackFragment defines interface; Activity implements itLegacy; avoid in new code
Navigation Component + argsSafe Args pass typed arguments via NavBackStackEntry or navigate()Navigation-driven data passing

Navigation Component with Fragments

// nav_graph.xml — declare navigation in one place
<navigation ...>
    <fragment android:id="@+id/homeFragment" android:name=".HomeFragment">
        <action android:id="@+id/action_home_to_detail"
                app:destination="@id/productDetailFragment" />
    </fragment>
    <fragment android:id="@+id/productDetailFragment" ...>
        <argument android:name="productId" app:argType="string" />
    </fragment>
</navigation>

// Navigate with Safe Args
val action = HomeFragmentDirections.actionHomeToproductDetail(productId = "abc123")
findNavController().navigate(action)

3 · Why and When to Use Fragments

Use caseFragment approach
Adaptive tablet/phone layoutsSame Fragment shown in single-pane (phone) or dual-pane (tablet)
Tab-based navigationEach tab is a Fragment; ViewPager2 + FragmentStateAdapter
Bottom sheet dialogsBottomSheetDialogFragment
Single-activity navigation (pre-Compose)Navigation Component + Fragment destinations
Reusable complex UI component with lifecycleFragment with its own ViewModel

When NOT to Use Fragments

  • Logic-only modules: Use ViewModel / UseCase instead — no need for Fragment lifecycle.
  • New Compose-only projects: Composable functions replace Fragments entirely. A Composable has no lifecycle complexity.
  • Simple UI elements: If you just need a reusable view, use a custom View or Composable, not a Fragment.

4 · Production Example (E-Commerce App)

Single-activity e-commerce app with Navigation Component: Home → Product List → Product Detail, plus a Cart bottom sheet.

Fragment with viewLifecycleOwner (critical pattern)

@AndroidEntryPoint
class ProductListFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_product_list) {

    private val viewModel: ProductListViewModel by viewModels()
    private var _binding: FragmentProductListBinding? = null
    private val binding get() = _binding!!

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onViewCreated(view, savedInstanceState)
        _binding = FragmentProductListBinding.bind(view)

        // ✅ Use viewLifecycleOwner — NOT 'this' (Fragment) — for observe/collect
        viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
            repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                viewModel.products.collect { products ->
                    adapter.submitList(products)
                }
            }
        }

        binding.cartFab.setOnClickListener {
            findNavController().navigate(R.id.action_products_to_cart)
        }
    }

    override fun onDestroyView() {
        super.onDestroyView()
        _binding = null   // ✅ Null binding to avoid view memory leak in back stack
    }
}

Shared ViewModel Between Fragments

// Both fragments share one CartViewModel scoped to the Activity
@AndroidEntryPoint
class ProductDetailFragment : Fragment() {
    // activityViewModels() — same instance as CartFragment's ViewModel
    private val cartViewModel: CartViewModel by activityViewModels()

    fun onAddToCart(product: Product) {
        cartViewModel.addItem(product)
    }
}

@AndroidEntryPoint
class CartFragment : Fragment() {
    private val cartViewModel: CartViewModel by activityViewModels()
    // Observes same CartViewModel instance
}

Fragment Result API — Confirmation Dialog

// Dialog Fragment sets result
class ConfirmDeleteDialog : DialogFragment() {
    override fun onCreateDialog(...): Dialog =
        AlertDialog.Builder(requireContext())
            .setTitle("Delete item?")
            .setPositiveButton("Delete") { _, _ ->
                setFragmentResult("deleteConfirmed", Bundle())
            }
            .create()
}

// Parent Fragment listens for result
override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    setFragmentResultListener("deleteConfirmed") { _, _ ->
        viewModel.deleteSelectedItem()
    }
}

5 · Alternatives and Trade-offs

ApproachProsConsWhen to pick
Fragments + Navigation Component Mature tooling, SafeArgs, deep links, ViewPager2 support View lifecycle complexity; onDestroyView/onCreateView pattern; boilerplate Standard modern Android pre-full-Compose migration
Jetpack Compose (no Fragments) No lifecycle complexity; composable = function; simpler state Less mature for very complex multi-module graphs; requires full investment New projects; greenfield; full Compose adoption
Multiple Activities Total isolation; independent back stacks Hard to share state; complex deep linking; more boilerplate Legacy; or when truly distinct independent user flows needed
Custom Views Simpler for self-contained UI components; no lifecycle overhead No built-in ViewModel, no back stack, no nav graph Reusable UI widgets (chart, custom button); not full screens

6 · Pitfalls and Best Practices

Pitfall 1: Observing with 'this' Instead of viewLifecycleOwner

❌ Bad — potential duplicate observers

// 'this' is the Fragment object lifecycle
// When Fragment goes to back stack: View destroyed but Fragment lives
// When returning: onCreateView() called again — new observer added
// Now TWO observers active — duplicate updates
viewModel.products.observe(this) { ... }

✅ Good — tied to View lifecycle

// viewLifecycleOwner starts fresh each onCreateView
// Auto-removed in onDestroyView — no duplicates
viewModel.products.observe(viewLifecycleOwner) { ... }

Pitfall 2: ViewBinding Memory Leak

❌ Bad — binding holds View reference

private lateinit var binding: FragmentBinding

override fun onCreateView(...): View {
    binding = FragmentBinding.inflate(inflater)
    return binding.root
    // binding never nulled — leaks View after back stack
}

✅ Good — null in onDestroyView

private var _binding: FragmentBinding? = null
private val binding get() = _binding!!

override fun onDestroyView() {
    super.onDestroyView()
    _binding = null   // releases View reference
}

Other Critical Pitfalls

  • Accessing view in onCreate(): View is not created yet — always use onViewCreated().
  • Fragment constructor arguments: Never pass arguments to Fragment constructors. Use Fragment.newInstance() with a Bundle or Safe Args. On recreation, the framework uses the no-arg constructor — custom constructors cause crashes.
  • commitAllowingStateLoss(): Called after onSaveInstanceState — state loss means the Fragment transaction may be lost. Use commit() and ensure transactions happen at the right lifecycle moment.
  • Nested fragments with wrong FragmentManager: Always use childFragmentManager for nested Fragments (inside another Fragment), not parentFragmentManager or supportFragmentManager.
  • Duplicate Fragments after rotation: Not using tags + findFragmentByTag before add creates duplicates after system-restored Fragments.

7 · Interview Answer Framework

30-Second Answer

"A Fragment is a reusable UI component hosted inside an Activity with its own lifecycle. The critical subtlety is that a Fragment has two separate lifecycles — the Fragment object lifecycle and the View lifecycle. Observers must be tied to viewLifecycleOwner, not the Fragment itself, to avoid duplicate observers when the Fragment returns from the back stack. In modern apps I use single-activity with Navigation Component and Fragments (or Compose for new projects), sharing state between Fragments via activityViewModels() and using Fragment Result API for one-shot communications."

2-Minute Structured Answer

What a Fragment is: A modular UI component hosted inside an Activity. It has its own view hierarchy, lifecycle, and can be added/removed at runtime via FragmentManager transactions.

Two lifecycles: The Fragment object lifecycle (onAttach → onDetach) and the View lifecycle (onCreateView → onDestroyView). When a Fragment is on the back stack, its View is destroyed (onDestroyView) but the Fragment object stays alive. This is why observers must use viewLifecycleOwner — not this — to avoid duplicate observers.

Communication: I share state between Fragments via a ViewModel scoped to the Activity (activityViewModels()). For one-shot results (dialog confirmations, pickers), I use the Fragment Result API — setFragmentResult/setFragmentResultListener. I avoid interface callbacks; they're legacy and create tight coupling.

ViewBinding leak: Always null the binding reference in onDestroyView to avoid holding a reference to the destroyed View while the Fragment object is still in the back stack.

Modern context: In new projects I prefer Compose which eliminates the dual-lifecycle complexity entirely. For XML-based codebases, Navigation Component manages the Fragment back stack automatically.

Must-Mention Points

  1. Fragment has TWO lifecycles: Fragment object + View lifecycle (viewLifecycleOwner).
  2. Use viewLifecycleOwner for observers — not 'this' — to prevent duplicate observers on back-stack return.
  3. Null ViewBinding in onDestroyView to prevent View memory leaks.
  4. Never pass constructor arguments — use Bundle/newInstance() or Safe Args.
  5. childFragmentManager for nested Fragments; parentFragmentManager to reach host.
  6. activityViewModels() for shared state between Fragments.
  7. Fragment Result API replaces interface callbacks and startActivityForResult.
  8. Navigation Component manages Fragment back stack — prefer over manual transactions.

Do Not Go Deeper Unless Asked

  • DialogFragment internals
  • ViewPager2 + FragmentStateAdapter details
  • Navigation Component internals (covered in 18A)
  • Compose interop with Fragments (ComposeView in Fragment)

Likely Follow-up Questions

QuestionShort Answer
What happens to a Fragment when it goes on the back stack?onDestroyView() is called — the View is destroyed. The Fragment object stays alive in memory (onCreate was called, but not onDestroy). When the user navigates back, onCreateView() and onViewCreated() are called again.
What is the difference between childFragmentManager and supportFragmentManager?supportFragmentManager is from the Activity — it manages top-level Fragments. childFragmentManager is from a Fragment — it manages nested Fragments inside that Fragment. Using supportFragmentManager inside a Fragment for nested fragments causes incorrect lifecycle ownership.
How do two Fragments communicate without coupling?Shared ViewModel via activityViewModels() for ongoing shared state. Fragment Result API for one-shot results. Both avoid direct Fragment-to-Fragment references.
Why use viewLifecycleOwner instead of this for observe()?The Fragment object can outlive its View (when on back stack). Using 'this' ties the observer to the Fragment lifecycle — when the Fragment returns from the back stack, a new observer is added while the old one is still active, causing duplicate updates.

Senior-Level Insight

"The dual-lifecycle problem in Fragments is a design flaw that Compose eliminates entirely. In Compose, there is no separate View lifecycle — a Composable is either in composition or not. But in XML Fragment apps, understanding the dual lifecycle is what separates junior from senior: specifically, the pattern of _binding = null in onDestroyView, using viewLifecycleOwner for all observers, and knowing that back-stack Fragments are alive but viewless. Navigation Component's Fragment back stack management encapsulates all of this, which is why I treat direct FragmentManager transaction code as a code smell in new projects — it should almost always be replaced by a NavController.navigate() call."

Fragment Lifecycle Order

Critical Rules

  • observe(viewLifecycleOwner) — NEVER observe(this) in Fragment
  • _binding = null in onDestroyView — ALWAYS for ViewBinding Fragments

9 · Interview Questions (Self-Check)

Basic What is the Fragment lifecycle and how does it differ from Activity lifecycle?
Fragment lifecycle has extra steps: onAttach (before onCreate), onCreateView (inflate layout), onViewCreated (view ready — most setup goes here), onDestroyView (view destroyed, Fragment may stay alive on back stack), and onDetach (after onDestroy). The key difference from Activity: a Fragment has two separate lifecycles — the Fragment object and its View. The Activity has only one lifecycle. Fragment's View is destroyed when it goes on the back stack, while the Fragment object persists.
Basic What is viewLifecycleOwner and why is it important?
viewLifecycleOwner is the LifecycleOwner tied to the Fragment's View lifecycle (created in onCreateView, destroyed in onDestroyView). It is different from the Fragment itself as a LifecycleOwner (which lives longer). Using viewLifecycleOwner for LiveData/Flow observers ensures the observer is removed in onDestroyView. Using 'this' (the Fragment) keeps observers active between onDestroyView and onCreateView — leading to duplicate observers when the Fragment returns from the back stack.
Basic How do you pass data to a Fragment correctly?
Use arguments Bundle with companion object newInstance(), or Safe Args via Navigation Component. Never use constructor arguments — the Fragment framework instantiates Fragments using the no-arg constructor on recreation (rotation, process death), so custom constructors cause InstantiationException.
companion object {
    fun newInstance(productId: String) = ProductDetailFragment().apply {
        arguments = Bundle().apply { putString("productId", productId) }
    }
}
// In Fragment: val id = requireArguments().getString("productId")
Intermediate What is the difference between add() and replace() in Fragment transactions?
add(): Adds the new Fragment on top of the existing one. Both Fragments exist simultaneously in the container. Used for overlapping UIs: BottomSheetDialogFragment, overlay Fragments. The previous Fragment's onStop() is NOT called (it's still visible underneath).
replace(): Removes all existing Fragments in the container and adds the new one. Previous Fragment goes through onStop → onDestroyView (if addToBackStack) or full destruction. Used for full-screen navigation between screens.
Intermediate How do two sibling Fragments communicate without coupling?
Two patterns: (1) Shared ViewModel — both Fragments use activityViewModels() to get the same ViewModel instance scoped to the Activity. One Fragment writes to it, the other observes it. (2) Fragment Result API — setFragmentResult("key", bundle) in the sender; setFragmentResultListener("key", viewLifecycleOwner) in the receiver. Avoids direct Fragment-to-Fragment references and interface callbacks.
Intermediate When would you use childFragmentManager vs parentFragmentManager?
childFragmentManager: used inside a Fragment to manage Fragments that are children (nested) within that Fragment. E.g., a ViewPager inside a Fragment uses childFragmentManager as the FragmentManager for its page Fragments. parentFragmentManager: used inside a Fragment to access the FragmentManager that owns this Fragment (the parent Fragment's childFragmentManager, or the Activity's supportFragmentManager). Wrong choice leads to lifecycle ownership issues and potential memory leaks.
Intermediate What is the Fragment Result API and when was it introduced?
Fragment Result API (introduced in Fragment 1.3.0, 2020) provides a type-safe, lifecycle-aware way to pass one-shot results between Fragments. It replaces the pattern of interface callbacks and the deprecated targetFragment API. The sender calls setFragmentResult("requestKey", bundle). The receiver registers a listener with setFragmentResultListener("requestKey", viewLifecycleOwner) { key, bundle -> }. The listener is only invoked when the Fragment is at least STARTED, and is automatically removed in onDestroyView.
Senior/Scenario [Scenario] After rotation, users report seeing duplicate list items. You suspect the Observer is firing twice. How do you diagnose and fix this?
Root cause: LiveData/Flow is being observed with 'this' (Fragment lifecycle) instead of viewLifecycleOwner. When the Fragment goes to back stack, its View is destroyed but the Fragment object is alive — observer 1 still active. When it returns, onCreateView is called again and a second observer is added — observer 2 now also active. After rotation (full Fragment recreation), there may be 2+ observers emitting to the same adapter.

Diagnose: Place a log in the observe lambda and count how many times it fires per update.

Fix: Change all observe() calls from this to viewLifecycleOwner. For StateFlow/Flow: use viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) { ... } } inside onViewCreated.
Senior/Scenario [Coding] Implement a Fragment with ViewBinding that correctly nulls the binding, uses viewLifecycleOwner for observation, and handles arguments safely. 
@AndroidEntryPoint
class OrderListFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_order_list) {

    private val viewModel: OrderListViewModel by viewModels()
    private var _binding: FragmentOrderListBinding? = null
    private val binding get() = _binding!!  // safe non-null accessor

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onViewCreated(view, savedInstanceState)
        _binding = FragmentOrderListBinding.bind(view)

        // ✅ viewLifecycleOwner — not 'this'
        viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
            repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                viewModel.orders.collect { binding.recyclerView.adapter?.let { a ->
                    (a as OrderAdapter).submitList(it)
                }}
            }
        }
    }

    override fun onDestroyView() {
        super.onDestroyView()
        _binding = null  // ✅ prevent View memory leak
    }

    companion object {
        fun newInstance(userId: String) = OrderListFragment().apply {
            arguments = Bundle().apply { putString("userId", userId) }
        }
    }
}
Senior/Scenario [Debug] "IllegalStateException: Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState" — when does this crash occur and how do you fix it?
This crash occurs when a Fragment transaction (commit()) is called after the Activity has saved its state (post-onSaveInstanceState). Common causes: async callback finishes after the Activity is paused (e.g., network response, dialog dismiss from a background thread).

Fix options:
1. Use commitAllowingStateLoss() — accepts state may be lost (acceptable for non-critical UI).
2. Check lifecycle before committing: if (lifecycle.currentState.isAtLeast(Lifecycle.State.STARTED)) { commit() }
3. Better: Don't commit transactions in async callbacks directly. Use a shared ViewModel to emit navigation events, and observe them in the Fragment with viewLifecycleOwner so they only fire when STARTED.
4. In Navigation Component: navController.navigate() is safe to call from lifecycle-aware coroutines — it handles the state check internally.

Answer Key Summary

  • Can you explain the dual lifecycle (Fragment + View) without prompting?
  • Can you write a correct ViewBinding Fragment with null in onDestroyView?
  • Do you know why viewLifecycleOwner prevents duplicate observers?
  • Can you compare activityViewModels vs viewModels and explain when to use each?
  • Can you fix the "Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState" crash?

2E — Intents

Tier 2 Explicit · Implicit · Intent Filters · PendingIntent · Deep Links · App Links

1 · Overview

An Intent is a messaging object used to request an action from another component — within your app or from the system/other apps. It is the primary mechanism for inter-component and inter-app communication on Android.

What problem it solves: Android's sandboxed process model means apps cannot call each other's code directly. Intents provide a declarative, system-mediated way to say "I want to do X" without needing to know which app or component will handle it. The OS routes the Intent to the correct recipient based on intent filters declared in the manifest.

Three uses of Intents:
  • Start an Activity (screen navigation)
  • Start or bind to a Service
  • Deliver a Broadcast (system or app-wide event)

2 · How It Works

Explicit Intent

Specifies the exact component (class) to start. Used for in-app navigation.

// Start a specific Activity in the same app
val intent = Intent(this, OrderDetailActivity::class.java).apply {
    putExtra("orderId", "ORD-123")
    putExtra("amount", 99.99)
}
startActivity(intent)

// Start a Service explicitly
val serviceIntent = Intent(this, SyncService::class.java)
startService(serviceIntent)

Implicit Intent

Does not specify a component. Declares an action; the OS resolves which app/component can handle it based on intent filters.

// Share text — OS shows chooser of apps that handle ACTION_SEND
val intent = Intent(Intent.ACTION_SEND).apply {
    type = "text/plain"
    putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_TEXT, "Check out this product!")
}
// ✅ Always check if a handler exists before starting
if (intent.resolveActivity(packageManager) != null) {
    startActivity(Intent.createChooser(intent, "Share via"))
}

// Dial a phone number
val dialIntent = Intent(Intent.ACTION_DIAL, Uri.parse("tel:+1234567890"))
startActivity(dialIntent)

Intent Filters

Declared in the manifest; tell the system what types of Intents a component can handle (for implicit Intents).

<activity android:name=".ShareReceiverActivity" android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.SEND" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
        <data android:mimeType="text/plain" />
    </intent-filter>
</activity>

PendingIntent

A PendingIntent is a token that grants another app (Notification system, AlarmManager, widget host) the ability to fire your Intent at a future time, with your app's permissions and identity — even if your app is not running.

Your App Android System Notification Manager │ │ │ ├─ createPendingIntent ──────────────────────►│ │ (stores Intent + your identity) │ │ │ │ │ [User taps notification] │ │ │◄───────────────────────┤ │ │ fires PendingIntent │ ├◄───────────────────┤ │ │ Activity started with your permissions │
// PendingIntent for notification tap — API 31+ requires FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE
val intent = Intent(this, OrderDetailActivity::class.java).apply {
    putExtra("orderId", orderId)
    flags = Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_SINGLE_TOP
}
val pendingIntent = PendingIntent.getActivity(
    context,
    orderId.hashCode(),       // requestCode — uniquely identifies this PendingIntent
    intent,
    PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE
)

// Use in Notification
NotificationCompat.Builder(context, CHANNEL_ID)
    .setContentIntent(pendingIntent)
    .setAutoCancel(true)
    .

Deep Links and App Links

TypeSchemeVerification?Disambiguation?
Deep LinkCustom scheme (myapp://) or HTTP(S)NoSystem may show chooser if multiple apps handle it
App Link (Android App Link)HTTPS onlyYes — via Digital Asset Links JSON at serverNo chooser — opens your app directly
<!-- Manifest: handle https://example.com/orders/{id} -->
<activity android:name=".OrderDetailActivity" android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter android:autoVerify="true">  <!-- autoVerify = App Link -->
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE" />
        <data android:scheme="https" android:host="example.com" android:pathPrefix="/orders" />
    </intent-filter>
</activity>

// Handle in Activity
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    val orderId = intent?.data?.lastPathSegment  // "ORD-123"
    orderId?.let { viewModel.loadOrder(it) }
}

3 · Why and When to Use Each

TypeUse when…Do NOT use when…
Explicit Intent In-app navigation between known components; starting your own Service Cross-app actions where you don't know the target — use implicit
Implicit Intent System actions (share, dial, map, camera); letting user choose which app handles the action In-app navigation — use explicit (security risk to expose your internals)
PendingIntent Notifications, AlarmManager, widgets — any deferred Intent fired by another process Immediate in-app navigation — use startActivity() directly
Deep Link Custom URL scheme for your app; marketing links; sharing app content When you need guaranteed single-app routing — use App Links
App Link HTTPS links that should always open your app (no chooser); bank account links; purchase confirmations If you can't serve the verification JSON at the domain — use deep link

4 · Production Example (Banking App)

FCM Notification with PendingIntent + TaskStackBuilder

// Notification for incoming payment — tap opens TransactionDetailActivity
// with correct back stack (Home → Transactions → Detail)
fun buildPaymentNotification(context: Context, txId: String): Notification {
    // TaskStackBuilder creates synthetic back stack for notification deep link
    val pendingIntent = TaskStackBuilder.create(context).apply {
        addNextIntentWithParentStack(
            Intent(context, TransactionDetailActivity::class.java).apply {
                putExtra("transactionId", txId)
            }
        )
    }.getPendingIntent(
        txId.hashCode(),
        PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE
    )

    return NotificationCompat.Builder(context, CHANNEL_PAYMENTS)
        .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_payment)
        .setContentTitle("Payment received")
        .setContentText("Transaction #$txId")
        .setContentIntent(pendingIntent)
        .setAutoCancel(true)
        .build()
}

App Links — HTTPS Deep Link Handling

// Manifest: android:autoVerify="true" + HTTPS scheme + your domain
// Server: /.well-known/assetlinks.json must return your app's SHA256 fingerprint

// In Activity (or Navigation Component handles this automatically)
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    val action = intent.action
    val data = intent.data

    if (Intent.ACTION_VIEW == action && data != null) {
        when {
            data.path?.startsWith("/account") == true -> navigateToAccount()
            data.path?.startsWith("/transactions") == true -> {
                val txId = data.lastPathSegment
                navigateToTransaction(txId)
            }
        }
    }
}

// With Navigation Compose — declare deep links in NavGraph instead
composable(
    route = "transaction/{id}",
    deepLinks = listOf(navDeepLink {
        uriPattern = "https://mybank.com/transactions/{id}"
    })
) { backStackEntry ->
    val id = backStackEntry.arguments?.getString("id")
    TransactionDetailScreen(id)
}

Implicit Intent — Share Bank Statement

fun shareStatement(fileUri: Uri) {
    val intent = Intent(Intent.ACTION_SEND).apply {
        type = "application/pdf"
        putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_STREAM, fileUri)
        // Grant temporary read permission to the receiving app
        addFlags(Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION)
    }
    // ✅ Use createChooser — always show picker even if one app handles it
    startActivity(Intent.createChooser(intent, "Share statement"))
}

5 · Alternatives and Trade-offs

ApproachProsConsWhen to pick
Explicit Intent Direct, fast, type-safe Couples caller to exact class; breaks modularization if used across modules In-app navigation where you own both sides
Implicit Intent Decoupled; works across apps No guarantee of handler; security risks if unvalidated; chooser UX Cross-app actions: share, dial, open URL
Navigation Component Type-safe Safe Args; centralized graph; deep link handling; no class coupling Overhead for very simple apps; requires migration In-app navigation in modern single-activity apps — preferred
Deep Link (custom scheme) Simple; no server setup Not unique — any app can declare same scheme; disambiguation dialog Internal app links; dev/testing; when you don't control the domain
App Link (HTTPS + verification) No disambiguation; OS opens your app directly; secure Requires domain + server-side assetlinks.json; verification process Production marketing links; push notification deep links; open from email

6 · Pitfalls and Best Practices

Implicit Intent with No Handler — Crash

❌ Bad — ActivityNotFoundException

// On devices without an email app — crashes
val intent = Intent(Intent.ACTION_SENDTO)
intent.data = Uri.parse("mailto:support@bank.com")
startActivity(intent)  // CRASH if no handler

✅ Good — check first

val intent = Intent(Intent.ACTION_SENDTO)
intent.data = Uri.parse("mailto:support@bank.com")
if (intent.resolveActivity(packageManager) != null) {
    startActivity(intent)
} else {
    showToast("No email app found")
}

PendingIntent — Missing FLAG_IMMUTABLE (API 31+)

API 31+ requires PendingIntent to explicitly specify FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE. Omitting this throws IllegalArgumentException. Almost always use FLAG_IMMUTABLE unless the PendingIntent needs to be modified by the receiving app (e.g. Android Auto inline replies).

Other Critical Pitfalls

  • Passing large objects via Intent extras: Intents go through the Binder IPC buffer (1 MB limit). Passing large Bitmaps or lists causes TransactionTooLargeException. Pass IDs and load data in the target component.
  • Receiving implicit Intents in unexported components: On API 31+, any component with an intent-filter must declare android:exported="true|false" explicitly or the app won't install.
  • Not using FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION: When sharing files via FileProvider, the receiving app needs temporary permission to read the URI. Missing this causes permission denied on the target app.
  • Deep link not handled after process death: If the Activity is killed and relaunched via a deep link, intent.data must be parsed in onCreate — not just in onNewIntent. Both paths must be handled.
  • PendingIntent requestCode collision: Using the same requestCode for different PendingIntents causes FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT to overwrite the previous one's extras. Use unique requestCodes (e.g., notification ID or entity ID hashCode).
Security best practice for implicit Intents received: Validate all data received via Intent. An implicit Intent can be sent by any app. Never trust extras without validation — especially in components marked android:exported="true".

7 · Interview Answer Framework

30-Second Answer

"Intents are the messaging system for starting Android components. Explicit Intents specify the exact component — used for in-app navigation. Implicit Intents declare an action and let the OS find an app to handle it — used for share, dial, open URL. PendingIntent wraps an Intent with your app's identity and permissions so another process can fire it later — used for notifications, AlarmManager, widgets. Deep links and App Links let external URLs open specific screens, with App Links requiring HTTPS domain verification to avoid the disambiguation chooser."

2-Minute Structured Answer

Explicit vs Implicit: Explicit Intent targets a specific class — used for in-app navigation. Implicit Intent declares an action (ACTION_SEND, ACTION_VIEW) — the OS resolves it via intent filters in the manifest. Always check resolveActivity() before firing an implicit Intent to avoid ActivityNotFoundException.

Intent filters: Declared in manifest; specifies what action + category + data MIME type a component can handle. For security, components that should not be accessed externally must be android:exported="false".

PendingIntent: A deferred Intent that another process (notification manager, alarm manager) can fire with your app's identity. API 31+ requires FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE explicitly. Use TaskStackBuilder to create a proper back stack when the PendingIntent opens a deep-linked screen.

Deep links vs App Links: Deep links use custom schemes or HTTPS but may show a chooser if multiple apps match. App Links use HTTPS with domain verification via assetlinks.json — no chooser, opens your app directly. For production push notification flows and marketing links, I always implement App Links.

Must-Mention Points

  1. Explicit (known component) vs Implicit (declared action, OS resolves).
  2. Intent filters in manifest — how implicit Intent routing works.
  3. PendingIntent — deferred Intent, fired by another process, carries your identity.
  4. FLAG_IMMUTABLE required on API 31+ for PendingIntent.
  5. TransactionTooLargeException — never pass large data via extras; pass IDs.
  6. Deep link vs App Link — HTTPS verification, no chooser with App Links.
  7. TaskStackBuilder for synthetic back stack on notification deep links.
  8. Always validate data received via exported components — any app can send Intents.

Do Not Go Deeper Unless Asked

  • Broadcast Intents and intent filters for receivers (covered in 16A)
  • FileProvider details for sharing files
  • Navigation Component deep link XML declaration details (18A)
  • AIDL for IPC (3C)

Likely Follow-up Questions

QuestionShort Answer
What is a PendingIntent and why is it needed?A token that grants another process (notification manager, alarm) the ability to execute a specific Intent with your app's identity and permissions, even if your app is not running. Without PendingIntent, other processes cannot start Activities or send broadcasts on your behalf.
What is the difference between a deep link and an App Link?Deep link: any scheme (custom or HTTPS), may show disambiguation chooser if multiple apps match. App Link: HTTPS only, requires domain verification via Digital Asset Links — opens your app directly without a chooser.
Why can't you put a Bitmap in an Intent extra?Intent extras go through Binder IPC, which has a ~1 MB transaction buffer. A Bitmap can easily exceed that, causing TransactionTooLargeException. Pass a file URI or resource ID instead.
What happens if resolveActivity() returns null?No app on the device can handle this implicit Intent. startActivity() would throw ActivityNotFoundException. Must handle gracefully — show error or fallback (e.g., open a WebView for the URL instead).

Senior-Level Insight

"In modern single-activity Compose apps, explicit Intents for in-app navigation are largely replaced by Navigation Component. But Intents are still critical for three scenarios: (1) cross-app communication via implicit Intents, (2) PendingIntents for FCM notifications — where TaskStackBuilder is essential to avoid broken back navigation, and (3) App Links for seamless HTTPS → app routing. The security angle is often overlooked: exported components with intent-filters are an attack surface — any app can fire an Intent at them. I always audit android:exported='true' components, validate all received data, and use FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION instead of making file URIs globally readable."

Golden Rules

  • Always check resolveActivity() before firing implicit Intents
  • PendingIntent API 31+: always add FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE
  • Use TaskStackBuilder for notification PendingIntents to ensure correct back stack
  • Never pass large objects (Bitmap, List) as Intent extras — pass IDs
  • Validate all data in exported components with intent-filters
  • Use FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION when sharing files via FileProvider

9 · Interview Questions (Self-Check)

Basic What is the difference between an explicit and an implicit Intent?
Explicit Intent specifies the exact component (Activity/Service class name) to start. Used for in-app navigation. Implicit Intent specifies an action (e.g. ACTION_SEND) and optional data type/category. The OS resolves which app/component can handle it based on manifest intent-filters. The system shows a chooser if multiple apps match.
Basic What is a PendingIntent and when is it used?
A PendingIntent is a token wrapping an Intent that grants another process the ability to execute it with your app's permissions, even when your app is not running. Used for: notification taps (NotificationCompat), scheduled alarms (AlarmManager), widget interactions, and deferred system actions. API 31+ requires FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE explicitly.
Basic What happens if you try to start an implicit Intent with no handler?
ActivityNotFoundException is thrown at runtime, crashing the app. Fix: always call intent.resolveActivity(packageManager) first and handle the null case gracefully. Note: On Android 11+ (API 30), resolveActivity() requires a <queries> element in the manifest for non-system apps to be visible.
Intermediate What is the difference between a deep link and an App Link?
Deep link: any URI scheme (custom myapp:// or https://). No domain verification. The OS may show a disambiguation chooser if multiple apps match. Simple to implement.
App Link: HTTPS URI only. Requires digital asset links verification — a JSON file at https://domain/.well-known/assetlinks.json that contains your app's SHA256 signing certificate. On verified devices, the OS opens your app directly with no chooser. Required: android:autoVerify="true" in the intent-filter.
Intermediate Why do you use TaskStackBuilder for notification PendingIntents?
When a user taps a notification that opens a deep screen (e.g. TransactionDetailActivity), the app may not have a back stack. Without TaskStackBuilder, pressing Back would exit the app instead of going to the expected parent screen. TaskStackBuilder.create(context).addNextIntentWithParentStack(targetIntent) constructs a synthetic back stack based on the Activity's parentActivityName in the manifest. This creates the full stack [HomeActivity → TransactionsActivity → TransactionDetailActivity] even if the app was cold-started from the notification.
Intermediate What security risk exists with exported Activities that have intent-filters?
Any app on the device can send an Intent to any exported component. If your exported Activity reads Intent extras and uses them (SQL queries, file paths, URLs), a malicious app can send crafted extras to cause SQL injection, path traversal, or open unintended URLs (deep link hijacking). Fix: always validate and sanitize data received from Intents. Use android:permission to restrict access. Keep non-public components exported="false". Audit all intent-filter declarations.
Intermediate What is FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION and when is it needed?
When you share a file via FileProvider (content:// URI), the receiving app doesn't normally have permission to read from your app's content provider. FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION grants the target app temporary read access to that specific URI. Without it, the receiving app gets "Permission Denied". Used in ACTION_SEND with EXTRA_STREAM for file sharing, and when opening files in third-party viewers.
Senior/Scenario [Scenario] Your FCM notification deep link opens the correct screen but pressing Back takes the user to an empty app/Home screen instead of the expected parent screens. How do you fix it?
Use TaskStackBuilder to construct a proper back stack for the notification PendingIntent. Declare parentActivityName in the manifest for each Activity's logical parent.
// Manifest
<activity android:name=".TransactionDetailActivity"
          android:parentActivityName=".TransactionsListActivity" />

// PendingIntent creation
val pendingIntent = TaskStackBuilder.create(context).apply {
    addNextIntentWithParentStack(
        Intent(context, TransactionDetailActivity::class.java)
            .putExtra("txId", txId)
    )
}.getPendingIntent(
    txId.hashCode(),
    PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE
)
Now pressing Back from TransactionDetailActivity goes to TransactionsListActivity (which goes to HomeActivity), matching the expected navigation flow.
Senior/Scenario [Coding] Implement file sharing via FileProvider in a banking app (share PDF statement). 
// 1. Provider declared in manifest
<provider
    android:name="androidx.core.content.FileProvider"
    android:authorities="com.mybank.app.fileprovider"
    android:exported="false"
    android:grantUriPermissions="true">
    <meta-data
        android:name="android.support.FILE_PROVIDER_PATHS"
        android:resource="@xml/file_paths" />
</provider>

// 2. res/xml/file_paths.xml
// <files-path name="statements" path="statements/" />

// 3. Sharing code
fun shareStatement(statementFile: File) {
    val uri = FileProvider.getUriForFile(
        context,
        "com.mybank.app.fileprovider",
        statementFile
    )
    val intent = Intent(Intent.ACTION_SEND).apply {
        type = "application/pdf"
        putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_STREAM, uri)
        addFlags(Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION)  // ✅ critical
    }
    context.startActivity(Intent.createChooser(intent, "Share statement"))
}
Senior/Scenario [Debug] Your app crashes with TransactionTooLargeException when navigating to a product detail screen. What is the root cause and fix?
Root cause: An oversized object (likely a Bitmap, large List, or Parcelable with many fields) is being passed via Intent extras. Intent extras are transmitted through the Binder IPC buffer which has a ~1 MB limit across the entire transaction queue.

Fix: Never pass large objects via Intent extras. Pass only an ID or key and load the data in the destination:
// ❌ Bad
intent.putExtra("product", product)  // large Parcelable

// ✅ Good — pass only the ID
intent.putExtra("productId", product.id)
// Load full product in destination ViewModel using the ID
For shared ViewModel patterns (single-activity), the data is already in memory — no need to pass it via Intent at all.

Answer Key Summary

  • Can you explain explicit vs implicit Intent in one clear sentence each?
  • Can you explain PendingIntent and FLAG_IMMUTABLE requirement?
  • Can you implement TaskStackBuilder for notification deep links?
  • Do you know when to use App Links vs deep links?
  • Can you diagnose and fix TransactionTooLargeException?
