5D — Cancellation & Exceptions

Cooperative cancellation, CancellationException, isActive/ensureActive/yield, NonCancellable, exception propagation, CoroutineExceptionHandler, SupervisorJob — everything about keeping coroutines safe.

ID: 5D ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

Cooperative cancellation

Coroutines can only be cancelled at suspension points. Code between suspension points runs to completion — you cannot interrupt a tight CPU loop from outside. The coroutine must actively check for cancellation.

  • isActive — check in tight loops: while (isActive) { ... }
  • ensureActive() — throws CancellationException if not active; use at loop top
  • yield() — checks cancellation AND yields control to other coroutines (fairness)
  • delay() — any suspension point, checks cancellation automatically

CancellationException is special

CancellationException is a subclass of IllegalStateException but is treated specially — it is not a failure from the structured concurrency perspective. It propagates downward only and does NOT cancel the parent. Catch it carefully.

⚙
2. How It Works

Cancellation check mechanisms

// 1. isActive — manual check, no exception thrown
while (isActive) {
    processItem(queue.poll())
}

// 2. ensureActive() — throws CancellationException if cancelled
for (item in items) {
    ensureActive()           // check at top of loop
    processItem(item)
}

// 3. yield() — checks + gives up thread for other coroutines
for (item in items) {
    yield()                   // check + fairness
    processItem(item)
}

// 4. Any suspend function (delay, withContext) checks automatically
for (item in items) {
    delay(0)                  // zero-delay still checks cancellation
    processItem(item)
}

NonCancellable — for cleanup work

// Problem: finally blocks run in cancelled coroutine context
// Suspend calls in finally fail with CancellationException
try {
    doWork()
} finally {
    // This throws if coroutine is cancelled:
    delay(100)            // ❌ CancellationException thrown
    db.closeConnection()  // ❌ Never reached
}

// Fix: withContext(NonCancellable) for cleanup
try {
    doWork()
} finally {
    withContext(NonCancellable) {
        delay(100)           // ✅ runs even if cancelled
        db.closeConnection() // ✅ cleanup completes
    }
}

CoroutineExceptionHandler

val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { context, exception ->
    Timber.e(exception, "Unhandled in ${context[CoroutineName]}")
    // Log to Crashlytics, show error UI, etc.
}

// Handler must be on the ROOT coroutine (not a child)
val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main + handler)
scope.launch {              // root — handler fires here
    launch {               // child — handler does NOT fire here
        throw IOException()  // propagates to root launch
    }
}

// ⚠️ Handler does NOT catch exceptions from async { }.await()
// Those must be caught with try/catch around await()

Exception propagation rules

ScenarioBehaviour
launch throws, regular Job parentException propagates to parent → cancels all siblings → crashes scope
launch throws, SupervisorJob parentException goes to CoroutineExceptionHandler → siblings unaffected
async throws, not awaitedException stored in Deferred — nothing happens yet
async throws, .await() calledException re-thrown at await() site — catch it there
CancellationException thrownNever treated as failure — scope NOT cancelled
🕑
3. When to Use

Cancellation pattern guide

SituationUse
Tight CPU loop that should be cancellableensureActive() or yield() at top of iteration
Cleanup (close socket, commit to DB) after cancellationfinally { withContext(NonCancellable) { ... } }
Catch all unhandled exceptions from root coroutinesCoroutineExceptionHandler on scope
Catch exceptions from asynctry/catch around .await()
Treat partial failures as oksupervisorScope + per-child try/catch
🏭
4. Production Example

E-commerce: resilient order processing

class OrderProcessor(
    private val ioDispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO
) {
    private val exceptionHandler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e ->
        if (e is CancellationException) return@CoroutineExceptionHandler
        Crashlytics.log(e)
        alertOpsTeam(e)
    }

    private val scope = CoroutineScope(
        SupervisorJob() + ioDispatcher + exceptionHandler
    )

    fun processOrders(orders: List<Order>) {
        scope.launch {
            for (order in orders) {
                ensureActive()  // check before each order
                try {
                    processOrder(order)
                } catch (e: OrderException) {
                    markFailed(order, e)   // one failure → next order
                }
            }
        }
    }

    private suspend fun processOrder(order: Order) {
        try {
            withContext(ioDispatcher) {
                paymentService.charge(order)
                inventoryService.reserve(order)
            }
        } finally {
            // Cleanup runs even if this coroutine is cancelled
            withContext(NonCancellable) {
                auditLog.record(order)    // audit must complete
            }
        }
    }

    fun cancel() = scope.cancel()
}

try/catch and CancellationException — critical rule

// ❌ WRONG: catching Exception swallows CancellationException
try {
    longRunningOp()
} catch (e: Exception) {
    log(e)  // CancellationException caught and dropped!
    // Coroutine continues running after cancel() — LEAK
}

// ✅ CORRECT: re-throw CancellationException
try {
    longRunningOp()
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e   // always re-throw
} catch (e: Exception) {
    handleError(e)
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs
PatternWhen to useCaveat
try/catch around await()Handle async failures inlineMust re-throw CancellationException
CoroutineExceptionHandlerGlobal catch-all for root coroutinesOnly works on root; not child coroutines; not async
runCatching { }Wrap suspend call, get Result<T>Also catches CancellationException — must check
supervisorScopeIndependent child failuresEach child still needs its own handler
runCatching Gotcha
runCatching { suspendFn() } catches ALL exceptions including CancellationException. This is dangerous: the coroutine appears to have been cancelled but the exception is trapped in a Result.Failure. Always check: result.exceptionOrNull()?.let { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Tight loop without cancellation check
A CPU-intensive loop with no suspension points is not cancellable. Even if you call job.cancel(), the coroutine keeps running until the loop finishes. Fix: add ensureActive() or yield() inside the loop.
Pitfall 2 — Catching CancellationException
Catching Exception or Throwable and not re-throwing will swallow CancellationException, breaking cooperative cancellation — the coroutine continues running after cancel() is called.
Pitfall 3 — Using CoroutineExceptionHandler on child coroutines
CoroutineExceptionHandler only fires on root coroutines (those whose parent is a Job without a coroutine parent, e.g. scope.launch). Adding it to a child launch { } has no effect — exceptions still propagate to the parent.
Best Practice — Always use NonCancellable for critical cleanup
Any suspend call in a finally block needs withContext(NonCancellable) { }. This includes: closing network connections, committing database transactions, writing audit logs, sending analytics events.
🎯
7. Interview Framework

30-second answer

"Coroutine cancellation is cooperative — it only happens at suspension points. The coroutine receives a CancellationException which must be propagated, not swallowed. For non-cancellable cleanup like closing connections, wrap suspend calls in withContext(NonCancellable) inside finally blocks. For unhandled exceptions from root coroutines, use CoroutineExceptionHandler."

2-minute answer

"Cancellation works by marking the Job as cancelling and throwing CancellationException at the next suspension point. This means a tight CPU loop without suspension is not cancellable — you need to add ensureActive() or yield() checks. CancellationException is special: it's not treated as a failure by the parent Job, so cancellation is a clean lifecycle event, not an error.

The most dangerous mistake is catching Exception and not re-throwing CancellationException — this breaks cancellation entirely, causing coroutine leaks.

For cleanup after cancellation, wrap suspend calls in withContext(NonCancellable) — this creates a context that ignores cancellation, allowing your cleanup to complete. For application-level error handling, put a CoroutineExceptionHandler on your root scope — not on child coroutines, where it has no effect."

Must-mention points

1
Cooperative cancellation — only happens at suspension points
2
Always re-throw CancellationException — never swallow it
3
NonCancellable for cleanup — finally block suspend calls need this
4
CoroutineExceptionHandler = root only — no effect on child coroutines or async
5
ensureActive() / yield() — add to tight loops for cancellability

Follow-up Q&A

Q: "What is the difference between ensureActive() and yield()?"

A: Both throw CancellationException if the coroutine is cancelled. ensureActive() only checks — no suspension, no thread switch. yield() also suspends briefly, giving other coroutines a chance to run — provides fairness in the thread pool. Use ensureActive() for tight loops where you just want cancellability; use yield() when the work is heavy and you want to be a good citizen in the coroutine pool.

Q: "Where does CoroutineExceptionHandler fit vs try/catch?"

A: CoroutineExceptionHandler is the "last resort" for exceptions that escape the coroutine hierarchy — like an UncaughtExceptionHandler for threads. It's for logging/reporting, not for recovery. For recoverable errors, use try/catch locally. For async results, use try/catch around .await(). The handler only fires on root coroutines inside a scope.

Senior insight

Senior Insight
In an automotive app processing continuous sensor streams, every processing loop must have ensureActive(). When the car park scenario ends, the system scope is cancelled — without this check, the sensor processor would continue consuming CPU and battery on a dead screen. This is the difference between a battery-draining app and a well-behaved one.
📋
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Cancellation checks

isActive       // check, no throw
ensureActive() // throw if cancelled
yield()        // throw + yield CPU
delay(0)       // also checks

CancellationException rules

// ALWAYS re-throw it!
catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e  // never swallow
}
catch (e: Exception) { handle() }

NonCancellable cleanup

finally {
  withContext(NonCancellable) {
    db.close()    // suspend ok
    audit.log()   // suspend ok
  }
}

ExceptionHandler scope

// ✅ Root coroutine — fires
scope.launch(handler) { throw E() }

// ❌ Child coroutine — no effect
scope.launch {
  launch(handler) { throw E() }
}
❓
9. Interview Questions
What does "cooperative cancellation" mean in coroutines?
Basic⌄
Cancellation is cooperative — the coroutine is not forcefully stopped; instead, calling cancel() marks the Job as cancelling and throws CancellationException at the next suspension point. Code between suspension points runs to completion. If a coroutine has no suspension points (e.g., a tight CPU loop), it cannot be cancelled unless you add explicit checks like ensureActive().
What is CancellationException and how should you handle it?
Basic⌄
CancellationException is a subclass of IllegalStateException used to signal cooperative cancellation. It should always be re-thrown when caught. Catching it with a broad catch (e: Exception) and not rethrowing breaks cancellation — the coroutine continues running after being cancelled. Rule: catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } always comes first.
When would you use withContext(NonCancellable)?
Basic⌄
When you need to run suspend calls inside a finally block after a coroutine has been cancelled. Normally, any suspension inside a cancelled coroutine throws CancellationException immediately, preventing cleanup. withContext(NonCancellable) overrides this, letting cleanup code (close connections, audit logs, commit transactions) complete even in a cancelled coroutine.
A tight data processing loop is not responding to cancel(). Why and how do you fix it?
Intermediate⌄
The loop has no suspension points — cancellation can only happen at suspension points. Fix: add ensureActive() at the top of each iteration (checks and throws CancellationException if cancelled) or yield() (also yields the thread to other coroutines). For example: for (item in items) { ensureActive(); process(item) }. Both options make the loop respect cancellation.
Where should you place CoroutineExceptionHandler — on the scope, root coroutine, or child coroutine?
Intermediate⌄
On the scope or root coroutine — never on a child coroutine. The handler only fires when an exception has propagated all the way up to the root of the coroutine hierarchy (a coroutine whose parent context is a bare Job, not another coroutine). Adding it to a child launch has no effect — the exception still propagates to the parent.
Does CoroutineExceptionHandler catch exceptions from async { }.await()?
Intermediate⌄
No. The handler only catches exceptions from launch-based coroutines. Exceptions from async { }.await() are re-thrown at the await() call site and must be caught with try/catch there. This is a common misconception — developers add a handler expecting it to catch all errors, but async failures still require local handling.
What is the danger of using runCatching with suspend functions?
Intermediate⌄
runCatching catches ALL exceptions, including CancellationException. If used inside a coroutine, it may silently trap a cancellation signal, breaking cooperative cancellation. The coroutine would continue executing as if nothing happened. Workaround: after calling runCatching, check if the result contains a CancellationException and re-throw it: result.exceptionOrNull()?.let { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }.
Design cancellation-safe order processing for a banking app that must always write an audit log, even when cancelled.
Senior⌄
Structure the processing as: try { processPayment(order) } catch (e: CancellationException) { markOrderCancelled(order); throw e } catch (e: Exception) { markOrderFailed(order, e) } finally { withContext(NonCancellable) { auditLog.write(order) } }. The finally with NonCancellable guarantees the audit log is written regardless of outcome. Re-throwing CancellationException after marking the order cancelled ensures structured concurrency still works. The catch for Exception handles business failures gracefully without breaking cancellation.
Explain why a coroutine can appear "stuck" even after calling scope.cancel().
Senior⌄
Three root causes: (1) The coroutine is in a tight loop with no suspension points — cancellation can't be delivered. Fix: add ensureActive(). (2) The code caught CancellationException and didn't rethrow — the coroutine thinks it's still running normally. Fix: always rethrow CancellationException. (3) The coroutine holds a NonCancellable context from a misused withContext(NonCancellable) not just in finally — if wrapped around a long operation, cancellation is indefinitely blocked. Fix: use NonCancellable only in finally blocks.
What is the difference between ensureActive() and yield() and when would you choose each?
Senior⌄
ensureActive() only checks the cancellation flag and throws CancellationException if cancelled — no suspension, no thread yield. It has minimal overhead and is ideal for high-speed loops that must remain cancellable but should not voluntarily give up the CPU. yield() also throws on cancellation but additionally suspends the coroutine, allowing other coroutines on the same dispatcher to run. Use yield() in CPU-heavy loops that run on a limited pool (Default) where fairness matters — without it, a single heavy coroutine can starve others on the same thread.

5E — Scopes, Concurrency & Testing

lifecycleScope, viewModelScope, custom scopes. Race conditions with Mutex/Semaphore/AtomicInteger. runTest, StandardTestDispatcher vs UnconfinedTestDispatcher, virtual time control.

ID: 5E ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

Lifecycle-aware scopes

  • viewModelScope — tied to ViewModel lifecycle; SupervisorJob + Dispatchers.Main.immediate; auto-cancelled on onCleared()
  • lifecycleScope — tied to Lifecycle owner (Activity/Fragment); auto-cancelled on DESTROYED state
  • repeatOnLifecycle(State.STARTED) — collect flows only when UI is visible; re-launches on STARTED, cancels on STOPPED

Concurrency primitives

  • Mutex — coroutine-aware lock; mutex.withLock { }; suspends instead of blocks
  • Semaphore — limits concurrent access to N coroutines at a time
  • AtomicInteger / AtomicLong — lock-free atomic operations for simple counters

Testing

  • runTest — replaces runBlocking for tests; uses virtual time
  • StandardTestDispatcher — coroutines don't start until you advance time or call idle
  • UnconfinedTestDispatcher — coroutines run eagerly (like Unconfined)
⚙
2. Scopes & Lifecycle

viewModelScope and lifecycleScope

// viewModelScope: auto-cancelled when ViewModel is cleared
class CartViewModel : ViewModel() {
    fun addItem(item: Item) {
        viewModelScope.launch {   // SupervisorJob + Main
            cartRepo.add(item)
        }
    }
}

// lifecycleScope: auto-cancelled on DESTROYED
class CartFragment : Fragment() {
    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, saved: Bundle?) {
        // repeatOnLifecycle: starts on STARTED, cancels on STOPPED
        // Re-starts on STARTED again — safe for background/foreground
        viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
            viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycle.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                viewModel.state.collect { state ->
                    render(state)   // only runs when UI is visible
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

Custom CoroutineScope

// For Repositories or Services not tied to ViewModel
class SyncService(
    private val ioDispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO
) {
    private val job = SupervisorJob()
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(job + ioDispatcher)

    fun startSync() { scope.launch { doSync() } }
    fun stop() { job.cancel() }
}
⚠
3. Race Conditions & Synchronisation

The problem: concurrent state mutation

// ❌ Race condition: multiple coroutines updating shared state
var counter = 0
repeat(1000) {
    viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
        counter++  // NOT atomic! Result: < 1000
    }
}

Mutex — coroutine-aware lock

private val mutex = Mutex()
var counter = 0

repeat(1000) {
    viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
        mutex.withLock {   // suspends other coroutines waiting for lock
            counter++       // safe: only one coroutine at a time
        }
    }
}
// Result: exactly 1000 — guaranteed

Semaphore — limit concurrent access

// Limit concurrent API calls to 3 (rate limiting)
val semaphore = Semaphore(3)

suspend fun fetchWithRateLimit(id: String) {
    semaphore.withPermit {   // blocks if 3 already active
        api.fetch(id)
    }
}

AtomicInteger — lock-free counter

// For simple increment/decrement without lock overhead
private val requestCount = AtomicInteger(0)

suspend fun trackRequest() {
    requestCount.incrementAndGet()  // lock-free, thread-safe
    try { makeRequest() }
    finally { requestCount.decrementAndGet() }
}
ToolUse caseSuspends?Lock-free?
MutexExclusive access to shared stateYesNo
Semaphore(n)Limit concurrent access to NYesNo
AtomicIntegerSimple counter, flagNoYes
Single-thread dispatcherConfine state to one threadNoYes
📋
4. Testing Coroutines

runTest — virtual time

import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*

@Test
fun `retry after delay works`() = runTest {
    // runTest uses TestCoroutineScheduler — virtual time
    // delay(5000) completes instantly in runTest!
    val result = withTimeout(6000) {
        fetchWithRetry()  // internally delay(5000) on each retry
    }
    assertEquals("success", result)
    // Real time elapsed: < 10ms
}

StandardTestDispatcher — manual time control

@Test
fun `loading state transitions`() = runTest {
    val testDispatcher = StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)
    val viewModel = MyViewModel(testDispatcher)

    viewModel.load()
    // Coroutine queued but NOT yet started (StandardTestDispatcher)
    assertEquals(UiState.Loading, viewModel.state.value)

    advanceUntilIdle()   // run all pending coroutines to completion
    assertEquals(UiState.Success(mockData()), viewModel.state.value)
}

UnconfinedTestDispatcher — eager execution

@Test
fun `flow collection`() = runTest(UnconfinedTestDispatcher()) {
    // UnconfinedTestDispatcher: coroutines run eagerly on current thread
    // Great for testing flows — collection starts immediately
    val results = mutableListOf<Int>()
    val job = launch {
        viewModel.countFlow.collect { results.add(it) }
    }
    viewModel.increment()
    viewModel.increment()
    assertEquals(listOf(0, 1, 2), results)
    job.cancel()
}

advanceTimeBy vs advanceUntilIdle

FunctionEffectUse when
advanceUntilIdle()Runs all pending coroutines + delaysFinal assertion — all work done
advanceTimeBy(ms)Fast-forwards virtual clock by msTesting time-sensitive delays
runCurrent()Runs pending coroutines without advancing timeChecking intermediate states
🏭
5. Production Example

Banking: rate-limited concurrent transfers with testing

// Production code
class TransferQueue(
    private val ioDispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO
) {
    private val semaphore = Semaphore(5)  // max 5 concurrent transfers
    private val completedCount = AtomicInteger(0)
    private val stateMutex = Mutex()
    private val pendingTransfers = mutableListOf<Transfer>()

    suspend fun enqueue(transfer: Transfer) {
        stateMutex.withLock { pendingTransfers.add(transfer) }
    }

    suspend fun processAll() = coroutineScope {
        val snapshot = stateMutex.withLock { pendingTransfers.toList() }
        snapshot.forEach { transfer ->
            launch(ioDispatcher) {
                semaphore.withPermit {       // limit concurrency
                    executeTransfer(transfer)
                    completedCount.incrementAndGet()
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

// Test
@Test
fun `processAll completes all transfers`() = runTest {
    val testDispatcher = StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)
    val queue = TransferQueue(testDispatcher)
    val fakeApi = FakeTransferApi()  // delays 100ms per transfer

    repeat(10) { queue.enqueue(Transfer(it)) }
    val job = launch { queue.processAll() }

    advanceTimeBy(100)    // first batch of 5 complete (semaphore)
    assertEquals(5, queue.completedCount.get())

    advanceUntilIdle()   // remaining 5 complete
    assertEquals(10, queue.completedCount.get())
    job.join()
}
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Mutex deadlock
Never call mutex.withLock from inside another mutex.withLock on the same Mutex. Unlike Java's reentrant locks, Kotlin's Mutex is NOT reentrant — it will deadlock.
Pitfall 2 — repeatOnLifecycle vs launchWhenStarted
launchWhenStarted (deprecated) pauses collection but does NOT cancel the upstream flow — the producer keeps emitting. repeatOnLifecycle cancels and re-starts the entire collector, stopping the upstream producer. Always use repeatOnLifecycle.
Pitfall 3 — runTest vs runBlocking in tests
Using runBlocking in tests runs coroutines with real time — delay(5000) waits 5 real seconds. Use runTest which uses virtual time — all delays are skipped unless you explicitly advance.
Best Practice — Prefer single-thread confinement over Mutex for state
Instead of Mutex, confine mutable state to a single-threaded dispatcher: val stateDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1). All reads/writes happen on one thread — no locks needed, no deadlock risk.
🎯
7. Interview Framework

30-second answer

"For lifecycle-aware coroutines, viewModelScope ties to ViewModel.onCleared() and lifecycleScope ties to the Lifecycle DESTROYED state. For race conditions, coroutines have Mutex for exclusive access, Semaphore for rate limiting, and AtomicInteger for lock-free counters. For tests, runTest uses virtual time so delays are free, and you control execution with advanceUntilIdle() or advanceTimeBy()."

2-minute answer

"viewModelScope uses SupervisorJob + Dispatchers.Main.immediate, so it starts immediately on the main thread. lifecycleScope tied to a Fragment should use viewLifecycleOwner, not the Fragment itself — the Fragment outlives its view. For flow collection in Fragments, always use repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED), which cancels and re-creates the collector as the app goes to background/foreground. launchWhenStarted is deprecated because it doesn't cancel the upstream.

For concurrency safety: Mutex is the coroutine-native lock — it suspends instead of blocking. For simple counters, AtomicInteger is lock-free and more efficient. For rate limiting concurrent API calls, Semaphore(n) is the clean solution.

For testing: runTest gives a virtual clock, StandardTestDispatcher queues coroutines without running them (so you can assert Loading state), UnconfinedTestDispatcher runs eagerly for flow tests."

Must-mention points

1
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope in Fragments — not this
2
repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) cancels upstream; launchWhenStarted does not
3
Mutex is NOT reentrant — deadlock if called twice on same lock
4
runTest = virtual time; StandardTestDispatcher = manual; UnconfinedTestDispatcher = eager
5
Inject dispatchers — use TestDispatcher in tests

Follow-up Q&A

Q: "Why use viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope instead of lifecycleScope in a Fragment?"

A: Fragments can be detached and re-attached without being destroyed. The Fragment's own lifecycleScope lives until the Fragment is destroyed. But the view is destroyed on back-stack. If you use this.lifecycleScope (the Fragment), view-accessing coroutines survive the view destruction, causing NullPointerExceptions. viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope is cancelled when the view is destroyed — the safe choice.

Q: "StandardTestDispatcher vs UnconfinedTestDispatcher?"

A: StandardTestDispatcher queues coroutines and doesn't start them until you advance time. This lets you assert intermediate states like Loading before the data arrives. UnconfinedTestDispatcher runs coroutines eagerly on the current thread — good for flow collection tests where you just want to verify emissions.

Senior insight

Senior Insight
In production, prefer state confinement over Mutex wherever possible. If all mutations to shared state go through a Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1) dispatcher, you get thread-safety without locks, no deadlock risk, and better performance. Mutex should be reserved for cases where you need to atomically read+modify+write across suspension points.
📋
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Scope summary

viewModelScope: SupervisorJob+Main
              cancelled in onCleared()
lifecycleScope: cancelled in DESTROYED
  → always use viewLifecycleOwner
repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) for flows

UnconfinedTest→ eager, runs inline

Test template

@Test fun test() = runTest {
  val vm = ViewModel(
    StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler))
  vm.load()
  assertEquals(Loading, vm.state.value)
  advanceUntilIdle()
  assertEquals(Success, vm.state.value)
}
❓
9. Interview Questions
What is viewModelScope and when is it cancelled?
Basic⌄
viewModelScope is a CoroutineScope provided by the ViewModel Kotlin extension. It uses SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate. It's automatically cancelled when ViewModel.onCleared() is called — which happens when the ViewModel is no longer needed (e.g., the associated Fragment/Activity is permanently destroyed). This means all coroutines are cancelled automatically, preventing leaks.
Why should you use repeatOnLifecycle instead of launchWhenStarted?
Basic⌄
launchWhenStarted only pauses collection when the lifecycle goes below STARTED — the upstream flow still runs and produces values (wasting resources, potential memory buildup). repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) cancels the entire collection block when STOPPED and re-launches it when STARTED — fully stopping the producer. This is the correct pattern for lifecycle-aware collection.
What is a Mutex and how does it differ from Java's synchronized?
Basic⌄
Kotlin's Mutex is coroutine-aware — it suspends the waiting coroutine instead of blocking the thread. Java's synchronized blocks the OS thread. This means with Mutex, a waiting coroutine frees the thread for other coroutines to run. Important: Mutex is NOT reentrant — a coroutine that already holds the lock and tries to acquire it again will deadlock. Java's synchronized is reentrant by default.
What is the difference between StandardTestDispatcher and UnconfinedTestDispatcher?
Intermediate⌄
StandardTestDispatcher: coroutines are queued but don't execute until you explicitly advance time (advanceUntilIdle(), advanceTimeBy(), runCurrent()). This lets you assert intermediate states (e.g., Loading before data arrives). UnconfinedTestDispatcher: coroutines run eagerly on the current thread as soon as launched. Better for flow collection tests where you want emissions to be immediately available.
How would you limit concurrent API calls to a maximum of 5 at a time?
Intermediate⌄
Use Semaphore(5): val semaphore = Semaphore(5). Wrap each API call: semaphore.withPermit { api.call() }. When 5 calls are active, additional coroutines suspend at withPermit until a permit is released. This is cleaner than managing a custom counter and doesn't block threads — suspended coroutines free the thread while waiting.
How do you test a ViewModel that has a 3-second loading delay?
Intermediate⌄
Inject a test dispatcher: class MyViewModel(private val dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO). In the test: runTest { val vm = MyViewModel(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)); vm.load(); assertEquals(Loading, vm.state.value); advanceUntilIdle(); assertEquals(Success(...), vm.state.value) }. The 3-second delay is skipped by the virtual clock — test runs instantly.
Two coroutines are simultaneously trying to update a list. What is the safest approach?
Intermediate⌄
Three options, ordered by preference: (1) State confinement: use Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1) — all mutations go through a single-threaded dispatcher, no locks needed. (2) Mutex: mutex.withLock { list.add(item) } — suspends waiting coroutines without blocking threads. (3) Use StateFlow/Channel: emit updates through a single-writer flow, never mutate shared state directly. Option 1 is usually preferred for simplicity.
Design a test that verifies a ViewModel shows Loading → Error states when an API throws after 2 seconds.
Senior⌄
runTest { val dispatcher = StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler); val fakeRepo = FakeRepo { delay(2000); throw IOException() }; val vm = MyViewModel(fakeRepo, dispatcher); vm.load(); assertEquals(Loading, vm.state.value); advanceTimeBy(2000); runCurrent(); // process exception; assertEquals(Error("network"), vm.state.value) }. Key: advanceTimeBy(2000) moves the virtual clock forward, then runCurrent() processes the resulting exception handling. StandardTestDispatcher gives precise control over state transitions.
What is the difference between collectAsStateWithLifecycle() and collectAsState() in Compose?
Senior⌄
collectAsState() collects the flow as long as the Composition is active — it doesn't respect Android lifecycle. If the app goes to background, collection continues (wasting resources, potentially processing stale data). collectAsStateWithLifecycle() (from lifecycle-compose library) uses repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) semantics — collection pauses when the app goes to background and resumes when it returns. Always prefer collectAsStateWithLifecycle() in production Android apps.
You notice that your Mutex-protected code sometimes deadlocks in production. What are the root causes and how do you diagnose?
Senior⌄
Root causes: (1) Non-reentrant deadlock — a coroutine holding the mutex calls a function that also tries to acquire the same mutex. (2) Nested Mutex acquisition in wrong order across two mutexes (classic ABBA deadlock). (3) withLock block suspends (via suspend call) and another coroutine holding a different lock tries to acquire this one. Diagnosis: enable coroutine debug mode (-Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug), check thread dumps, look for coroutines in Waiting state at Mutex.lock(). Prevention: never call unknown suspend functions inside a locked block; prefer state confinement over Mutex.

6A — Flow Core

Cold Flow vs hot StateFlow vs hot SharedFlow. collect vs collectLatest. The definitive StateFlow vs SharedFlow vs LiveData comparison. Most-asked Flow questions.

ID: 6A ⭐ Tier 1 🔥 Highest Priority
🔍
1. Overview

Three Flow types

  • Flow<T> — cold: does nothing until collected; each collector gets its own independent execution; like a function that you call
  • StateFlow<T> — hot: always has a value; emits current state to new collectors immediately; single shared execution; like a property
  • SharedFlow<T> — hot: configurable replay buffer; multi-cast; for events like navigation, one-time UI messages; like a broadcast

Cold vs hot — the key mental model

Cold: the flow block runs fresh for each collector. Think of it as a lazy factory — no work until you call collect(). If two collectors subscribe, the upstream runs twice, independently.

Hot: the source runs regardless of collectors. A collector joining late gets the current/recent state. StateFlow and SharedFlow are hot — they exist independently of any collector.

Senior Mental Model
Flow = cold = pull model. StateFlow/SharedFlow = hot = push model. Repository functions should return cold Flow<T> (each collection triggers a new network/db request). ViewModels should expose hot StateFlow<UiState> (the current UI state always exists, new subscribers get it immediately without re-triggering the data source).
⚙
2. How It Works

Cold Flow — runs per collector

// Cold: each collect() runs the block independently
fun userFlow(): Flow<User> = flow {
    println("Fetching user...")  // runs for EACH collector
    val user = api.getUser()
    emit(user)
}

val f = userFlow()
// Nothing has run yet! No network call.
f.collect { println(it) }  // NOW fetches — prints "Fetching user..."
f.collect { println(it) }  // fetches AGAIN — second independent call

StateFlow — hot, always has value

// StateFlow: always has a value, replays current value to new collectors
private val _state = MutableStateFlow(UiState.Loading)
val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _state.asStateFlow()

// Collector 1 subscribes now — gets Loading immediately
state.collect { render(it) }

// 2 seconds later, data arrives:
_state.value = UiState.Success(data)

// Collector 2 subscribes NOW — gets Success immediately (current value)
state.collect { render(it) }  // gets Success(data) right away

// StateFlow uses equals() to deduplicate — won't emit same value twice
_state.value = UiState.Success(data)  // IGNORED if data == existing value

SharedFlow — hot, configurable

// SharedFlow: for one-time events (navigation, snackbar, dialogs)
private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<UiEvent>(
    replay = 0,         // no replay — events not re-sent to late collectors
    extraBufferCapacity = 1  // buffer 1 event if no collector
)
val events: SharedFlow<UiEvent> = _events.asSharedFlow()

fun showError(msg: String) {
    viewModelScope.launch {
        _events.emit(UiEvent.ShowSnackbar(msg))
    }
}

collect vs collectLatest

// collect: processes EVERY emission — blocks until lambda completes
flow.collect { value ->
    expensiveOperation(value)  // new value waits until this finishes
}

// collectLatest: cancels previous lambda when new emission arrives
flow.collectLatest { value ->
    delay(300)                   // if new value arrives during delay,
    expensiveOperation(value)  // this run is CANCELLED
}
// Use collectLatest for search queries — only process the latest input
⚖
3. StateFlow vs SharedFlow vs LiveData
FeatureFlowStateFlowSharedFlowLiveData
Hot or ColdColdHotHotHot
Always has valueNoYes (initial required)No (configurable)No (nullable)
Replay to new collectorsN/ALatest value (1)Configurable (0–n)Latest value
DeduplicationNoYes (equals())NoYes
Lifecycle awareNoNo (manual)No (manual)Yes (built-in)
Thread safeDependsYesYesYes (postValue)
Typical use caseRepository streamsUI state in ViewModelOne-time events, navigationLegacy UI state
Multiple collectorsIndependentShared (multicast)Shared (multicast)Shared
When to choose what
StateFlow: ViewModel UI state — always has a value, new subscribers see current state immediately.
SharedFlow: navigation commands, snackbars, dialogs — one-time events that should NOT be replayed on config change.
Flow: repository data streams, database queries (Room returns Flow), any data that should restart per collector.
LiveData: legacy code, or if you're not yet using Compose (even then, prefer StateFlow).
🏭
4. Production Example

E-commerce: product screen with state + events

class ProductViewModel(
    private val repo: ProductRepository
) : ViewModel() {

    // StateFlow: UI state (always has a value)
    private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow<ProductUiState>(ProductUiState.Loading)
    val uiState: StateFlow<ProductUiState> = _uiState.asStateFlow()

    // SharedFlow: one-time events (no replay)
    private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<ProductEvent>(extraBufferCapacity = 1)
    val events: SharedFlow<ProductEvent> = _events.asSharedFlow()

    fun loadProduct(id: String) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            // collectLatest: if a new load() is called while loading,
            // cancel the previous and start fresh
            repo.getProduct(id)  // returns cold Flow from Room
                .collect { product ->
                    _uiState.value = ProductUiState.Success(product)
                }
        }
    }

    fun addToCart(productId: String) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            try {
                cartRepo.add(productId)
                _events.emit(ProductEvent.ShowSnackbar("Added to cart"))
            } catch (e: Exception) {
                _events.emit(ProductEvent.ShowError(e.message!!))
            }
        }
    }
}

// Fragment collection (safe lifecycle)
override fun onViewCreated(view: View, saved: Bundle?) {
    viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
        viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycle.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
            launch { viewModel.uiState.collect { renderState(it) } }
            launch { viewModel.events.collect { handleEvent(it) } }
        }
    }
}
📊
5. Comparison Table

StateFlow vs SharedFlow — detailed

MutableStateFlowMutableSharedFlow
Initial valueRequiredNot required
Replay default1 (current value)0 (configurable)
Value access.value propertyNo value property
Equality checkUses equals() — deduplicatesNo deduplication
Good forUI state (boolean, data class)Events, navigation, commands
Config changeReplays current state to new collectorreplay=0 → events lost; replay=1 → replayed
BackpressureDrops old value (conflated)BufferOverflow strategy configurable
One-Time Events Pattern
For navigation/snackbar events, use SharedFlow(replay=0, extraBufferCapacity=1, onBufferOverflow=DROP_OLDEST). replay=0 means rotating the device won't replay the navigation event. extraBufferCapacity=1 means if no one is collecting (e.g., activity in background), one event is buffered rather than suspending the ViewModel.
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — StateFlow for events
Using StateFlow for one-time UI events (navigation, snackbar) causes the event to replay on configuration change — the user sees the navigation happen again or the snackbar re-appears. Use SharedFlow(replay=0) for events.
Pitfall 2 — Missing StateFlow deduplication
StateFlow uses equals() to check if a new value differs from the current. If your state class doesn't implement equals() correctly (e.g., a regular class, not a data class), StateFlow may silently drop updates. Always use data classes for state.
Pitfall 3 — Collecting Flow in ViewModel
Calling flow.collect { } inside a ViewModel is usually wrong — it creates an infinite suspension that never returns. Use stateIn() or shareIn() to convert a Flow to a StateFlow/SharedFlow that the ViewModel exposes. (See 6D for stateIn/shareIn.)
Best Practice — Expose StateFlow, not MutableStateFlow
Always expose the read-only StateFlow<T> interface: val state: StateFlow<T> = _state.asStateFlow(). The UI should never mutate state directly. Only the ViewModel mutates via _state.value = ... or _state.update { ... }.
🎯
7. Interview Framework

30-second answer

"Flow is cold — it does nothing until collected, and each collector gets its own execution. StateFlow is hot — it always has a current value and replays it to new collectors; perfect for ViewModel UI state. SharedFlow is hot with configurable replay — for one-time events like navigation where replay=0 prevents re-triggering on config change."

2-minute answer

"The cold vs hot distinction is fundamental. Cold Flow is a factory — calling collect() triggers a fresh execution, so two collectors each trigger their own network/database call. This is correct for repositories. Hot StateFlow/SharedFlow exist independently of collectors — they have ongoing state.

StateFlow is specifically designed for UI state: it requires an initial value, uses equals() deduplication so the same state isn't re-rendered, and always replays the current value to new subscribers. When Compose recomposition happens or a Fragment is re-attached, it immediately gets the current state without triggering a new data fetch.

SharedFlow is for events — things that happen once. For navigation commands, set replay=0 so a device rotation doesn't re-navigate. For the collect vs collectLatest choice: use collectLatest for search — cancel processing the previous query when a new keystroke arrives."

Must-mention points

1
Cold Flow: each collector triggers fresh execution; hot StateFlow/SharedFlow: shared execution
2
StateFlow deduplicates using equals() — data class states are required
3
SharedFlow replay=0 for events — prevents replay on config change
4
collectLatest cancels previous when new emission arrives — use for search/debounce
5
Always expose StateFlow (not MutableStateFlow) from ViewModel

Follow-up Q&A

Q: "When would you use SharedFlow over StateFlow?"

A: When the data represents an event, not state. State = what the UI should currently show (always relevant, can be replayed). Event = something that happened once (navigation, show snackbar, play sound — should not re-happen on config change). SharedFlow with replay=0 models this correctly; StateFlow would re-trigger the event every time a new subscriber joins.

Q: "How does StateFlow handle equals()?"

A: StateFlow uses structural equality (==) to decide whether to emit. If the new value equals the current value, the emission is dropped. For data classes, this is automatic. For custom classes without equals(), all updates emit. This deduplication is important for performance — you don't want to recompose the UI for an identical state.

Senior insight

Senior Insight
In banking apps where UI state includes balance data, StateFlow deduplication can cause bugs if the balance wrapper doesn't override equals() correctly. A data class BalanceState(val amount: BigDecimal, val lastUpdated: Instant) — even if amount hasn't changed, a new lastUpdated will trigger a re-render. Design state classes carefully: include only data that should trigger a render when it changes.
📋
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Flow types

Flow<T>      cold  each collector fresh
StateFlow<T> hot   always has value
SharedFlow<T>hot   configurable replay

StateFlow pattern

private val _state = MutableStateFlow(Loading)
val state: StateFlow<T> = _state.asStateFlow()
// Update:
_state.value = Success(data)
_state.update { it.copy(loading=false) }

MutableSharedFlow<Event>(
  replay = 0,           // no replay
  extraBufferCapacity=1 // buffer 1
)

collect        // process all, sequential
collectLatest  // cancel previous on new emit
               // use for: search, debounce
❓
9. Interview Questions
What is the difference between a cold and hot Flow?
Basic⌄
Cold Flow: the block runs fresh for each collector — nothing executes until collect() is called. Each collector gets its own independent execution. Hot Flow (StateFlow/SharedFlow): runs independently of collectors, always producing values. New collectors get the current/recent values without triggering a new execution.
What is StateFlow and what makes it different from a regular Flow?
Basic⌄
StateFlow is a hot flow that always holds a current value (requires an initial value). It replays the current value to every new subscriber. It uses equals() to deduplicate — if you set the same value again, no emission occurs. Unlike regular Flow, it's multicast — multiple collectors share one execution. It's the recommended ViewModel UI state holder in Android.
When would you use SharedFlow instead of StateFlow?
Basic⌄
Use SharedFlow for one-time events that should not be replayed on configuration changes: navigation commands, showing snackbars, triggering dialogs, playing sounds. With replay=0, rotating the device won't re-trigger the event. StateFlow would replay the current value to every new collector — wrong for events.
What is the difference between collect and collectLatest?
Intermediate⌄
collect processes every emission sequentially — if the lambda takes time, the next emission waits. collectLatest cancels the current lambda when a new emission arrives and starts fresh with the new value. Use collectLatest for search queries (only process the latest keystroke), live updates where only the freshest value matters.
Why should you always use data classes for StateFlow state objects?
Intermediate⌄
StateFlow uses equals() for deduplication. Data classes auto-generate structural equals() — two instances with the same fields are equal, so updating state to the same values won't trigger unnecessary recompositions. Regular classes don't override equals(), so every assignment emits even if nothing changed, causing unnecessary UI updates. Also, data classes support copy() for immutable updates.
A cold Flow is collected from two places in the UI simultaneously. What happens?
Intermediate⌄
Each collector starts an independent execution of the flow's block — two network/database calls happen. This is correct for some use cases (e.g., two independent widgets both need the latest price) but often undesirable (duplicate network calls, inconsistent data). The fix is to convert the cold Flow to a hot StateFlow using stateIn() in the ViewModel — then both collectors share one upstream execution.
Why should you expose StateFlow<T> instead of MutableStateFlow<T> from a ViewModel?
Intermediate⌄
Encapsulation. MutableStateFlow exposes .value as settable — any code that gets the reference can modify state. This breaks the UDF (Unidirectional Data Flow) principle where state should only flow down from the ViewModel. Expose val state: StateFlow<T> = _state.asStateFlow() — read-only, the UI can only observe, never write.
Your ViewModel navigation event fires twice after a screen rotation. What is the root cause and fix?
Senior⌄
Root cause: the event is stored in a StateFlow or a SharedFlow with replay > 0. After rotation, the new collector immediately receives the last emitted event and triggers navigation again. Fix: use MutableSharedFlow(replay=0) for events. replay=0 means new collectors don't receive past events. Also ensure collection is inside repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) so the collector is recreated, not just a stale collector receiving past buffered events.
Compare StateFlow with LiveData — when would you still use LiveData in 2024?
Senior⌄
StateFlow advantages over LiveData: fully coroutine-native, no Android framework dependency (testable without AndroidX), richer operator chain (map, filter, combine), works with Flow operators. LiveData advantages: built-in lifecycle awareness (no repeatOnLifecycle boilerplate), automatic dispatch to main thread. In 2024, prefer StateFlow + collectAsStateWithLifecycle() for all new code. LiveData is acceptable in legacy XML-view code where the automatic lifecycle handling reduces boilerplate, or in Room queries that you don't want to migrate.
Design the state and event architecture for a checkout screen that has: loading state, form validation errors, a payment processing state, and a navigation-to-confirmation event.
Senior⌄
Use a sealed state class in StateFlow: sealed class CheckoutState { object Loading; data class Form(val errors: List<Error>, val isSubmitting: Boolean); object Success }. For navigation event: SharedFlow<CheckoutEvent>(replay=0, extraBufferCapacity=1) where CheckoutEvent.NavigateToConfirmation(orderId). The distinction: state represents what the screen should currently show (StateFlow replaying current state on rotation is correct). Navigation event should NOT replay — use SharedFlow replay=0 to prevent duplicate navigation after rotation.

6B — Flow Operators

Transforming, combining, flatMapping, timing, error handling, and lifecycle operators. Production examples for each. flatMapConcat vs flatMapMerge vs flatMapLatest comparison.

ID: 6B ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

Operator categories

  • Transforming: map, filter, transform — change the data in the stream
  • Combining: combine, zip, merge — merge multiple flows into one
  • FlatMapping: flatMapConcat, flatMapMerge, flatMapLatest — map each value to a new Flow
  • Timing: debounce, sample, throttle, distinctUntilChanged — control emission rate
  • Error handling: catch, retry, retryWhen — handle upstream errors
  • Lifecycle: onStart, onCompletion, onEach — side effects in the chain
Mental Model
Flow operators are lazy — they don't execute until collect() is called. Each operator creates a new Flow that wraps the upstream. Think of the chain as a pipeline declaration, not execution. The entire chain runs when collected.
⚙
2. Transform & Filter
// map: transform each value
repo.getPrices()                  // Flow<RawPrice>
    .map { raw -> formatPrice(raw) } // Flow<String>
    .collect { displayPrice(it) }

// filter: drop values that don't match predicate
transactionFlow
    .filter { it.amount > BigDecimal.ZERO }  // only positive
    .collect { showTransaction(it) }

// transform: most flexible — can emit multiple values or skip
userFlow
    .transform { user ->
        if (user.isVerified) {
            emit(user)                  // emit the user
            emit(user.copy(cached = true)) // emit modified copy
        }
        // if not verified: emit nothing (skip)
    }
    .collect { handleUser(it) }

// mapNotNull: map + filter null results
eventFlow
    .mapNotNull { event -> event as? PaymentEvent }
    .collect { handlePayment(it) }
📊
3. Combining Flows

combine — emit when any source changes

// combine: re-emits when EITHER source emits (uses latest from other)
val searchFlow: Flow<String> = searchInput.asFlow()
val filterFlow: Flow<FilterOptions> = activeFilters

searchFlow.combine(filterFlow) { query, filters ->
    repo.search(query, filters)
}.collect { results -> showResults(results) }
// If user types OR changes filter → new search triggered

zip — pair values one-to-one

// zip: pairs emissions 1:1, waits for BOTH to emit
val namesFlow = flowOf("Alice", "Bob", "Carol")
val scoresFlow = flowOf(95, 87, 92)

namesFlow.zip(scoresFlow) { name, score ->
    "$name: $score"
}.collect { println(it) }
// Outputs: "Alice: 95", "Bob: 87", "Carol: 92"
// Zip ends when shorter flow completes

merge — interleave emissions

// merge: combines multiple flows, emits as they arrive
val uiUpdates = merge(
    networkStatusFlow,   // emits when connectivity changes
    batteryLevelFlow,    // emits when battery changes
    userActionFlow       // emits on user interaction
)
uiUpdates.collect { update -> handleUpdate(update) }
OperatorEmits whenUses latest from other?Use case
combineEither source emitsYesSearch + filter, form validation
zipBoth sources emitNo (1:1 pairing)Paired data from two sources
mergeAny source emitsN/AMultiple event sources into one
⚧
4. FlatMap Operators

FlatMap operators transform each emission into a new Flow, then flatten the results. The key difference is how concurrent inner flows are handled.

flatMapConcat — sequential, in-order

// flatMapConcat: waits for each inner flow to complete before starting next
// Preserves order, sequential — like a queue
orderIds.flatMapConcat { id ->
    repo.getOrderDetails(id)  // returns Flow<OrderDetail>
}.collect { detail -> showDetail(detail) }
// Order 1 fully loaded before Order 2 starts

flatMapMerge — concurrent

// flatMapMerge: starts all inner flows concurrently, interleaves results
// Faster, but order is NOT guaranteed
productIds.flatMapMerge { id ->
    priceApi.getPriceStream(id)  // live price updates per product
}.collect { price -> updatePriceDisplay(price) }
// All price streams run in parallel — fastest delivery

flatMapLatest — cancel previous on new emission

// flatMapLatest: cancels the PREVIOUS inner flow when a new source emits
// Only the latest inner flow survives
searchQuery
    .debounce(300)
    .flatMapLatest { query ->
        repo.search(query)  // if user types again, this is cancelled
    }
    .collect { results -> showResults(results) }
// ✅ Perfect for search — only the latest query matters
OperatorConcurrencyOrderOn new emissionUse case
flatMapConcatSequentialGuaranteedQueued after currentOrdered processing (pagination)
flatMapMergeConcurrentNot guaranteedStarts immediatelyParallel fetches (product prices)
flatMapLatestCancel + restartN/ACancels previousSearch, live updates
🕑
5. Timing & Error Handling

Timing operators

// debounce: emit only after X ms of silence
searchInput.debounce(300).collect { query -> search(query) }
// User types "kotlin" — only "kotlin" sent after 300ms pause

// distinctUntilChanged: skip if value same as previous
userFlow.distinctUntilChanged().collect { render(it) }
// Only re-renders when actual user data changes

// sample: emit most recent value every X ms interval
sensorFlow.sample(1000).collect { reading -> updateUI(reading) }
// Sensor fires 60fps — sample(1000) → 1 update/second to UI

Error handling operators

// catch: handle upstream exceptions, emit fallback
repo.getBalance()
    .catch { e ->
        emit(Balance.Unavailable)  // emit fallback value
        logError(e)
    }
    .collect { showBalance(it) }

// retry: re-subscribe on error
networkFlow
    .retry(3) { e -> e is IOException }  // retry up to 3 times for IO errors
    .collect { handleData(it) }

// retryWhen: retry with exponential backoff
apiFlow
    .retryWhen { cause, attempt ->
        if (cause is IOException && attempt < 3) {
            delay(1000L * (2.pow(attempt.toInt()))) // 1s, 2s, 4s
            true   // retry
        } else false   // don't retry
    }
    .collect { handleData(it) }
📋
6. Lifecycle Operators

onStart, onEach, onCompletion

// onStart: called before flow starts collecting
repo.getProducts()
    .onStart { _loading.value = true }
    .onEach { product -> cacheProduct(product) }  // side effect per item
    .onCompletion { cause ->
        _loading.value = false
        if (cause != null) logError(cause)
    }
    .collect { displayProduct(it) }

// Production: full pipeline with loading, error, completion
fun getTransactionFlow(accountId: String) =
    repo.transactions(accountId)
        .onStart { emit(Resource.Loading) }
        .map { Resource.Success(it) }
        .catch { emit(Resource.Error(it)) }
        .onCompletion { /* cleanup */ }
🎯
7. Interview Framework

30-second answer

"Flow operators are lazy — they build a pipeline that executes on collect. Key operators: map/filter for transformation, combine/zip/merge for combining flows, flatMapLatest for search (cancel previous on new query), debounce for typing delays, catch/retry for error handling, and onStart/onCompletion for loading states."

2-minute answer

"The most important distinction is the three flatMap operators. flatMapConcat is sequential — each inner flow must complete before the next starts, preserving order. flatMapMerge is concurrent — all inner flows run simultaneously, results interleave. flatMapLatest cancels the previous inner flow when a new source emission arrives — essential for search where only the latest query matters.

For combining flows: combine fires when either source emits using the latest from the other — perfect for search + filter combinations. zip pairs emissions 1:1, waiting for both — good for correlated datasets. merge interleaves from multiple sources — good for event aggregation.

For error handling: catch handles exceptions and can emit fallback values. retryWhen gives you control over retry timing — exponential backoff for network resilience. debounce with 300ms is the standard search debounce pattern in Android."

Must-mention points

1
flatMapLatest for search — cancels previous; flatMapConcat for ordered; flatMapMerge for parallel
2
combine vs zip — combine = either emits with latest; zip = 1:1 pairing
3
debounce(300) — standard search debounce
4
catch — handles upstream errors, can emit fallback; does NOT catch downstream errors
5
Operators are lazy — pipeline executes only on collect

Follow-up Q&A

Q: "What's the difference between debounce and sample?"

A: debounce(n) waits until the source has been silent for n ms before emitting — useful for typing (only emit after user stops). sample(n) emits the most recent value every n ms on a fixed schedule — useful for sensor data where you want regular UI updates regardless of how fast the sensor fires.

Q: "Does catch handle errors thrown by the collector?"

A: No. catch only handles exceptions from the upstream (the flow chain above it). Exceptions thrown inside the collect { } lambda are NOT caught by catch. Use a try/catch inside the collect lambda for downstream errors.

Senior insight

Senior Insight
In a banking app, combine the search query flow with the account filter flow and the sort preference flow using combine: combine(searchFlow, filterFlow, sortFlow) { q, f, s → Query(q,f,s) }.flatMapLatest { query → repo.search(query) }.catch { emit(Error(it)) }. This creates a reactive search that automatically re-fetches whenever any input changes, with only the latest result kept.
📋
8. Quick Revision Sheet

FlatMap comparison

flatMapConcat  sequential, ordered
flatMapMerge   concurrent, unordered
flatMapLatest  cancel prev on new emit

Combining

combine(a,b) { x,y -> }  either emits
zip(a) { x, y -> }       1:1 pair

Error handling

.catch { e -> emit(fallback) }
.retry(3) { e -> e is IOException }
.retryWhen { cause, attempt ->
  delay(2.pow(attempt) * 1000L)
  attempt < 3
}

Timing

debounce(300)          wait 300ms silence
distinctUntilChanged() skip duplicates
sample(1000)           emit every 1s
❓
9. Interview Questions
What is the difference between map and transform in Flow?
Basic⌄
map transforms each emission 1:1 — one input always produces exactly one output. transform is more flexible — you can call emit() zero or multiple times. Use transform to skip some emissions (like filter) or to expand one value into multiple (like a 1:n mapping).
What does debounce do and when would you use it?
Basic⌄
debounce(n) only emits a value after n milliseconds of silence from the upstream. If a new value arrives before n ms, the timer resets. Classic use case: search-as-you-type — don't fire an API call for every keystroke; wait until the user pauses typing for 300ms.
Explain the difference between combine and zip.
Basic⌄
combine: emits a new combined value whenever either source emits, using the latest value from the other. If flow A emits 3 times and flow B emits 2 times, you can get up to 5 combined emissions. zip: pairs emissions 1:1. Waits for both sources to emit before combining. If A emits 3 times and B emits 2 times, you get 2 paired emissions (stops when the shorter one completes).
What is the difference between flatMapConcat, flatMapMerge, and flatMapLatest?
Intermediate⌄
flatMapConcat: sequential — waits for each inner flow to complete before starting the next. Order guaranteed. Use for ordered operations like paginated loading. flatMapMerge: concurrent — starts all inner flows simultaneously. Results arrive in any order. Use for parallel fetches. flatMapLatest: when a new outer emission arrives, the previous inner flow is cancelled and a new one starts. Only the latest matters. Use for search queries.
Does the catch operator handle exceptions thrown inside the collect lambda?
Intermediate⌄
No. catch is a transparent operator that only catches exceptions thrown by the upstream (the flow chain above it in the pipeline). Exceptions thrown inside the collect { } collector lambda are downstream and are NOT intercepted by catch. To handle collector exceptions, wrap the collect call in a try/catch.
How would you implement exponential backoff retry in a Flow?
Intermediate⌄
Use retryWhen: .retryWhen { cause, attempt -> if (cause is IOException && attempt < 3) { delay(1000L * (1 shl attempt.toInt())); true } else false }. The attempt starts at 0. Delays: 1000ms, 2000ms, 4000ms (powers of 2). Only retry IOExceptions, not business logic errors. After 3 attempts, return false to stop retrying and let the exception propagate.
Build a search pipeline that: debounces 300ms, ignores blank input, cancels stale requests, and handles network errors gracefully.
Intermediate⌄
searchQuery.debounce(300).filter { it.isNotBlank() }.distinctUntilChanged().flatMapLatest { query -> repo.search(query).catch { emit(SearchResult.Error(it)) } }.collect { result -> renderResult(result) }. Explanation: debounce waits for typing pause; filter ignores empty; distinctUntilChanged avoids re-searching same query; flatMapLatest cancels previous request on new keystroke; catch inside the flatMapLatest handles errors per query without breaking the outer flow.
What is onEach and how does it differ from map?
Senior⌄
onEach is for side effects — it performs an action on each emission but passes the original value through unchanged. map transforms the value into a different value. Use onEach for logging, caching, analytics tracking, or setting loading states without changing the stream's data type. Example: flow.onEach { cache.save(it) }.map { toUiModel(it) } — cache the raw data, then transform to UI model.
How would you merge live price updates for 100 products into a single UI-updating stream without overwhelming the main thread?
Senior⌄
Use flatMapMerge(concurrency = 20) to limit concurrent inner flows: productIds.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 20) { id -> priceSocket.streamPrice(id) }.conflate(). The concurrency parameter prevents 100 simultaneous socket connections. conflate() at the end drops intermediate updates if the UI can't keep up — only the latest price per product matters. Then collect on Main dispatcher for UI updates. The concurrency limit matches realistic socket pool size.
Explain how you would use the Resource pattern (Loading/Success/Error) with Flow operators.
Senior⌄
Wrap the repository flow: fun getDataFlow(id: String): Flow<Resource<Data>> = repo.getStream(id).map<Data, Resource<Data>> { Resource.Success(it) }.onStart { emit(Resource.Loading) }.catch { emit(Resource.Error(it)) }. The onStart emits Loading before any data arrives. map wraps success data. catch catches upstream errors and emits Error. The UI collects a single flow that handles all three states. Important: onStart must come before catch so the Loading emission isn't caught by catch.

6C — Builders & Channels

flow{}, flowOn, callbackFlow, channelFlow. Channel types: Rendezvous, Buffered, Conflated, Unlimited. Backpressure strategies.

ID: 6C ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

Flow builders

  • flow { } — simplest builder; cold; sequential; cannot emit from a different coroutine
  • flowOf(vararg) — emit a fixed set of values
  • callbackFlow { } — bridge callback-based APIs (location, sensors, WebSocket) to Flow
  • channelFlow { } — like callbackFlow but allows multiple concurrent emissions from different coroutines
  • flowOn(dispatcher) — change the upstream context; does NOT affect the collector

Channels

A Channel is a communication primitive between coroutines — like a queue with suspend-aware send/receive. Unlike Flow, channels are hot and stateful. They're the foundation of channelFlow and callbackFlow internally.

Senior Mental Model
Use callbackFlow to bridge legacy callback APIs (Bluetooth, location, Firebase) into the reactive Flow world. Use flowOn to change the dispatcher for upstream work without changing where the collector runs. Channels are low-level — in most Android code you don't need raw Channels; prefer Flow.
⚙
2. Flow Builders

flow { } — basic cold builder

// Simple cold flow — sequential emissions
fun countdownFlow(): Flow<Int> = flow {
    for (i in 10 downTo 0) {
        emit(i)
        delay(1000)
    }
}
// Constraint: cannot call emit() from a different coroutine inside flow{}

flowOn — change upstream context

// flowOn affects ONLY the upstream operators — NOT the collector
repo.getItems()                    // runs on IO (set by flowOn)
    .map { it.toUiModel() }          // also runs on IO
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)          // sets context for above ops
    .collect { renderItem(it) }       // runs on collector's context (Main)

// Multiple flowOn: each applies to everything above it
flow.map { /* on Default */ }
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)
    .map { /* on IO */ }
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)
    .collect { /* on Main */ }

callbackFlow — bridge callbacks to Flow

// Bridge LocationManager callback to Flow
fun locationFlow(context: Context): Flow<Location> = callbackFlow {
    val manager = context.getSystemService(LocationManager::class.java)

    val listener = LocationListener { location ->
        trySend(location)  // non-suspend send (from callback thread)
    }

    manager.requestLocationUpdates(
        LocationManager.GPS_PROVIDER, 1000L, 0f, listener
    )

    // awaitClose: runs when flow is cancelled / collector stops
    awaitClose {
        manager.removeUpdates(listener)  // cleanup!
    }
}

// Usage
locationFlow(context)
    .collect { location -> updateMap(location) }
// When collector cancels, awaitClose removes the listener

channelFlow — concurrent emissions

// channelFlow: allows emission from different coroutines
fun parallelFetch(ids: List<String>): Flow<Item> = channelFlow {
    ids.forEach { id ->
        launch {                    // multiple coroutines emit concurrently
            val item = api.fetchItem(id)
            send(item)               // suspend-aware send
        }
    }
}
// Regular flow{} would throw: "Flow invariant is violated"
📊
3. Channel Types
TypeBuffer sizeSend behaviourReceive behaviourUse case
Rendezvous0Suspends until receiver readySuspends until sender readyStrict handshake between coroutines
Buffered(n)nSuspends when buffer fullSuspends when buffer emptyProducer slightly faster than consumer
Conflated1Overwrites old value, never suspendsGets latestSensor data — only latest matters
Unlimited∞Never suspendsSuspends when emptyBurst events; be careful of OOM
// Creating channels
val rendezvous = Channel<Int>()                    // default: Rendezvous
val buffered = Channel<Int>(Channel.BUFFERED)       // default 64
val conflated = Channel<Int>(Channel.CONFLATED)     // overwrite old
val unlimited = Channel<Int>(Channel.UNLIMITED)     // unbounded

// Custom buffer size
val custom = Channel<Order>(capacity = 100,
    onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)
⚖
4. Backpressure Strategies

Backpressure occurs when the producer emits faster than the consumer can process. Flow operators to handle it:

// buffer: add a coroutine boundary between producer and consumer
// Producer and consumer run concurrently
fastSensorFlow
    .buffer(64)              // up to 64 items buffered while consumer processes
    .collect { slowProcess(it) }

// conflate: keep only the latest value, drop intermediate
// Consumer always gets freshest data
locationFlow
    .conflate()              // if consumer is busy, old locations are dropped
    .collect { updateMap(it) }

// collectLatest: cancel current processing when new value arrives
priceFlow
    .collectLatest { price ->
        delay(1000)          // simulate slow rendering
        renderPrice(price)   // if new price arrives, this is cancelled
    }
StrategyHow it worksData loss?Use case
buffer(n)Concurrent producer/consumer with queueNo (suspends when full)Bursty producer, need all items
conflate()Keep only latest, drop intermediateYes (intermediate dropped)UI refresh — only latest matters
collectLatestCancel current on new arrivalYes (cancelled work)Search, live preview
Channel(DROP_OLDEST)Overwrite buffer with newer valuesYes (old values)Sensor data, rate-limited events
🏭
5. Production Example

Automotive: GPS sensor to location service via callbackFlow

// Bridge Android FusedLocationProvider to Flow
fun FusedLocationProviderClient.locationFlow(): Flow<Location> = callbackFlow {
    val request = LocationRequest.create()
        .setInterval(1000)
        .setPriority(PRIORITY_HIGH_ACCURACY)

    val callback = object : LocationCallback() {
        override fun onLocationResult(result: LocationResult) {
            result.lastLocation?.let { location ->
                trySend(location)  // non-blocking send from callback
            }
        }
    }

    requestLocationUpdates(request, callback, Looper.getMainLooper())

    awaitClose { removeLocationUpdates(callback) }
}

// Processing pipeline with backpressure + context switch
class NavigationViewModel(
    private val client: FusedLocationProviderClient
) : ViewModel() {

    val route: StateFlow<RouteState> = client.locationFlow()
        .conflate()                          // only latest GPS position
        .map { location ->                   // heavy route calculation
            routeEngine.calculate(location)
        }
        .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)         // route calc on CPU pool
        .map { route -> RouteState.Active(route) }
        .catch { emit(RouteState.Error(it)) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5000), RouteState.Idle)
}

Banking: WebSocket price feed via callbackFlow

fun priceFlow(symbol: String): Flow<Price> = callbackFlow {
    val ws = webSocketClient.connect(symbol)

    ws.onMessage { msg ->
        val price = parsePrice(msg)
        trySend(price)  // may drop if buffer full
    }
    ws.onError { e -> close(e) }

    awaitClose { ws.disconnect() }
}
    .buffer(Channel.CONFLATED)   // only latest price if consumer is slow
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Missing awaitClose in callbackFlow
If you don't call awaitClose { } in a callbackFlow, the flow completes immediately after the block ends — before any callbacks fire. You also miss the chance to unregister the callback, causing memory leaks.
Pitfall 2 — emit() from different coroutine inside flow{}
flow { } is single-coroutine only. Calling emit() from a coroutine launched inside flow { } throws "Flow invariant violated". Use channelFlow { } instead for concurrent emissions.
Pitfall 3 — flowOn affects upstream, not downstream
A common mistake: putting flowOn(IO) after collect { }. flowOn only applies to operators above it. The collector always runs on the coroutine that called collect (e.g., viewModelScope's Main dispatcher).
Best Practice — trySend vs send in callbackFlow
Use trySend(value) in callbacks — it's non-suspending and returns a ChannelResult. send(value) suspends until there's space in the buffer, which is not valid in a regular (non-suspending) callback. If you need to know if the send was dropped, check the result.
🎯
7. Interview Framework

30-second answer

"callbackFlow is the standard way to bridge legacy callback APIs like location, sensors, or WebSocket to Kotlin Flow. It provides trySend() for non-suspending emission from callbacks and awaitClose() for cleanup. flowOn changes the upstream context without affecting the collector. Channels are the underlying mechanism — Rendezvous (no buffer), Buffered, Conflated (latest only), Unlimited."

2-minute answer

"callbackFlow solves a fundamental problem: callback-based APIs (LocationManager, Bluetooth, Firebase Realtime) don't fit the sequential coroutine model. callbackFlow creates a Channel internally — trySend() puts values into it from callback threads, and collect() reads from it. awaitClose() is critical: it runs when the flow collector cancels, unregistering the callback to prevent leaks.

flowOn is more subtle than it appears: it only affects operators upstream (above it). Multiple flowOn operators create separate coroutine boundaries between sections. The collector always runs in its calling context — usually Main in a ViewModel.

For backpressure: buffer(n) allows the producer to run ahead by n items. conflate() drops intermediate values, keeping only the latest. For sensor data, conflate is usually right — processing stale GPS readings is wasteful. For financial transactions, buffer is right — you don't want to lose any transaction events."

Must-mention points

1
callbackFlow + awaitClose — always cleanup in awaitClose, never skip it
2
trySend (not send) in callbacks — callbacks are not suspend-aware
3
flowOn affects upstream only — collector runs on its own context
4
Channel types: Rendezvous=0, Buffered, Conflated=1-latest, Unlimited
5
conflate() for sensor data; buffer() when all items matter

Follow-up Q&A

Q: "What's the difference between callbackFlow and channelFlow?"

A: callbackFlow and channelFlow are nearly identical in implementation. Both create a Channel and allow concurrent emissions. The key difference: callbackFlow checks that awaitClose() is called and throws a runtime error if it's missing. channelFlow does not enforce this. In practice, always use callbackFlow when bridging callbacks (the enforcement helps catch bugs), and channelFlow for internal concurrent producers.

Q: "What does trySend return when the buffer is full?"

A: It returns a ChannelResult — a failure result if the channel is full or closed. You can check trySend(value).isFailure. For a conflated channel, it never fails — it overwrites the old value. The caller in a callback should decide: log the drop, increment a dropped-events counter, or simply ignore it depending on the use case.

Senior insight

Senior Insight
In an automotive app with 10+ sensor streams (GPS, accelerometer, LIDAR), use callbackFlow for each sensor and merge them with merge(). Apply conflate() on each sensor stream to drop stale readings, then flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) for sensor fusion processing. This gives you one clean reactive stream that always processes the freshest sensor data available.
📋
