7D — Compose Performance

Smart recomposition, stability system, @Stable/@Immutable, unstable List<>, LazyColumn keys, remember for expensive computations, derivedStateOf, lambda stability, Compose compiler metrics.

ID: 7D ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

What triggers recomposition — and what should NOT

Recomposition is triggered by State changes. The performance question is: how much of the tree recomposes? Compose can skip composables where all parameters are equal — this is called smart recomposition. For a composable to be skippable, all its parameters must be stable.

The stability contract

  • Stable type: if a == b then a will never produce a different result for the same inputs — Compose can safely skip it
  • Immutable type: stronger — value never changes after creation (primitives, String, @Immutable data class)
  • Unstable type: Compose cannot trust equals() — cannot skip (List<>, MutableList, regular classes without @Stable)
Senior Mental Model
Every composable parameter that is an unstable type prevents the composable from being skippable — it MUST re-run on every parent recomposition, even if the actual value didn't change. In a 500-item list, this means 500 items recompose when the parent recomposes. Understanding stability is the key to Compose performance at scale.
⚙
2. Stability System

@Stable annotation

// @Stable: promises that equals() is reliable AND observable
// (Compose will be notified when observable properties change)
@Stable
class UserState {
    var name by mutableStateOf("")  // observable via State
    var email by mutableStateOf("")
}
// Compose can skip composables with UserState params if the reference
// is the same — it trusts the State fields to trigger recomposition

@Immutable annotation

// @Immutable: all public properties never change after construction
// Strongest stability guarantee
@Immutable
data class ProductUiModel(
    val id: String,
    val name: String,
    val price: Double
)
// data class is @Immutable IF all fields are val and stable types
// Compose compiler may infer this automatically in some cases

What the compiler infers automatically

TypeStabilityWhy
Int, String, Boolean, FloatStable (immutable)Primitives never change
data class with stable fieldsStableCompiler infers if all fields are val + stable
List<T>, MutableList<T>UnstableMutable interface, equals() unreliable
HashMap, ArrayListUnstableMutable collections
ViewModelStableNever changes reference in the composable
Regular class (non-data)UnstableNo reliable equals() override
⚠
3. Unstable Types — The List Problem

Why List<T> is unstable

// List<T> is an interface — Compose sees it as potentially mutable
// Even if you pass a listOf(), Compose can't trust equals()

// ❌ UNSTABLE: composable cannot be skipped
@Composable
fun ProductList(products: List<Product>) { /* ... */ }
// Parent recomposes → ProductList ALWAYS recomposes, even if list unchanged

// ✅ Fix 1: @Immutable wrapper
@Immutable
data class ProductList(val items: List<Product>)

@Composable
fun ProductListScreen(products: ProductList) { /* stable ✅ */ }

// ✅ Fix 2: kotlinx.collections.immutable
implementation("org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-collections-immutable:0.3.7")

@Composable
fun ProductListScreen(products: ImmutableList<Product>) { /* stable ✅ */ }

Lambda stability

// Lambdas that capture unstable values are themselves unstable
@Composable
fun Parent() {
    val list: List<String> = remember { listOf("a", "b") }

    // ❌ Lambda captures unstable list — unstable lambda
    Child(onClick = { process(list) })
}

// ✅ Fix: stabilize the list, or move lambda out of recomposition scope
val stableList: ImmutableList<String> = remember { persistentListOf("a", "b") }
Child(onClick = { process(stableList) })  // ✅ stable
📌
4. LazyColumn Keys & remember

LazyColumn keys — stable item identity

// ❌ Without key: index is the identity
// Insert an item → all positions shift → all items recompose
LazyColumn {
    items(products) { product ->
        ProductCard(product)  // identity = index in list
    }
}

// ✅ With key: item.id is the identity
// Insert an item → only new item created, others keep their composition
LazyColumn {
    items(products, key = { it.id }) { product ->  // stable String ID
        ProductCard(product)
    }
}
// Keys enable: correct animations, proper remember state per item,
// efficient reuse of composition for unchanged items

remember for expensive computations in composables

// ❌ Expensive computation runs every recomposition
@Composable
fun ChartComposable(data: List<DataPoint>) {
    val chartPath = buildBezierPath(data)  // ❌ O(n) on every recompose
    Canvas { drawPath(chartPath) }
}

// ✅ Memoize with remember(key)
@Composable
fun ChartComposable(data: List<DataPoint>) {
    val chartPath = remember(data) {    // ✅ only recomputes when data changes
        buildBezierPath(data)
    }
    Canvas { drawPath(chartPath) }
}

Modifier.graphicsLayer — avoid recomposition for visual changes

// ❌ alpha in modifier triggers recomposition to update UI
Box(Modifier.alpha(animatedAlpha))  // recomposes on alpha change

// ✅ graphicsLayer: runs in draw phase, no recomposition
Box(
    Modifier.graphicsLayer(alpha = animatedAlpha)
) // No recomposition — handled by render layer
🏭
5. Production Example

E-commerce: performant product list

// ✅ Stable state wrapper for list
@Immutable
data class ProductScreenState(
    val products: ImmutableList<ProductUiModel> = persistentListOf(),
    val isLoading: Boolean = false
)

@Immutable
data class ProductUiModel(
    val id: String,
    val name: String,
    val price: String,       // Pre-formatted string — stable
    val imageUrl: String
)

@Composable
fun ProductListScreen(
    state: ProductScreenState,    // @Immutable → stable
    onAddToCart: (String) -> Unit  // lambdas on stable types → stable
) {
    LazyColumn {
        items(
            items = state.products,
            key = { it.id }  // stable String key
        ) { product ->
            // ProductCard: all params are @Immutable types → skippable
            ProductCard(
                product = product,
                onAddToCart = { onAddToCart(product.id) }
            )
        }
    }
}

// ✅ Skippable ProductCard — all params stable
@Composable
fun ProductCard(
    product: ProductUiModel,       // @Immutable → stable
    onAddToCart: () -> Unit        // no capture → stable
) {
    // derivedStateOf for expensive display computation
    val displayPrice by remember(product.price) {
        derivedStateOf { formatWithCurrency(product.price) }
    }
    /* ... */
}
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Passing List<T> to composables
List<T> is unstable — any composable that takes it as a parameter cannot be skipped. In a list screen, this means every item recomposes whenever the parent updates. Use ImmutableList<T> (kotlinx.collections.immutable) or wrap in an @Immutable data class.
Pitfall 2 — Lambdas capturing non-stable values
A lambda that captures a List<T> or any unstable value is itself unstable. This prevents the composable receiving it from skipping. Fix: ensure captured values are stable, or use remember { { ... } } to stabilize the lambda reference.
Pitfall 3 — LazyColumn without keys
Without stable keys in LazyColumn, inserting or removing items causes all items to recompose and loses per-item state (expanded state, animations). Always provide key = { item.id }.
Best Practice — Compose compiler metrics
Enable compiler reports: freeCompilerArgs += ["-P", "plugin:androidx.compose.compiler.plugins.kotlin:reportsDestination=build/compose_reports"]. The output shows skippable vs restartable composables and identifies unstable parameters. Use this to find performance bottlenecks.
🎯
7. Interview Framework

30-second answer

"Compose performance is about minimizing unnecessary recomposition. A composable is skippable only if all its parameters are stable — equals() is reliable and Compose trusts the value hasn't changed. The biggest issue is List<T>, which is unstable. Fix it with ImmutableList from kotlinx.collections.immutable or an @Immutable wrapper. LazyColumn keys give items stable identity. derivedStateOf prevents over-recomposition from high-frequency state changes."

2-minute answer

"The stability system is the performance foundation. A stable type means Compose can trust equals() — if a == b, the composable doesn't need to re-run. Primitives and Strings are stable. data classes with stable fields are stable. But List<T> is an interface — Compose cannot guarantee it's immutable, so it's marked unstable. This means a composable with a List parameter is non-skippable: it recomposes every time its parent recomposes, even if the list didn't change.

The fix is ImmutableList from kotlinx.collections.immutable, or wrapping in @Immutable data class. The @Immutable annotation is a promise — you're telling Compose 'trust this class, its contents won't change after construction.'

For LazyColumn: keys give items stable identity. Without keys, inserting at position 0 shifts everything, causing all 500 items to recompose. With keys, Compose moves items and only creates the new one.

Use the Compose compiler metrics to discover unstable parameters and non-skippable composables — it generates reports showing exactly which composables have issues."

Must-mention points

1
Stable = trustworthy equals() → composable can be skipped on recompose
2
List<T> is unstable — use ImmutableList or @Immutable wrapper
3
LazyColumn keys — stable identity prevents full-list recompose
4
derivedStateOf — avoid over-recomposition from high-freq state (scroll, sensors)
5
Compiler metrics — diagnose unstable params in production

Follow-up Q&A

Q: "What is the difference between @Stable and @Immutable?"

A: @Immutable: stronger contract — all public properties never change after construction. The compiler treats all fields as constants for stability purposes. @Stable: weaker — equals() is reliable AND changes to public properties are observable (via State/observable property). Use @Immutable for pure value objects (UI models). Use @Stable for observable state holders (StateHolder classes with mutableStateOf fields).

Q: "How do you enable Compose compiler reports?"

A: In your app's build.gradle: kotlinOptions { freeCompilerArgs += ["-P", "plugin:androidx.compose.compiler.plugins.kotlin:reportsDestination=${project.buildDir}/compose_reports"] }. Run a build and inspect the `*-composables.txt` file — it shows each composable as skippable/restartable and lists stable/unstable parameters.

Senior insight

Senior Insight
In a banking transaction list with real-time updates, use @Immutable data class TransactionUiModel with pre-computed display strings (formatted amount, date string) rather than passing BigDecimal and Instant. This ensures all fields are stable primitives/strings, the composable is fully skippable, and formatting happens once in the ViewModel — not on every recomposition.
📋
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Stability rules

Stable:   primitives, String,
          data class (all val+stable),
          @Stable, @Immutable
Unstable: List<T>, MutableList,
          HashMap, regular class

Fix unstable List

// Option 1: wrapper
@Immutable data class Items(val list: List<T>)

// Option 2: ImmutableList
ImmutableList<T> // kotlinx.collections.immutable

LazyColumn key

items(
  items = list,
  key = { it.id }  // ← always provide
) { item -> ItemCard(item) }

Performance toolbox

derivedStateOf { } // for high-freq state
remember(key) { }  // memoize expensive ops
graphicsLayer { }  // draw-phase changes
@Immutable class   // trust equals()
compiler metrics   // diagnose issues
❓
9. Interview Questions
What does it mean for a composable to be "skippable"?
Basic⌄
A skippable composable can be skipped during recomposition if all its parameters are equal to their previous values. Compose checks each parameter using equals(). If all are equal, it assumes the output would be the same and skips executing the function — saving CPU time. For a composable to be skippable, all parameters must be stable types.
Why is List<T> unstable in Compose?
Basic⌄
List<T> is a Kotlin interface. Compose cannot verify that the implementation won't change after the composable receives it — a mutable list could change without notifying Compose. Since Compose can't trust that equals() reliably indicates whether the content changed, it marks List as unstable. Any composable receiving a List parameter is non-skippable and will recompose whenever its parent recomposes.
What is the difference between @Stable and @Immutable?
Basic⌄
@Immutable: all public properties never change after construction — strongest guarantee. Every field is treated as a compile-time constant for stability. Use for value objects (UI models). @Stable: weaker — equals() is reliable AND any changes to public properties are observable (the Compose runtime will be notified). Use for mutable state holders that use mutableStateOf internally. In practice, most UI model classes should use @Immutable.
Why should you always provide keys in LazyColumn?
Intermediate⌄
Without keys, each item's identity is its index. Inserting an item at position 0 shifts all other items' indices — Compose thinks every item changed and recomposes all of them. Remember state per item is also lost. With key = { item.id }, each item has a stable identity. Compose can correctly identify which items moved, which are new, and which are unchanged — only recomposing what actually changed and preserving per-item state.
How do you fix the performance issue caused by passing List<T> to a composable?
Intermediate⌄
Two approaches: (1) Use ImmutableList<T> from the kotlinx.collections.immutable library — it's a stable type by design. Convert in ViewModel: _state.update { it.copy(products = newList.toImmutableList()) }. (2) Wrap in an @Immutable data class: @Immutable data class ProductListState(val items: List<T>) — the annotation makes the wrapper stable, and the inner List is treated as immutable by contract.
When should you use Modifier.graphicsLayer vs setting a modifier property directly?
Intermediate⌄
Modifier.alpha(value) updates a modifier that Compose reads during composition — if the alpha changes, a recomposition is needed to apply the new modifier. Modifier.graphicsLayer { alpha = value } applies the change in the draw phase — no recomposition required. For animated values that change every frame (alpha, scale, translation), graphicsLayer skips the composition phase entirely, giving better performance. For static properties that only change occasionally, direct modifiers are fine.
A product list screen shows 200 items. Typing in a search box causes all 200 items to flicker/recompose. What is the root cause and fix?
Intermediate⌄
Root cause: either (1) ProductCard takes a List parameter (unstable, non-skippable), or (2) the state update changes the list reference even if content is the same, or (3) the search query state is being read by the parent that contains the LazyColumn, causing the LazyColumn's parent to recompose, and without stable/skippable ProductCard, all 200 items recompose. Fix: ensure ProductCard takes @Immutable ProductUiModel (not List). Hoist the search query state to a ViewModel so it doesn't live in the same composable as the list. Add stable keys to LazyColumn.
How do you use Compose compiler metrics to diagnose performance issues?
Senior⌄
Add to app build.gradle: kotlinOptions { freeCompilerArgs += ["-P", "plugin:androidx.compose.compiler.plugins.kotlin:reportsDestination=${buildDir}/compose_reports", "-P", "plugin:androidx.compose.compiler.plugins.kotlin:metricsDestination=${buildDir}/compose_metrics"] }. Run an assembleDebug/Release. Open build/compose_reports/*-composables.txt. Each composable is marked: skippable/non-skippable, restartable/non-restartable. Non-skippable composables list their unstable parameters. The metrics JSON provides counts. Focus on non-skippable composables in hot paths (list items).
Explain why a lambda that captures a non-stable type is itself unstable and how to fix it.
Senior⌄
Compose compiler analyzes lambda capture sites. If a lambda captures an unstable value (e.g., List<T>), the compiler cannot guarantee the lambda's output is stable — calling it with the same "arguments" might produce different results because the captured state may have changed. The lambda is therefore marked unstable, preventing composables that receive it from skipping. Fix: (1) ensure the captured value is stable (ImmutableList, @Immutable class); (2) use remember { { } } to create a stable lambda reference; (3) in Compose 1.5+, lambdas with stable captures are automatically stabilized by the compiler.
An automotive dashboard has a speedometer recomposing at 60fps. The needle is animated but the rest of the dashboard should not recompose. How do you architect this?
Senior⌄
Isolate the high-frequency state. The speed value from sensors updates at 60fps — keep it in a separate StateFlow or animatable. The Speedometer composable reads this directly. Use Modifier.graphicsLayer { rotationZ = needleAngle } for the needle rotation — this runs in the draw phase without recomposition. For the rest of the dashboard (current music, temperature, warnings), use derivedStateOf for threshold-crossing booleans. Structure: DashboardScreen (reads all states) → SpeedGauge (reads only speed via derivedStateOf thresholds) + StaticDashboardPanels (@Stable, skippable). The needle rotation via graphicsLayer avoids even SpeedGauge recomposition at 60fps.

● Android Interview Prep

8A — Architecture Patterns

MVC, MVP, MVVM, MVI — what each solves and its trade-offs. Full layered architecture: UI → ViewModel → UseCase → Repository → Data Sources. When to use each pattern.

ID: 8A ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

Why architecture patterns matter

Architecture patterns solve the same fundamental problem: separation of concerns. In Android, without architecture, Activities and Fragments become God objects — containing business logic, UI code, data fetching, and state management all tangled together. The result: untestable, fragile, impossible-to-maintain code.

The evolution

  • MVC — classic pattern; Controller = Activity; View = XML; Model = data; Controller too big
  • MVP — Presenter separates logic; testable; but Presenter leaks View references; boilerplate
  • MVVM — ViewModel + LiveData/StateFlow; lifecycle-aware; two-way binding optional; Android recommended
  • MVI — strict UDF; immutable state; sealed Intents; single state object; most predictable
Senior Mental Model
In interviews, say: "We use MVVM with Clean Architecture layers — UI → ViewModel → UseCase → Repository → Remote/Local data sources. UseCases encapsulate single business rules, making them independently testable. Repository provides a single data access abstraction, hiding whether data comes from network or cache. We could layer MVI on top of MVVM if we need stricter state management."
⚙
2. MVC, MVP, MVVM

MVC — Model-View-Controller

LayerAndroid mappingResponsibility
ModelData classes, DB, APIBusiness data and logic
ViewXML layoutsDisplay only
ControllerActivity / FragmentGlue — handles events, updates View, calls Model

Problem: In Android, Activity is both Controller AND part of the lifecycle. Business logic in Activity = untestable. God Activity anti-pattern.

MVP — Model-View-Presenter

LayerAndroid mappingResponsibility
ModelRepository, data layerData and business logic
ViewActivity/Fragment (behind interface)UI only, delegates all logic
PresenterPlain Kotlin classBusiness logic, mediates between View and Model

Improvement: Presenter is testable (no Android deps). Problem: Presenter holds a View reference → memory leaks on rotation. Weak references or detach pattern needed. 1:1 Presenter-View coupling is boilerplate-heavy.

MVVM — Model-View-ViewModel

// View observes ViewModel state — no direct reference from VM to View
class OrderViewModel(
    private val placeOrder: PlaceOrderUseCase
) : ViewModel() {

    // ViewModel never holds a reference to View/Activity
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(OrderState())
    val state: StateFlow<OrderState> = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun submitOrder(order: Order) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _state.update { it.copy(isLoading = true) }
            val result = placeOrder(order)
            _state.update { it.copy(isLoading = false, result = result) }
        }
    }
}
// View lifecycle: Activity destroyed → ViewModel survives rotation
// View lifecycle: navigated away → ViewModel.onCleared() called
⚗
3. MVI — Model-View-Intent

MVI takes UDF to its strictest form: a single immutable state object, sealed class Intents (user actions), and pure reducers that produce new state from old state + intent. No side effects in state — everything is explicit.

// Intent: sealed class representing all possible user actions
sealed class TransferIntent {
    data class AmountChanged(val amount: String) : TransferIntent()
    data class RecipientSelected(val id: String) : TransferIntent()
    object SubmitTransfer : TransferIntent()
}

// State: single immutable data class
data class TransferState(
    val amount: String = "",
    val recipientId: String? = null,
    val isLoading: Boolean = false,
    val error: String? = null,
    val isSuccess: Boolean = false
)

// ViewModel processes intents → produces new state
class TransferViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(TransferState())
    val state = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun processIntent(intent: TransferIntent) {
        when (intent) {
            is TransferIntent.AmountChanged ->
                _state.update { it.copy(amount = intent.amount) }
            is TransferIntent.RecipientSelected ->
                _state.update { it.copy(recipientId = intent.id) }
            TransferIntent.SubmitTransfer -> submitTransfer()
        }
    }

    private fun submitTransfer() {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _state.update { it.copy(isLoading = true) }
            // ... call use case
        }
    }
}
📊
4. Clean Architecture Layers
UI Layer (Compose Screens + ViewModels)
    ↕ StateFlow / Events
Domain Layer (UseCases / Interactors)
    ↕ suspend functions / Flow<T>
Data Layer (Repositories)
    ↕ suspend functions / Flow<T>
Data Sources (Remote API + Room DB + Preferences)

Each layer's responsibilities

// UI Layer: display state, forward events
@Composable
fun TransferScreen(viewModel: TransferViewModel) {
    val state by viewModel.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    /* render state, send intents to viewModel */
}

// Domain Layer: business rules, no Android deps
class ValidateTransferUseCase {
    operator fun invoke(
        amount: BigDecimal, balance: BigDecimal
    ): ValidationResult = when {
        amount <= BigDecimal.ZERO -> ValidationResult.InvalidAmount
        amount > balance -> ValidationResult.InsufficientFunds
        else -> ValidationResult.Valid
    }
}

class ExecuteTransferUseCase(
    private val repository: TransferRepository
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(
        from: Account, to: Account, amount: BigDecimal
    ): Result<Transfer> = runCatching {
        repository.executeTransfer(from.id, to.id, amount)
    }
}

// Data Layer: data access abstraction
interface TransferRepository {
    suspend fun executeTransfer(fromId: String, toId: String, amount: BigDecimal): Transfer
}

class TransferRepositoryImpl(
    private val remoteApi: TransferApi,    // Retrofit
    private val localDao: TransferDao     // Room
) : TransferRepository {
    override suspend fun executeTransfer(fromId: String, toId: String, amount: BigDecimal): Transfer {
        val transfer = remoteApi.postTransfer(TransferRequest(fromId, toId, amount))
        localDao.insert(transfer.toEntity())
        return transfer
    }
}
🏭
5. Production Example

Banking: full transfer flow with all layers

// ViewModel: MVVM orchestrator
class TransferViewModel(
    private val validateTransfer: ValidateTransferUseCase,
    private val executeTransfer: ExecuteTransferUseCase,
    private val getAccount: GetAccountUseCase
) : ViewModel() {

    val uiState: StateFlow<TransferUiState> =
        getAccount()
            .map { account -> TransferUiState(balance = account.formattedBalance()) }
            .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), TransferUiState.Loading)

    private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<TransferEvent>(extraBufferCapacity = 1)
    val events = _events.asSharedFlow()

    fun submitTransfer(amount: BigDecimal, recipientId: String) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            val account = (uiState.value as? TransferUiState.Ready)?.account ?: return@launch

            val validation = validateTransfer(amount, account.balance)
            if (validation != ValidationResult.Valid) {
                _events.emit(TransferEvent.ValidationError(validation))
                return@launch
            }

            executeTransfer(account, recipientId, amount)
                .onSuccess { _events.emit(TransferEvent.Success(it)) }
                .onFailure { _events.emit(TransferEvent.Error(it)) }
        }
    }
}

Comparison table — when to choose each

PatternTestabilityComplexityBest for
MVCPoor (logic in Activity)LowPrototypes only
MVPGood (Presenter pure)MediumLegacy codebases
MVVMExcellentMediumMost Android apps — Google recommended
MVIExcellent + auditableHighComplex flows with many state transitions (checkout, onboarding)
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Fat ViewModel
Moving all business logic to the ViewModel without UseCases creates a "Fat ViewModel" anti-pattern — the same problem as Fat Controller in MVC, just moved. UseCases should encapsulate discrete business rules; the ViewModel should only orchestrate them.
Pitfall 2 — Repository doing too much
The Repository should be a clean data access abstraction — not the place for business logic. If a Repository method is called "validateAndSaveIfFundsAvailable", the validate part belongs in a UseCase, not the Repository.
Pitfall 3 — Domain layer depending on Android
UseCases should be pure Kotlin with zero Android dependencies — no Context, no ViewModel, no Room entities. This is what makes them unit-testable with JUnit without Robolectric.
Best Practice — Repository interface in domain layer
Define the Repository interface in the domain layer, implementation in the data layer. This inverts the dependency — data layer depends on domain, not the other way. Enables mocking in UseCase tests without a real DB or network.
🎯
7. Interview Framework

30-second answer

"We use MVVM with Clean Architecture. The UI layer has Compose composables and ViewModels. ViewModels expose StateFlow and receive events. The domain layer has UseCases — pure Kotlin, no Android deps, one business rule each. The data layer has Repositories that abstract Remote API and local Room database. Dependencies only flow inward: UI → Domain ← Data."

2-minute answer

"The architecture evolution: MVC had Activity as the Controller — god class, untestable. MVP extracted a Presenter but it held a View reference, causing memory leaks on rotation. MVVM solved this — ViewModel survives rotation, never holds a View reference, exposes observable state that the View subscribes to. Android Jetpack's ViewModel + LiveData/StateFlow makes MVVM lifecycle-safe.

On top of MVVM, Clean Architecture adds layers: UI calls UseCases, not Repositories directly. Each UseCase does one thing and is unit-testable without Robolectric. Repository interfaces live in the domain layer — implementations in the data layer — this inverts the dependency, enabling proper mocking in tests.

MVI adds stricter UDF on top: sealed class Intents describe all actions, a single immutable State describes all UI state, and a reducer maps Intent + State → new State. It's more boilerplate but makes complex checkout-style flows auditable — you can replay every state transition."

Must-mention points

1
MVVM + Clean Architecture = the Android standard; ViewModel has no View reference
2
UseCases = pure Kotlin — no Android deps, one business rule, independently testable
3
Repository interface in domain — dependency inversion; data layer depends on domain
4
MVI = strict UDF — sealed Intents, single immutable state, for complex flows
5
Layer diagram: UI → ViewModel → UseCase → Repository → API/DB

Follow-up Q&A

Q: "Why use a UseCase between ViewModel and Repository?"

A: Three reasons: (1) Testability — UseCases can be unit-tested with JUnit, injecting a mock Repository. (2) Reuse — multiple ViewModels can use the same UseCase without duplicating logic. (3) Single responsibility — each UseCase encapsulates exactly one business rule. Without UseCases, business logic leaks into ViewModels, making them fat and hard to test.

Q: "When would you choose MVI over MVVM?"

A: For complex, multi-step flows with many possible states and transitions — checkout flows, onboarding, complex forms with multiple validation rules. MVI's single state object and sealed Intents make the state machine explicit and auditable. You can log every Intent and replay the state transitions for debugging. For simpler screens (list + detail), MVVM is less boilerplate and equally appropriate.

Senior insight

Senior Insight
In a banking app, we use MVVM for most screens but MVI for the payment flow. The payment screen has 12+ possible states (form idle, amount entered, recipient selected, validating, payment pending, 3DS challenge, success, various error states). MVI's sealed state class makes every state explicit — no boolean flags, no "can this be null here?" guessing. The reducer is a pure function — testable with exhaustive when expressions. This is exactly the kind of complex flow where MVI pays its boilerplate cost.
📋

class GetUserUseCase(

9. Interview Questions
What is the main problem with MVC in Android?
Basic⌄
In Android MVC, Activity/Fragment acts as the Controller. This creates a God Class — Activities handle button clicks, network calls, database queries, navigation, lifecycle management, and UI updates all in one place. The Controller is tightly coupled to Android SDK, making it untestable with JUnit. It's also lifecycle-unsafe: the Controller is destroyed on rotation, interrupting ongoing work.
What is the key difference between MVP and MVVM?
Basic⌄
In MVP, the Presenter holds a direct reference to the View interface and calls methods on it — tight coupling that requires careful lifecycle management (detach on destroy). In MVVM, the ViewModel exposes observable state (LiveData/StateFlow) and never holds a View reference. The View subscribes and unsubscribes independently. This makes MVVM lifecycle-safe automatically — ViewModel survives rotation, View re-subscribes on recreation.
Why use UseCases between ViewModel and Repository?
Basic⌄
Three reasons: (1) Single Responsibility — each UseCase encapsulates one business rule; (2) Testability — UseCases are pure Kotlin, no Android dependencies, unit-testable with JUnit using mock Repositories; (3) Reuse — multiple ViewModels can use the same UseCase. Without UseCases, business logic accumulates in ViewModels (Fat ViewModel anti-pattern) or Repositories.
What is MVI and how does it differ from MVVM?
Intermediate⌄
MVI (Model-View-Intent) enforces strict UDF with three components: sealed Intent class (all user actions explicit), immutable State data class (all UI state in one object), and a reducer (Intent + State → new State). Unlike MVVM where ViewModels may have multiple state flows and methods, MVI has one state object and one entry point (processIntent). This makes state transitions auditable and the complete state machine visible. Tradeoff: more boilerplate.
Where should the Repository interface be defined — in the domain layer or data layer?
Intermediate⌄
Domain layer. This is the Dependency Inversion Principle — the domain layer should not depend on the data layer. By defining the interface in domain and the implementation in data, the data layer depends on the domain (not the other way). This means UseCases can reference the interface without knowing about Retrofit or Room. In tests, you inject a fake Repository that implements the domain interface — zero Android SDK needed.
What dependencies should a UseCase have?
Intermediate⌄
Only Repository interfaces (defined in domain) and other UseCases or domain services. A UseCase should have zero Android SDK dependencies — no Context, no ViewModel, no Room entities, no Retrofit annotations. This purity makes it unit-testable with plain JUnit5. If you find yourself adding import android.* in a UseCase, that's a code smell — the logic probably belongs in the data layer or a domain-specific service.
When would you choose MVI over MVVM for a feature?
Intermediate⌄
Use MVI when a screen has many possible states and transitions that are hard to track with boolean flags across multiple StateFlows — checkout flows, complex onboarding, multi-step forms, game UIs. MVI's single state object makes every combination of booleans explicit; you can't have an "impossible state" (loading AND error simultaneously) if the State is a sealed class. Use MVVM for simpler screens — list/detail, settings, profile — where the overhead of sealed Intents and reducers isn't justified.
A junior dev put network retry logic in the ViewModel. Is this correct? Where should it go?
Senior⌄
Not correct for reusable retry logic. Network retry is a data-layer concern — it applies regardless of which screen triggers the request. Retry logic belongs in: (1) Repository (retryWhen on Flow, or manual retry in suspend function), or (2) a generic data source interceptor (OkHttp Interceptor for HTTP retries). The ViewModel should handle UI state for retries (show retry button, update loading state) but not implement the retry policy itself. If it's a business-level retry (e.g., retry payment only if network error, not if card declined), a UseCase can add retry semantics before calling the repository.
How would you test a UseCase that executes a bank transfer?
Senior⌄
class ExecuteTransferUseCaseTest { private val fakeRepo = FakeTransferRepository(); private val sut = ExecuteTransferUseCase(fakeRepo); @Test fun `transfer succeeds when funds available`() = runTest { val result = sut(fromAccount, toAccount, 100.toBigDecimal()); assertTrue(result.isSuccess); assertEquals(1, fakeRepo.recordedTransfers.size) }; @Test fun `transfer fails when API throws`() = runTest { fakeRepo.shouldThrow = IOException(); val result = sut(fromAccount, toAccount, 100.toBigDecimal()); assertTrue(result.isFailure) } }. FakeTransferRepository implements the domain interface — no Retrofit, no Room, no Hilt. Tests run on JVM in milliseconds.
Design the full architecture for a real-time price tracking screen in a banking app.
Senior⌄
UI: Compose screen collecting StateFlow. ViewModel: exposes PriceScreenState via stateIn(WhileSubscribed(5000)); uses SubscribeToPriceUpdatesUseCase. UseCase: SubscribeToPriceUpdatesUseCase(repo): returns Flow<PriceUpdate> — pure kotlin, composable with Flow operators. Repository interface (in domain): PriceRepository.observePrices(symbols): Flow<PriceUpdate>. Repository impl (in data): bridges WebSocket via callbackFlow; shareIn(appScope, WhileSubscribed(5000)) to share one socket among multiple subscribers. Local fallback: Room observeLatestPrices() on network error. Dependencies: ViewModel depends on UseCase; UseCase depends on Repository interface; RepositoryImpl depends on WebSocket client and Room DAO.

8B — Clean Architecture

Three concentric layers, the Dependency Rule, and the art of keeping your domain pure. The architecture standard for production Android apps.

ID: 8B ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

What is Clean Architecture?

Clean Architecture (Robert C. Martin, 2012) organises code into concentric layers where dependencies only point inward. The innermost layer (Domain) has zero knowledge of Android, databases, or network — it is pure Kotlin business logic. Each outer layer depends on the layer inside it, never the reverse.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ PRESENTATION LAYER │ │ ViewModel · UI State · Composable / Fragment │ │ │ │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ DOMAIN LAYER (pure Kotlin) │ │ │ │ UseCase · Repository Interface │ │ │ │ Domain Models · Business Rules │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ │ DATA LAYER │ │ │ │ │ │ Repository Impl · Remote DS │ │ │ │ │ │ Local DS · DTO · Mapper │ │ │ │ │ └────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Dependencies flow INWARD only ──►

The Three Layers

LayerContentsDependencies
PresentationViewModel, UI State, Composables/Fragments/ActivitiesDomain layer only
DomainUseCases, Repository interfaces, Domain models, Business rulesNone — pure Kotlin
DataRepository implementations, Remote/Local data sources, DTOs, MappersDomain layer (implements interfaces)
Senior Mental Model
The Domain layer is the most stable part of your app. It should compile without any Android SDK, Retrofit, or Room imports. If your UseCase imports retrofit2.Response, you have violated the Dependency Rule.
⚙
2. How It Works

The Dependency Rule

Source code dependencies must point inward only. A class in the Data layer can implement a Domain interface, but the Domain layer never imports anything from Data. This is enforced at compile time by structuring them as separate Gradle modules.

Dependency Inversion in Practice

The Domain layer defines the PaymentRepository interface. The Data layer implements it. The Domain UseCase receives it via constructor injection — it never knows whether it's talking to Room or Retrofit.

// domain/repository/PaymentRepository.kt  (pure Kotlin interface)
interface PaymentRepository {
    suspend fun processPayment(request: PaymentRequest): Result<PaymentReceipt>
    fun getTransactionHistory(accountId: String): Flow<List<Transaction>>
}

// domain/model/PaymentRequest.kt  (Domain model — no JSON annotations)
data class PaymentRequest(
    val fromAccountId: String,
    val toAccountId: String,
    val amount: BigDecimal,
    val currency: Currency
)

// domain/usecase/ProcessPaymentUseCase.kt
class ProcessPaymentUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val repository: PaymentRepository,  // interface, not impl
    private val validator: PaymentValidator
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(request: PaymentRequest): Result<PaymentReceipt> {
        validator.validate(request).getOrElse { return Result.failure(it) }
        return repository.processPayment(request)
    }
}

DTO → Domain Model Mapper

DTOs carry network/database-specific concerns (JSON field names, nullable API fields). Mappers convert them to clean domain models at the boundary.

// data/remote/dto/TransactionDto.kt
data class TransactionDto(
    @SerializedName("txn_id") val txnId: String,
    @SerializedName("amount_cents") val amountCents: Long,
    @SerializedName("status_code") val statusCode: Int?
)

// data/mapper/TransactionMapper.kt
fun TransactionDto.toDomain(): Transaction = Transaction(
    id = txnId,
    amount = BigDecimal(amountCents).movePointLeft(2),
    status = TransactionStatus.fromCode(statusCode ?: 0)
)

Repository Implementation (Data Layer)

// data/repository/PaymentRepositoryImpl.kt
class PaymentRepositoryImpl @Inject constructor(
    private val remoteDataSource: PaymentRemoteDataSource,
    private val localDataSource: PaymentLocalDataSource
) : PaymentRepository {

    override suspend fun processPayment(request: PaymentRequest) =
        runCatching {
            remoteDataSource.processPayment(request.toDto()).toDomain()
        }

    override fun getTransactionHistory(accountId: String): Flow<List<Transaction>> =
        localDataSource.getTransactions(accountId).map { list ->
            list.map { it.toDomain() }
        }
}
Unidirectional Data Flow
UI → ViewModel → UseCase → Repository → DataSource. Data flows back up via Flow/StateFlow. No circular dependencies. Each step is independently testable with mocks.
💡
3. When to Use

Use Clean Architecture when:

  • Team size > 2: clear boundaries prevent merge conflicts and ownership disputes
  • Long-lived app: the separation pays off over months, not weeks
  • Multiple data sources: combining Room + Retrofit + third-party SDKs
  • High test coverage requirement: UseCases are pure Kotlin — unit tests need no Android framework
  • Feature parity across platforms: domain module can be shared with KMM (Kotlin Multiplatform Mobile)

Consider a simpler approach when:

  • Prototype or throwaway code — the boilerplate overhead isn't worth it
  • Single-feature, single-developer, short-lived app
  • Simple CRUD app with no business logic (a ViewModel directly calling a Repository may suffice)
Pragmatic Note
Many teams skip the UseCase layer for trivial screens (e.g., a settings toggle) and only introduce UseCases when business logic accumulates. That's fine — Clean Architecture is a spectrum, not a binary.

Module Structure (Gradle)

:app (Android module — Hilt entry point, navigation) :feature:payments :presentation (Android module — ViewModel, Composables) :domain (pure Kotlin module — UseCases, interfaces, models) :data (Android module — Room, Retrofit, repositories) :core:network (shared Retrofit/OkHttp setup) :core:database (shared Room setup)
🏭
4. Production Example

Banking App — Transfer Money Feature

A complete vertical slice through all three layers for a funds transfer flow:

// ── DOMAIN LAYER ──────────────────────────────────────────────

// domain/model/TransferResult.kt
sealed class TransferResult {
    data class Success(val receipt: TransferReceipt) : TransferResult()
    data class InsufficientFunds(val available: BigDecimal) : TransferResult()
    data class DailyLimitExceeded(val limit: BigDecimal) : TransferResult()
    data class Error(val cause: Throwable) : TransferResult()
}

// domain/usecase/TransferFundsUseCase.kt
class TransferFundsUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val accountRepo: AccountRepository,
    private val transferRepo: TransferRepository,
    private val limitsRepo: LimitsRepository
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(params: TransferParams): TransferResult {
        val balance = accountRepo.getBalance(params.fromAccountId)
        if (balance < params.amount) return TransferResult.InsufficientFunds(balance)

        val dailyLimit = limitsRepo.getDailyTransferLimit(params.fromAccountId)
        val usedToday = transferRepo.getTodayTransferTotal(params.fromAccountId)
        if (usedToday + params.amount > dailyLimit)
            return TransferResult.DailyLimitExceeded(dailyLimit)

        return runCatching { transferRepo.execute(params) }
            .fold(
                onSuccess = { TransferResult.Success(it) },
                onFailure = { TransferResult.Error(it) }
            )
    }
}
// ── PRESENTATION LAYER ────────────────────────────────────────

@HiltViewModel
class TransferViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val transferFunds: TransferFundsUseCase
) : ViewModel() {

    private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow<TransferUiState>(TransferUiState.Idle)
    val uiState = _uiState.asStateFlow()

    fun onTransfer(params: TransferParams) {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _uiState.emit(TransferUiState.Loading)
            val result = transferFunds(params)
            _uiState.emit(when (result) {
                is TransferResult.Success          -> TransferUiState.Success(result.receipt)
                is TransferResult.InsufficientFunds -> TransferUiState.InsufficientFunds
                is TransferResult.DailyLimitExceeded -> TransferUiState.LimitExceeded
                is TransferResult.Error              -> TransferUiState.Error(result.cause.message)
            })
        }
    }
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs
ArchitectureLayersProsCons
Clean Architecture3 (Presentation/Domain/Data)Testable, scalable, platform-agnostic domainBoilerplate, learning curve
MVI + Repository2 (UI/Data)Simpler, less filesBusiness logic bleeds into ViewModel
MVVM (no UseCase)2 (ViewModel/Repository)Quick to set up, Google's starter recommendationRepos become god objects over time
MVC (Activity)1No boilerplateUntestable, spaghetti code

Clean Architecture vs "MVVM with Repository"

Google's official guide shows MVVM + Repository without a Domain layer. That works for simple apps. As business rules grow, UseCases act as an extraction point — each one has a single responsibility, is independently testable, and prevents the ViewModel from becoming a god object.

KMM Advantage
If you structure the Domain layer as a pure Kotlin module, it can be shared between Android and iOS via Kotlin Multiplatform. Business logic is written once; only the Presentation and Data layers differ per platform.
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Common Violations

Anti-Pattern: Domain importing Android/Retrofit
import retrofit2.Response or import android.content.Context inside a UseCase or domain model instantly breaks the Dependency Rule and makes the domain untestable without Robolectric.
Anti-Pattern: Repository returning DTOs
If UserRepository.getUser() returns UserDto (with JSON annotations), the mapping responsibility leaks into the Presentation layer. Always map to domain models at the Data/Domain boundary.

Best Practices

  • One UseCase per action: GetUserUseCase, UpdateProfileUseCase — not a UserUseCase with ten methods
  • Domain models have no annotations: no @SerializedName, no @ColumnInfo, no @Parcelize (those belong in Data/Presentation)
  • UseCases are operator fun invoke: the idiomatic Kotlin style allows calling them like a function: getUser(userId)
  • Mappers as extension functions: fun UserDto.toDomain() keeps mapping code co-located with the DTO
  • Repository interface in Domain, impl in Data: enforced by separate Gradle modules so you cannot accidentally import the wrong one
  • Test UseCases with pure unit tests: no Mockk Android extensions needed — just mock the repository interface
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"Clean Architecture splits an Android app into three layers: Presentation (ViewModel + UI), Domain (UseCases + Repository interfaces + domain models), and Data (Repository implementations + Room + Retrofit). The key rule is that dependencies only point inward — the Domain layer knows nothing about Android, databases, or network. This makes business logic independently testable and swappable."

2-Minute Deep Dive

"On top of the three layers, I apply the Dependency Inversion Principle: the Domain layer defines repository interfaces, and the Data layer implements them. This means if we swap Retrofit for a GraphQL client, the Domain and Presentation layers don't change at all. I use the Mapper pattern to convert DTOs (which have JSON annotations) into clean domain models at the Data/Domain boundary — the domain model is annotation-free and testable without Android. UseCases are single-responsibility interactors — they orchestrate business rules, validate inputs, and delegate to repositories. The ViewModel only talks to UseCases and exposes a StateFlow of sealed UI states. The whole flow is unidirectional: UI → ViewModel → UseCase → Repository → DataSource, with data flowing back up via Flow."

Must-Mention Points

1
Dependency Rule: source code dependencies only point inward — outer layers depend on inner, never the reverse
2
Domain layer is pure Kotlin: no Android SDK, no Retrofit, no Room — compiles standalone
3
DIP: Domain defines interface PaymentRepository; Data implements it. ViewModel/UseCase depend on abstraction
4
Mapper pattern: DTO (data concern) → Domain Model (business concern) at the Data layer boundary
5
UseCase = single responsibility: operator fun invoke, one business action, independently unit testable
6
Unidirectional data flow: UI → ViewModel → UseCase → Repository → DS, results via Flow/StateFlow
7
Gradle modules: enforced at compile time — cannot import Data classes into Domain module

Do NOT Go Deeper On

  • Hexagonal Architecture / Ports and Adapters (same idea, different name — mention only if asked)
  • The full Gradle multi-module setup syntax (mention the concept, not the Gradle DSL)
  • KMM shared domain module (mention as a benefit, don't deep-dive unless asked)

Follow-up Q&A

QuestionAnswer
"Why not just use ViewModel + Repository?"Works for simple apps, but repos become god objects. UseCases isolate business logic, making it testable and reusable across features.
"Isn't it too much boilerplate?"The layers pay dividends in large teams: parallel development, isolated testing, and swappable data sources.
"What if a UseCase just delegates to a repository?"That's fine — a passthrough UseCase still provides a stable interface and a place to add logic later without touching the ViewModel.
"How do you enforce the Dependency Rule?"Separate Gradle modules: :domain is a pure Kotlin module with no Android dependencies. Any bad import causes a compile error.

Senior Insight

Senior Signal
Mention that the real value of Clean Architecture isn't the layers themselves — it's that it creates natural seams for testing. A UseCase with a mocked repository interface can be tested in <1ms with no emulator. At scale, this means thousands of fast unit tests instead of slow integration tests. That's the business case for the boilerplate.
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Layer Responsibilities

Presentation: ViewModel, UI State,
  Composables — talks to UseCases

Domain: UseCase, Interfaces,
  Domain Models — PURE KOTLIN

Data: Repository Impls, DTOs,
  Mappers, Room, Retrofit

Dependency Rule

Presentation
  └─depends on─► Domain
Data
  └─implements─► Domain interfaces
Domain
  └─depends on─► NOTHING

UseCase Pattern

class GetUserUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val repo: UserRepository
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(id: String) =
        repo.getUser(id)
}

Mapper Pattern

// In :data module
fun UserDto.toDomain() = User(
    id = userId,
    name = fullName,
    email = emailAddress
)
🅾
9. Interview Questions
Basic What are the three layers of Clean Architecture and what goes in each? ⌄
Presentation: ViewModel, UI State, Composables/Fragments — handles display logic and user events.

Domain: UseCases, Repository interfaces, Domain models, business rules — pure Kotlin, no Android imports.

Data: Repository implementations, DTOs, Mappers, Room DAOs, Retrofit API interfaces — bridges the domain to external systems.
Basic What is the Dependency Rule and why does it matter? ⌄
Source code dependencies must point inward only. Outer layers (Data, Presentation) can depend on inner layers (Domain), but Domain can never import anything from Data or Presentation. This means the business logic is decoupled from framework details, making it independently testable and replaceable.
Basic Why should Domain models be free of JSON/Room annotations? ⌄
Annotations like @SerializedName and @ColumnInfo are data concerns tied to specific frameworks. If you put them on domain models, your business logic becomes coupled to Gson and Room. When you switch serialisation libraries or databases, you'd have to modify domain models — violating OCP and the Dependency Rule. The solution is separate DTOs in the Data layer with mappers at the boundary.
Intermediate Explain the Mapper pattern with a concrete example. ⌄
A mapper converts between layers' models. A UserDto from Retrofit has @SerializedName annotations and potentially nullable fields due to API inconsistency. The domain User has validated, non-null fields. An extension function fun UserDto.toDomain(): User in the Data layer performs this conversion — handling nulls, renaming fields, and transforming types — so the Domain and Presentation layers work with clean, safe models.
Intermediate When would you skip the UseCase layer? ⌄
For screens with no business logic — like a settings toggle that just calls repository.saveTheme(theme) — a passthrough UseCase adds ceremony without benefit. In those cases, having the ViewModel call the repository directly is fine. The UseCase layer pays off when there's real orchestration: validating inputs, combining data from multiple repositories, handling business-specific error cases, or reusing the same logic across ViewModels.
Intermediate How does Dependency Inversion work between Domain and Data? ⌄
The Domain layer defines a interface ProductRepository with methods the UseCase needs. The Data layer provides class ProductRepositoryImpl : ProductRepository. Hilt binds the implementation to the interface via @Binds. The UseCase only knows about the interface — it never imports or instantiates the implementation. This means swapping Room for SQLDelight only requires changing the Data module; Domain and Presentation are untouched.
Intermediate How do you handle errors across the layers? ⌄
The Data layer catches network/database exceptions and converts them into domain errors — either via Kotlin's Result<T> or a custom sealed class. The UseCase propagates or transforms these into business-meaningful sealed results (e.g., InsufficientFunds instead of HttpException(402)). The ViewModel maps these to UI states. The Presentation layer never sees raw IOException — it sees domain-specific failure cases it can display meaningfully.
Senior How do you enforce Clean Architecture boundaries at scale? ⌄
Gradle modules are the primary enforcement mechanism — the :domain module declares no Android or framework dependencies, so any bad import fails the build. For monolithic single-module projects, tools like ArchUnit (via JVM tests) can assert that no class in the domain package imports anything from data or presentation. On large teams, a custom Lint rule or a modularisation guide in the team wiki prevents drift. The key is making violations visible at CI time, not code review time.
Senior Design a Clean Architecture structure for an e-commerce app with offline support. ⌄
Domain: ProductRepository interface with getProducts(): Flow<List<Product>>, GetFeaturedProductsUseCase, domain models Product, Cart, Order.

Data: ProductRepositoryImpl that first emits Room data (instant), then fetches from Retrofit, maps DTOs, saves to Room — so the Flow automatically re-emits the updated list. Room is the single source of truth. TTL-based cache invalidation triggers background refresh.

Presentation: ProductListViewModel collects the Flow, emits UiState.Loading / UiState.Success(products) / UiState.Offline(cachedProducts).

The offline-first pattern works naturally because Room's Flow re-emits whenever the local DB updates, regardless of whether the update came from the network or a local action.
Senior A colleague says UseCases are just "extra classes that call repository methods". How do you respond? ⌄
They're right for trivial cases, and that's fine — not every UseCase needs to justify its existence. The value emerges when:

1. Multiple ViewModels need the same logic — without a UseCase, you'd duplicate it or put it in the repository (wrong layer).
2. Business rules accumulate — a "place order" flow that started as a single repo call now involves inventory check, payment processing, loyalty points, and audit logging. A UseCase is the right seam for that.
3. Testing — a UseCase with mocked repos tests business logic at <1ms, no emulator needed.

The pragmatic approach: start without UseCases, extract them when ViewModels grow beyond display logic. The architecture supports that evolution.

● Android Interview Prep

9A — SOLID Principles

Five object-oriented design principles that produce maintainable, scalable Android code. Each principle with definition, Android violation, and correct fix.

ID: 9A ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

What are the SOLID principles?

SOLID is an acronym coined by Robert C. Martin for five design principles that, when applied together, produce code that is easy to understand, maintain, extend, and test. They are not rules — they are guidelines for managing complexity as a codebase grows.

LetterPrincipleOne-line definition
SSingle ResponsibilityA class should have one, and only one, reason to change
OOpen/ClosedOpen for extension, closed for modification
LLiskov SubstitutionSubtypes must be substitutable for their base types
IInterface SegregationClients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they don't use
DDependency InversionDepend on abstractions, not concretions
Senior Mental Model
SOLID principles are forces that counter entropy. Every codebase drifts toward tangled dependencies and god classes over time. SOLID provides the vocabulary and patterns to actively push back. In interviews, always connect each principle to a real Android violation and its concrete fix.
⚙
2. How It Works

S — Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

"A class should have one, and only one, reason to change."

Android Violation: An Activity that makes network calls, accesses SharedPreferences, formats dates, and updates UI — it changes whenever the network layer, database, UI, or business logic changes.

// ❌ VIOLATION: Activity doing everything
class OrderActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    fun loadOrders() {
        // Network call directly in Activity
        Retrofit.create(OrderApi::class.java).getOrders()
        // Database access directly
        AppDatabase.getInstance().orderDao().getAll()
        // Business logic directly
        val total = orders.sumOf { it.price * it.quantity }
    }
}
// ✅ FIX: Each class has one responsibility
class OrderRepository() { /* data concern */ }
class CalculateOrderTotalUseCase() { /* business logic */ }
class OrderViewModel(val repo: OrderRepository, val calcTotal: CalculateOrderTotalUseCase) { /* UI logic */ }
class OrderActivity { /* display only */ }

O — Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

"Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification."

Android Violation: A method with a growing when statement that must be modified every time a new payment type is added.

// ❌ VIOLATION: adding a new payment type requires modifying this class
fun processPayment(type: String, amount: BigDecimal) {
    when (type) {
        "credit"  -> chargeCreditCard(amount)
        "paypal"  -> chargePayPal(amount)
        // every new type requires modifying this file
    }
}
// ✅ FIX: Strategy pattern + sealed class — closed for modification
sealed class PaymentMethod {
    abstract suspend fun charge(amount: BigDecimal): PaymentResult

    class CreditCard(val token: String) : PaymentMethod() {
        override suspend fun charge(amount: BigDecimal) = /* ... */
    }
    class PayPal(val email: String) : PaymentMethod() {
        override suspend fun charge(amount: BigDecimal) = /* ... */
    }
}
// New payment methods extend PaymentMethod — processPayment never changes
suspend fun processPayment(method: PaymentMethod, amount: BigDecimal) =
    method.charge(amount)

L — Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

"Objects of a subtype should be substitutable for objects of their base type without altering program correctness."

Android Violation: A subclass overrides a method to throw an exception or do nothing — code using the base type breaks unexpectedly.

// ❌ VIOLATION: ReadOnlyRepository cannot honour the full contract
open class UserRepository {
    open fun save(user: User) { /* saves to DB */ }
    open fun delete(user: User) { /* deletes from DB */ }
}
class ReadOnlyUserRepository : UserRepository() {
    override fun save(user: User) { throw UnsupportedOperationException() } // 💥 LSP violated
}
// ✅ FIX: Separate interfaces — ReadableRepository and WritableRepository
interface ReadableUserRepository { fun getUser(id: String): User? }
interface WritableUserRepository { fun save(user: User); fun delete(user: User) }
interface UserRepository : ReadableUserRepository, WritableUserRepository

I — Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

"Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use."

Android Violation: A fat Repository interface that every screen must implement, even screens that only need one or two methods.

// ❌ VIOLATION: ProductListFragment only needs getProducts() but depends on this fat interface
interface ProductRepository {
    fun getProducts(): Flow<List<Product>>
    suspend fun createProduct(p: Product)
    suspend fun deleteProduct(id: String)
    suspend fun bulkImport(csv: String)
    suspend fun exportToCsv(): String
}
// ✅ FIX: Split into role-specific interfaces
interface ProductReader { fun getProducts(): Flow<List<Product>> }
interface ProductWriter { suspend fun createProduct(p: Product); suspend fun deleteProduct(id: String) }
interface ProductImportExport { suspend fun bulkImport(csv: String); suspend fun exportToCsv(): String }

// ProductListViewModel only depends on ProductReader
class ProductListViewModel @Inject constructor(val reader: ProductReader)

D — Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

"High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions."

Android Violation: ViewModel directly instantiates or imports a concrete repository class.

// ❌ VIOLATION: ViewModel is coupled to the concrete Retrofit implementation
class UserViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val repo = UserRepositoryImpl(RetrofitClient.create())  // concrete class
}
// ✅ FIX: ViewModel depends on the interface; Hilt provides the impl
@HiltViewModel
class UserViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val repo: UserRepository   // interface — can be mocked in tests
) : ViewModel()
💡
3. When to Use

These are default — not optional

SOLID principles aren't situational. They are default design hygiene for any codebase you expect to maintain or hand off to other developers. However, their application is graduated:

  • SRP: Apply from day one. God classes create an ever-growing change surface.
  • OCP: Apply when you identify variation points — places where new types or behaviours will be added. Don't over-engineer stable code.
  • LSP: Apply when designing inheritance or interface hierarchies. Prefer composition over inheritance to avoid LSP traps.
  • ISP: Apply when interfaces grow beyond 3–4 methods or when different callers need different subsets.
  • DIP: Apply to any class that needs to be testable. If you can't inject a mock, you're probably violating DIP.
The Litmus Test
"Can I write a unit test for this class in under 30 seconds — without setting up a Room database, Retrofit, or an Android emulator?" If the answer is no, at least one SOLID principle is being violated.
🏭
4. Production Example

E-Commerce App — Checkout Feature Refactor

A realistic before/after showing all five principles applied to a checkout flow:

// ❌ BEFORE: CheckoutManager violates SRP, OCP, DIP
class CheckoutManager {
    fun checkout(cart: Cart, paymentType: String) {
        // Validates cart (SRP violation)
        if (cart.items.isEmpty()) throw Exception("Empty cart")

        // Chooses payment (OCP violation — must modify for new types)
        when (paymentType) {
            "card"   -> StripeClient().charge(cart.total)   // DIP violation
            "paypal" -> PayPalClient().charge(cart.total)  // DIP violation
        }

        // Saves order and sends email (SRP violation)
        AppDatabase.getInstance().orderDao().insert(cart.toOrder())
        EmailClient().sendConfirmation(cart.email)
    }
}
// ✅ AFTER: Each responsibility extracted, depends on abstractions

// ISP: split interfaces
interface CartValidator { fun validate(cart: Cart): ValidationResult }
interface PaymentProcessor { suspend fun charge(amount: BigDecimal): PaymentResult }
interface OrderPersistence { suspend fun save(order: Order) }
interface NotificationService { suspend fun sendConfirmation(order: Order) }

// OCP: new payment methods extend this, CheckoutUseCase never changes
sealed class Payment : PaymentProcessor {
    class Card(val token: String) : Payment() { override suspend fun charge(amount: BigDecimal) = /* ... */ }
    class PayPal(val email: String) : Payment() { override suspend fun charge(amount: BigDecimal) = /* ... */ }
}

// SRP: one class orchestrates the flow, delegates everything
// DIP: depends only on interfaces injected via Hilt
class CheckoutUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val validator: CartValidator,
    private val persistence: OrderPersistence,
    private val notifications: NotificationService
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(cart: Cart, payment: PaymentProcessor): CheckoutResult {
        validator.validate(cart).onFailure { return CheckoutResult.ValidationFailed(it) }
        val paymentResult = payment.charge(cart.total)
            .onFailure { return CheckoutResult.PaymentFailed(it) }
        val order = cart.toOrder(paymentResult)
        persistence.save(order)
        notifications.sendConfirmation(order)
        return CheckoutResult.Success(order)
    }
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs

Over-applying SOLID

SOLID can be over-engineered. A simple settings screen that just toggles a flag doesn't need five interfaces and three UseCases. Premature abstraction creates indirection without benefit.

PrincipleBenefitOver-application risk
SRPFocused, small classesExcessive fragmentation — too many tiny classes to trace
OCPAdding types without breaking existing codePremature abstraction of stable code that never changes
LSPSafe polymorphismForcing inheritance where composition is cleaner
ISPLean interfacesInterface explosion — too many one-method interfaces
DIPTestability, swappable implementationsInterface-for-everything anti-pattern when only one impl exists
Rule of Three
Create an abstraction when you see a concept appearing in three or more places, or when you need to mock it in a test. Before that, the "wrong" code is often the simplest code.
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

SRP in Android — The Activity God Class

Most Common Android SOLID Violation
Activities/Fragments that contain network calls, business logic, database access, date formatting, and navigation. This is the top anti-pattern in legacy Android code. The fix: ViewModel for UI logic, UseCase for business logic, Repository for data, separate formatters and mappers.

DIP in Tests

The most immediate payoff of DIP is testability. When CheckoutViewModel depends on interface PaymentProcessor, you can inject a FakePaymentProcessor in tests. When it depends on class StripeClient, you can't test it without hitting the network.

LSP and Kotlin Sealed Classes

Sealed classes are naturally LSP-compliant: all subtypes are declared in the same file, so you always know the complete set. A when expression on a sealed class is exhaustive — the compiler forces you to handle all cases, preventing substitution surprises.

ISP and Click Listeners

// ❌ Fat listener — every implementer must implement all methods
interface OnItemInteractionListener {
    fun onItemClick(id: String)
    fun onItemLongClick(id: String)
    fun onItemSwipeLeft(id: String)
    fun onItemSwipeRight(id: String)
}

// ✅ Specific lambdas passed only where needed
class OrderAdapter(
    private val onClick: (String) -> Unit,
    private val onSwipeDelete: ((String) -> Unit)? = null
)
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"SOLID is five design principles: Single Responsibility — one reason to change; Open/Closed — extend without modifying; Liskov Substitution — subtypes are safely substitutable; Interface Segregation — small, focused interfaces; Dependency Inversion — depend on abstractions. In Android, the most common violation is an Activity doing networking, database access, and UI — SRP says those belong in separate ViewModel, Repository, and UseCase classes."

2-Minute Deep Dive

"Let me give Android-specific examples for each. SRP: an Activity that makes Retrofit calls violates SRP — extract to Repository, UseCase, and ViewModel. OCP: a when(paymentType) switch that grows every sprint violates OCP — replace with a sealed class hierarchy where each subtype implements a charge() interface. LSP: a read-only repository subclassing a read-write repository and throwing UnsupportedOperationException violates LSP — separate the interfaces. ISP: a fat Repository interface where each ViewModel uses only two of its ten methods violates ISP — split into role interfaces. DIP: a ViewModel constructing a concrete Retrofit client violates DIP — inject the interface, let Hilt provide the implementation. The unified benefit: every one of these makes the class unit-testable without Android framework setup."

Must-Mention Points

1
SRP: Activity doing everything = classic violation. Extract ViewModel, Repository, UseCase
2
OCP: sealed classes + strategy pattern let you add types without modifying existing code
3
LSP: prefer composition over inheritance; sealed classes are naturally LSP-safe
4
ISP: split fat Repository interfaces into role interfaces (ProductReader, ProductWriter)
5
DIP: ViewModel depends on interface Repository injected by Hilt — not on class RepositoryImpl
6
Testability link: every SOLID principle ultimately enables unit testing without Android framework

Do NOT Go Deeper On

  • Academic definitions and history (Robert Martin, 2000s publications)
  • Contrived examples that don't connect to Android
  • Every possible interpretation of LSP (keep it practical)

Follow-up Q&A

QuestionAnswer
"Which SOLID principle does Clean Architecture enforce?"DIP primarily — Domain defines interfaces, Data implements them. Also SRP via layer separation.
"Can you violate SOLID even with Hilt?"Yes. Hilt only enforces DIP if you inject interfaces. If you inject concrete classes, DIP is still violated.
"How does OCP relate to the open keyword in Kotlin?"Kotlin's open keyword is syntactic, not principled. OCP is about design — using polymorphism so callers never change. Not all open classes follow OCP.

Senior Insight

Senior Signal
The five principles aren't independent — they reinforce each other. SRP limits class scope, which makes ISP natural. DIP requires ISP (you need interfaces to invert). OCP is enabled by DIP. In practice, applying one principle to a violation usually requires applying two or three simultaneously. That's the sign of mature design thinking.
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

SRP — One Reason to Change

Activity → just inflate & observe
ViewModel → UI state logic
UseCase → business rules
Repository → data access

OCP — Extend, Don't Modify

sealed class Payment {
    class Card(...) : Payment()
    class PayPal(...) : Payment()
    // add Crypto here — no other change
}

LSP — Safe Substitution

// Prefer interfaces over open classes
// Sealed classes = safe exhaustive when
// Avoid: subclass that throws on override

ISP + DIP

// ISP: split fat interfaces
interface ProductReader { getProducts() }
interface ProductWriter { save(); delete() }
// DIP: inject the interface
class VM @Inject constructor(
    val repo: ProductReader  // not Impl!
)
🅾
9. Interview Questions
Basic What does SRP mean and give an Android example of a violation? ⌄
SRP: a class should have only one reason to change. Classic Android violation: an Activity that contains Retrofit calls, SharedPreferences access, date formatting, and UI updates. It changes when the API changes, when the database schema changes, when the UI design changes, and when the business logic changes. Fix: extract to ViewModel (UI state), Repository (data), UseCase (business logic), and Formatter (display formatting).
Basic What is DIP and how does Hilt enforce it? ⌄
DIP: high-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concretions. In Android, a ViewModel should depend on interface UserRepository, not class UserRepositoryImpl. Hilt enforces this via @Binds in a @Module, which maps the interface to its implementation at compile time. The ViewModel only knows the interface — in tests, you inject a fake; in production, Hilt injects the real impl.
Basic How does OCP apply to handling different payment methods in an app? ⌄
A when(paymentType: String) that keeps growing with new cases violates OCP — every new method modifies existing code. The fix is to define a PaymentProcessor interface with a charge() method, and represent each payment type as a sealed class subtype implementing it. The checkout logic calls processor.charge(amount) and never changes when a new payment type is added — it only extends via a new subclass.
Intermediate Spot the SOLID violations in this code and suggest fixes. ⌄
Scenario: class ProfileViewModel : ViewModel() { val retrofit = Retrofit.Builder().build(); fun loadUser() { retrofit.create(Api::class.java).getUser(); Room.databaseBuilder(...).build().userDao().getAll() } }

SRP violation: ViewModel constructs Retrofit and Room directly — data access is not its responsibility.
DIP violation: Depends on concrete Retrofit and AppDatabase classes, not interfaces.
Fix: Inject a UserRepository interface via Hilt. The ViewModel calls repository.getUser() and knows nothing about HTTP or SQL.
Intermediate Explain ISP with a RecyclerView listener example. ⌄
A fat OnItemInteractionListener with onClick, onLongClick, onSwipeLeft, onSwipeRight forces every implementer to implement all four methods, even if only one is used. ISP says: give clients only what they need. The fix: accept separate lambdas — onClick: (String) -> Unit, onSwipeDelete: ((String) -> Unit)? = null — so the screen only provides what it actually handles.
Intermediate How do sealed classes relate to LSP and OCP? ⌄
LSP: sealed class subtypes are all declared in one file with full visibility — you always know every possible subtype. A when on a sealed type is exhaustive, so the compiler enforces that all cases are handled. No subtype can introduce unexpected behaviour because the set is closed.

OCP: a sealed class with a when expression in a single place isn't OCP (adding a subtype requires modifying the when). But using the subtypes polymorphically — e.g., each subtype implements render() — achieves OCP because calling code never changes.
Intermediate Why can a class that uses Hilt still violate DIP? ⌄
Hilt is a DI framework, not a DIP enforcer. If you write @Inject constructor(val repo: UserRepositoryImpl), you're injecting a concrete class — DIP is still violated. For Hilt to enforce DIP, you must: (1) define an interface UserRepository in the domain layer, (2) implement it as UserRepositoryImpl in the data layer, (3) use @Binds to map the interface to the impl in a Hilt module, (4) inject the interface everywhere. Hilt automates the wiring; you must choose to depend on the interface.
Senior A PR adds a new feature by subclassing a Fragment and overriding onResume() to throw if a condition isn't met. What principle does this violate and what's the correct fix? ⌄
This violates LSP. Any code that uses the base Fragment type and calls resume() now has to defensively check whether it might throw — the subtype is not safely substitutable for the base type. The precondition (the condition that must be met) is stronger in the subtype than in the base, which is precisely what LSP forbids.

Fix: represent the precondition check as part of the Fragment's visible state machine. Use a UiState.RequiresCondition sealed class variant and navigate away or show an error screen. Never throw exceptions from lifecycle methods — the calling framework doesn't expect it and won't recover gracefully.
Senior How would you identify SOLID violations in a codebase of 200,000 lines during a technical interview review? ⌄
I'd look for these signals:

SRP: Classes >300 lines, or classes with methods that import 3+ different subsystems (network + db + UI).
OCP: Files with large when blocks on string/int types, especially in service or handler classes.
LSP: Overridden methods that throw UnsupportedOperationException, or empty overrides.
ISP: Interfaces with 8+ methods; implementers that stub half the methods with empty bodies.
DIP: Classes that construct their own dependencies (val x = ConcreteClass()) inside constructors or init blocks.

Tooling: Detekt rules enforce class/method line counts. ArchUnit assertions verify layer dependencies. These run in CI so violations are caught automatically.
Senior SOLID was defined for OOP. How relevant is it for Kotlin with its functional features? ⌄
Still very relevant, but Kotlin's features change the implementation idioms:

SRP: Even more relevant — Kotlin's extension functions let you decompose behaviour without subclassing.
OCP: Sealed classes are Kotlin's native way to express a closed-for-modification set of types with compile-time exhaustiveness.
LSP: Less of a problem because Kotlin discourages inheritance (open must be explicit) and favours interfaces and composition.
ISP: Functional interfaces (fun interface) and lambdas are naturally segregated — a lambda is a single-method interface.
DIP: Extension functions on interfaces allow default behaviour without breaking DIP. The principle remains; the syntax is more concise.
