11A — DI & Hilt Basics

Why dependency injection, constructor vs field injection, and Hilt's core annotations: @Inject, @Module, @Provides, @Binds, @InstallIn, scopes, and qualifiers.

ID: 11A ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

Why Dependency Injection?

Dependency Injection (DI) is the practice of providing a class with its dependencies from outside rather than having the class create them. This produces three critical benefits:

  • Testability: swap real implementations with fakes/mocks without modifying production code
  • Loose coupling: classes depend on interfaces, not concrete types (DIP)
  • Single source of truth: one place creates and configures dependencies — a Hilt module, not scattered new calls throughout the codebase

DI Without Framework (Manual DI)

// Manual DI — valid for small apps, but scales poorly
class AppContainer(context: Context) {
    val database = AppDatabase.getInstance(context)
    val orderDao = database.orderDao()
    val retrofit = Retrofit.Builder().baseUrl("https://api.example.com").build()
    val orderApi = retrofit.create(OrderApi::class.java)
    val orderRepo: OrderRepository = OrderRepositoryImpl(orderApi, orderDao)
    val getOrders = GetOrdersUseCase(orderRepo)
    fun orderViewModelFactory() = OrderViewModelFactory(getOrders)
}
// Problem: tedious, error-prone, no lifecycle management
Senior Mental Model
Hilt is Dagger with an opinionated, Android-aware setup. Dagger does the heavy lifting (compile-time code generation, validated dependency graph); Hilt provides the Android-specific component hierarchy and @AndroidEntryPoint so you don't write boilerplate component code. Understanding Hilt = understanding Dagger's core concepts + Android lifecycle.
⚙
2. How It Works

Constructor Injection (Preferred)

The cleanest form — dependencies are declared in the constructor, making them visible, testable, and immutable.

// @Inject on constructor — Hilt knows how to create this class
class GetOrdersUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val repository: OrderRepository  // interface — resolved by Hilt
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(): Flow<List<Order>> = repository.getOrders()
}

@Provides — Providing Third-Party Classes

When you can't annotate a class with @Inject (e.g., OkHttpClient, Retrofit, Room), use @Provides in a module.

@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object NetworkModule {

    @Singleton
    @Provides
    fun provideOkHttpClient(
        tokenStore: TokenStore  // Hilt injects this parameter automatically
    ): OkHttpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
        .addInterceptor(AuthInterceptor(tokenStore))
        .build()

    @Singleton
    @Provides
    fun provideRetrofit(client: OkHttpClient): Retrofit =
        Retrofit.Builder()
            .baseUrl("https://api.commerce.com/")
            .client(client)
            .addConverterFactory(MoshiConverterFactory.create())
            .build()
}

@Binds — Interface Binding (Preferred over @Provides for interfaces)

@Binds is more efficient than @Provides for binding an interface to its implementation — no code is generated for the function body, it's purely a Dagger hint.

@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
abstract class RepositoryModule {  // must be abstract for @Binds

    @Singleton
    @Binds
    abstract fun bindOrderRepository(
        impl: OrderRepositoryImpl  // Hilt injects the impl, returns as interface
    ): OrderRepository

    @Singleton
    @Binds
    abstract fun bindPaymentRepository(impl: PaymentRepositoryImpl): PaymentRepository
}

Scopes

AnnotationScopeLifetime
@SingletonSingletonComponentApplication lifetime
@ActivityRetainedScopedActivityRetainedComponentActivity lifetime across config changes
@ViewModelScopedViewModelComponentViewModel lifetime
@ActivityScopedActivityComponentActivity instance (destroyed on config change)
@FragmentScopedFragmentComponentFragment instance
@ViewModelScoped  // lives as long as the ViewModel
class CartSessionManager @Inject constructor() { /* ... */ }

@HiltViewModel
class CartViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val session: CartSessionManager  // same instance throughout ViewModel lifetime
) : ViewModel()

Qualifiers — Distinguishing Multiple Bindings

// Custom qualifier annotations
@Qualifier @Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY)
annotation class AuthenticatedOkHttpClient

@Qualifier @Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY)
annotation class UnauthenticatedOkHttpClient

@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object NetworkModule {
    @AuthenticatedOkHttpClient
    @Provides
    fun provideAuthClient(store: TokenStore) =
        OkHttpClient.Builder().addInterceptor(AuthInterceptor(store)).build()

    @UnauthenticatedOkHttpClient
    @Provides
    fun providePublicClient() = OkHttpClient.Builder().build()
}

// Injection site — specify which binding you want
class TokenRefreshService @Inject constructor(
    @UnauthenticatedOkHttpClient private val client: OkHttpClient
)

Entry Points — Injecting into Non-Hilt-Managed Classes

// For classes Hilt can't inject directly (e.g., ContentProvider, custom View)
@EntryPoint
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
interface SyncWorkerEntryPoint {
    fun syncService(): SyncService
}

// Use in a non-Hilt class
class DataSyncWorker(context: Context, params: WorkerParameters) : Worker(context, params) {
    private val syncService = EntryPointAccessors
        .fromApplication(applicationContext, SyncWorkerEntryPoint::class.java)
        .syncService()
}
💡
3. When to Use

Constructor Injection vs Field Injection

TypeSyntaxProsCons
Constructor injection@Inject constructor(val dep: Dep)Immutable, visible, testable without DI frameworkRequires a non-Android class or @HiltViewModel
Field injection@Inject lateinit var dep: DepRequired for Activity/Fragment (system-instantiated)Mutable, not visible in constructor, needs @AndroidEntryPoint
Rule of Thumb
Use constructor injection everywhere possible. Use field injection only for Activities, Fragments, and Views — classes that Android instantiates via reflection and where you can't control the constructor call.

When to Use @Provides vs @Binds

  • @Provides: when you need to call a constructor or configure the object (Retrofit, Room, OkHttp). The function body creates the instance.
  • @Binds: when you have an interface and an @Inject-annotated implementation. No function body — just tells Dagger which type to use. More efficient (generates less code).
🏭
4. Production Example

Banking App — Full DI Setup

// ── Application setup ─────────────────────────────────────────
@HiltAndroidApp
class BankApplication : Application()

// ── Database module ───────────────────────────────────────────
@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object DatabaseModule {
    @Singleton
    @Provides
    fun provideDatabase(@ApplicationContext context: Context): BankDatabase =
        Room.databaseBuilder(context, BankDatabase::class.java, "bank.db")
            .addMigrations(MIGRATION_1_2, MIGRATION_2_3)
            .build()

    @Provides
    fun provideTransactionDao(db: BankDatabase) = db.transactionDao()
}

// ── Repository binding module ─────────────────────────────────
@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
abstract class RepositoryModule {
    @Singleton
    @Binds
    abstract fun bindTransactionRepository(
        impl: TransactionRepositoryImpl
    ): TransactionRepository

    @Singleton
    @Binds
    abstract fun bindAccountRepository(impl: AccountRepositoryImpl): AccountRepository
}

// ── ViewModel (auto-injected via @HiltViewModel) ──────────────
@HiltViewModel
class TransactionHistoryViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val getTransactions: GetTransactionHistoryUseCase
) : ViewModel() {
    val transactions = getTransactions()
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5000), emptyList())
}

// ── Fragment — field injection via @AndroidEntryPoint ─────────
@AndroidEntryPoint
class TransactionHistoryFragment : Fragment() {
    private val viewModel: TransactionHistoryViewModel by viewModels()
    // No @Inject needed — viewModels() delegate works via Hilt ViewModel injection
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs
ApproachProsCons
HiltCompile-time validation, Android component hierarchy, minimal boilerplateBuild-time annotation processing, steep learning curve
Manual DI (AppContainer)No framework dependency, easy to understandManual lifetime management, no compile-time validation
KoinPure Kotlin, simpler setup, runtime resolutionRuntime errors (not compile-time), slower for large graphs
KodeinKotlin DSL, lightweightLess popular, runtime resolution

Hilt vs Koin

The critical difference: Hilt/Dagger validates the entire dependency graph at compile time. A missing binding is a compile error, not a runtime crash. Koin resolves at runtime — a missing binding crashes on the first use. For production apps with large dependency graphs, Hilt's compile-time safety is the decisive advantage.

⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Scope Mismatch

Scope Mismatch — Most Common Hilt Bug
Injecting a @ActivityScoped dependency into a @Singleton component. The Singleton lives longer than the Activity — Dagger catches this at compile time with a "cannot be provided without an @Singleton scope" error. Always match the scope to the shortest-lived component that needs the dependency.

Field Injection and Lateinit

Accessing Field-Injected Property Before Injection
@Inject lateinit var service: MyService — accessing service before super.onCreate() in an Activity (where Hilt performs injection) causes a UninitializedPropertyAccessException. Always access injected fields after super.onCreate().

@Provides vs @Binds

  • Prefer @Binds for interface-to-implementation bindings — it's a compile-time hint, not a function call
  • Never have both @Binds and @Provides for the same type in the same module
  • @Binds requires an abstract class for the module; @Provides can be in an object

@ApplicationContext vs Context

// ✅ Use @ApplicationContext qualifier for Context in Singleton-scoped modules
@Provides
fun provideDatabase(@ApplicationContext ctx: Context): AppDatabase = /* ... */

// ✅ Use @ActivityContext for Activity-scoped components
@Provides
fun provideNavigator(@ActivityContext ctx: Context): Navigator = /* ... */
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"Hilt is Android's dependency injection framework built on Dagger. The three main benefits: testability (inject a fake instead of a real implementation), loose coupling (depend on interfaces, not concrete classes), and single source of truth (one Hilt module creates and configures each dependency). You annotate the Application with @HiltAndroidApp, Activities/Fragments with @AndroidEntryPoint, ViewModels with @HiltViewModel, and constructor dependencies with @Inject. For third-party types you can't annotate, you use @Module + @Provides or @Binds."

2-Minute Deep Dive

"The key distinction between @Provides and @Binds: use @Provides when you need to instantiate the object yourself (Retrofit, OkHttp, Room). Use @Binds when you're mapping an interface to its implementation — it's a pure Dagger hint with no function body, more efficient. Scopes control object lifetime: @Singleton = one instance for the app's lifetime, @ViewModelScoped = one per ViewModel. A scope mismatch — injecting a shorter-lived dependency into a longer-lived scope — is a compile error in Hilt, which is the critical advantage over runtime DI like Koin. For qualifiers: when two OkHttpClient instances exist (authenticated and unauthenticated), custom qualifier annotations tell Hilt which one to inject at each injection site."

Must-Mention Points

1
Why DI: testability (swap fakes), loose coupling (interfaces), single source of truth
2
Constructor injection preferred; field injection only for Android-system-instantiated classes
3
@Binds for interface → impl (abstract module, no body); @Provides for construction logic
4
Scopes: @Singleton app-wide; @ViewModelScoped per ViewModel; scope mismatch = compile error
5
Qualifiers: distinguish multiple bindings of the same type (two OkHttpClients)
6
Compile-time validation: Hilt/Dagger catches missing bindings at build time; Koin at runtime
7
@HiltAndroidApp / @AndroidEntryPoint / @HiltViewModel: three required entry-point annotations

Do NOT Go Deeper On

  • Raw Dagger 2 component boilerplate (Hilt handles it)
  • SubComponent vs Component dependencies details (covered in 11B)
  • Koin/Kodein implementation details

Follow-up Q&A

QuestionAnswer
"What's the difference between @Singleton and object in Kotlin?"Kotlin object is a static, untestable global. Hilt @Singleton is a single instance managed by the DI graph — injectable and replaceable in tests via a test module.
"How do you inject into a WorkManager Worker?"Use @HiltWorker on the Worker class and @AssistedInject on the constructor. Hilt generates the required WorkerFactory that WorkManager uses.
"What happens if a binding is missing?"The build fails with a "cannot be provided without an @Provides-annotated method" error. This is the key advantage — you find it at build time, not in production.

Senior Insight

Senior Signal
The compile-time graph validation is Hilt/Dagger's most underappreciated feature. In a large app with 200 classes in the DI graph, adding a new dependency and getting a build error is a feature, not a bug. It means you find missing bindings before the QA team does. The extra build time annotation processing pays for itself in prevented runtime crashes in production.
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Core Annotations

@HiltAndroidApp   → Application class
@AndroidEntryPoint → Activity/Fragment
@HiltViewModel    → ViewModel
@Inject           → constructor or field
@Singleton        → app-wide scope

@Provides vs @Binds

// @Provides — construction needed
@Provides fun provideRetrofit(...) = Retrofit.Builder()...build()

// @Binds — interface mapping
@Binds abstract fun bindRepo(
    impl: RepoImpl
): Repository

Qualifiers

@Qualifier @Retention(BINARY)
annotation class AuthClient

@AuthClient @Provides
fun provideAuthOkHttp() = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor(AuthInterceptor()).build()

Scopes

@Singleton        → App lifetime
@ViewModelScoped  → ViewModel lifetime
@ActivityScoped   → Activity instance
@FragmentScoped   → Fragment instance
🅾
9. Interview Questions
Basic What are the three main benefits of Dependency Injection? ⌄
1. Testability: inject a fake or mock implementation instead of the real one — test the class in isolation. 2. Loose coupling: classes depend on interfaces, not concrete types — changing the implementation doesn't require changing the consumer. 3. Single source of truth: dependency creation is centralised in Hilt modules — no scattered new SomeClass() calls, consistent configuration everywhere.
Basic What is the difference between constructor injection and field injection? ⌄
Constructor injection: class Foo @Inject constructor(val dep: Bar) — dependencies are declared in the constructor, immutable, visible, and testable by passing them directly. Preferred everywhere possible.

Field injection: @Inject lateinit var dep: Bar — Hilt sets the field after the object is created. Required for Activities, Fragments, and Views because Android's system creates them using the no-arg constructor and you can't inject via constructor. Fields are mutable and can be accessed before injection.
Basic What is @Binds and when do you use it over @Provides? ⌄
@Binds tells Dagger to use a specific implementation class when a given interface is requested. It's in an abstract module method with no body: @Binds abstract fun bindRepo(impl: RepoImpl): Repository. Use it when the implementation has its own @Inject constructor and you just need to map the interface to it.

Use @Provides when you need to execute code to create the object — calling a builder, configuring a client, or using a constructor with non-injectable parameters. @Binds generates less code and is preferred for pure interface bindings.
Intermediate What does @ViewModelScoped mean and how does it differ from @Singleton? ⌄
@Singleton: one instance per Application component — lives as long as the app process. All ViewModels and classes in the app share the same instance.

@ViewModelScoped: one instance per ViewModel — lives as long as the ViewModel. Different ViewModel instances get different instances. The ViewModel's onCleared() destroys the scoped dependency. Use this for dependencies that logically belong to one ViewModel's operation (e.g., a cart session manager, a paging data source).
Intermediate How do qualifiers solve the "multiple bindings of the same type" problem? ⌄
When you have two OkHttpClient instances — one with auth interceptor, one without — Hilt/Dagger can't distinguish them by type alone. Qualifier annotations act as labels. You define @Qualifier annotation class AuthClient and @Qualifier annotation class PublicClient, annotate each @Provides method with the appropriate qualifier, and annotate the injection site: @AuthClient @Inject val client: OkHttpClient. Dagger matches the qualifier at compile time.
Intermediate How do you inject into a class that Hilt doesn't manage (e.g., a custom View)? ⌄
Use @EntryPoint. Define an interface annotated with @EntryPoint and @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class) that exposes the dependencies you need. In the custom View or ContentProvider, retrieve the entry point via EntryPointAccessors.fromApplication(context, MyEntryPoint::class.java) and call the accessor methods. This is the "manual injection" escape hatch — use it sparingly, as it's more fragile than normal injection.
Intermediate Why is Hilt preferred over Koin in large production apps? ⌄
Compile-time validation: Hilt/Dagger validates the entire dependency graph during compilation. Missing bindings, scope mismatches, and circular dependencies are build errors. Koin resolves at runtime — a missing dependency crashes the first time the code path is hit in production. For a banking or e-commerce app with hundreds of dependencies, finding a missing binding in CI (build failure) rather than in production (crash report) is critical.
Senior How do you write a unit test for a ViewModel that has Hilt-injected dependencies? ⌄
For a pure unit test, don't use Hilt at all — just instantiate the ViewModel directly with constructor injection, passing fakes:
val fakeRepo = FakeOrderRepository(); val vm = OrderViewModel(GetOrdersUseCase(fakeRepo))

For integration tests using Hilt (e.g., @HiltAndroidTest): create a test module annotated with @TestInstallIn that replaces the production module with fakes. The test Hilt component uses the test module. Use @UninstallModules(ProductionModule::class) on the test class to exclude the real module.

Prefer the first approach (no Hilt in unit tests) — it's faster and requires no instrumentation.
Senior Explain a scope mismatch error and how to fix it. ⌄
Scenario: @Singleton class UserDashboard @Inject constructor(val activityNav: Navigator) where Navigator is @ActivityScoped. Dagger error: "Navigator cannot be provided without an @ActivityScoped scope".

Why: A Singleton lives forever; an ActivityScoped dependency lives only while the Activity is alive. The Singleton would hold a reference to a dead Navigator after the Activity is destroyed — memory leak and crash.

Fix options: (1) Make Navigator also @Singleton if it doesn't truly require Activity context. (2) Move UserDashboard to @ActivityScoped if it logically belongs to an Activity. (3) Use Provider<Navigator> to defer Navigator creation and always get the current Activity's instance.
Senior How would you migrate a large app from manual DI (AppContainer pattern) to Hilt? ⌄
Incremental migration strategy:

1. Add Hilt to the project; annotate Application with @HiltAndroidApp.
2. Start with leaf nodes of the dependency graph — classes with no dependencies of their own. Add @Inject constructor.
3. Work up the graph: for each class whose dependencies are now injectable, add @Inject constructor. For third-party classes, create Hilt modules.
4. For interfaces, add @Binds modules.
5. Once a subsystem is fully in Hilt, annotate the consuming Activity/Fragment with @AndroidEntryPoint and annotate ViewModels with @HiltViewModel.
6. Remove the corresponding AppContainer code for that subsystem.

Key: don't try to migrate everything at once. The AppContainer and Hilt can coexist during migration — keep the old container for unmigrated parts.

11B — Hilt Components & Dagger Internals

Component hierarchy and lifetimes, Dagger code generation, @HiltViewModel internals, compile-time graph validation, and SubComponents vs Component dependencies.

ID: 11B ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

The Hilt Component Hierarchy

Hilt generates a hierarchy of Dagger components that mirror the Android lifecycle. Each component can access bindings from its parent (they form a parent-child tree). A component is created when its corresponding Android object is created and destroyed when that object is destroyed.

SingletonComponent (Application lifetime) └── ActivityRetainedComponent (survives config changes) ├── ViewModelComponent (ViewModel lifetime) └── ActivityComponent (Activity instance) ├── FragmentComponent (Fragment instance) │ └── ViewComponent (Fragment) └── ViewComponent (Activity) ServiceComponent (Service lifetime, parallel to Activity)
ComponentScope AnnotationCreated WhenDestroyed When
SingletonComponent@SingletonApplication.onCreate()Application destroyed
ActivityRetainedComponent@ActivityRetainedScopedActivity.onCreate()Activity.onDestroy() (NOT on rotation)
ViewModelComponent@ViewModelScopedViewModel createdViewModel.onCleared()
ActivityComponent@ActivityScopedActivity.onCreate()Activity.onDestroy() (INCLUDING rotation)
FragmentComponent@FragmentScopedFragment.onAttach()Fragment.onDestroy()
Senior Mental Model
ActivityRetainedComponent survives configuration changes — it's the component backing the ViewModel lifecycle. That's why @ViewModelScoped dependencies don't re-create on rotation. ActivityComponent does NOT survive rotation — never inject something that holds a reference to an Activity View into ActivityRetainedComponent.
⚙
2. How It Works

Dagger Code Generation

Dagger is an annotation processor that runs at compile time. It reads your @Inject, @Module, @Provides, @Binds annotations and generates concrete Java/Kotlin classes: a Factory for each injectable class, and a Component implementation for each component.

// Your code
class GetOrdersUseCase @Inject constructor(
    val repo: OrderRepository
)

// Dagger generates (simplified):
class GetOrdersUseCase_Factory(val repoProvider: Provider<OrderRepository>) : Factory<GetOrdersUseCase> {
    override fun get() = GetOrdersUseCase(repoProvider.get())
    companion object { fun create(repoProvider: Provider<OrderRepository>) = GetOrdersUseCase_Factory(repoProvider) }
}

@HiltViewModel — What Dagger Generates

// Your code
@HiltViewModel
class OrderViewModel @Inject constructor(
    val getOrders: GetOrdersUseCase
) : ViewModel()

// Dagger generates a Factory class:
class OrderViewModel_HiltModules_KeyModule_ProvideFactory
// + registers it in the ViewModelComponent
// Hilt's DefaultViewModelFactories uses the generated factory to create ViewModel instances

Compile-Time Graph Validation

When Dagger processes annotations, it builds a complete dependency graph. It performs several compile-time checks:

  • Missing binding: A type is requested but no @Provides/@Binds/injectable constructor provides it → "cannot be provided without an @Provides-annotated method"
  • Scope mismatch: A shorter-lived dependency injected into a longer-lived component → compile error
  • Circular dependency: A depends on B, B depends on A → compile error (can be broken with Provider<T> lazy injection)
  • Duplicate bindings: Two @Provides methods return the same type without qualifiers
// Example compile error: AnalyticsService is not provided anywhere
@HiltViewModel
class DashboardViewModel @Inject constructor(
    val analytics: AnalyticsService  // ← no @Inject on AnalyticsService, no @Provides
) : ViewModel()
// Build error: AnalyticsService cannot be provided without an @Provides-annotated method

SubComponents vs Component Dependencies

ApproachAccess to parent bindingsHow specifiedHilt equivalent
SubComponentFull access to all parent bindings@Subcomponent declared inside parentAll Hilt components are subcomponents of their parent
Component dependencyOnly explicitly exposed bindings@Component(dependencies=[ParentComponent::class])Not used in standard Hilt (Hilt uses subcomponents)

In Hilt's hierarchy, all components are SubComponents — each child has full access to the bindings of its parent (e.g., ActivityComponent can use Singleton-scoped bindings). This is why a @Singleton-scoped dependency can be injected into an Activity-scoped class.

Provider<T> — Breaking Circular Dependencies and Deferring Creation

// Provider<T> defers creation — the dependency is retrieved lazily on each get() call
class LoginFlowCoordinator @Inject constructor(
    private val authViewModelProvider: Provider<AuthViewModel>  // lazy + fresh instance each call
) {
    fun createAuthViewModel() = authViewModelProvider.get()
}

// Lazy<T> — like Provider but caches the first result
class FeatureFlagService @Inject constructor(
    private val remoteConfig: Lazy<FirebaseRemoteConfig>  // first access initialises, then cached
)
💡
3. When to Use

Choosing the Right Component Scope

ScenarioComponentScope
HTTP client, Room database, token storeSingletonComponent@Singleton
Shared state that must survive rotationActivityRetainedComponent@ActivityRetainedScoped
Dependency used by one ViewModel onlyViewModelComponent@ViewModelScoped
Navigator that needs Activity contextActivityComponent@ActivityScoped
Screen-specific analytics trackerFragmentComponent@FragmentScoped
Key Decision Criterion
Ask: "What is the shortest lifecycle that ALL consumers of this dependency have in common?" Use that component's scope. When in doubt, scope to @Singleton for stateless services (they're cheap to share) and @ViewModelScoped for stateful per-screen state.
🏭
4. Production Example

E-Commerce App — Scoped Dependencies Across Components

// ── Singleton (app-wide) ───────────────────────────────────────
@Singleton
class ProductCatalogCache @Inject constructor(
    private val clock: Clock
) {
    private val cache = LruCache<String, Product>(200)
    // Shared across the entire app — cache is populated once, used everywhere
}

// ── ActivityRetained (survives rotation, not Activity death) ──
@ActivityRetainedScoped
class CheckoutSessionManager @Inject constructor() {
    var selectedAddress: Address? = null
    var paymentMethod: PaymentMethod? = null
    // Survives screen rotation — user's checkout state is preserved
}

// ── ViewModelScoped (lives with one ViewModel) ─────────────────
@ViewModelScoped
class CartPagingSourceFactory @Inject constructor(
    private val dao: CartDao
) {
    fun create() = CartPagingSource(dao)
    // New factory per ViewModel instance — scoped to avoid stale sources
}

@HiltViewModel
class CheckoutViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val session: CheckoutSessionManager,    // ActivityRetainedScoped
    private val cache: ProductCatalogCache,          // Singleton
    private val pagingFactory: CartPagingSourceFactory // ViewModelScoped
) : ViewModel() {
    // Hilt injects the correct scoped instance for each dependency
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs

SubComponents vs Component Dependencies

Hilt uses SubComponents exclusively. Raw Dagger offers both: SubComponents have full access to the parent's bindings (tighter coupling, simpler configuration). Component dependencies are explicit — the child only sees what the parent exposes (looser coupling, better for library modules or multi-project setups). Hilt's choice of SubComponents simplifies usage at the cost of slightly less control over what's visible.

Eager vs Lazy Injection

TypeSyntaxBehaviour
Regular injection@Inject val dep: DepDep is created when the parent is created
Provider<T>@Inject val depProvider: Provider<Dep>Dep is created on each call to get()
Lazy<T>@Inject val dep: Lazy<Dep>Dep is created once, on first get() call
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

ActivityRetainedScoped vs ActivityScoped Confusion

Most Common Scope Confusion
@ActivityRetainedScoped survives rotation — it's the scope backing the ViewModel. @ActivityScoped does NOT survive rotation — it's a new instance every time the Activity is recreated. Never put something that holds a View reference into ActivityRetainedScoped; Views don't survive rotation and you'll leak the old Activity.

Build Errors — Common Dagger Error Messages

Error messageRoot causeFix
"cannot be provided without an @Provides"Type has no binding in the graphAdd @Inject constructor or @Provides method
"is bound multiple times"Two modules provide the same typeAdd qualifiers or remove duplicate binding
"depends on scoped components"Scope mismatchMatch scope to the shortest-lived consumer
"found a dependency cycle"A → B → A circular dependencyUse Provider<T> to break the cycle

@HiltViewModel vs SavedStateHandle

// SavedStateHandle is automatically available in @HiltViewModel constructors
@HiltViewModel
class ProductDetailViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle,  // injected by Hilt — no @Provides needed
    private val getProduct: GetProductUseCase
) : ViewModel() {
    private val productId = requireNotNull(savedStateHandle.get<String>("product_id"))
}
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"Hilt has a predefined component hierarchy that mirrors the Android lifecycle: SingletonComponent (app lifetime), ActivityRetainedComponent (survives rotation), ViewModelComponent (ViewModel lifetime), ActivityComponent (Activity instance), FragmentComponent. Dagger generates Factory classes at compile time for each injectable type, validates the entire graph, and catches missing bindings as build errors. When you annotate a ViewModel with @HiltViewModel, Dagger generates a Factory for it that the ViewModelProvider uses to create instances with injected dependencies."

2-Minute Deep Dive

"The key lifecycle insight: ActivityRetainedComponent survives configuration changes — that's the component behind ViewModel's survival. ActivityComponent does not survive rotation. So @ActivityRetainedScoped dependencies persist through rotation; @ActivityScoped ones don't. A scope mismatch — injecting an ActivityScoped dependency into an ActivityRetainedScoped class — is a compile-time error, not a runtime bug. Under the hood, Dagger runs as an annotation processor (kapt or KSP), reads all the annotations, and emits Java classes: a Factory per injectable class, an implementation class for each component. The factory pattern means every instantiation is explicit and traceable. For ViewModel injection specifically, Dagger generates a ViewModelFactory entry into the ViewModelComponent, and Hilt's DefaultViewModelFactories bridges that to Android's ViewModelProvider."

Must-Mention Points

1
Component hierarchy: Singleton → ActivityRetained → ViewModel → Activity → Fragment — child can access parent bindings
2
ActivityRetained ≠ Activity: survives rotation; ActivityScoped does not
3
Compile-time generation: Dagger (kapt/KSP) generates Factory classes and Component impls at build time
4
@HiltViewModel generates a Factory: registered in ViewModelComponent, used by Hilt's DefaultViewModelFactories
5
Graph validation at compile time: missing bindings, scope mismatches, circular deps = build errors
6
All Hilt components are SubComponents: full parent binding access — no explicit exposure needed

Do NOT Go Deeper On

  • Raw Dagger SubComponent annotation syntax (Hilt abstracts it away)
  • kapt vs KSP implementation details (just say "annotation processing")

Follow-up Q&A

QuestionAnswer
"Why does Hilt use SubComponents instead of Component dependencies?"SubComponents have full access to parent bindings — simpler for Android where components naturally nest (Fragment inside Activity inside Application). Component dependencies require explicit exposure of each binding, which is more verbose for the standard hierarchy.
"How does SavedStateHandle work with Hilt?"Hilt automatically provides SavedStateHandle in the ViewModelComponent — no @Provides needed. It's created from the Activity's or Fragment's saved state bundle.
"What's the difference between Provider<T> and Lazy<T>?"Provider<T>: new instance on each get() call. Lazy<T>: first get() creates the instance and caches it — same instance on subsequent calls.

Senior Insight

Senior Signal
Understanding what Dagger generates is what separates Hilt users from Hilt practitioners. When you add @Singleton to a class, you're not adding concurrency safety — you're telling Dagger to reuse one instance in the SingletonComponent. If the class has mutable state, you still need synchronisation. The scope only controls how many instances Dagger creates; you're responsible for thread safety inside the instance.
⚡

Component Lifetimes

Singleton       → App process
ActivityRetained→ Survives rotation
ViewModel       → onCleared()
Activity        → onDestroy() (incl. rotation)
Fragment        → Fragment.onDestroy()

Dagger Code Generation

  → generates Foo_Factory

@HiltViewModel
  → generates ViewModel factory
  → registered in ViewModelComponent

Build fails if binding is missing!

Common Build Errors

  → add @Inject or @Provides
"depends on scoped components"
  → scope mismatch — fix scope
"found a dependency cycle"
  → use Provider<T> to break it

Provider vs Lazy

Lazy<T>

  → cached for subsequent calls

9. Interview Questions
Basic List the Hilt component hierarchy from outermost to innermost. ⌄
SingletonComponent (Application) → ActivityRetainedComponent → ViewModelComponent and ActivityComponent (siblings) → FragmentComponent (child of Activity) → ViewComponent. ServiceComponent runs parallel to the Activity hierarchy, created/destroyed with a Service.
Basic What does Dagger generate when you annotate a class with @Inject constructor? ⌄
Dagger generates a Foo_Factory class that implements Factory<Foo>. The factory has a get() method that creates an instance of Foo by calling its constructor with the required dependencies (obtained from their own Providers). The factory is also used by Dagger to respect scope — if Foo is @Singleton, the component wraps the factory with a DoubleCheck to create only one instance.
Basic What is the difference between @ActivityScoped and @ActivityRetainedScoped? ⌄
@ActivityRetainedScoped: the instance lives inside ActivityRetainedComponent, which is preserved across configuration changes (rotation). One instance per Activity "logical session".

@ActivityScoped: the instance lives inside ActivityComponent, which is destroyed and recreated on rotation. A new instance is created every time the Activity is recreated. Use ActivityScoped for things that depend on the specific Activity instance (e.g., a Navigator using startActivity()).
Intermediate What does Dagger generate for a @HiltViewModel-annotated ViewModel? ⌄
Dagger generates: (1) A ViewModel_Factory that creates the ViewModel with all its injected constructor parameters. (2) A module that provides this factory, installed in the ViewModelComponent. (3) An entry point that Hilt's DefaultViewModelFactories can query to obtain the factory for a specific ViewModel class. When you call viewModels(), Android's ViewModelProvider asks Hilt's factory for the ViewModel type; Hilt looks up the generated factory and creates the ViewModel with injected dependencies.
Intermediate Explain how a child component accesses parent bindings. ⌄
In Hilt, all components are SubComponents. A SubComponent holds a reference to its parent component instance. When a binding is requested in a child component, Dagger first looks in the child's own modules. If not found, it looks in the parent's modules, then the grandparent's, up the hierarchy. This is why a FragmentComponent can inject a @Singleton-scoped OkHttpClient defined in the SingletonComponent — the request propagates up until it's satisfied. This is implicit in Hilt; with raw Dagger Component dependencies, you'd need to explicitly expose each binding.
Intermediate How does Hilt validate the dependency graph at compile time? ⌄
Dagger runs as an annotation processor (kapt or KSP). During the processing phase, it reads all @Module, @Provides, @Binds, @Inject annotations and builds an in-memory graph. Before generating any code, it validates: (1) every requested type has exactly one binding, (2) scope annotations are consistent (no parent-scope type in child component), (3) no cycles, (4) no duplicate bindings. Any violation produces a compiler error with a clear message pointing to the offending class. This happens before .class files are generated, so no runtime overhead.
Intermediate When would you use Provider<T> vs regular injection? ⌄
Use Provider<T> when: (1) You need a fresh instance on each call (not a singleton). (2) The dependency is expensive and may not always be needed — defer creation until first use. (3) You have a circular dependency — Provider<T> breaks the cycle because Dagger doesn't resolve T immediately on component creation. (4) The dependency comes from a child scope and you need to access the current instance at call time (e.g., getting the current Activity's Navigator from a longer-lived class).
Senior How does @Singleton scope work at the Dagger level — what code is generated? ⌄
When you scope a binding with @Singleton, Dagger wraps the generated Factory with a DoubleCheck wrapper in the component implementation. The simplified generated code:

private volatile Object myService = UNINITIALIZED;
On get(): checks if myService == UNINITIALIZED. If so, synchronized(this) check again, then create and store. Otherwise return the cached instance. This is the classic double-checked locking pattern.

Important: @Singleton does NOT make the class thread-safe internally. It only guarantees that Dagger creates one instance. If the class has mutable state accessed from multiple threads, you still need synchronisation inside the class.
Senior A Hilt build fails with "cannot be provided without an @Provides-annotated method" for a class that does have @Inject constructor. What are the possible causes? ⌄
1. One of the constructor's parameters is the missing binding — not the annotated class itself. Read the full error: Dagger traces the chain from the requesting site down to the unresolved leaf.
2. The class is in a Gradle module that isn't visible to the Hilt component module — transitive dependency not configured.
3. The class is abstract or an interface — @Inject constructor doesn't work on interfaces; you need @Binds.
4. Module is not installed — the @Module class exists but @InstallIn is missing or uses the wrong component.
5. Qualifier mismatch — the requesting site has a qualifier annotation but no binding with that qualifier exists.
Senior Design a multi-module Hilt setup for a feature module that needs to register its own bindings. ⌄
In a multi-module app, each feature module can define its own Hilt modules. Hilt aggregates them automatically at compile time via the app module's Hilt component:

:feature:payments module: @Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class) abstract class PaymentModule { @Binds abstract fun bindPaymentRepo(impl: PaymentRepositoryImpl): PaymentRepository }

:app module: just needs @HiltAndroidApp on the Application class. Hilt's annotation processing scans all included modules and their transitive dependencies, finds all @InstallIn modules, and includes them in the generated component.

Key rule: the feature module must be on the compile-time classpath of the app module. Dynamic feature modules (DFM) require a separate Hilt component since they're loaded at runtime — use @DefineComponent for custom components in DFMs.

12A — REST & HTTP

HTTP verbs, status codes, headers, authentication, timeouts, retry strategies, HTTP caching, and pagination — the networking fundamentals every Android engineer must know cold.

ID: 12A ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

REST Principles

REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for distributed hypermedia systems. Six constraints make an API RESTful:

  • Client-Server: UI and data storage are separated
  • Stateless: each request contains all information needed; no server-side session state
  • Cacheable: responses can be cached with appropriate headers
  • Uniform Interface: standard HTTP verbs, resource URIs, representation (JSON/XML)
  • Layered System: client can't tell if it's talking to the actual server or an intermediary
  • Code on Demand (optional): server can send executable code
HTTP Request Structure: POST /api/v1/payments HTTP/1.1 Host: api.bank.com Content-Type: application/json Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci... Accept: application/json { "amount": 100.00, "currency": "GBP", "toAccountId": "ACC-456" } HTTP Response Structure: HTTP/1.1 201 Created Content-Type: application/json Location: /api/v1/payments/PAY-789 ETag: "abc123def" Cache-Control: no-store { "paymentId": "PAY-789", "status": "PENDING" }
⚙
2. How It Works

HTTP Verbs

VerbSemanticsIdempotent?Safe?Android use
GETRetrieve a resourceYesYesFetch product list, user profile
POSTCreate a new resourceNoNoSubmit order, upload file
PUTReplace entire resourceYesNoUpdate full profile
PATCHPartial updateNo (usually)NoUpdate single field (status, name)
DELETERemove resourceYesNoRemove cart item, cancel order

Status Codes — The Essential Set

CodeMeaningWhen you see it
200 OKSuccess with bodyGET/PUT/PATCH response
201 CreatedResource createdPOST that creates a resource; response includes Location header
204 No ContentSuccess, no bodyDELETE success, PUT with no response body
304 Not ModifiedUse cached versionConditional GET with If-None-Match/If-Modified-Since
400 Bad RequestMalformed requestInvalid JSON, missing required field
401 UnauthorizedNot authenticatedMissing or expired token — trigger token refresh
403 ForbiddenAuthenticated but not authorisedUser lacks permission for this resource
404 Not FoundResource doesn't existInvalid product ID, deleted item
409 ConflictState conflictDuplicate order, optimistic lock violation
422 UnprocessableValidation failureBusiness rule violation (insufficient funds)
429 Too Many RequestsRate limitedRespect Retry-After header; exponential backoff
500 Internal Server ErrorServer crashedRetry with backoff
503 Service UnavailableServer overloadedRetry with Retry-After header

Key Headers

HeaderDirectionPurpose
Authorization: Bearer {token}RequestJWT or OAuth access token
Content-Type: application/jsonRequest/ResponseBody format
Accept: application/jsonRequestExpected response format
Cache-Control: max-age=300ResponseCache for 300 seconds
Cache-Control: no-storeResponseNever cache (for sensitive data)
ETag: "v12abc"ResponseResource version identifier
If-None-Match: "v12abc"RequestConditional GET — return 304 if unchanged
Retry-After: 30ResponseSeconds before retrying after 429/503

HTTP Caching with ETag

First request: Client ──GET /products──────────────────────► Server Client ◄──200 OK, ETag: "v5abc", body────── Server Second request (same URL): Client ──GET /products, If-None-Match: "v5abc"──► Server If unchanged: Server ◄──304 Not Modified──── (no body) If changed: Server ◄──200 OK, ETag: "v6xyz", new body── 
// OkHttp handles conditional GETs automatically if you set up a cache
val cache = Cache(File(context.cacheDir, "http_cache"), maxSize = 10L * 1024 * 1024)
val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .cache(cache)
    .build()
// OkHttp stores ETag from response; sends If-None-Match on next request automatically

Timeouts

TimeoutWhat it coversTypical value
connectTimeoutTime to establish TCP connection10–15 seconds
readTimeoutTime between packets during data transfer30 seconds
writeTimeoutTime to finish sending the request body30 seconds
callTimeoutTotal end-to-end call time (OkHttp 3.12+)60 seconds

Retry with Exponential Backoff

suspend fun <T> retryWithBackoff(
    maxAttempts: Int = 3,
    initialDelayMs: Long = 1000,
    maxDelayMs: Long = 8000,
    factor: Double = 2.0,
    block: suspend () -> T
): T {
    var currentDelay = initialDelayMs
    repeat(maxAttempts - 1) { attempt ->
        try { return block() }
        catch (e: IOException) {
            delay(currentDelay + Random.nextLong(0, 500))  // jitter
            currentDelay = minOf((currentDelay * factor).toLong(), maxDelayMs)
        }
    }
    return block()  // final attempt, let exception propagate
}

Pagination Patterns

PatternRequest paramsProsCons
Offset pagination?offset=20&limit=10Simple, random accessMissing items if content changes during pagination
Page-based?page=2&pageSize=10SimpleSame as offset
Cursor-based?after=eyJpZCI6MTAwfQ&limit=10Stable, no missing items, works with infinite feedsNo random access; cursor must be opaque
Keyset?lastId=100&limit=10Efficient DB query (indexed)Sorting is fixed
💡
3. When to Use

Choosing the Right HTTP Verb

  • GET: any read operation — always safe to repeat
  • POST: creating a resource where the server assigns the ID, or non-idempotent actions (submit payment)
  • PUT: full replacement; the client supplies the final representation
  • PATCH: partial updates — prefer when you only want to change one field
  • DELETE: removal — safe to retry (idempotent)

When to Retry

  • Retry: 429 (rate limit — wait for Retry-After), 500, 503, network timeouts (connect/read), SocketTimeoutException, UnknownHostException
  • Do NOT retry: 400 (bad request — same request will fail again), 401 (need new token first), 403, 404, 409, 422
  • Conditionally retry: POST payments — only retry if the API has idempotency keys
Idempotency Keys for Payments
POST is not idempotent. For payment APIs, send an Idempotency-Key: {uuid} header. The server will return the same response for duplicate requests with the same key, preventing double charges on retry.
🏭
4. Production Example

Banking App — API Error Mapping + Retry

// Sealed API result type — maps HTTP status codes to domain errors
sealed class ApiResult<out T> {
    data class Success<T>(val data: T) : ApiResult<T>()
    sealed class Failure : ApiResult<Nothing>() {
        data class HttpError(val code: Int, val message: String) : Failure()
        data class NetworkError(val cause: IOException) : Failure()
        object Unauthorized : Failure()
        data class ValidationError(val errors: List<String>) : Failure()
    }
}

// Map HTTP response to ApiResult
fun <T> Response<T>.toApiResult(): ApiResult<T> = when {
    isSuccessful    -> ApiResult.Success(requireNotNull(body()))
    code() == 401  -> ApiResult.Failure.Unauthorized
    code() == 422  -> {
        val errors = errorBody()?.string().parseValidationErrors() ?: emptyList()
        ApiResult.Failure.ValidationError(errors)
    }
    else            -> ApiResult.Failure.HttpError(code(), message())
}

// Repository using ApiResult
class PaymentRepositoryImpl @Inject constructor(
    private val api: PaymentApi
) : PaymentRepository {
    override suspend fun processPayment(request: PaymentRequest): ApiResult<PaymentReceipt> =
        retryWithBackoff(maxAttempts = 3) {
            api.processPayment(request.toDto(),
                idempotencyKey = request.idempotencyKey)  // prevents double charge on retry
        }.toApiResult()
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs

REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC

ProtocolProsConsAndroid use
RESTSimple, cacheable, wide tooling supportOver/under-fetching, multiple round tripsStandard — Retrofit
GraphQLFetch exactly what you need, single endpointNo HTTP caching on POST, complex toolingApollo Kotlin
gRPCBi-directional streaming, binary protocol (fast), schema-firstNo browser support, harder debugginggRPC-Kotlin, good for internal microservices
WebSocketFull-duplex real-timeNot request/response, need reconnect logicChat, live prices — OkHttp WebSocket

Pagination: Offset vs Cursor

For social feeds and real-time content, cursor-based pagination prevents the "page drift" problem: if a new item is inserted at the top while the user is on page 2, offset-based pagination would show the same item twice. Cursor-based pagination always continues from the last seen item regardless of insertions.

⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Status Code Pitfalls

401 vs 403 Confusion
401 = authentication problem (not logged in or token expired). 403 = authorisation problem (logged in but no permission). Handle them differently: 401 triggers token refresh; 403 shows "permission denied" and does NOT trigger a retry or refresh — the token is valid, the user just doesn't have access.
Retrying non-idempotent requests
Never blindly retry POST requests for financial operations. A retry after a timeout on POST /payments could charge the user twice. Always use idempotency keys for payment POST requests, and only retry with the same key.

Caching Sensitive Data

Never Cache Sensitive Responses
Account balances, transaction details, PII — always return Cache-Control: no-store, private. OkHttp respects this header and will not write the response to disk cache.

Best Practices

  • Version your API: /api/v1/ — never make breaking changes without a version bump
  • Use meaningful 4xx codes — don't return 500 for a validation error
  • Always set appropriate Content-Type on requests and responses
  • Add jitter to retry delays (random 0–500ms added to calculated backoff) to prevent thundering herd
  • Log request/response in debug only; never log Authorization headers or request bodies containing PII
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"REST uses standard HTTP verbs — GET to retrieve, POST to create, PUT to replace, PATCH to partially update, DELETE to remove. The most important status codes: 200 success, 201 created, 400 bad request, 401 trigger token refresh, 403 no permission, 404 not found, 429 rate limited, 500/503 retry with backoff. Caching uses ETags — server sends ETag with response, client sends If-None-Match on next request, server returns 304 Not Modified if unchanged, saving bandwidth."

2-Minute Deep Dive

"For retry strategy: retry 500, 503, 429 (respect Retry-After), and network errors like SocketTimeoutException with exponential backoff plus jitter. Never retry POST payments without idempotency keys — you'd charge users twice. The distinction between 401 and 403 is critical: 401 means unauthenticated — trigger token refresh and retry. 403 means authenticated but unauthorised — show error, don't retry. For caching: OkHttp supports disk cache with ETag-based conditional GETs automatically. For sensitive data like account balances, the server must send Cache-Control: no-store. For pagination, cursor-based is superior to offset for real-time feeds — offset pagination has a page drift problem when items are inserted during pagination."

Must-Mention Points

1
Verb semantics: idempotent = GET/PUT/DELETE; non-idempotent = POST/PATCH (usually)
2
401 vs 403: 401 = unauthenticated (refresh token); 403 = unauthorised (show error, don't retry)
3
ETag caching: server sends ETag; client sends If-None-Match; 304 = use cache
4
Retry strategy: exponential backoff + jitter for 5xx/429/network errors; idempotency key for POST payments
5
Timeouts: connectTimeout (TCP), readTimeout (data), writeTimeout (body) — set all three
6
Cursor pagination: no page drift; preferred over offset for real-time feeds

Do NOT Go Deeper On

  • HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 internals (mention that OkHttp supports HTTP/2 if asked)
  • Full OAuth 2.0 flow details (covered in 12C)
  • WebSocket frame protocol details

Follow-up Q&A

QuestionAnswer
"What's an idempotency key?"A UUID sent in a request header (e.g., Idempotency-Key). If the same request is sent twice with the same key, the server returns the same response without processing it again — preventing duplicate actions on retry.
"When would you use PATCH vs PUT?"PATCH for partial updates (change one field without sending the whole object). PUT for full replacement (client sends the complete representation). PUT is safer for conflict resolution — you always know the full state being set.
"What is a thundering herd?"When many clients all retry at the same time after a failure, overwhelming the server again. Jitter (random delay added to backoff) spreads retry attempts over time to prevent this.

Senior Insight

Senior Signal
In a banking or e-commerce app, the most dangerous HTTP mistake is blindly retrying POST requests. Network timeout doesn't mean the server didn't process the request — it might have. Always use idempotency keys for any non-idempotent operation that has real-world consequences (payments, orders, bookings). This is the difference between robust production code and code that occasionally charges users twice.
⚡

ETag Caching

9. Interview Questions
Basic What is the difference between GET and POST? ⌄
GET is safe (no side effects), idempotent (same result every call), and cacheable. Parameters go in the URL query string. POST is unsafe (may cause side effects like creating a record), not idempotent, and not cached by default. Body carries the payload. GET for reading; POST for creating or triggering non-idempotent actions.
Basic What should an app do when it receives a 401 response? ⌄
401 means the request lacked valid authentication — typically an expired JWT. The app should: (1) Pause the current request. (2) Attempt to refresh the access token using the refresh token. (3) If refresh succeeds, retry the original request with the new token. (4) If refresh fails (e.g., refresh token expired), redirect the user to the login screen. This logic lives in an OkHttp Authenticator or AuthInterceptor to avoid duplicating it everywhere.
Basic What does Cache-Control: no-store mean and when should you use it? ⌄
Cache-Control: no-store means the response must not be stored in any cache — not memory cache, not disk cache, not intermediary proxy cache. The entire response is discarded after use. Use it for sensitive data: account balances, transaction history, authentication tokens, personal information. no-cache is different — it allows caching but requires re-validation with the server before each use.
Intermediate Explain ETag-based conditional GET and its benefit. ⌄
The server includes an ETag: "version_hash" header with its response. The client caches the response and the ETag. On the next request, the client adds If-None-Match: "version_hash". If the resource hasn't changed, the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body — saving bandwidth and processing. If the resource changed, the server returns 200 with the new body and a new ETag. The benefit: freshness check happens every time (no stale data), but bandwidth is only used when the data actually changed.
Intermediate Describe a correct retry strategy for a mobile banking app. ⌄
1. Only retry transient failures: 500, 503, 429, SocketTimeoutException, ConnectException, UnknownHostException.
2. Exponential backoff + jitter: 1s, 2s, 4s ± random(0-500ms) to spread load.
3. Respect Retry-After: for 429/503, wait the specified duration.
4. Max 3 attempts: beyond that, fail and show the user an actionable error.
5. Idempotency keys for payments: generate a UUID before the first attempt; use the same key for all retries of the same payment.
6. Do NOT retry: 400, 401, 403, 404, 422 — retrying won't help.
Intermediate What is the difference between connectTimeout and readTimeout in OkHttp? ⌄
connectTimeout: how long OkHttp waits to establish a TCP connection to the server. A slow DNS lookup or an unresponsive server will trigger this. Typically 10–15 seconds.

readTimeout: how long OkHttp waits between receiving consecutive bytes from the server during data transfer. A server that starts responding but then stalls mid-response will trigger this. Typically 30 seconds for APIs; may need to be longer for large file downloads.

writeTimeout: how long OkHttp waits to finish sending the request body. Important for file uploads on slow connections.
Intermediate Compare cursor-based and offset-based pagination. ⌄
Offset: ?offset=20&limit=10 — skip the first 20 records. Simple to implement. Problem: if a new item is inserted at the top while the user is on page 2, page 3 will show one item they already saw on page 2 (page drift). Also slow for large offsets (database must scan rows to skip them).

Cursor: ?after=eyJpZCI6MTAwfQ&limit=10 — start from after the item with that cursor. The cursor encodes the position (usually last item's ID + sort field). No page drift — you always get items after your last position, regardless of insertions. DB query is efficient (WHERE id > cursor instead of OFFSET). No random access. Best for infinite scroll/feed content.
Senior A payment POST times out. How do you handle it correctly to avoid double charges? ⌄
Network timeout doesn't mean the payment failed — the server may have processed it and the response was lost. Strategy:

1. Before the first POST, generate a UUID as an idempotency key and store it (DataStore/SharedPreferences) alongside the payment state.
2. Add the key to the request: Idempotency-Key: {uuid}.
3. On timeout, retry the same POST with the same idempotency key. The payment API returns the original response (e.g., 200 with the receipt) if already processed.
4. On success: clear the idempotency key.
5. If all retries fail: show a "payment pending" state. Check payment status via a separate GET endpoint using the idempotency key as a reference.
6. On app restart: check for any pending idempotency keys and resolve their status via GET before allowing new payments.
Senior How do you design API error handling that works across the full Android stack? ⌄
Layered error handling:

Data layer (Repository): wraps raw Response<T> in a sealed ApiResult type. Maps status codes: 401 → Unauthorized, 422 → ValidationError with parsed field errors, 5xx → ServerError, IOException → NetworkError.

Domain layer (UseCase): maps ApiResult to domain-specific results: InsufficientFunds, AccountFrozen, etc. The ViewModel never sees HTTP concepts.

Presentation layer (ViewModel): maps domain errors to UI states: UiState.Error("Insufficient balance"). Provides user-visible strings, not error codes.

Benefit: the API's error model can change without touching the ViewModel; the ViewModel's error display can change without touching the repository.
Senior How would you implement HTTP caching for a product catalogue in a Retrofit/OkHttp app? ⌄
1. Add an OkHttp Cache object: Cache(File(cacheDir, "http"), 10 * 1024 * 1024).
2. Set it on the OkHttpClient: .cache(cache).
3. Server must send Cache-Control: max-age=300 (5 min) and ETag: "v5abc".
4. For offline mode, add a network interceptor: if no network, override the request's Cache-Control to only-if-cached, max-stale=86400 — OkHttp will serve stale cache rather than failing.
5. Combine with a Room single source of truth for offline-first: on network response, update Room; UI observes Room's Flow. Even with cache miss, the user sees stale data from Room rather than an error.

● Android Interview Prep

12B — Retrofit & OkHttp

Retrofit annotations, suspend vs Call, Moshi/Gson/kotlinx.serialization, OkHttp interceptors, Application vs Network interceptors, and how Retrofit wraps OkHttp.

ID: 12B ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

How Retrofit and OkHttp Compose

Your code Retrofit layer OkHttp layer ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── suspend fun getProduct() → Retrofit processes AnnotationProcessor annotations, builds reads @GET, @Path, etc. HTTP request creates OkHttp Request calls OkHttpClient.newCall() ApplicationInterceptors ↓ Cache check ↓ NetworkInterceptors ↓ TCP connection ↓ Server ↑ (response) ConverterFactory parses response body (Moshi/Gson) maps JSON to data class Returns typed object ◄──────────────────────────────────────────
Senior Mental Model
Retrofit is a type-safe HTTP client — it turns your interface into a working implementation at runtime using dynamic proxies. OkHttp is the actual HTTP engine. Retrofit handles the annotation processing and serialisation; OkHttp handles the connection pool, caching, and interceptors. They're designed to be used together but are independently useful.
⚙
2. How It Works

Retrofit API Interface

interface OrderApi {
    // @GET + @Path — GET /orders/{orderId}
    @GET("orders/{orderId}")
    suspend fun getOrder(
        @Path("orderId") orderId: String
    ): OrderDto

    // @GET + @Query — GET /orders?status=PENDING&page=1&pageSize=20
    @GET("orders")
    suspend fun getOrders(
        @Query("status") status: String? = null,
        @Query("page") page: Int = 1,
        @Query("pageSize") pageSize: Int = 20
    ): PagedResponse<OrderDto>

    // @POST + @Body — POST /orders with JSON body
    @POST("orders")
    suspend fun createOrder(
        @Body request: CreateOrderRequest,
        @Header("Idempotency-Key") idempotencyKey: String
    ): OrderDto

    // @PUT — full update
    @PUT("orders/{orderId}")
    suspend fun updateOrder(
        @Path("orderId") orderId: String,
        @Body request: UpdateOrderRequest
    ): OrderDto

    // @DELETE
    @DELETE("orders/{orderId}")
    suspend fun cancelOrder(
        @Path("orderId") orderId: String
    ): Unit  // 204 No Content

    // Response<T> — access the full HTTP response (headers, code, etc.)
    @POST("payments")
    suspend fun processPayment(@Body body: PaymentRequest): Response<PaymentDto>
}

suspend fun vs Call<T>

Return typeUsageThreading
suspend fun getX(): TCoroutines — preferred in new codeRuns on OkHttp thread pool, coroutine dispatcher handles switching
fun getX(): Call<T>Old code or if you need to cancel manuallyYou must call enqueue() on the right thread
suspend fun getX(): Response<T>When you need headers, error body, or status codeSame as suspend fun

Converter Factories

LibraryFactoryProsCons
GsonGsonConverterFactory.create()Widely used, simpleReflection-based, no null safety, no default values
MoshiMoshiConverterFactory.create()Kotlin-aware, null safety, codegen optionRequires adapters for custom types
kotlinx.serializationserializationConverterFactory()Multiplatform, KSP-based codegen, fastContent-type negotiation can be tricky
// Moshi with KSP codegen (preferred)
val moshi = Moshi.Builder()
    .add(KotlinJsonAdapterFactory())  // reflection fallback for classes without @JsonClass
    .add(BigDecimalAdapter())           // custom adapter
    .build()

val retrofit = Retrofit.Builder()
    .baseUrl("https://api.commerce.com/")
    .addConverterFactory(MoshiConverterFactory.create(moshi))
    .client(okHttpClient)
    .build()

OkHttp Interceptors

// Application Interceptor — runs before cache, for every call
class AuthInterceptor(private val tokenStore: TokenStore) : Interceptor {
    override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response {
        val token = tokenStore.getAccessToken() ?: return chain.proceed(chain.request())
        val newRequest = chain.request().newBuilder()
            .header("Authorization", "Bearer $token")
            .build()
        return chain.proceed(newRequest)
    }
}

// Logging Interceptor — debug only
val loggingInterceptor = HttpLoggingInterceptor { message ->
    if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) Timber.d(message)
}.apply {
    level = if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) HttpLoggingInterceptor.Level.BODY
            else HttpLoggingInterceptor.Level.NONE
}

Application vs Network Interceptors

TypeRuns whenCache hit?Best for
Application interceptor (addInterceptor)Before OkHttp's core logic, for every callYes — even for cached responsesAuth header, retry logic, business-level logging
Network interceptor (addNetworkInterceptor)After OkHttp decides a network request is neededNo — skipped for cache hitsGzip, low-level wire tracing, adding Cache-Control
💡
3. When to Use

Use suspend fun — Always in new code

Retrofit 2.6+ natively supports Kotlin coroutines with suspend fun. This integrates naturally with coroutine scopes, structured concurrency, and cancellation. Prefer it over Call<T> in all new code.

Use Response<T> when you need HTTP metadata

// Use Response<T> when you need the status code, headers, or error body
@POST("payments")
suspend fun createPayment(@Body body: PaymentRequest): Response<PaymentDto>

// In repository:
val response = api.createPayment(request)
if (response.isSuccessful()) {
    val locationHeader = response.headers()["Location"]  // e.g. /payments/PAY-123
    val dto = response.body()!!
} else {
    val errorJson = response.errorBody()?.string()
}

Converter Factory Selection

For new projects: Moshi with KSP codegen (@JsonClass(generateAdapter = true)) or kotlinx.serialization. Both avoid reflection, support Kotlin null safety, and generate adapters at compile time. Avoid Gson for new code — it doesn't understand Kotlin nullable types correctly.

🏭
4. Production Example

E-Commerce App — Full Retrofit + OkHttp Setup

// ── Retrofit interface ───────────────────────────────────────
interface CommerceApi {
    @GET("v1/products")
    suspend fun getProducts(
        @Query("categoryId") categoryId: String?,
        @Query("cursor") cursor: String? = null,
        @Query("limit") limit: Int = 20
    ): CursorPageResponse<ProductDto>

    @POST("v1/cart/items")
    suspend fun addToCart(
        @Body item: AddToCartRequest,
        @Header("Idempotency-Key") key: String
    ): CartItemDto
}

// ── Full OkHttp + Retrofit setup in Hilt module ──────────────
@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object NetworkModule {

    @Singleton
    @Provides
    fun provideOkHttpClient(
        tokenStore: TokenStore,
        @ApplicationContext context: Context
    ): OkHttpClient {
        val cache = Cache(File(context.cacheDir, "http"), 10L * 1024 * 1024)
        return OkHttpClient.Builder()
            .cache(cache)
            .connectTimeout(15, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
            .readTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
            .writeTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
            .addInterceptor(AuthInterceptor(tokenStore))          // auth first
            .addInterceptor(buildLoggingInterceptor())             // logging after auth
            .build()
    }

    @Singleton
    @Provides
    fun provideCommerceApi(client: OkHttpClient): CommerceApi =
        Retrofit.Builder()
            .baseUrl("https://api.commerce.com/")
            .client(client)
            .addConverterFactory(MoshiConverterFactory.create(buildMoshi()))
            .build()
            .create(CommerceApi::class.java)

    private fun buildLoggingInterceptor() = HttpLoggingInterceptor().apply {
        level = if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) HttpLoggingInterceptor.Level.BODY
                else HttpLoggingInterceptor.Level.NONE
    }

    private fun buildMoshi() = Moshi.Builder()
        .addLast(KotlinJsonAdapterFactory())
        .build()
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs

Retrofit vs Ktor Client vs Manual OkHttp

LibraryProsConsUse when
RetrofitType-safe, annotation-driven, huge ecosystemReflection-based proxy, extra dependencyStandard Android REST APIs
Ktor ClientKMM-compatible, first-class coroutines, flexible DSLLess familiar, more boilerplate for simple APIsKotlin Multiplatform projects
Raw OkHttpFull control, no abstractionsNo type safety, manual serialisationComplex streaming, WebSocket, when Retrofit isn't available

Gson vs Moshi vs kotlinx.serialization

Gson Null Safety Problem
Gson ignores Kotlin's null safety — it will happily set a non-nullable Kotlin field to null if the JSON is missing the field, causing NPE at runtime. Always use Moshi or kotlinx.serialization for Kotlin code.
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Common Mistakes

Creating Multiple Retrofit Instances
Retrofit and OkHttpClient are expensive to create and should be singletons. Creating a new instance per request or per screen causes multiple connection pools, multiple thread pools, and wasted memory. Always inject via Hilt as @Singleton.
Logging Authorization Headers in Production
HttpLoggingInterceptor.Level.BODY logs the full Authorization header and request bodies. Guard with if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) — never ship BODY logging to production users. Sensitive data in logs is a security violation.

@Path Encoding

// By default, @Path URL-encodes the value
@GET("users/{userId}/orders")
suspend fun getOrders(@Path("userId") userId: String)
// userId = "user/123" → encodes to "user%2F123" (safe)

// To allow slashes (when path segment contains a full path):
@GET("{fullPath}")
suspend fun getResource(@Path("fullPath", encoded = true) path: String)

ConnectionPool

// OkHttp default: 5 connections, 5 min idle timeout — usually fine
// For high-throughput: increase maxIdleConnections
val connectionPool = ConnectionPool(maxIdleConnections = 10, keepAliveDuration = 5, TimeUnit.MINUTES)
val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectionPool(connectionPool)
    .build()
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"Retrofit is a type-safe HTTP client that sits on top of OkHttp. You define your API as an interface with Retrofit annotations — @GET, @POST, @Path, @Query, @Body, @Header. Retrofit generates a proxy implementation at runtime, reads annotations to build OkHttp requests, passes them to OkHttp, and converts the response using a converter factory like Moshi. OkHttp handles the actual TCP connection, connection pooling, caching, and interceptor chains."

2-Minute Deep Dive

"The interceptor chain is the key OkHttp concept. Application interceptors run for every call including cache hits — used for auth headers and logging. Network interceptors run only for actual network requests — used for low-level headers. Order matters: I always put auth first, then logging, so the log shows the authenticated request. For serialisation: never use Gson in new Kotlin code — it ignores null safety and can set non-nullable fields to null from JSON, causing NPEs. Use Moshi with @JsonClass(generateAdapter = true) for compile-time adapter generation, or kotlinx.serialization. For suspend vs Call: always use suspend in new code — it integrates with structured concurrency, and cancellation happens automatically when the coroutine scope is cancelled."

Must-Mention Points

1
Retrofit wraps OkHttp: Retrofit = annotation processing + converter; OkHttp = HTTP engine + interceptors + pool
2
suspend fun preferred over Call<T> — integrates with structured concurrency
3
Moshi over Gson: Gson doesn't respect Kotlin null safety; Moshi does with codegen
4
Application vs Network Interceptor: Application = every call; Network = only actual HTTP calls
5
Singleton OkHttpClient: one instance per app — connection pool, thread pool, cache are shared
6
Never log in production: Level.BODY is debug-only — logs full headers including auth tokens

Do NOT Go Deeper On

  • Retrofit Rx/Java adapters (replaced by coroutines)
  • Full Moshi/Gson annotation reference
  • OkHttp HTTP/2 multiplexing internals

Follow-up Q&A

QuestionAnswer
"How does Retrofit create the API implementation?"Via Java's dynamic proxy (Proxy.newProxyInstance()). The InvocationHandler intercepts every method call, reads annotations to build an OkHttp Request, executes it, and converts the response.
"What happens if Retrofit has multiple converter factories?"Retrofit tries each factory in order, using the first one that claims it can handle the type. Add the most specific factory first, fallback factory last.
"How do you handle multipart file uploads?"Use @Multipart on the method and @Part on parameters. Wrap files in MultipartBody.Part.createFormData("file", filename, requestBody).

Senior Insight

Senior Signal
The most important production concern is that OkHttp's interceptors run synchronously on OkHttp's thread pool. Never do UI work in an interceptor. Also: if you need to make another network call inside an interceptor (e.g., refresh token), use a synchronous execute() call on the new client, not a coroutine — interceptors aren't coroutine-aware and using suspending functions there requires careful handling to avoid deadlocks.
⚡

9. Interview Questions
Basic What is the role of a Retrofit converter factory? ⌄
A converter factory serialises your Kotlin objects into a request body (e.g., data class → JSON string) and deserialises the response body into Kotlin objects (JSON string → data class). Without a converter factory, you'd have to handle raw ResponseBody and call body.string() manually. Factories are added to Retrofit.Builder; Retrofit tries each in order until one claims it can handle the type.
Basic What is the difference between @Path and @Query in Retrofit? ⌄
@Path("id") replaces a placeholder in the URL path: @GET("products/{id}") with @Path("id") productId: String → GET /products/abc123. The value is URL-encoded by default.

@Query("status") appends a query parameter: @GET("products") with @Query("status") status: String → GET /products?status=ACTIVE. Null values are omitted from the URL.
Basic Why should you not use Gson with Kotlin? ⌄
Gson was designed for Java and doesn't understand Kotlin's type system. If a JSON field is missing, Gson sets the corresponding Kotlin property to null — even if it's declared as non-nullable. This bypasses Kotlin's null safety guarantees and causes NullPointerException at runtime when accessing the property. Moshi and kotlinx.serialization are Kotlin-aware and throw a descriptive exception if a required non-nullable field is missing.
Intermediate Explain the difference between Application Interceptors and Network Interceptors. ⌄
Application Interceptors (addInterceptor()): added to the application layer, before OkHttp's core. They run for every call — including responses served from cache (no network request is made). They see the final URL after redirects. Best for: adding auth headers (so cached responses also get the header for consistency), retry logic, and request/response logging at the business level.

Network Interceptors (addNetworkInterceptor()): added to the network layer. They only run when an actual network connection is established. They don't run for cache hits. Best for: modifying response headers, adding Cache-Control headers, low-level traffic analysis or compression.
Intermediate Why should OkHttpClient be a singleton, and what happens if it's not? ⌄
Each OkHttpClient instance maintains its own: thread pool (for async calls), connection pool (open TCP connections), DNS cache, and HTTP response cache. Creating a new client per request means: no connection reuse (expensive TCP handshake every call), no shared cache (disk cache opens/closes repeatedly), wasted threads. A Singleton client reuses connections across requests (HTTP keep-alive), shares the thread pool efficiently, and has a single cache. This significantly reduces latency and memory usage.
Intermediate How do you access the HTTP status code and error body when using Retrofit? ⌄
Change the return type from T to Response<T>: suspend fun getUser(): Response<UserDto>. The Response wrapper provides: response.code() (HTTP status), response.isSuccessful() (200–299), response.body() (parsed body if successful), response.errorBody() (raw error body string for 4xx/5xx), response.headers() (all response headers). Parse the error body with your Moshi instance to get structured error objects.
Intermediate How would you build a Moshi instance with a custom adapter for BigDecimal? ⌄
class BigDecimalAdapter { @FromJson fun fromJson(value: String) = BigDecimal(value); @ToJson fun toJson(value: BigDecimal) = value.toPlainString() }

val moshi = Moshi.Builder().add(BigDecimalAdapter()).addLast(KotlinJsonAdapterFactory()).build()

Add adapters before KotlinJsonAdapterFactory so they take priority. Use addLast() for KotlinJsonAdapterFactory as a general fallback. Register the Moshi instance with Retrofit: .addConverterFactory(MoshiConverterFactory.create(moshi)).
Senior Describe in detail how Retrofit creates the implementation of your API interface. ⌄
When you call retrofit.create(OrderApi::class.java):

1. Retrofit uses Proxy.newProxyInstance(classLoader, arrayOf(OrderApi::class.java), handler) to create a Java dynamic proxy.
2. The InvocationHandler intercepts every method call on the proxy.
3. On getOrder("123"): Retrofit reads annotations (@GET("orders/{orderId}"), @Path("orderId")) from the method's reflection metadata.
4. It builds an OkHttp Request with the resolved URL, headers, and body.
5. For suspend fun: Retrofit uses a SuspendCallAdapterFactory that converts Call<T> to a coroutine-compatible execution using suspendCancellableCoroutine.
6. The request passes through OkHttp's interceptor chain and returns a Response.
7. The configured ConverterFactory deserialises response.body() into the return type.
Senior How would you make a synchronous network call inside an OkHttp interceptor to refresh a token? ⌄
Use a separate, unauthenticated OkHttpClient instance and call .execute() (synchronous, not .enqueue()) on a new Call:

val refreshResponse = unauthClient.newCall(refreshRequest).execute()

Key rules: (1) Use the unauthenticated client — never the same client, or you'll infinite loop. (2) Use execute(), not enqueue() — interceptors run synchronously; enqueue() would require a callback and block the interceptor thread awkwardly. (3) Use a Mutex to ensure only one refresh request happens concurrently when multiple API calls fail with 401 simultaneously. (4) After refreshing, update the token store and retry the original request with chain.proceed(newRequest).
Senior A production app is making too many connections. What OkHttp settings would you investigate? ⌄
1. Multiple OkHttpClient instances: each has its own connection pool. Consolidate to a singleton. Check via profiling — unique pool objects.
2. ConnectionPool configuration: default is 5 idle connections, 5 min keep-alive. For high traffic, increase maxIdleConnections so connections aren't closed and reopened.
3. HTTP/2 not being used: HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple requests over one connection. Verify server supports HTTP/2; OkHttp enables it automatically if the server supports ALPN.
4. Aggressive timeouts: very short timeouts cause premature connection closure. Check if keepAliveDuration aligns with server's connection timeout.
5. retryOnConnectionFailure: if true, OkHttp opens new connections on failure — can compound connection issues during server outages.
