12C — Advanced Networking

Certificate pinning, token refresh with Mutex, concurrent refresh problem, API error handling with sealed Result, and offline-first networking strategies.

ID: 12C ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

Advanced Production Networking Topics

TopicProblem solved
Certificate PinningPrevents MITM attacks even if a rogue CA is trusted
Network Security ConfigDeclarative security policy — no code needed for basic pinning
Token RefreshSilently refreshes expired JWT and retries original request
Concurrent Refresh ProblemMultiple simultaneous 401s — only one refresh call is made
Sealed Result + Error MapperType-safe error propagation across layers
Offline-FirstApp works without network; data syncs when connectivity returns
Senior Mental Model
These are the topics that distinguish senior Android engineers from mid-level ones. Certificate pinning is a requirement in banking/healthcare apps. The concurrent token refresh problem is a classic race condition — every banking app must solve it. Offline-first is about more than caching — it's about designing the Room + Retrofit data flow so the UI never shows an error when the network is slow.
⚙
2. How It Works

1. Certificate Pinning

Certificate pinning prevents MITM attacks by hardcoding the expected certificate (or its public key hash) in the app. Even if a user installs a malicious CA certificate, a pinned connection will fail.

// OkHttp CertificatePinner — pin the server's leaf or intermediate certificate
val certificatePinner = CertificatePinner.Builder()
    .add("api.bank.com", "sha256/AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=")
    .add("api.bank.com", "sha256/BACKUP_PIN_HASH_HERE=")  // backup pin for rotation
    .build()

val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .certificatePinner(certificatePinner)
    .build()

Network Security Config (Declarative, XML)

<!-- res/xml/network_security_config.xml -->
<network-security-config>
    <domain-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="false">
        <domain includeSubdomains="true">api.bank.com</domain>
        <pin-set expiration="2026-01-01">
            <pin digest="SHA-256">AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=</pin>
            <pin digest="SHA-256">BACKUP_PIN=</pin>
        </pin-set>
    </domain-config>
</network-security-config>

<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<application android:networkSecurityConfig="@xml/network_security_config" ... />

2. Token Refresh — The Concurrent Problem

When a JWT expires, multiple in-flight API calls all get 401 simultaneously. Without coordination, each call would try to refresh the token independently — causing multiple refresh requests and race conditions.

PROBLEM (no mutex): Thread 1: GET /orders → 401 → starts refresh Thread 2: GET /cart → 401 → starts refresh (duplicate!) Thread 3: GET /user → 401 → starts refresh (triplicate!) → 3 concurrent refresh calls → server confusion, possible logout SOLUTION (with Mutex): Thread 1: GET /orders → 401 → acquires Mutex → refreshes token → releases Mutex → retries Thread 2: GET /cart → 401 → waits for Mutex → (token already refreshed) → retries with new token Thread 3: GET /user → 401 → waits for Mutex → retries with new token → 1 refresh call, all requests succeed 
class TokenRefreshInterceptor @Inject constructor(
    private val tokenStore: TokenStore,
    @UnauthenticatedOkHttpClient private val refreshClient: OkHttpClient
) : Interceptor {

    private val mutex = Mutex()  // Coroutine Mutex — only one refresh at a time

    override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response {
        val response = chain.proceed(chain.request())
        if (response.code != 401) return response

        response.close()

        // Synchronous token refresh with Mutex to prevent concurrent refreshes
        val newToken = runBlocking {
            mutex.withLock {
                // Check if another thread already refreshed the token while we waited
                val currentToken = tokenStore.getAccessToken()
                val requestToken = chain.request().header("Authorization")?.removePrefix("Bearer ")
                if (currentToken != requestToken) {
                    // Token was already refreshed by another thread — use the new one
                    return@withLock currentToken
                }
                // We are the first thread — perform the refresh
                val refreshResponse = refreshClient.newCall(
                    buildRefreshRequest(tokenStore.getRefreshToken())
                ).execute()
                if (!refreshResponse.isSuccessful()) {
                    tokenStore.clearTokens()  // force logout
                    return@withLock null
                }
                val newToken = refreshResponse.parseToken()
                tokenStore.saveTokens(newToken)
                newToken.accessToken
            }
        } ?: return buildUnauthorizedResponse(chain.request())

        // Retry original request with new token
        return chain.proceed(
            chain.request().newBuilder().header("Authorization", "Bearer $newToken").build()
        )
    }
}

3. Sealed Result Type + Error Mapper

sealed class NetworkResult<out T> {
    data class Success<T>(val data: T)                     : NetworkResult<T>()
    data class HttpError(val code: Int, val error: ApiError?) : NetworkResult<Nothing>()
    data class NetworkError(val exception: IOException)          : NetworkResult<Nothing>()
    object Loading                                                : NetworkResult<Nothing>()
}

// Extension function — wrap any Retrofit call in a NetworkResult
suspend fun <T> safeApiCall(call: suspend () -> Response<T>): NetworkResult<T> =
    try {
        val response = call()
        if (response.isSuccessful()) NetworkResult.Success(requireNotNull(response.body()))
        else NetworkResult.HttpError(response.code(), response.errorBody()?.parseApiError())
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        NetworkResult.NetworkError(e)
    }

4. Offline-First Networking

// Pattern: emit Room data immediately, then fetch from network and update Room
// Room's Flow re-emits when the DB updates → UI automatically shows fresh data
fun getProducts(): Flow<List<Product>> = flow {
    // 1. Emit cached data immediately (UI is usable right away)
    emitAll(productDao.getProducts().map { it.map(ProductEntity::toDomain) })
}.onStart {
    // 2. Fetch from network in parallel — updates Room, which re-emits the Flow
    refreshProductsFromNetwork()
}

private suspend fun refreshProductsFromNetwork() {
    runCatching { api.getProducts() }
        .onSuccess { dtos -> productDao.replaceAll(dtos.map(ProductDto::toEntity)) }
        .onFailure { /* silently fail — cached data is already shown */ }
}
💡
3. When to Use

Certificate Pinning — Required for

  • Banking, payments, healthcare apps — any app handling sensitive personal or financial data
  • Apps in regulated industries (PCI-DSS, HIPAA)
  • Internal corporate apps where the server certificate is known and stable
Certificate Rotation Warning
Always include a backup pin. If the server's certificate is rotated and you've only pinned one certificate hash, all previously installed app versions will stop working until users update. With an expiration date in Network Security Config and a backup pin, you can rotate gracefully.

Mutex Token Refresh — Required when

  • The app makes multiple concurrent API calls
  • The authentication token has a TTL and can expire mid-session

Offline-First — Use when

  • Users are in areas with intermittent connectivity (mobile apps in general)
  • The app shows lists of data that should be available instantly
  • A network failure should degrade gracefully, not show an error screen
🏭
4. Production Example

Banking App — Complete Auth Interceptor with Concurrent Refresh

// TokenStore — persists tokens securely (EncryptedSharedPreferences)
interface TokenStore {
    fun getAccessToken(): String?
    fun getRefreshToken(): String?
    fun saveTokens(accessToken: String, refreshToken: String)
    fun clearTokens()
}

// Full interceptor with all production considerations
class BankingAuthInterceptor @Inject constructor(
    private val tokenStore: TokenStore,
    @UnauthenticatedOkHttpClient
    private val authClient: OkHttpClient,
    private val moshi: Moshi
) : Interceptor {

    companion object {
        private val mutex = Mutex()  // static — shared across all interceptor instances
    }

    override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response {
        // 1. Add current token to request
        val token = tokenStore.getAccessToken()
        val request = if (token != null)
            chain.request().newBuilder().header("Authorization", "Bearer $token").build()
        else chain.request()

        val response = chain.proceed(request)
        if (response.code != 401) return response

        response.close()  // IMPORTANT: close before retrying

        // 2. Try to refresh token, coordinated with Mutex
        val newToken = runBlocking {
            mutex.withLock {
                // Was token already refreshed while waiting for Mutex?
                val latestToken = tokenStore.getAccessToken()
                if (latestToken != token) {
                    return@withLock latestToken  // use the already-refreshed token
                }
                // Perform the refresh
                val refreshToken = tokenStore.getRefreshToken()
                    ?: return@withLock null

                val refreshResult = runCatching {
                    authClient.newCall(
                        Request.Builder()
                            .url("https://auth.bank.com/v1/token/refresh")
                            .post(jsonBody("""{"refreshToken":"$refreshToken"}"""))
                            .build()
                    ).execute()
                }

                refreshResult.getOrNull()?.let { refreshResponse ->
                    if (refreshResponse.isSuccessful()) {
                        val tokens = refreshResponse.parseTokenResponse(moshi)
                        tokenStore.saveTokens(tokens.accessToken, tokens.refreshToken)
                        tokens.accessToken
                    } else {
                        tokenStore.clearTokens()  // session expired — force re-login
                        null
                    }
                }
            }
        }

        return if (newToken != null) {
            chain.proceed(request.newBuilder().header("Authorization", "Bearer $newToken").build())
        } else {
            // Build 401 response to propagate up to the ViewModel
            Response.Builder().request(request).protocol(Protocol.HTTP_1_1)
                .code(401).message("Unauthorized")
                .body("".toResponseBody()).build()
        }
    }
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs

Token Refresh: Mutex vs Authenticator vs Queue

ApproachProsCons
OkHttp AuthenticatorBuilt-in OkHttp support; called on 401 automaticallyOkHttp uses its own internal locking; can conflict with manual retry logic
Interceptor + MutexFull control; clear logic; works with coroutinesRequires careful runBlocking usage in interceptor
Queue-based (pending calls)Queues all pending calls; replays with new tokenComplex implementation; more memory usage

Offline-First: Cache-then-Network vs Network-then-Cache vs Cache-only

StrategyShow stale data?When to use
Cache-then-Network (offline-first)Yes (briefly)Lists, feeds, catalogue — data freshness matters but offline usability is critical
Network-then-CacheNoAccount balance, live prices — accuracy more important than speed
Cache-only (with background sync)YesNotes apps, todo lists — edited locally, synced later
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Certificate Pinning Pitfalls

Forgotten Backup Pin = App Broken on Certificate Rotation
If you pin only the production certificate and the server rotates to a new cert, every installed version of the app breaks until the user updates. Always pin the production certificate AND a backup certificate (can be a pre-generated cert you haven't deployed yet). Include an expiration date in Network Security Config so Trustpilot/Google Play's review catches stale pins.

Token Refresh Pitfalls

Infinite Refresh Loop
If the refresh endpoint itself returns 401 (e.g., refresh token expired), and your interceptor retries on 401, you'll loop infinitely. Always check: if the request is already to the refresh endpoint, don't retry — propagate the 401 up and force re-login.

Offline-First Pitfalls

Not Closing Response Bodies
When you call chain.proceed(), OkHttp returns a Response with an open body stream. If you check the status code and decide to retry without calling response.close(), you leak the connection. Always call response.close() before retrying or returning a different response.

Best Practices

  • Store the Mutex as a companion object property — shared across all interceptor instances
  • Use EncryptedSharedPreferences (or DataStore with encryption) to store refresh tokens — never plain SharedPreferences
  • Seal the NetworkResult type — forces callers to handle all cases at compile time
  • Room as single source of truth: always write network data to Room first; let Room's Flow deliver it to the UI
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"For production Android networking: certificate pinning pins the server's certificate hash in the app so MITM attacks fail even with a rogue CA — OkHttp's CertificatePinner or Network Security Config XML handles this. Token refresh: when a JWT expires, multiple concurrent 401s can trigger multiple refresh calls — use a Mutex so only one refresh happens; others wait and reuse the new token. Offline-first: Room is the single source of truth; the repository emits Room's Flow immediately, then fetches from network and writes to Room — the Flow re-emits automatically with fresh data."

2-Minute Deep Dive

"The concurrent token refresh problem is a race condition: if 5 API calls are in-flight and the token expires, all 5 get 401 simultaneously and would each try to refresh — potentially logging the user out. The fix: a Mutex in the auth interceptor. Thread 1 acquires the Mutex and refreshes. Threads 2–5 wait. When they finally acquire the Mutex, they check if the token changed since their 401 — it has, so they skip the refresh and retry with the new token directly. Always store the Mutex as a companion object property — a new interceptor instance per request would have different Mutexes and the protection fails. For pinning: always include a backup pin to survive certificate rotation, and set an expiration date so you remember to update it."

Must-Mention Points

1
Certificate pinning: OkHttp CertificatePinner or Network Security Config XML; always include backup pin
2
Concurrent 401 problem: Mutex ensures only one refresh call happens; others reuse the result
3
Check token changed before refreshing: avoids redundant refresh when waiting on Mutex
4
Never loop on refresh endpoint 401: detect and force re-login
5
Offline-first: Room as single source of truth; emit cache immediately, update from network
6
Always close Response before retrying: prevents OkHttp connection leaks

Do NOT Go Deeper On

  • Full OAuth 2.0 PKCE flow (mention if asked, don't volunteer)
  • TLS handshake mechanics (just say "certificate pinning validates the server cert")
  • Network Security Config for debug builds (mention only if asked about proxy debugging)

Follow-up Q&A

QuestionAnswer
"What's the difference between CertificatePinner and Network Security Config?"Both pin certificates. CertificatePinner is in code — works for one host at a time, easy to update with app release. NSC is XML — declarative, also controls cleartext traffic and custom CAs, applied at OS level.
"What is stale-while-revalidate?"Serve the cached response immediately, then fetch fresh data in the background. The UI sees instant data; if the background fetch differs, the UI updates. This is essentially the offline-first pattern described above.
"How do you store tokens securely?"EncryptedSharedPreferences (wraps Android Keystore) for access and refresh tokens. Never plain SharedPreferences or files. Never in-memory only — tokens are lost on process death.

Senior Insight

Senior Signal
The subtle part of the Mutex solution is the "check if token changed" step. Without it, threads 2–5 wake up after Thread 1's refresh and each also try to refresh — the Mutex prevents parallel refreshes, but without the stale-token check, you'd refresh N times sequentially. The check makes the solution O(1) refreshes regardless of how many calls failed with 401. This is the kind of detail that separates a correct implementation from a production-ready one.
⚡

🅾
9. Interview Questions
Basic What is certificate pinning and why is it needed? ⌄
Certificate pinning hardcodes the expected server certificate (or its public key hash) in the app. Standard TLS trusts any certificate signed by a trusted CA. If an attacker installs a rogue CA certificate on the device (or does a corporate MITM), they can intercept TLS traffic. Certificate pinning rejects any certificate not matching the pinned hash — even if it's signed by a "trusted" CA. This is required for apps handling financial or health data where MITM attacks must be prevented.
Basic What is the concurrent token refresh problem? ⌄
When a JWT expires, multiple in-flight API calls all receive 401 simultaneously. Without coordination, each call would attempt to refresh the token independently — potentially making 5 simultaneous refresh calls, overwhelming the auth server, causing race conditions (which refresh response is "correct"?), and possibly invalidating other refresh tokens in the process. The solution: a Mutex that serialises refresh attempts. The first thread refreshes; subsequent threads wait, then reuse the new token without refreshing again.
Basic What does "offline-first" mean in Android development? ⌄
Offline-first means the app is designed to work without network connectivity. The architecture uses Room as the single source of truth: the UI always reads from Room (never directly from the network), so data is instantly available even without a network. When the network is available, the repository fetches fresh data and writes it to Room — Room's Flow automatically re-emits the update to the UI. The user never sees "no connection" errors for data that was previously loaded; they see slightly stale data, which is preferable to a blank screen.
Intermediate Why must the Mutex be in a companion object in the token refresh interceptor? ⌄
OkHttp creates a new interceptor invocation context per call — but if the Mutex is an instance property, each call could potentially use a different Mutex instance if new interceptor instances are created. The Mutex must be shared across all concurrent calls to the same interceptor. Declaring it in companion object makes it a class-level (static) property, so all instances share the same Mutex. Even if multiple interceptors of the same type exist (which shouldn't happen in production, but might in tests), they share the lock.
Intermediate How does the "check if token changed" optimisation work in the Mutex refresh pattern? ⌄
When Thread 1 acquires the Mutex and refreshes the token, Threads 2–5 are waiting. When they each acquire the Mutex (one at a time), they check: "Is the current token in the token store different from the token that was in my 401 request?" If yes — Thread 1 already refreshed — they skip the refresh and return the new token immediately. Without this check, Threads 2–5 would each perform a sequential refresh, refreshing the token 5 times and invalidating previously issued refresh tokens. The check makes it so only Thread 1 does real work; the rest benefit from it.
Intermediate What should happen when the token refresh request itself returns 401? ⌄
A 401 on the refresh endpoint means the refresh token itself has expired (or been revoked). The session is invalid and cannot be recovered silently. The interceptor should: (1) Call tokenStore.clearTokens() — remove all stored credentials. (2) Return null from the refresh logic. (3) Build a 401 response to propagate up the call chain. (4) The ViewModel observes the 401 state and navigates to the login screen.

Critical: guard against infinite loops — if the request URL is the refresh endpoint, skip the 401 retry logic entirely and propagate the 401 immediately.
Intermediate What is the difference between OkHttp CertificatePinner and Network Security Config? ⌄
CertificatePinner (code-based): configured in OkHttpClient builder. Per-host configuration. Checked by OkHttp on every request to the pinned hostname. More flexible — can be dynamically updated (e.g., via remote config, though that defeats the purpose). Easy to test.

Network Security Config (XML): declared in res/xml/network_security_config.xml, referenced in AndroidManifest. Applied at the OS networking layer — affects all connections from the app including those not using OkHttp. Also controls cleartext traffic (cleartextTrafficPermitted), custom CAs for debug builds, and domain-specific policies. Has an expiration date feature. Verified by Google Play on upload.
Senior Design the full offline-first architecture for a banking transaction history feature. ⌄
Room: TransactionEntity with all fields. TransactionDao returns Flow<List<TransactionEntity>>.

Repository: getTransactions() returns a Flow that: (1) immediately emits Room data (mapped to domain models). Separately, a background refresh: (2) fetches from Retrofit, writes to Room via dao.replaceAll(). Room's Flow auto-re-emits the fresh data.

Stale data handling: each transaction has a server-assigned timestamp. On Room insert, also store a fetchedAt timestamp. Show a "last updated X minutes ago" label in the UI based on this. If fetchedAt is older than 5 minutes and no network is available, show a "data may be outdated" banner.

Balance (accuracy-critical): do NOT use offline-first for balance. Always fetch from network. Show a loading state until fresh data arrives. Cache for display only during temporary connection loss, with a clear "as of [time]" label.
Senior A user's token refresh is failing intermittently in production. How would you debug it? ⌄
Debugging strategy:

1. Add logging (to a secure backend — not Logcat in production): log refresh request timestamps, HTTP status codes, and whether the token-changed check triggered. Never log token values.
2. Check for clock skew: JWT expiry is time-based. If the device's clock is ahead/behind the server's, tokens may appear expired before they are. Check the token's exp claim vs system time at the point of 401.
3. Check for Mutex deadlock: if the Mutex is never released (exception in the refresh block), all calls will hang. Ensure withLock is used (auto-releases on exception).
4. Verify single Mutex instance: check if the Mutex is actually in companion object — a test configuration change could have moved it to an instance property.
5. Server logs: check if multiple refresh requests are hitting the server from the same device — indicating the Mutex isn't working as expected.
Senior How would you handle certificate pinning when using a CDN that rotates certificates frequently? ⌄
CDNs like CloudFront rotate leaf certificates frequently (every 30–90 days), making leaf certificate pinning impractical. Solution: pin the intermediate CA certificate instead. CDN providers control which intermediate CA they use, and these rotate far less frequently (years). This gives you MITM protection without breaking on every leaf cert rotation.

Alternative: use the public key hash (sha256/ of the SubjectPublicKeyInfo) rather than the certificate hash. The public key is stable even when the certificate is renewed — same public key, new certificate = same pin hash.

Also: implement a remote kill-switch — a mechanism to disable pinning for a specific version via a remote config, in case a pin break in production requires an emergency bypass while an app update propagates.

● Android Interview Prep

13A — Room

Room's full API — @Entity, @Dao, @Database, relations, @TypeConverter, @Transaction, migrations, Flow integration, FTS, and indexing.

ID: 13A ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

What is Room?

Room is Google's ORM (Object-Relational Mapping) library built on top of SQLite. It provides compile-time query verification, type-safe access to the database, and seamless integration with Kotlin Flow and coroutines.

ComponentAnnotationResponsibility
Entity@Entity(tableName = "orders")Defines a database table — maps a data class to a table row
DAO@DaoData Access Object — interface with query methods
Database@Database(entities=[...], version=1)Creates/manages the SQLite database file
Senior Mental Model
Room's biggest advantage over raw SQLite: compile-time query verification. If your SQL has a typo, references a non-existent column, or returns the wrong type, the build fails. This catches data access bugs before they reach production. The Flow integration turns a static SQL query into a live, reactive data source.
⚙
2. How It Works

@Entity — Table Definition

@Entity(
    tableName = "transactions",
    indices = [Index(value = ["account_id"]),  // speed up queries by accountId
               Index(value = ["transaction_date"])]
)
data class TransactionEntity(
    @PrimaryKey val id: String,
    @ColumnInfo(name = "account_id") val accountId: String,
    @ColumnInfo(name = "amount_cents") val amountCents: Long,
    @ColumnInfo(name = "transaction_date") val date: LocalDate,  // needs TypeConverter
    @ColumnInfo(name = "status") val status: TransactionStatus  // needs TypeConverter
)

@TypeConverter — Custom Types

class Converters {
    @TypeConverter
    fun fromLocalDate(date: LocalDate): String = date.toString()  // ISO-8601
    @TypeConverter
    fun toLocalDate(value: String): LocalDate = LocalDate.parse(value)

    @TypeConverter
    fun fromStatus(status: TransactionStatus) = status.name
    @TypeConverter
    fun toStatus(value: String) = TransactionStatus.valueOf(value)
}

@Dao — Data Access Object

@Dao
interface TransactionDao {
    // Flow — re-emits automatically when table changes
    @Query("SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id = :accountId ORDER BY transaction_date DESC")
    fun getTransactions(accountId: String): Flow<List<TransactionEntity>>

    // Suspend — for one-shot operations
    @Query("SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE id = :transactionId")
    suspend fun getTransaction(transactionId: String): TransactionEntity?

    @Insert(onConflict = OnConflictStrategy.REPLACE)
    suspend fun insertAll(transactions: List<TransactionEntity>)

    @Update
    suspend fun update(transaction: TransactionEntity): Int  // returns rows affected

    @Delete
    suspend fun delete(transaction: TransactionEntity)

    @Query("DELETE FROM transactions WHERE account_id = :accountId")
    suspend fun deleteByAccount(accountId: String)

    // @Transaction — multiple queries in one atomic operation
    @Transaction
    @Query("SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id = :accountId")
    fun getTransactionsWithDetails(accountId: String): Flow<List<TransactionWithDetails>>
}

@Relation — One-to-Many and Many-to-Many

// One-to-Many: Account has many Transactions
data class AccountWithTransactions(
    @Embedded val account: AccountEntity,
    @Relation(parentColumn = "id", entityColumn = "account_id")
    val transactions: List<TransactionEntity>
)
// Must mark DAO query as @Transaction — Room fetches both in one atomic operation
@Transaction
@Query("SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = :accountId")
suspend fun getAccountWithTransactions(accountId: String): AccountWithTransactions?

// Many-to-Many: Order can have many Products; Product can be in many Orders
@Entity(primaryKeys = ["order_id", "product_id"])
data class OrderProductCrossRef(
    @ColumnInfo(name = "order_id") val orderId: String,
    @ColumnInfo(name = "product_id") val productId: String
)
data class OrderWithProducts(
    @Embedded val order: OrderEntity,
    @Relation(parentColumn = "id", entityColumn = "product_id",
              associateBy = Junction(OrderProductCrossRef::class))
    val products: List<ProductEntity>
)

@Database and Migrations

@Database(
    entities = [TransactionEntity::class, AccountEntity::class, OrderProductCrossRef::class],
    version = 3,
    exportSchema = true  // exports schema JSON to assets — track in git
)
@TypeConverters(Converters::class)
abstract class AppDatabase : RoomDatabase() {
    abstract fun transactionDao(): TransactionDao
    abstract fun accountDao(): AccountDao
}

// Migration 2→3: add index on transaction_date
val MIGRATION_2_3 = object : Migration(2, 3) {
    override fun migrate(database: SupportSQLiteDatabase) {
        database.execSQL("CREATE INDEX index_transactions_transaction_date ON transactions (transaction_date)")
    }
}

// Database builder — in Hilt module
Room.databaseBuilder(context, AppDatabase::class.java, "app.db")
    .addMigrations(MIGRATION_1_2, MIGRATION_2_3)
    .fallbackToDestructiveMigration()  // ⚠️ dev only — wipes data if migration missing
    .build()

Full-Text Search (FTS)

// FTS4 virtual table — enables fast full-text search
@Fts4(contentEntity = ProductEntity::class)
@Entity(tableName = "products_fts")
data class ProductFtsEntity(
    @PrimaryKey @ColumnInfo(name = "rowid") val rowId: Int,
    val name: String,
    val description: String
)

// FTS search query — MATCH operator
@Query("SELECT * FROM products JOIN products_fts ON products.rowid = products_fts.rowid WHERE products_fts MATCH :query")
suspend fun searchProducts(query: String): List<ProductEntity>
💡
3. When to Use

Room is the Right Choice for

  • Any structured relational data that must be queried, filtered, or sorted
  • Offline-first apps where the database is the single source of truth
  • Large data sets with millions of rows where query performance matters
  • Complex relationships between entities (one-to-many, many-to-many)

Use @Transaction When

  • Fetching a parent entity and its related child entities — prevents inconsistent reads
  • Writing multiple related records atomically — either all succeed or all fail
  • Any multi-step operation that must be atomic (e.g., delete then re-insert)

Room + Flow

Reactive Database
When a DAO method returns Flow<List<T>>, Room automatically observes the table for changes. Every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE to the observed table triggers a new emission. This is what makes the offline-first pattern work — the UI never polls; it just reacts to database changes.
🏭
4. Production Example

E-Commerce App — Orders with Products

// ── Entities ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
@Entity(tableName = "orders", indices = [Index("user_id"), Index("created_at")])
data class OrderEntity(
    @PrimaryKey val id: String,
    @ColumnInfo(name = "user_id") val userId: String,
    @ColumnInfo(name = "total_cents") val totalCents: Long,
    @ColumnInfo(name = "status") val status: String,
    @ColumnInfo(name = "created_at") val createdAt: Instant  // TypeConverter needed
)

// ── DAO ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
@Dao
interface OrderDao {
    @Transaction
    @Query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = :userId ORDER BY created_at DESC")
    fun getOrdersWithProducts(userId: String): Flow<List<OrderWithProducts>>

    @Transaction
    suspend fun upsertOrderWithItems(order: OrderEntity, items: List<OrderItemEntity>) {
        upsertOrder(order)
        deleteOrderItems(order.id)
        insertOrderItems(items)
    }

    @Insert(onConflict = OnConflictStrategy.REPLACE)
    suspend fun upsertOrder(order: OrderEntity)

    @Query("DELETE FROM order_items WHERE order_id = :orderId")
    suspend fun deleteOrderItems(orderId: String)

    @Insert
    suspend fun insertOrderItems(items: List<OrderItemEntity>)
}

// ── Repository using the DAO ──────────────────────────────────
class OrderRepositoryImpl @Inject constructor(
    private val dao: OrderDao,
    private val api: OrderApi
) : OrderRepository {

    override fun getOrders(userId: String): Flow<List<Order>> =
        dao.getOrdersWithProducts(userId).map { it.map(OrderWithProducts::toDomain) }
            .onStart { refreshOrders(userId) }

    private suspend fun refreshOrders(userId: String) {
        runCatching { api.getOrders(userId) }
            .onSuccess { orders ->
                orders.forEach { dto ->
                    dao.upsertOrderWithItems(dto.toEntity(), dto.items.map(OrderItemDto::toEntity))
                }
            }
    }
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs

Migration Strategies

StrategyUse whenRisk
addMigrations()Production app with user data — always preferredRequires writing correct SQL migration
fallbackToDestructiveMigration()Development only — wipes all data if migration is missingDestroys all user data — NEVER in production
allowDestructiveMigrationOnDowngrade()When version downgrade is possible in testingData loss on downgrade

OnConflictStrategy

StrategyBehaviour
REPLACEDelete old row, insert new — triggers re-emission of observers
IGNORESkip insert if row exists — use for "insert if not exists"
ABORTRollback and throw exception (default)
⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Common Mistakes

Querying on Main Thread
Room throws IllegalStateException: Cannot access database on the main thread if you call a non-Flow, non-suspend DAO method on the main thread. Always use suspend fun or Flow. Never call .allowMainThreadQueries() in production — it blocks UI rendering.
@Relation without @Transaction
Loading a parent + its children requires at least two SQL queries. Without @Transaction, another thread could modify a child between the two queries, giving you an inconsistent result. Always add @Transaction to any DAO method that returns a type with @Relation.

Database Migration Best Practices

  • Set exportSchema = true — tracks the schema JSON file in git. This lets you verify migrations haven't missed columns
  • Write migration tests using MigrationTestHelper from Room's test dependency
  • Never use fallbackToDestructiveMigration() in production builds
  • Always run migrations on a background thread (Room handles this, but ensure you're not blocking the main thread during startup)

@Index Best Practices

  • Add indexes on foreign key columns (e.g., account_id on the transactions table)
  • Add indexes on columns used in WHERE clauses in frequent queries
  • Indexes slow down INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE — don't index every column
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"Room is Android's SQLite ORM with three main components: @Entity maps a data class to a database table, @Dao is an interface with annotated query methods, and @Database ties everything together and provides DAO instances. The key advantage over raw SQLite: queries are verified at compile time — a typo in your SQL is a build error, not a runtime crash. Returning Flow<List<T>> from a DAO makes it reactive — the Flow re-emits whenever the underlying table changes."

2-Minute Deep Dive

"For relations: @Relation maps a one-to-many or many-to-many relationship. Always pair it with @Transaction — loading a parent and its children requires two queries, and without a transaction another thread could modify the children between queries giving you an inconsistent result. For custom types like LocalDate or enums, use @TypeConverter to convert to/from a SQLite-supported type. For migrations: write explicit Migration objects for every version bump — never use fallbackToDestructiveMigration in production. For performance: add @Index on foreign key columns and frequently queried columns. For FTS: @Fts4 creates a virtual table that enables fast full-text search with the MATCH operator."

Must-Mention Points

1
Compile-time query verification: SQL typos and type mismatches are build errors
2
Flow reactive queries: Room auto-re-emits when the queried table changes
3
@Transaction required with @Relation: prevents inconsistent reads across multiple queries
4
@TypeConverter: converts non-primitive types (LocalDate, enums, BigDecimal)
5
Migration objects: never fallbackToDestructiveMigration in production
6
@Index on foreign keys: critical for query performance on large tables

Do NOT Go Deeper On

  • Paging 3 + Room integration (separate topic — PagingSource)
  • Room's code generation internals (just say "annotation processing")
  • WAL mode details (mention it exists for multi-process access if asked)

Follow-up Q&A

QuestionAnswer
"How does Room emit Flow updates?"Room registers an InvalidationTracker.Observer on the queried tables. When a write occurs to any tracked table, Room posts an update, and the Flow collector re-runs the query and emits the new result.
"What is @Embedded used for?"Flattens a nested object's fields into the parent table. Unlike @Relation (separate query), @Embedded is part of the same row. Used for ValueObjects like Address embedded in a UserEntity.
"What happens if a migration is missing?"Room throws IllegalStateException: A migration from version X to Y was required but not found on database open. Without fallbackToDestructiveMigration, the app crashes. With it, the database is wiped and recreated.

Senior Insight

Senior Signal
The @Transaction-with-@Relation requirement is the most commonly missed Room concept. Room's relation loading is not a JOIN — it's multiple separate queries. Without a transaction wrapping them, you have a TOCTOU (time-of-check-to-time-of-use) race condition. Mentioning this demonstrates real-world Room knowledge beyond the happy path.
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Core Annotations

@Entity(tableName="orders")   → table
@PrimaryKey val id: String    → PK
@ColumnInfo(name="user_id")   → column
@TypeConverters(Converters::class) → custom types
@Dao  → query interface
@Database(entities=[...], version=3)

DAO Methods

@Query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE...")
fun getOrders(): Flow<List<OrderEntity>>

@Insert(onConflict = REPLACE)
suspend fun insert(order: OrderEntity)

@Transaction
suspend fun upsertOrderWithItems(...)

Relations

data class OrderWithProducts(
    @Embedded val order: OrderEntity,
    @Relation(parentColumn = "id",
              entityColumn = "order_id")
    val items: List<OrderItemEntity>
)
// Always add @Transaction to the DAO method!

Migrations

val MIGRATION_2_3 = object : Migration(2,3) {
    override fun migrate(db: SupportSQLiteDatabase) {
        db.execSQL("ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN notes TEXT")
    }
}
// In builder: .addMigrations(MIGRATION_2_3)
// NEVER .fallbackToDestructiveMigration() in prod!
🅾
9. Interview Questions
Basic What are the three main components of Room and what does each do? ⌄
@Entity: annotates a data class to define a database table. Fields map to columns. @PrimaryKey defines the primary key; @ColumnInfo customises column names.

@Dao: interface that defines methods to interact with the table. Methods are annotated with @Query, @Insert, @Update, or @Delete. Room generates the implementation at compile time.

@Database: abstract class extending RoomDatabase. Declares all entities, the database version, and abstract methods returning DAO instances. Built via Room.databaseBuilder().
Basic How does Room's Flow integration work? ⌄
When a DAO method returns Flow<List<T>>, Room wraps the query in an InvalidationTracker observer. Whenever a row in the queried table is inserted, updated, or deleted, Room marks the table as invalid and re-runs the query. The new result is emitted to all active collectors. This makes Room queries reactive — the UI doesn't need to manually refresh; it just collects the Flow and reacts to emissions.
Basic What is a TypeConverter and when do you need one? ⌄
SQLite natively supports: INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB, and NULL. For any other type — LocalDate, Instant, BigDecimal, enums, List<String> — you need a TypeConverter. A TypeConverter class has two methods: one converting FROM the Kotlin type TO a SQLite-supported type, and one converting back. Register it with @TypeConverters(Converters::class) on the @Database class.
Intermediate Why must @Relation DAO methods be annotated with @Transaction? ⌄
Room's @Relation is NOT a SQL JOIN. It executes multiple SQL queries: one to fetch the parent entities, then one (or more) separate queries to fetch the related children. Between these two queries, another thread could write to the child table — you might get a parent with outdated children or missing children. @Transaction wraps all these queries in a single SQLite transaction, ensuring you get a consistent snapshot of the database at a single point in time.
Intermediate How do you add a column to a Room table in an existing production app? ⌄
1. Add the new column to the @Entity data class. If nullable: val notes: String? = null; if non-nullable, provide a default.
2. Increment the @Database(version = N+1).
3. Write a Migration: val MIGRATION_N_N1 = object : Migration(N, N+1) { override fun migrate(db) { db.execSQL("ALTER TABLE my_table ADD COLUMN notes TEXT") } }.
4. Register: Room.databaseBuilder(...).addMigrations(MIGRATION_N_N1).build().
5. Test with MigrationTestHelper to verify migration works on the old schema.
Never use fallbackToDestructiveMigration in production — it destroys all user data.
Intermediate What is @Fts4 and when would you use it? ⌄
@Fts4 creates an SQLite FTS (Full-Text Search) virtual table. Regular SQL LIKE '%query%' performs a full table scan — O(n) on every search. FTS creates an inverted index, enabling fast token-based searches with the MATCH operator. Use it when: users type search queries against large text content (product descriptions, notes, messages), you need relevance ranking, or you need prefix matching. Trade-off: FTS tables don't support standard SQL operations like JOIN directly — you typically JOIN back to the original table via rowid.
Intermediate Explain the difference between @Embedded and @Relation. ⌄
@Embedded: flattens a nested object's fields directly into the same table row. @Embedded val address: Address means Address's fields (street, city, zip) are columns in the parent table. One row, one query. Good for value objects that belong to one entity.

@Relation: represents a relationship between two different tables. Room runs separate queries for parent and children. Requires @Transaction. Good for one-to-many or many-to-many associations where children are stored in a separate table with a foreign key.
Senior Design the Room schema for a banking app with accounts, transactions, and categories. ⌄
AccountEntity: PK=id, userId, name, type (CHECKING/SAVINGS), balanceCents. Index on userId.

TransactionEntity: PK=id, FK=accountId, FK=categoryId (nullable), amountCents, type (DEBIT/CREDIT), description, date (Instant→TypeConverter), status. Index on accountId, date.

CategoryEntity: PK=id, name, iconName, color.

Relations: AccountWithTransactions(@Embedded account, @Relation transactions). TransactionWithCategory(@Embedded transaction, @Relation category). Both DAOs methods annotated with @Transaction.

Indexes: account_id on transactions (FK queries), date on transactions (sort/filter), userId on accounts.

TypeConverters: Instant, TransactionType enum, TransactionStatus enum.
Senior What happens at compile time when Room processes your DAO annotations? ⌄
Room uses an annotation processor (KSP or kapt). For each DAO interface, Room:

1. Parses SQL strings: validates syntax, resolves column names against the @Entity field names, checks that return types match query result types. A SELECT * FROM orders WHERE uer_id = :id typo is caught here.
2. Generates a concrete implementation class: e.g., OrderDao_Impl. For Flow methods, the generated code wraps the query in RoomTrackingLiveData / CoroutinesRoom.createFlow() with the table invalidation tracker.
3. Generates the Database implementation: AppDatabase_Impl that creates tables, runs migrations, and returns DAO instances.
4. Validates relationships: ensures @Relation column names exist in the referenced entities.
Any error (bad SQL, missing column, type mismatch) is a compile error — not a runtime crash.
Senior A query that was fast in development is slow in production with 100k rows. How do you investigate? ⌄
1. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN: run the SQL with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN prefix on the production database (copy it to dev). Look for "SCAN TABLE" (full scan) vs "SEARCH TABLE USING INDEX" (fast). Full scans on large tables = missing index.

2. Add @Index: on the column(s) in the WHERE clause. Re-run EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to verify it uses the index.

3. Check query complexity: multiple JOINs or nested SELECT → consider a denormalised view or restructuring the query.

4. Room profiling: enable SQLite WAL mode and use Android Studio's Database Inspector to trace query execution times.

5. Paging: if the query returns large lists, paginate with Paging 3 — never load 100k rows at once.

● Android Interview Prep

13B — Room vs SQLite

Full comparison — compile-time safety, type safety, LiveData/Flow support, migration DSL, @RawQuery, and when raw SQLite still makes sense.

ID: 13B ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

Room Abstracts SQLite

Room is not a replacement for SQLite — it is an abstraction layer on top of it. Under the hood, Room generates code that calls the Android SQLiteOpenHelper APIs. The generated code is equivalent to what you'd write manually with raw SQLite, but Room adds compile-time verification, type mapping, and reactive integration.

FeatureRoomRaw SQLite
Query verificationCompile time — SQL errors are build errorsRuntime — crashes in production
Type safetyFull — data classes, TypeConverters, FlowManual — Cursor with string column names
Reactive (Flow/LiveData)Built-in — Flow<List<T>>Manual — polling or custom observers
MigrationsMigration DSL with exportSchemaManual — onUpgrade() with raw SQL
BoilerplateMinimal — annotations + code generationHigh — open, cursor, extract, close
Performance overheadNegligible (compile-time code gen)None
Complex dynamic queriesLimited — use @RawQueryFull control
Multi-process accessLimited supportMore flexible
Senior Mental Model
"Room vs SQLite" is often a false dichotomy. Room IS SQLite — it's compiled into efficient SQLiteOpenHelper calls. The question is really: "Do you need the safety and productivity of Room's abstractions, or do you need the raw control that only direct SQLite access provides?" In 2024, the answer is Room for 95% of cases.
⚙
2. How It Works

Compile-Time Query Verification Side by Side

// ── Room ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
@Query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = :userId AND staus = 'ACTIVE'")
//                                              ^^^^^ typo
// BUILD ERROR: There is a problem with the query: [SQLITE_ERROR] SQL error or missing database
// (no such column: staus) → caught at COMPILE TIME

// ── Raw SQLite ───────────────────────────────────────────────
val cursor = db.rawQuery(
    "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = ? AND staus = 'ACTIVE'",
    arrayOf(userId)
)
// Cursor is empty at runtime — no exception, just silently wrong results
// Typo discovered in production via user bug report 😢

Type Safety

// ── Room — type-safe, auto-mapped ────────────────────────────
@Query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = :orderId")
suspend fun getOrder(orderId: String): OrderEntity?
// Room maps columns to OrderEntity fields automatically, with type checking

// ── Raw SQLite — manual, error-prone ─────────────────────────
val cursor = db.rawQuery("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ?", arrayOf(orderId))
return if (cursor.moveToFirst()) {
    OrderEntity(
        id = cursor.getString(cursor.getColumnIndexOrThrow("id")),
        userId = cursor.getString(cursor.getColumnIndexOrThrow("user_id")),
        totalCents = cursor.getLong(cursor.getColumnIndexOrThrow("total_cents")),
        status = cursor.getString(cursor.getColumnIndexOrThrow("status"))
    ).also { cursor.close() }
} else {
    cursor.close(); null
}

Migration DSL vs onUpgrade

// ── Room Migration ───────────────────────────────────────────
val MIGRATION_2_3 = object : Migration(2, 3) {
    override fun migrate(database: SupportSQLiteDatabase) {
        database.execSQL("ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN delivery_notes TEXT")
    }
}
// Room validates the resulting schema against the @Entity definition

// ── Raw SQLiteOpenHelper ─────────────────────────────────────
override fun onUpgrade(db: SQLiteDatabase, oldVersion: Int, newVersion: Int) {
    if (oldVersion < 3) {
        db.execSQL("ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN delivery_notes TEXT")
    }
    // No automatic schema validation — must manually verify correctness
    // Easy to forget an if-block for a new version jump
}

@RawQuery — Dynamic Queries in Room

// @RawQuery for dynamic query construction (e.g., user-configurable filters)
@Dao
interface ProductDao {
    @RawQuery(observedEntities = [ProductEntity::class])
    fun getProductsDynamic(query: SupportSQLiteQuery): Flow<List<ProductEntity>>
}

// Build the query dynamically
fun buildProductQuery(
    categoryId: String?,
    minPrice: Long?,
    sortBy: String
): SupportSQLiteQuery {
    val sb = StringBuilder("SELECT * FROM products")
    val args = mutableListOf<Any>()
    val conditions = mutableListOf<String>()
    if (categoryId != null) { conditions.add("category_id = ?"); args.add(categoryId) }
    if (minPrice != null) { conditions.add("price_cents >= ?"); args.add(minPrice) }
    if (conditions.isNotEmpty()) sb.append(" WHERE ${conditions.joinToString(" AND ")}")
    sb.append(" ORDER BY $sortBy")
    return SimpleSQLiteQuery(sb.toString(), args.toTypedArray())
}
@RawQuery and SQL Injection
Never concatenate user input directly into a RawQuery string — use positional arguments (?) to prevent SQL injection. The SimpleSQLiteQuery(sql, args) constructor uses parameterised queries safely.
💡
3. When to Use

Use Room when:

  • Building any new Android feature that needs local data persistence
  • You want compile-time safety, type safety, and reactive queries
  • The schema is known at compile time (covers 95% of use cases)
  • You need coroutine-based APIs and Flow integration
  • The team has mixed experience — Room prevents common SQLite mistakes

Consider Raw SQLite when:

  • Multi-process access: Room's locking isn't designed for concurrent access from multiple processes (e.g., app + ContentProvider + background service in separate processes). Raw SQLite with WAL mode handles this better.
  • Existing legacy code: migrating an existing SQLiteOpenHelper that works correctly is only worthwhile if there's a benefit to the migration
  • Complex dynamic SQL that Room's annotation model can't express — though @RawQuery covers most of these
  • Minimal dependency requirements in an SDK/library where adding Room's dependencies is undesirable
The Answer in Most Interviews
"Room in 95% of cases. Raw SQLite only for multi-process access, legacy code with no benefit to migration, or SDK development where dependencies must be minimal."
🏭
4. Production Example

Same Feature: Room vs Raw SQLite

Get all active orders for a user, sorted by date descending:

// ── ROOM (10 lines, type-safe, compile-verified, reactive) ────
@Query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = :userId AND status = 'ACTIVE' ORDER BY created_at DESC")
fun getActiveOrders(userId: String): Flow<List<OrderEntity>>

// ── RAW SQLITE (30+ lines, manual, error-prone, no reactivity) ─
fun getActiveOrders(userId: String): List<OrderEntity> {
    val db = readableDatabase
    val orders = mutableListOf<OrderEntity>()
    var cursor: Cursor? = null
    try {
        cursor = db.rawQuery(
            "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = ? AND status = 'ACTIVE' ORDER BY created_at DESC",
            arrayOf(userId)
        )
        while (cursor.moveToNext()) {
            orders.add(OrderEntity(
                id = cursor.getString(cursor.getColumnIndexOrThrow("id")),
                userId = cursor.getString(cursor.getColumnIndexOrThrow("user_id")),
                totalCents = cursor.getLong(cursor.getColumnIndexOrThrow("total_cents")),
                status = cursor.getString(cursor.getColumnIndexOrThrow("status")),
                createdAt = cursor.getString(cursor.getColumnIndexOrThrow("created_at"))
                    .let { Instant.parse(it) }
            ))
        }
    } finally {
        cursor?.close()  // must not forget this
    }
    return orders
    // No reactivity — caller must re-call this manually to get updates
}

@RawQuery for Advanced Search

// E-commerce app: user selects any combination of category, price, rating filters
// Static @Query cannot express this — @RawQuery with SimpleSQLiteQuery is the solution
class ProductSearchRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val dao: ProductDao
) {
    fun searchProducts(filters: ProductFilters): Flow<List<Product>> =
        dao.getProductsDynamic(buildProductQuery(filters))
            .map { it.map(ProductEntity::toDomain) }
}
⚖
5. Alternatives & Trade-offs

Room vs SQLDelight vs Realm vs ObjectBox

LibraryApproachProsCons
Room (Google)ORM on SQLite, annotation-basedOfficial, great tooling, Flow/coroutine supportAndroid-only (unless KMM)
SQLDelightSQL-first, generates Kotlin APIs from .sq filesKMM-compatible, strong type safety, SQL is the source of truthDifferent mental model, less familiar
RealmObject database (not SQLite)Fast writes, live objects, offline syncNot SQL, separate runtime, Atlas sync cost
ObjectBoxNoSQL embedded databaseVery fast writes, no SQL knowledge neededNot SQL, proprietary, less community support

Room Performance vs Raw SQLite

Room's overhead is negligible for normal usage. Since Room generates code at compile time (not reflection at runtime), the generated DAO implementation is nearly identical to hand-written SQLite code. The only overhead is the InvalidationTracker for Flow queries — which adds a small observer registration on writes. For most apps this is unmeasurable.

⚠
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

SQL Injection in @RawQuery

Never Concatenate User Input into SQL Strings
SimpleSQLiteQuery("SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = '$userInput'") is vulnerable to SQL injection. Always use parameterised queries: SimpleSQLiteQuery("SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = ?", arrayOf(userInput)). Room's static @Query methods are automatically safe — Room never concatenates parameters into the SQL string.

Cursor Leaks in Raw SQLite

Always Close Cursors
Unclosed Cursors leak file descriptors. Always close them in a finally block or use Kotlin's use extension: cursor.use { ... }. Room never has this problem — it manages Cursor lifecycle in generated code. This is one of the most common raw SQLite bugs in production apps.

Best Practices for @RawQuery

  • Always specify observedEntities on @RawQuery — Room needs to know which tables to watch for Flow invalidation
  • Validate the sortBy column name against a whitelist before passing to SimpleSQLiteQuery — don't let users inject column names directly
  • Test @RawQuery methods with Room's test database using real data — static analysis can't verify dynamic queries
🏆
7. Interview Framework

30-Second Answer

"Room is an abstraction layer on top of SQLite with three key advantages: compile-time query verification — a SQL typo is a build error, not a runtime crash; type safety — no manual Cursor reading; and reactive queries via Flow — the UI auto-updates when the database changes. Raw SQLite gives full control and zero overhead, but you write 3x more code with no compile-time safety. I'd use Room for virtually all production Android work. The only exceptions are multi-process access, existing legacy code that works correctly, or library/SDK development where dependencies must be minimal."

2-Minute Deep Dive

"Room's compile-time verification is worth emphasising: when you write @Query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = :userId'), Room's annotation processor verifies the SQL against the schema before the .class files are generated. A typo in a column name, a type mismatch between the return type and the SELECT columns, or referencing a non-existent table — all are build errors. With raw SQLite, these produce silent bugs (wrong data) or runtime crashes. For dynamic queries that Room's static annotation model can't express, @RawQuery with SimpleSQLiteQuery preserves the Flow reactive behaviour while allowing runtime query construction. Always use parameterised queries to prevent SQL injection. Room's migration DSL is also safer than SQLiteOpenHelper.onUpgrade() — Room validates the schema after migration against the @Entity definition."

Must-Mention Points

1
Room IS SQLite: generates efficient SQLiteOpenHelper calls — no magic, no performance cost
2
Compile-time query verification: SQL errors are build errors; raw SQLite errors are runtime crashes
3
Type safety: no Cursor column index juggling; Room maps to/from data classes automatically
4
@RawQuery for dynamic SQL — preserves Flow reactivity; use parameterised queries to prevent injection
5
Raw SQLite for: multi-process, legacy code, SDK/library with minimal deps

Do NOT Go Deeper On

  • SQLiteOpenHelper full API (just mention it exists as Room's underlying mechanism)
  • ContentProvider with SQLite (mention if asked about multi-process)

Follow-up Q&A

QuestionAnswer
"Is Room slower than SQLite?"No measurable difference for normal use. Room generates compile-time code (not reflection). The InvalidationTracker for Flow adds trivial overhead on writes. At Google I/O, Room benchmarks show no significant performance gap vs hand-written SQLite.
"Can Room and raw SQLite be used in the same app?"Yes — Room builds on top of SQLiteOpenHelper. You can get the underlying database via database.openHelper.writableDatabase and run raw queries on it. Useful for complex analytical queries that @RawQuery can't express cleanly.
"What is @RawQuery observedEntities for?"Tells Room which tables to watch for changes when using a Flow-returning @RawQuery. Without it, Room wouldn't know which table changes should trigger a new emission.

Senior Insight

Senior Signal
The compile-time verification difference is the decisive argument. In a production banking app, a SQL typo that returns wrong data (wrong column, wrong type) discovered via a user bug report costs 10-100x more to fix than a build failure during development. Room's annotation processing is the only Android database approach that catches these errors automatically before any code ships.
⚡
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Room Advantages

✓ Compile-time SQL verification
✓ Type safety (data classes, not Cursor)
✓ Flow<List<T>> reactive queries
✓ Migration DSL + schema export
✓ No cursor leak risk

Raw SQLite Advantages

✓ Multi-process access
✓ Zero dependencies
✓ Full SQL control
✓ No annotation processing build time

Use for: SDKs, multi-process, legacy migration-not-worth-it

@RawQuery Pattern

@RawQuery(observedEntities = [ProductEntity::class])
fun searchDynamic(q: SupportSQLiteQuery): Flow<List<ProductEntity>>

// Build query — always use parameterised:
SimpleSQLiteQuery("SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = ?", arrayOf(input))

Cursor Safety (Raw SQLite)

// Always close cursors!
val cursor = db.rawQuery(sql, args)
try {
    while (cursor.moveToNext()) { ... }
} finally {
    cursor.close()
}
// OR: cursor.use { while (it.moveToNext()) { ... } }
🅾
9. Interview Questions
Basic What is the main advantage of Room over raw SQLite? ⌄
Compile-time query verification. Room's annotation processor validates your SQL queries against the database schema during compilation. Typos in table/column names, type mismatches between the query result and the return type, and invalid SQL syntax are all build errors — not runtime crashes. Raw SQLite discovers these errors in production via user bug reports or crash logs.
Basic What is a Cursor in raw SQLite and why is it error-prone? ⌄
A Cursor is the result of a raw SQLite query — a pointer into the result set that you iterate manually with cursor.moveToNext(). Pitfalls: (1) you access columns by string name or integer index — typos compile fine but throw IllegalArgumentException at runtime. (2) Cursors are file descriptor resources that must be explicitly closed — forgetting cursor.close() leaks file descriptors and eventually crashes the app. (3) There's no automatic type mapping — you manually call getString(), getLong(), etc., and must cast correctly. Room eliminates all of these.
Basic What is @RawQuery and when would you use it? ⌄
@RawQuery lets you execute a dynamically-constructed SQL query through Room's DAO, while still retaining Room's type mapping and Flow reactive capabilities. Use it when the query can't be expressed as a static @Query annotation — e.g., a search screen where users can select any combination of filters (category, price range, rating, sort order). The observedEntities parameter tells Room which tables to watch for Flow invalidation.
Intermediate Room is built on SQLite, so why doesn't it add performance overhead? ⌄
Room uses annotation processing (KSP or kapt) to generate DAO implementations at compile time — not reflection at runtime. The generated code in OrderDao_Impl is essentially the same boilerplate you'd write manually: open database, build the SQL string, create a Cursor, iterate it, close it. There's no reflection, no dynamic dispatch, no serialisation layer. The only runtime overhead is the InvalidationTracker for Flow queries, which registers a lightweight observer on table writes — this overhead is typically under 1ms.
Intermediate Describe a scenario where you'd choose raw SQLite over Room. ⌄
Multi-process access: If a ContentProvider in one process, the main app in another, and a background service in a third all need database access, Room's locking assumptions may not hold. Raw SQLite with WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode handles multi-reader, single-writer access more predictably across processes.

SDK/library development: A library that embeds SQLite doesn't want to force its consumers to add Room as a dependency — especially if they already use Room for their own data and might get version conflicts.

Legacy working code: Migrating a 5-year-old SQLiteOpenHelper that works correctly provides no user-visible benefit and carries migration risk.
Intermediate How does Room's migration approach differ from SQLiteOpenHelper.onUpgrade()? ⌄
SQLiteOpenHelper.onUpgrade(): called with old and new version numbers; you write nested if (oldVersion < N) checks. No automatic schema validation — if your migration is incorrect, Room won't tell you (unless you test it). Easy to miss a version jump when adding new migrations over time.

Room Migration objects: each Migration(fromVersion, toVersion) is registered separately via .addMigrations(). Room chains them automatically for large version jumps (e.g., 1→3 runs MIGRATION_1_2 then MIGRATION_2_3). With exportSchema = true, Room saves the schema JSON to disk — you can use MigrationTestHelper to verify that your migration produces the exact expected schema.
Intermediate How do you prevent SQL injection with @RawQuery? ⌄
Use SimpleSQLiteQuery with positional parameters (?) instead of string concatenation:

SAFE: SimpleSQLiteQuery("SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = ?", arrayOf(userInput))
UNSAFE: SimpleSQLiteQuery("SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = '$userInput'")

The parameterised form escapes the user input before embedding it in the query. Additionally, validate any user-controlled column names (e.g., sort order) against a whitelist of allowed column names before including them in the SQL string — column names cannot be parameterised.
Senior A colleague argues "Room is unnecessary overhead — our app should use raw SQLite for performance." How do you respond? ⌄
The performance argument is incorrect: Room generates identical code to hand-written SQLite at compile time — no reflection, no runtime overhead. Benchmark data from Google confirms this.

The real trade-offs are: (1) Safety: Room catches SQL errors at build time; raw SQLite at runtime in production. In a banking app, a wrong column reference that silently returns null instead of throwing means incorrect data displayed to users — far worse than a build failure. (2) Productivity: 3 lines of Room vs 30 lines of raw SQLite for a basic query. Over a codebase of 500 queries, that's 13,500 fewer lines of boilerplate. (3) Maintainability: when a column is renamed, Room gives a compile error at every affected query. With raw SQLite, you do a global text search and hope you didn't miss anything.

The only legitimate performance concern: Room's InvalidationTracker for Flow queries adds minimal overhead on writes. If you're doing millions of writes per second (atypical), this might matter. Otherwise, it's a non-issue.
Senior How would you migrate a 50,000-line legacy app from raw SQLiteOpenHelper to Room? ⌄
Incremental migration — never big-bang:

1. Assess first: is migration worth it? Identify which tables are most active, have the most bugs, or would benefit most from Flow reactivity.
2. Keep existing SQLiteOpenHelper: create Room entities and DAOs for one table only. Configure Room to use the same database file as the existing helper: Room.databaseBuilder(...).openHelperFactory(...) or use a separate database for new tables.
3. Write migration scripts: Room's schema must be compatible with the existing SQLite schema. Set the database version to the current version; add a Migration that does nothing (schema is already correct).
4. Migrate table by table: replace each SQLiteOpenHelper access with Room DAO calls. Run the full test suite after each table migration.
5. Export schema from the start: version control the JSON — it becomes the audit trail of schema changes.
6. Remove SQLiteOpenHelper once all tables are migrated.
Senior How does Room handle multi-threaded writes and reads? ⌄
Room configures SQLite in WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode by default on Android (API 16+). WAL allows: multiple concurrent readers, one concurrent writer, and readers don't block writers. Room's generated DAO code uses SupportSQLiteDatabase, which handles transaction management. Suspend DAO functions run on Room's Dispatchers.IO dispatcher — they're safe to call from multiple coroutines simultaneously.

Room uses ThreadLocal-based transaction management for @Transaction-annotated functions, ensuring all operations within a transaction block use the same database connection. For Flow queries, Room's InvalidationTracker uses a background thread to coalesce invalidation events and re-run queries. This is safe for single-process apps. For multi-process access, Room's documentation explicitly states it's not designed for that use case — use raw SQLite with explicit locking.

13C — Other Storage

SharedPreferences (legacy), DataStore (Preferences + Proto), Files (internal/external/FileProvider), Android Keystore, and EncryptedSharedPreferences.

ID: 13C ⭐ Tier 1
🔍
1. Overview

Android Storage Options

StorageBest forType-safe?Async?Encrypted?
SharedPreferencesSimple key-value settings (legacy)NoNo (main thread)No (unless Encrypted)
Preferences DataStoreKey-value settings, modern replacementNo (key-based)Yes (Flow/coroutines)No (unless encrypted)
Proto DataStoreTyped structured settings with schemaYes (protocol buffers)Yes (Flow/coroutines)No (unless encrypted)
Files (internal)App-private data files, cachesN/AManualNo
Files (external)Media shared with other appsN/AManualNo
Android KeystoreCryptographic keys (hardware-backed)N/AYesYes (hardware)
EncryptedSharedPreferencesEncrypted key-value storeNoNoYes (Keystore)
Senior Mental Model
The storage hierarchy in Android: Keystore (keys in hardware) → EncryptedSharedPreferences (Keystore-backed, for sensitive prefs like tokens) → DataStore (coroutine-safe, atomic) → Files (blobs, media) → Room (structured relational). SharedPreferences is legacy — avoid in new code. DataStore is the modern replacement.
⚙
2. How It Works

1. SharedPreferences (Legacy)

XML-based key-value storage. Simple but has serious problems: not type-safe, not thread-safe, blocking I/O on the main thread, no error propagation, and no observability without workarounds.

// DO NOT USE in new code — legacy only
val prefs = context.getSharedPreferences("settings", Context.MODE_PRIVATE)
prefs.edit().putBoolean("dark_mode", true).apply()  // apply() = async write (not guaranteed)
prefs.edit().putBoolean("dark_mode", true).commit() // commit() = sync write (blocks!)
val isDark = prefs.getBoolean("dark_mode", false)    // no type safety on key name

2. Preferences DataStore

DataStore is the modern replacement for SharedPreferences. Uses Kotlin coroutines and Flow; atomic writes; handles exceptions gracefully; no main thread I/O.

// Define keys
val DARK_MODE_KEY = booleanPreferencesKey("dark_mode")
val USER_ID_KEY   = stringPreferencesKey("user_id")
val FONT_SIZE_KEY = intPreferencesKey("font_size")

// Create DataStore (one per file name)
val dataStore: DataStore<Preferences> by preferencesDataStore(name = "settings")
// Inject via Hilt as @Singleton

// READ — returns a Flow; null if key not set
val darkModeFlow: Flow<Boolean> = context.dataStore.data
    .map { prefs -> prefs[DARK_MODE_KEY] ?: false }
    .catch { e -> if (e is IOException) emit(false) else throw e }

// WRITE — atomic; only via edit lambda
suspend fun setDarkMode(enabled: Boolean) {
    context.dataStore.edit { prefs ->
        prefs[DARK_MODE_KEY] = enabled
    }
}

3. Proto DataStore

Type-safe, schema-driven DataStore using Protocol Buffers. Define the schema in a .proto file; Protocol Buffers generates Kotlin classes.

// settings.proto
// syntax = "proto3";
// message UserSettings {
//   bool dark_mode = 1;
//   string locale = 2;
//   int32 font_size = 3;
// }

// Serializer for Proto DataStore
object UserSettingsSerializer : Serializer<UserSettings> {
    override val defaultValue: UserSettings = UserSettings.getDefaultInstance()
    override suspend fun readFrom(input: InputStream): UserSettings =
        UserSettings.parseFrom(input)
    override suspend fun writeTo(t: UserSettings, output: OutputStream) =
        t.writeTo(output)
}

val protoDataStore: DataStore<UserSettings> by dataStore(
    fileName = "user_settings.pb",
    serializer = UserSettingsSerializer
)

// READ — type-safe access to settings fields
val darkMode: Flow<Boolean> = protoDataStore.data.map { it.darkMode }

// WRITE — copy with modified field (immutable proto)
suspend fun setDarkMode(enabled: Boolean) {
    protoDataStore.updateData { current ->
        current.toBuilder().setDarkMode(enabled).build()
    }
}

4. Android Keystore

The Keystore system generates and stores cryptographic keys in a hardware-backed secure element (TEE/StrongBox). Private keys never leave the hardware — they're used in-place for operations.

// Generate an AES key stored in Keystore
val keyGenerator = KeyGenerator.getInstance(KeyProperties.KEY_ALGORITHM_AES, "AndroidKeyStore")
keyGenerator.init(
    KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder("myKeyAlias", KeyProperties.PURPOSE_ENCRYPT or KeyProperties.PURPOSE_DECRYPT)
        .setBlockModes(KeyProperties.BLOCK_MODE_GCM)
        .setEncryptionPaddings(KeyProperties.ENCRYPTION_PADDING_NONE)
        .setKeySize(256)
        .setUserAuthenticationRequired(false)  // true = requires biometric unlock
        .build()
)
keyGenerator.generateKey()  // key is stored in Keystore, never in app memory

// Use the key for encryption — key stays in hardware
val keyStore = KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore").apply { load(null) }
val key = keyStore.getKey("myKeyAlias", null) as SecretKey
val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key)
val encrypted = cipher.doFinal(plaintext)

5. EncryptedSharedPreferences

Uses Android Keystore to encrypt both keys and values in a SharedPreferences file. The encryption/decryption key is stored in hardware, never in app memory. This is the recommended way to store sensitive small data like tokens.

// EncryptedSharedPreferences — backed by Keystore, API-compatible with SharedPreferences
val encryptedPrefs = EncryptedSharedPreferences.create(
    context,
    "secure_prefs",                  // file name
    MasterKeys.getOrCreate(MasterKeys.AES256_GCM_SPEC),  // master key in Keystore
    EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefKeyEncryptionScheme.AES256_SIV,
    EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefValueEncryptionScheme.AES256_GCM
)

// Use exactly like SharedPreferences — but encrypted at rest
encryptedPrefs.edit().putString("access_token", token).apply()
val token = encryptedPrefs.getString("access_token", null)

6. Files — Internal vs External

// Internal storage — private to your app, deleted on uninstall
val internalFile = File(context.filesDir, "report.pdf")
val cacheFile = File(context.cacheDir, "temp_image.jpg")  // system may delete if low space

// External storage — shared with other apps (requires WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE or Scoped Storage)
// API 29+: Scoped Storage — use MediaStore API for media, FileProvider for sharing

// FileProvider — share a file with another app without exposing internal path
// In FileProvider.xml:
// <files-path name="reports" path="reports/" />
val fileUri: Uri = FileProvider.getUriForFile(
    context,
    "${context.packageName}.fileprovider",
    File(context.filesDir, "reports/statement.pdf")
)
// Share via Intent — only the receiving app gets temporary read permission
💡
3. When to Use
ScenarioStorage choiceReason
Auth tokens (access + refresh)EncryptedSharedPreferencesEncrypted at rest with hardware key; simple API
App settings (theme, locale, font size)Preferences DataStoreCoroutine-safe, atomic, Flow reactive
Typed settings with schemaProto DataStoreType-safe, schema versioning, efficient binary format
User-generated files (exports, reports)Internal files + FileProviderPrivate by default; FileProvider for controlled sharing
Biometric key pair generationAndroid Keystore (asymmetric)Private key never leaves hardware
Legacy integrationSharedPreferencesOnly if existing code can't be migrated
Never Store Tokens in Plain SharedPreferences
Plain SharedPreferences stores data as plain XML in /data/data/com.app/shared_prefs/. On rooted devices, this is readable by any app. Always use EncryptedSharedPreferences (backed by hardware Keystore) for tokens, user credentials, or any sensitive small data.
🏭
4. Production Example

Banking App — Token Store with EncryptedSharedPreferences + DataStore

// ── Encrypted Token Store ─────────────────────────────────────
class SecureTokenStore @Inject constructor(
    @ApplicationContext private val context: Context
) : TokenStore {

    private val prefs: SharedPreferences by lazy {
        EncryptedSharedPreferences.create(
            context, "auth_tokens",
            MasterKeys.getOrCreate(MasterKeys.AES256_GCM_SPEC),
            EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefKeyEncryptionScheme.AES256_SIV,
            EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefValueEncryptionScheme.AES256_GCM
        )
    }

    override fun getAccessToken(): String? = prefs.getString("access_token", null)
    override fun getRefreshToken(): String? = prefs.getString("refresh_token", null)

    override fun saveTokens(accessToken: String, refreshToken: String) {
        prefs.edit()
            .putString("access_token", accessToken)
            .putString("refresh_token", refreshToken)
            .apply()
    }

    override fun clearTokens() = prefs.edit().clear().apply()
}

// ── DataStore for User Preferences ────────────────────────────
val Context.settingsDataStore: DataStore<Preferences> by preferencesDataStore("settings")

class UserSettingsDataSource @Inject constructor(
    @ApplicationContext private val context: Context
) {
    private companion object {
        val DARK_MODE     = booleanPreferencesKey("dark_mode")
        val NOTIFICATIONS = booleanPreferencesKey("notifications_enabled")
        val CURRENCY      = stringPreferencesKey("preferred_currency")
    }

    val settings: Flow<AppSettings> = context.settingsDataStore.data
        .catch { if (it is IOException) emit(emptyPreferences()) else throw it }
        .map { prefs ->
            AppSettings(
                darkMode = prefs[DARK_MODE] ?: false,
                notificationsEnabled = prefs[NOTIFICATIONS] ?: true,
                currency = prefs[CURRENCY] ?: "GBP"
            )
        }

    suspend fun setDarkMode(enabled: Boolean) {
        context.settingsDataStore.edit { it[DARK_MODE] = enabled }
    }
}
